0.title: 2 Chronicles: If My People
0.overview:
The message. Second Chronicles tells a people who have lost almost everything that the way back to God is still open. It begins with the temple filled with the glory of the LORD and ends with that temple burned and the people in Babylon. But all the way through, God holds out the promise he gave the night after the temple was dedicated: “if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land” (7:14). Every king is measured by it. No king keeps faith to the end, yet God keeps his word to David, and the book closes not in the ashes but with a door thrown open: “Let him go up” (36:23).

Background: the writer. First and Second Chronicles were one book in the Hebrew Bible, and 2 Chronicles takes up the story as Solomon succeeds David. The writer is unnamed, and is usually called the Chronicler. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, named Ezra, and the last verses of this book are the first of Ezra (36:22–23; Ezra 1:1–3). Many scholars think rather of a Levite, because he cares so much for the temple’s singers and gatekeepers. Nothing depends on the answer. He names his sources, the annals of the kings and the writings of prophets such as Nathan and Isaiah (9:29; 32:32), and this commentary reads him as writing true history from trustworthy records.

When and where. The story runs from Solomon’s accession, about 970 BC, to the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. At Solomon’s death, about 930 BC, the ten northern tribes broke away under Jeroboam. Chronicles follows only Judah, the kingdom of David’s line (see Kings of Israel and Judah). The empires press in: Shishak of Egypt about 925 BC, Sennacherib of Assyria in 701 BC, then Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, who burned the temple. The book ends as Cyrus of Persia sends the exiles home, about 538 BC.

The first readers. David’s line in 1 Chronicles 3 runs several generations past Zerubbabel, who led the first exiles home, so the book probably dates from about 400 BC. Its readers were a small community under Persian rule, with a rebuilt temple so plain that old men who remembered the first one wept (Ezra 3:12), and no king on David’s throne. Were they still God’s people? Had his promise to David failed? The Chronicler answers by retelling their history.

The kind of writing. This is history, but preached history. The Chronicler had Samuel and Kings and often follows them word for word, so what he adds and omits shows his aim. He passes over Solomon’s foreign wives, not to hide them, since his readers knew Kings, but because his subject is God’s promise to David’s house and the worship of God. He adds Abijah’s sermon, Jehoshaphat’s choir, Hezekiah’s Passover and Manasseh’s repentance in chains. Watch his key words: to seek the LORD, to humble oneself, and to be unfaithful, the sin that ended in exile (36:14). And watch his pattern: blessing or judgment often comes within the same reign, so each generation stands before God for itself.

How the book makes its case. First come Solomon and the temple [1–9]. God gives him wisdom; he builds the house on Mount Moriah; and as the singers praise, “the glory of the LORD filled the house of God” (5:14). Solomon confesses that “heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you” (6:18), yet asks God to hear prayer made toward this house; fire falls, and God answers with 7:14. Then the kings of Judah [10–36], each reign a sermon on that verse. The kingdom splits under Rehoboam [10–12]. Asa seeks the LORD and is helped, then leans on Syria [14–16]. Jehoshaphat, outnumbered, prays, “We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you” (20:12), and hears, “the battle is not yours but God’s” (20:15). Athaliah nearly wipes out David’s line [21–23]; Joash, Amaziah and Uzziah begin well and end badly [24–26]; Ahaz shuts the temple doors [28]. Hezekiah opens them and calls north and south to the Passover [29–32]. Manasseh does worse than the nations, yet when he humbles himself in prison, God hears him [33]. Josiah hears the rediscovered Book of the Law [34–35]. Then the end: God “sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people”, but they mocked them “until there was no remedy” (36:15–16). The temple burns, the land lies desolate seventy years as Jeremiah had said, and Cyrus proclaims the return (36:17–23).

Does 7:14 promise to heal a nation today? Some Christians claim it for any nation whose believers repent. But it was spoken to Israel, a covenant people with a temple God had chosen and a land he had given by oath, and the drought and plague of 7:13 were the covenant’s warnings on that land. No nation now stands in Israel’s place. This commentary’s view is that what carries over is the people called by God’s name, the church of Jesus Christ, and the four verbs: God still hears those who humble themselves, pray, seek his face and turn, for “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). The full healing of the land waits for the new creation.

When Chronicles and Kings differ. Some numbers do not match: Solomon has 4,000 stalls for horses here (9:25) and 40,000 in 1 Kings 4:26. Numbers were easily miscopied in Hebrew manuscripts. This commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as first given is without error, takes such differences as copying slips, names each where it arises, and says when no answer is certain. None touches what the book teaches.

Where it leads: to Christ. Second Chronicles leads to Christ first by promise. God would not destroy David’s house, “since he had promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever” (21:7), and Matthew carries the line on “after the deportation to Babylon” (Matthew 1:12) to Jesus. It leads by pattern. The glory that filled Solomon’s temple came to dwell in a man: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14), and Jesus spoke of “the temple of his body” (John 2:21). The queen of Sheba crossed the world for Solomon’s wisdom; Jesus said, “something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). And it leads by the need it exposes. Even Hezekiah grew proud, and the nation sinned on until there was no remedy. Jesus traced the martyrs’ blood “from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (Luke 11:51), a priest stoned in this book’s temple court (24:20–22), the last martyr in the traditional Hebrew order, where Chronicles stands at the end. Zechariah died asking God to avenge; the blood of Jesus “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). The remedy Chronicles could not find is the Son of David who humbled himself to death, so that God might hear from heaven and forgive.

For us. Chronicles was written for discouraged believers with a small temple and no king, and it speaks to every church that feels small and late. God is still found by those who seek him: “If you seek him, he will be found by you” (15:2). If God heard Manasseh, no one is past return. When you do not know what to do, Jehoshaphat’s prayer is yours. And we no longer pray toward a house in Jerusalem, for “we have a great priest over the house of God” (Hebrews 10:21). The last word of this book is the gospel’s word too: come home.

1.title: Ask What I Shall Give You
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Solomon the son of David established himself in his kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him and made him exceedingly great.<sup>2</sup>Solomon spoke to all Israel, to the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, to the judges, and to all the leaders in all Israel, the heads of fathers' houses.<sup>3</sup>And Solomon, and all the assembly with him, went to the high place that was at Gibeon, for the tent of meeting of God, which Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness, was there.<sup>4</sup>(But David had brought up the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim to the place that David had prepared for it, for he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem.)<sup>5</sup>Moreover, the bronze altar that Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, had made, was there before the tabernacle of the LORD. And Solomon and the assembly sought it out.<sup>6</sup>And Solomon went up there to the bronze altar before the LORD, which was at the tent of meeting, and offered a thousand burnt offerings on it.<sup>7</sup>In that night God appeared to Solomon, and said to him, "Ask what I shall give you."<sup>8</sup>And Solomon said to God, "You have shown great and steadfast love to David my father, and have made me king in his place.<sup>9</sup>O LORD God, let your word to David my father be now fulfilled, for you have made me king over a people as numerous as the dust of the earth.<sup>10</sup>Give me now wisdom and knowledge to go out and come in before this people, for who can govern this people of yours, which is so great?"<sup>11</sup>God answered Solomon, "Because this was in your heart, and you have not asked for possessions, wealth, honor, or the life of those who hate you, and have not even asked for long life, but have asked for wisdom and knowledge for yourself that you may govern my people over whom I have made you king,<sup>12</sup>wisdom and knowledge are granted to you. I will also give you riches, possessions, and honor, such as none of the kings had who were before you, and none after you shall have the like."<sup>13</sup>So Solomon came from the high place at Gibeon, from before the tent of meeting, to Jerusalem. And he reigned over Israel.<sup>14</sup>Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.<sup>15</sup>And the king made silver and gold as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah.<sup>16</sup>And Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt and Kue, and the king's traders would buy them from Kue for a price.<sup>17</sup>They imported a chariot from Egypt for 600 shekels of silver, and a horse for 150. Likewise through them these were exported to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria.
1.overview:
Where we are. Second Chronicles opens where 1 Chronicles closed: David has died, Solomon sits on his throne, and the house David prepared for is still to be built (see the introduction). This first chapter shows the new king before a stone is laid: at worship, at prayer, and in possession of everything God gave him.

The message. The greatness of Solomon’s kingdom is God’s gift, given to a king who knew that the people were God’s and asked for wisdom to serve them. God delights to answer prayer that leans on his promise and seeks the good of his people, and he gives more than is asked. But the chapter ends with a warning folded into the blessing: gifts from God can still be held in ways God has forbidden.

Why it was said. The first readers had no king, little wealth and a plain temple (see the introduction). This chapter reminds them where Israel’s greatness had always come from: “the LORD his God was with him and made him exceedingly great” (v. 1). What God gave once he could give again, and what spoiled it was never a lack of gifts but the way they were held.

How the chapter makes its case. Solomon begins his reign by leading the whole nation to worship at Gibeon, where Moses’ tent and Bezalel’s altar stand, while the ark waits in Jerusalem (vv. 1–6). That night God says, “Ask what I shall give you”, and Solomon, leaning on God’s promise to David, asks for wisdom to lead “this people of yours” (vv. 7–10). God grants it and adds riches and honour (vv. 11–13). The closing inventory shows the promise kept, and also horses brought from Egypt, which the law for Israel’s king forbade (vv. 14–17).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the need the chapter exposes. Solomon asked for wisdom; in Christ “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3), and Jesus said of himself, “something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). To his Son the Father says, “Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage” (Psalm 2:8), and the Son asked for a people and laid down his life for them. Solomon gathered horses from Egypt; the greater Son of David came to Jerusalem “humble and mounted on a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9), the king who never trusted in chariots.

For us. Every believer may pray as Solomon prayed, leaning on what God has promised in Christ, and ask for wisdom without fear of reproach (James 1:5). Those who lead others, in a home, a church or a workplace, hold them as God’s people, not their own. And whatever God has given, hold it on his terms, for a gift does not make wrong terms right.
1.theology:
Solomon prays the way his father prayed. David, given the covenant, asked God to do as you have spoken; Solomon, told to ask for anything, says let your word to David my father be now fulfilled. Both take what God has already said and turn it into a request. That is how people pray once they have listened to God.

Jesus measured himself against this man. Something greater than Solomon is here (Matthew 12:42): Solomon asked for wisdom, and Christ is the one in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). And the shape of verses 11–12, wisdom sought and the rest added, is the shape of Jesus' own promise to his disciples: seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you (Matthew 6:33), in a sermon that mentions Solomon in all his glory in the same breath.

The chapter closes on a tension the Chronicler does not resolve: the horses and silver are both a promise kept and a law broken (vv. 14–17). Much of the book that follows shows what happens when God’s gifts are used in ways he has forbidden.
1.examples: Ask what I shall give you came at night, without warning, and what came out of Solomon was simply what was in him: because this was in your heart. The same God still gives wisdom to those who ask, not because they have earned it but because he gives generously to all without reproach (James 1:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The King Goes to Gibeon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon’s reign begins with worship, and the Chronicler names God as the cause of his greatness before anything else (v. 1). The new king gathers every commander, judge and head of a family and leads the whole assembly to Gibeon, where Moses’ tent of meeting and Bezalel’s bronze altar still stand (vv. 2–3, 5). An aside explains why worship is in two places: David had brought the ark to a tent in Jerusalem (v. 4). There Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings, gifts wholly given up to God (v. 6). Before any policy or building, the nation is at the altar.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's worship is still in two places, as it has been since David brought the ark to Jerusalem, and the new king goes first to the half that has the altar.
verseByVerse.examples: Before any policy or building, the new reign begins with a whole nation at worship. Whatever a person is about to take on, that is the right place to start.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon the son of David established himself in his kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him and made him exceedingly great. Solomon spoke to all Israel, to the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, to the judges, and to all the leaders in all Israel, the heads of fathers' houses. And Solomon, and all the assembly with him, went to the high place that was at Gibeon, for the tent of meeting of God, which Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness, was there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made Solomon great, and the first thing Solomon did with his kingdom was to lead the whole nation to worship. The Chronicler names the cause of the greatness before he records a single deed, and the first deed is a pilgrimage.

Established himself in his kingdom. Kings spends a whole chapter on how Solomon secured the throne (1 Kings 2): Adonijah executed; Joab struck down while holding the horns of the altar; Abiathar sent home to his fields; Shimei confined to Jerusalem and then put to death for leaving it. None of that is here, just as this writer told of the spring when kings go out to battle and left out David’s sin against Uriah (1 Chronicles 20:1). He is not hiding it, since his readers had Kings; he is telling how Israel came to have a temple, and the purge is not part of that story.

The LORD his God was with him and made him exceedingly great. What he does print is the clause he printed over David’s reign: the LORD was with him (1 Chronicles 11:9). The cause of the greatness is named, and it is not the man.

The high place that was at Gibeon. He calls in every commander, judge and family head, and the whole assembly goes six miles north-west to Gibeon, because the tent of meeting Moses made was there. It had stood somewhere in Israel for nearly five centuries, on the reckoning of 1 Kings 6:1: at Sinai, in the wilderness, probably at Gilgal, then at Shiloh and Nob, and now on a height outside Jerusalem. A high place was a hilltop shrine, and most are condemned in the chapters to come; this one held the lawful altar, where the priests offered the daily sacrifices the law required (1 Chronicles 16:39–40).

A greater Son made great. Solomon’s greatness was given, though his throne had been made safe by the sword. Of David’s greater Son something deeper is said: he “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:8–9). His throne was secured not by removing his rivals but by dying for his enemies.
verseByVerse.note: 2 Chronicles retells the history of Judah from Solomon to the exile, focusing on the temple and on kings who sought the LORD. It largely omits the northern kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: (But David had brought up the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim to the place that David had prepared for it, for he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem.) Moreover, the bronze altar that Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, had made, was there before the tabernacle of the LORD. And Solomon and the assembly sought it out. And Solomon went up there to the bronze altar before the LORD, which was at the tent of meeting, and offered a thousand burnt offerings on it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s worship was divided between the ark in Jerusalem and Moses’ altar at Gibeon, and Solomon began his reign with a costly offering at the lawful altar. Everything from here to chapter 7 is about bringing the two together in one house.

But David had brought up the ark of God. Verse 4 is an aside, in brackets in the ESV, and it answers the question a reader would ask: why is the king worshipping at a high place six miles away when the ark of the covenant is in his city? Because Israel’s worship has been divided for a generation. The ark, God’s throne, sits in a tent on Zion with singers around it and no altar (1 Chronicles 16:37); the tabernacle Moses made stands at Gibeon with the bronze altar before it and an empty Most Holy Place (1 Chronicles 16:39–40; 21:29). Neither site is complete, yet worship at both is lawful. Only Chronicles tells us so.

The bronze altar that Bezalel the son of Uri. This detail is Chronicles’ own. Bezalel is the craftsman God named to Moses at Sinai and filled “with the Spirit of God” to make the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3; 38:1–2), the first person Scripture describes in those words. His altar is still in service centuries later, and the richest king Israel ever had offers on it rather than commissioning a better one.

Solomon and the assembly sought it out. To seek is one of the Chronicler’s key words (see the introduction). The pronoun may mean the altar or the LORD, and the two come to the same thing: they went to the place God had appointed for meeting him. The first act of the reign is the very thing every later king will be measured by.

A thousand burnt offerings. Not peace offerings, which were shared and eaten, but burnt offerings, consumed whole on the altar and leaving the worshipper nothing (Leviticus 1:9). It is the right way for a reign to open: the new king spends a day giving away what he will never get back.

The throne and the altar joined. A thousand animals died that day, and none of them could finish the work: “every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins” (Hebrews 10:11). The divide Solomon’s worship lived with, a throne in one place and an altar in another, is closed in Christ, who is both the king on the throne and the offering on the altar, made once for all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — Ask What I Shall Give You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s open offer reveals Solomon’s heart, and God answers a request shaped by his own promise with more than was asked. “Ask what I shall give you” (v. 7). Solomon begins not with himself but with God’s steadfast love to David, and asks God to keep his word (vv. 8–9). What he wants is wisdom and knowledge to lead “this people of yours” (v. 10). God names the five things he did not ask for, grants the wisdom, and adds riches, possessions and honour beyond any king before or after (vv. 11–12). Then Solomon returns to Jerusalem and reigns (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Solomon's prayer leans its whole weight on what God has already said.
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday terms: anyone given charge of others, in a home, a church or a workplace, holds them as God's people rather than their own, and may ask for wisdom on that footing.

verseByVerse.quote: In that night God appeared to Solomon, and said to him, "Ask what I shall give you." And Solomon said to God, "You have shown great and steadfast love to David my father, and have made me king in his place. O LORD God, let your word to David my father be now fulfilled, for you have made me king over a people as numerous as the dust of the earth. Give me now wisdom and knowledge to go out and come in before this people, for who can govern this people of yours, which is so great?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Given an open offer, Solomon asked God to keep his promise to David by giving him wisdom to lead God’s people. The prayer shows his heart: it begins with God’s faithfulness, rests on God’s word, and asks for what will serve others.

Ask what I shall give you. An open question, with nothing ruled out and no time to prepare. It is the most revealing thing that can happen to a person, because the answer shows what was already in the heart (v. 11).

Great and steadfast love to David my father. He does not begin with himself. His first sentence is about another man’s history with God, and the word he reaches for is steadfast love (hesed), God’s loyal covenant love, which the singers at the ark had been praising: “his steadfast love endures forever” (1 Chronicles 16:34, 41).

Let your word to David my father be now fulfilled. Then the request, anchored to a promise. His father prayed the same way on the night the covenant was given: “do as you have spoken” (1 Chronicles 17:23). Neither asks God for something new. Solomon learned to pray from his father.

A people as numerous as the dust of the earth. The phrase echoes God’s promise to Abraham (Genesis 13:16), and Solomon sees it fulfilled in the nation in front of him. Its size is not his boast but his burden: who could govern so many?

To go out and come in before this people. This is the old phrase for leading people as a shepherd leads a flock. Moses asked God for a successor “who shall go out before them and come in before them”, so that Israel would not be “as sheep that have no shepherd” (Numbers 27:17), and the tribes said David had led them out and brought them in even while Saul was king (1 Chronicles 11:2).

This people of yours. The reason turns on one word, yours. He has barely begun to reign and already knows that the nation is not his. What he asks for is the ability to look after what belongs to God.

The Shepherd who knew whose the sheep were. Solomon’s prayer finds its full answer in the Son of David who saw the crowds and “had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd” (Mark 6:34), and who prayed for “those whom you have given me, for they are yours” (John 17:9). The Father said to his Son, “Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage” (Psalm 2:8). What the Son asked for was a people, and he laid down his life for them (John 10:11).

verseByVerse.quote: God answered Solomon, "Because this was in your heart, and you have not asked for possessions, wealth, honor, or the life of those who hate you, and have not even asked for long life, but have asked for wisdom and knowledge for yourself that you may govern my people over whom I have made you king, wisdom and knowledge are granted to you. I will also give you riches, possessions, and honor, such as none of the kings had who were before you, and none after you shall have the like." So Solomon came from the high place at Gibeon, from before the tent of meeting, to Jerusalem. And he reigned over Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God was pleased that Solomon asked for wisdom to serve rather than gifts for himself, and he granted it and added riches and honour that Solomon had not asked for. The request showed what was in Solomon’s heart, and God gave far more than was asked.

Because this was in your heart. God treats the request as showing what Solomon is, not as a clever answer. He is seeing the man.

You have not asked for possessions. God’s answer begins by naming what was not said: possessions, wealth, honour, the death of his enemies, a long life. Every one is what a new king in that world would have wanted.

Wisdom and knowledge are granted to you. He gets what he asked for, and three of the five things he did not ask for come with it: riches, possessions and honour beyond any king before or after.

The condition left out. Kings has one more clause at this point: if Solomon walks in God’s ways and keeps his statutes, his days will be lengthened (1 Kings 3:14). Chronicles prints only the gift. Hold that in mind, because the chapter is about to show what Solomon did with the riches.

Wiser than Solomon. Solomon received wisdom as a gift and in old age turned his heart after other gods (1 Kings 11:4). Jesus “increased in wisdom” as a boy (Luke 2:52), is himself “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), and never once turned aside.

May believers ask for wisdom as Solomon did? Yes: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him” (James 1:5). The riches were God’s added gift to Solomon, not a promise to every believer; God promises to meet his people’s needs, not to make them rich.

What it does not mean. Not that asking for the right things is a technique for getting the rest: the riches were an overflow of grace, and the next verses show how quickly they became a snare.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes with God’s promise kept, and a quiet warning. Solomon gathers 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen (v. 14), and silver and gold become “as common in Jerusalem as stone” (v. 15): the riches of verse 12, in figures. But the supply line is named: horses from Egypt and Kue, bought by the king’s traders and sold on to the Hittite and Syrian kings (vv. 16–17). Deuteronomy had forbidden Israel’s king to gather many horses or to send the people back to Egypt for them. The Chronicler sets the blessing and the breach side by side and lets the reader see both.
verseByVerse.theology: The same inventory reads as verse 12 coming true and as the law for Israel’s king being broken, since Deuteronomy 17:16 forbade him to gather horses from Egypt. The Chronicler offers no verdict.
verseByVerse.examples: A gift from God can still be held on the wrong terms, and the gift does not make the terms right.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem. And the king made silver and gold as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah. And Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt and Kue, and the king's traders would buy them from Kue for a price. They imported a chariot from Egypt for 600 shekels of silver, and a horse for 150. Likewise through them these were exported to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon’s wealth was God’s promise kept, but his horses from Egypt broke the law God gave for Israel’s king, and the Chronicler sets the two side by side. A gift from God can still be held on terms God has forbidden.

As common in Jerusalem as stone. Silver and gold become as common as stone, and cedar as plentiful as the scrubby sycamore-figs of the Shephelah, the low hills towards the coast. Read one way, this is verse 12 coming true in figures.

Solomon’s import of horses was from Egypt. Then verse 16 names the supplier. The law for the king said that “he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses” (Deuteronomy 17:16). Two prohibitions in one sentence, and the chapter has just recorded both broken: many horses, and Egypt named as the source.

David’s different answer. His father faced the same question and answered it the other way. When David captured a thousand chariots from Hadadezer, he hamstrung the horses and kept only enough for a hundred chariots (1 Chronicles 18:4), crippling the most valuable weapon in the region rather than build the sort of army that teaches a nation to trust its weapons instead of God. The son bought fourteen hundred chariots and set up a trade selling horses and chariots on to the Hittite and Syrian kings.

The Chronicler’s silence. He makes no comment. He reports the wealth as the promise kept, which it is, and the source, which the law had forbidden, and leaves the two facts side by side. Within five years of Solomon’s death an Egyptian king will empty Jerusalem’s treasuries (12:2, 9).

The king without war horses. “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7). Zechariah promised a king who would come “humble and mounted on a donkey”, and said that the LORD would “cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem” (Zechariah 9:9–10). Jesus rode into the city that way (Matthew 21:5), the Son of David who won his kingdom not with chariots but by a cross.

In everyday life. God’s gifts rarely become snares by being taken away; they become snares by being held on our own terms, when the money God gave becomes the thing we trust, or the ability he gave becomes our security. Ask not only “Is this from God?” but “Am I holding it the way he said?”

Uncertain wording. Kue is Cilicia, in the south-east of modern Turkey. Some scholars think “Egypt” in verses 16–17 may be Musri, a region in Asia Minor near Kue, since the two names look alike in Hebrew; if so, the breach was less glaring. The ESV and most translations keep Egypt, and the gathering of many horses stands either way.

keyVerse.quote: Give me now wisdom and knowledge to go out and come in before this people, for who can govern this people of yours, which is so great?
keyVerse.note: Solomon’s request shows the heart of a true king: he knows the people are God’s, not his, and that he cannot lead them without God’s gift. It is a prayer every believer who cares for others may pray, and it is answered in full in the Son of David, the good shepherd who knew his sheep were his Father’s and laid down his life for them.

1.reflection:
God asked Solomon, “Ask what I shall give you” (v. 7), and his answer showed what was in his heart (v. 11). If God asked you that question tonight, what would you be tempted to ask for, and what would that reveal?

Solomon’s prayer rested on what God had already promised to David (vv. 8–9). Which of God’s promises in Christ could shape your prayers this week, and how would praying from them change the way you pray?

Solomon called Israel “this people of yours” (v. 10). Whom has God given you to care for, at home, at church or at work, and how does it change your care for them to remember that they belong to him?

The horses from Egypt were both part of God’s gift and a breach of his command (vv. 14–17; Deuteronomy 17:16). Where might you be holding a good gift from God on terms he has forbidden, and what would it look like to trust him instead, as the King who rode a donkey did?

2.title: Who Am I to Build a House?
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Solomon purposed to build a temple for the name of the LORD, and a royal palace for himself.<sup>2</sup>And Solomon assigned 70,000 men to bear burdens and 80,000 to quarry in the hill country, and 3,600 to oversee them.<sup>3</sup>And Solomon sent word to Hiram the king of Tyre: "As you dealt with David my father and sent him cedar to build himself a house to dwell in, so deal with me.<sup>4</sup>Behold, I am about to build a house for the name of the LORD my God and dedicate it to him for the burning of incense of sweet spices before him, and for the regular arrangement of the showbread, and for burnt offerings morning and evening, on the Sabbaths and the new moons and the appointed feasts of the LORD our God, as ordained forever for Israel.<sup>5</sup>The house that I am to build will be great, for our God is greater than all gods.<sup>6</sup>But who is able to build him a house, since heaven, even highest heaven, cannot contain him? Who am I to build a house for him, except as a place to make offerings before him?<sup>7</sup>So now send me a man skilled to work in gold, silver, bronze, and iron, and in purple, crimson, and blue fabrics, trained also in engraving, to be with the skilled workers who are with me in Judah and Jerusalem, whom David my father provided.<sup>8</sup>Send me also cedar, cypress, and algum timber from Lebanon, for I know that your servants know how to cut timber in Lebanon. And my servants will be with your servants,<sup>9</sup>to prepare timber for me in abundance, for the house I am to build will be great and wonderful.<sup>10</sup>I will give for your servants, the woodsmen who cut timber, 20,000 cors of crushed wheat, 20,000 cors of barley, 20,000 baths of wine, and 20,000 baths of oil."<sup>11</sup>Then Hiram the king of Tyre answered in a letter that he sent to Solomon, "Because the LORD loves his people, he has made you king over them."<sup>12</sup>Hiram also said, "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, who made heaven and earth, who has given King David a wise son, who has discretion and understanding, who will build a temple for the LORD and a royal palace for himself.<sup>13</sup>"Now I have sent a skilled man, who has understanding, Huram-abi,<sup>14</sup>the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre. He is trained to work in gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone, and wood, and in purple, blue, and crimson fabrics and fine linen, and to do all sorts of engraving and execute any design that may be assigned him, with your craftsmen, the craftsmen of my lord, David your father.<sup>15</sup>Now therefore the wheat and barley, oil and wine, of which my lord has spoken, let him send to his servants.<sup>16</sup>And we will cut whatever timber you need from Lebanon and bring it to you in rafts by sea to Joppa, so that you may take it up to Jerusalem."<sup>17</sup>Then Solomon counted all the resident aliens who were in the land of Israel, after the census of them that David his father had taken, and there were found 153,600.<sup>18</sup>Seventy thousand of them he assigned to bear burdens, 80,000 to quarry in the hill country, and 3,600 as overseers to make the people work.
2.overview:
Where we are. At Gibeon God has given Solomon wisdom and wealth (chapter 1). Now the king turns to the work his father prepared for and God gave to him: building the house for the LORD’s name.

The message. God is too great for any house, yet in his kindness he gives his people a place to meet him. The temple is not built to contain God but to be “a place to make offerings before him” (v. 6), and building it is an act of humility and service. God gathers even foreign kings and foreign hands to the work.

Why it was said. The first readers had a plain second temple and lived under a foreign empire (see the introduction). They learn that the first house was never a box for God, so a smaller house did not mean a smaller God; and that a foreign king had once blessed Israel’s God and helped build his house, as the Persian kings had now funded theirs (Ezra 1:2–4; 6:3–8).

How the chapter makes its case. Solomon resolves to build and musters his workforce (vv. 1–2). His letter to Hiram of Tyre names what the house is for, the daily and festival worship God ordained, argues its greatness from God’s greatness, and confesses that heaven itself cannot contain him (vv. 3–6); then it asks for a craftsman and timber and sets the wages (vv. 7–10). Hiram replies with a blessing on the LORD, maker of heaven and earth, who made Solomon king because he loves his people, and sends Huram-abi, a craftsman gifted like Bezalel (vv. 11–16). The heavy work falls to the resident aliens (vv. 17–18).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern. The God whom heaven cannot contain came to dwell in a body: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and Jesus spoke of “the temple of his body” (John 2:21). “Something greater than the temple is here” (Matthew 12:6). Solomon asked, “Who am I to build a house for him?” and the prophets answered that another son of David would build the true temple (Zechariah 6:12). He builds it now of people from every nation, Jew and Gentile together, growing “into a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:21).

For us. No building can hold God, and none is needed to reach him, for in Christ God has come near. So give him your best gladly, knowing he needs nothing from you, and treasure the ordinary, repeated worship he delights in. And let wisdom show as it did in Solomon: in humility, fair dealing and gladness to work alongside others.
2.theology:
Verses 5 and 6 settle what a temple is before one is built: not a house that holds God, but a place to make offerings before him.

And a foreign king says what Israel’s kingship is for better than most Israelites did: because the LORD loves his people, he has made you king over them. The throne exists for the sake of the people, and the people because God loves them.

No house could contain God, and yet God came to dwell: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). Stephen made this very point, that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands (Acts 7:48–50), and Jesus called his own body the temple (John 2:19–21). The building was a place to bring offerings toward a God it could not hold. In Christ the God who cannot be contained has come near in a body, and has himself become the offering.
2.examples:
Solomon's newly given wisdom shows first in small things: he admits that Hiram's men are better at felling timber than his own, and he settles the woodsmen's wages before anyone asks. Wise leadership is often as plain as that.

The most expensive building in the nation's history existed to make a routine possible: bread set out, incense burned, sacrifices morning and evening. Faithful worship is mostly ordinary, repeated and unspectacular, and that is no mark against it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon’s first act as builder is to define the house rightly: it will be great because God is great, and yet no house can contain him. He resolves to build a temple for the LORD’s name and a palace for himself, and musters his workforce (vv. 1–2). His letter to Hiram of Tyre asks for the friendship Hiram showed David (v. 3), names the purpose of the house, the daily and festival worship ordained for Israel (v. 4), and confesses that heaven itself cannot contain God, so the house can only be a place to make offerings before him (vv. 5–6). Then he asks for a master craftsman and timber and sets the woodsmen’s wages (vv. 7–10).
verseByVerse.theology: Solomon states the paradox before a stone is laid, and so defines the building correctly in the letter that commissions the timber.
verseByVerse.examples: The list in verse 4 is ordinary on purpose: bread, incense, sacrifices morning and evening, and the feasts as they come round.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Solomon purposed to build a temple for the name of the LORD, and a royal palace for himself. And Solomon assigned 70,000 men to bear burdens and 80,000 to quarry in the hill country, and 3,600 to oversee them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon resolves to build the house for the LORD’s name, and gathers a vast workforce to do it. The temple is built “for the name of the LORD”: not to house God, but as the place where he has chosen to be known and called upon.

A temple for the name of the LORD. God’s name stands for God himself as he has made himself known. Moses spoke of “the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there” (Deuteronomy 12:11). The phrase holds together the two truths of verse 6: God is truly present there, and not contained there.

And a royal palace for himself. Temple and palace come in one sentence, with no comment on either. Kings supplies the figures that make the pairing uncomfortable: seven years on the house of the LORD and thirteen on his own (1 Kings 6:38; 7:1). Chronicles lets the two projects stand side by side, and a reader is free to notice which took longer.

70,000 men to bear burdens. Seventy thousand to carry, eighty thousand to quarry, three thousand six hundred to supervise. The figure comes back exactly at the end of the chapter, where the Chronicler says who they were (vv. 17–18).

Kings and Chronicles compared. Kings gives 3,300 overseers (1 Kings 5:16) where Chronicles has 3,600, and 550 chief officers (1 Kings 9:23) where Chronicles has 250 (8:10). Both totals come to 3,850, so the two books are probably dividing the same staff differently.

verseByVerse.quote: And Solomon sent word to Hiram the king of Tyre: "As you dealt with David my father and sent him cedar to build himself a house to dwell in, so deal with me. Behold, I am about to build a house for the name of the LORD my God and dedicate it to him for the burning of incense of sweet spices before him, and for the regular arrangement of the showbread, and for burnt offerings morning and evening, on the Sabbaths and the new moons and the appointed feasts of the LORD our God, as ordained forever for Israel. The house that I am to build will be great, for our God is greater than all gods. But who is able to build him a house, since heaven, even highest heaven, cannot contain him? Who am I to build a house for him, except as a place to make offerings before him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon tells Hiram that the house is for the daily worship God commanded, and that it must be great because God is great; yet he confesses that no house could ever contain him. The temple is not a home for God but a place where his people may come before him with their offerings.

So deal with me. The letter opens with a friendship Solomon inherited. Hiram had sent cedar and craftsmen to build David a house (1 Chronicles 14:1), and the son builds on his father’s alliance.

For the burning of incense of sweet spices. Then he says what the house is for, and the list is startlingly plain: incense, the bread set out in rows, burnt offerings morning and evening, on the Sabbaths and the new moons and the appointed feasts. Not a monument, but a place where the same things happen at the same hours. It is the calendar of Numbers 28 and 29, and the very routine the returned exiles restored on their rebuilt altar before the second temple’s foundation was laid (Ezra 3:3–5): the Chronicler’s readers were keeping what Solomon wrote down.

Heaven, even highest heaven, cannot contain him. Two sentences keep the whole enterprise honest. The greatness of the building is argued from the greatness of God, and in the next breath the argument is turned round: if he is that great, no building can hold him, and neither can the highest heaven, so God is not simply living somewhere else instead. The house is therefore not a residence but “a place to make offerings before him”, where a nation can bring its sacrifices and know they are received. Solomon will say the same at the dedication (6:18).

Who am I to build a house for him? He says all this in a letter ordering timber, and the phrase at its centre is his father’s. David said “Who am I” before the ark when God promised him a house (1 Chronicles 17:16), and again when the people gave for the temple (1 Chronicles 29:14).

The true builder. Solomon’s question has a fuller answer than he knew. The prophets spoke of another son of David, “the man whose name is the Branch”, and said, “he shall build the temple of the LORD” (Zechariah 6:12). Jesus builds it of living stones, his people (Matthew 16:18; 1 Peter 2:5), and he himself is the place where God and man meet, the temple no hands could make (John 2:19–21).

What it does not mean. Not that buildings for worship are wrong, or that how we worship does not matter; Solomon built with all his strength. But no church building is God’s house as this one was. God’s people are his temple now (1 Corinthians 3:16), and a congregation in a rented hall meets the same God as one under a cathedral roof.

verseByVerse.quote: So now send me a man skilled to work in gold, silver, bronze, and iron, and in purple, crimson, and blue fabrics, trained also in engraving, to be with the skilled workers who are with me in Judah and Jerusalem, whom David my father provided. Send me also cedar, cypress, and algum timber from Lebanon, for I know that your servants know how to cut timber in Lebanon. And my servants will be with your servants, to prepare timber for me in abundance, for the house I am to build will be great and wonderful. I will give for your servants, the woodsmen who cut timber, 20,000 cors of crushed wheat, 20,000 cors of barley, 20,000 baths of wine, and 20,000 baths of oil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon asks Hiram for a master craftsman and fine timber, and fixes fair wages for the workers before he is asked. His new wisdom shows first in humble, practical things.

A man skilled to work in gold. The request is specific: not labourers, of whom Solomon has a hundred and fifty thousand, but one master of metals, fabrics and engraving, to work alongside the craftsmen David had gathered (1 Chronicles 22:15–16).

Your servants know how to cut timber. A king just given wisdom beyond all others admits that the Phoenicians are better at something. Wisdom is quite compatible with hiring people who can do what you cannot; often it is the first sign of it (see Cedars of Lebanon).

I will give for your servants. He names the wages before he is asked, as provisions for the woodsmen rather than a lump sum to the king of Tyre: twenty thousand cors each of wheat and barley (a cor was about six bushels), and twenty thousand baths each of wine and oil (a bath was about six gallons). Kings records a different payment, yearly wheat and oil for Hiram’s own household (1 Kings 5:11); the two are most naturally read as separate parts of one contract.

Uncertain wording. Algum timber (v. 8) has not been identified. Kings calls it almug and says Hiram’s ships brought it from Ophir (1 Kings 10:11; 2 Chronicles 9:10), while here Solomon asks for it from Lebanon; perhaps Hiram could supply it through his trade, or the name covered more than one fine wood. Red sandalwood and a kind of juniper are among the guesses. Nothing in the passage depends on it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — Hiram's Answer, and the Craftsman
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hiram’s reply confesses that Solomon’s throne is a gift of God’s love for his people, and he sends the skill the house needs. He blesses the LORD God of Israel as maker of heaven and earth, who has given David a wise son (vv. 11–12). He sends Huram-abi, son of a Danite mother and a Tyrian father, skilled in every craft the tabernacle once needed (vv. 13–14). He accepts the wages and promises timber by raft to Joppa (vv. 15–16). Then Solomon counts the resident aliens from David’s census, 153,600 men, and sets them to carry, quarry and oversee (vv. 17–18). The house of Israel’s God is built with the help of the nations.
verseByVerse.theology: A Phoenician king's confession may be no more than good diplomacy. The Chronicler prints it and passes no verdict.
verseByVerse.examples: God gives skill of hand as truly as skill of speech. The temple is built by the same kind of craftsman as the tabernacle, and ordinary trades can still serve him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Hiram the king of Tyre answered in a letter that he sent to Solomon, "Because the LORD loves his people, he has made you king over them." Hiram also said, "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, who made heaven and earth, who has given King David a wise son, who has discretion and understanding, who will build a temple for the LORD and a royal palace for himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A foreign king blesses Israel’s God as Creator and says that Solomon’s throne exists because the LORD loves his people. Hiram puts into words what Israel’s kingship was for: the good of the people God loves.

Because the LORD loves his people. The first sentence of Hiram’s reply is not about cedar. A Phoenician king, whose city worshipped Melqart and whose region would give Israel Jezebel a century later, gives the reason for Solomon’s throne and gets it right: the king is there for the people, because God loves them. The Chronicler said the same when Hiram’s cedar first arrived in David’s Jerusalem: David’s kingdom “was highly exalted for the sake of his people Israel” (1 Chronicles 14:2).

Who made heaven and earth. Then a blessing on the LORD by name, as maker of heaven and earth: not one god among the region’s many, but the one.

A foreign king’s witness. How much Hiram meant of it cannot be known, and the Chronicler adds nothing. His readers lived under Persian rule, and had every reason to notice that a foreign king had once put that sentence in writing about their God, as Cyrus had put another: “The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem” (Ezra 1:2).

A King given in love. Hiram’s sentence is truest of the last King God gave. “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son” (John 3:16), and God “gave him as head over all things to the church” (Ephesians 1:22). Christ reigns not for his own sake but for his people’s, and he proved it by giving himself for them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now I have sent a skilled man, who has understanding, Huram-abi, the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre. He is trained to work in gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone, and wood, and in purple, blue, and crimson fabrics and fine linen, and to do all sorts of engraving and execute any design that may be assigned him, with your craftsmen, the craftsmen of my lord, David your father. Now therefore the wheat and barley, oil and wine, of which my lord has spoken, let him send to his servants. And we will cut whatever timber you need from Lebanon and bring it to you in rafts by sea to Joppa, so that you may take it up to Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hiram sends a master craftsman whose skills match Bezalel’s, so that the temple is made by the same kind of gifted hands that made the tabernacle. God supplies the skill his house needs, even from outside Israel.

A skilled man, who has understanding. Hiram’s craftsman is described at more length than anyone else in the chapter. Set his skills beside the man God named to Moses at Sinai: Bezalel, filled with the Spirit of God to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver and bronze, in cutting stones and carving wood, and, with Oholiab, in engraving and weaving blue, purple and scarlet yarns and fine linen (Exodus 31:1–6; 35:30–35). It is the same list. And Oholiab was of the tribe of Dan, as Huram-abi’s mother was. The temple’s craftsman is described in the same terms as the tabernacle’s: God’s house is still being made by the gifts he gives.

Dan or Naphtali? Kings says Huram-abi’s mother was a widow of the tribe of Naphtali (1 Kings 7:14); Chronicles says Dan. Perhaps she was a Danite by birth who married into Naphtali, or lived in its territory; it cannot be proved, and nothing in the chapter turns on it.

In rafts by sea to Joppa. The logs come down the coast lashed together as rafts, to Joppa, and are then hauled thirty-five miles uphill to Jerusalem.

Uncertain wording. Huram-abi means “Huram my father”, and in 4:16 the Hebrew has “Huram his father”. Many think “father” is a title of honour, something like “master craftsman”, as Joseph said God had made him “a father to Pharaoh” (Genesis 45:8). Kings simply calls him Hiram (1 Kings 7:13), and the ESV treats Huram-abi as his name. Either way, he is the master of the work.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon counted all the resident aliens who were in the land of Israel, after the census of them that David his father had taken, and there were found 153,600. Seventy thousand of them he assigned to bear burdens, 80,000 to quarry in the hill country, and 3,600 as overseers to make the people work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heavy labour on the temple was laid on the foreigners living in Israel, and the Chronicler records the conscription without defending it. The house that God would call a house of prayer for all peoples was built by outsiders’ hands.

There were found 153,600. The figure matches verse 2 exactly. The men are the resident aliens (Hebrew gerim), foreigners settled in the land, counted from a register David drew up when he set them to cutting stone for a building he would never see (1 Chronicles 22:2).

Forced labour. It was conscription, and the Chronicler does not dress it up (see Slavery in the Ancient World). He makes one distinction, stated in chapter 8: of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves for his work (8:9). The burden fell on residents who were not Israelites, and the book records it rather than defending it. Recording is not approving. Israel’s own law said, “Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 10:19), and the resentment that forced labour bred will split the kingdom in chapter 10.

A house of prayer for all peoples. So the stones of the house were squared by conscripted foreigners. Through Isaiah God promised the foreigner who joined himself to the LORD a name within its walls better than sons and daughters, and said, “my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples” (Isaiah 56:5–7). Jesus quoted those words when he cleared the temple courts (Mark 11:17), and in him the outsider receives that name: “you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19).

keyVerse.quote: But who is able to build him a house, since heaven, even highest heaven, cannot contain him? Who am I to build a house for him, except as a place to make offerings before him?
keyVerse.note: Before a stone is laid, Solomon defines what the temple is and is not: not a container for God, but a place where sinners may come before him with an offering. That humility governs the whole building project. It is fulfilled when the God no house could hold came to dwell among us in Christ, who is both the true temple and the offering that opens the way to God.

2.reflection:
Solomon said the house must be great because God is great, yet no house could contain him (vv. 5–6). How do you hold together giving God your very best and knowing that he needs nothing from you?

The temple existed for ordinary, repeated worship: bread, incense, morning and evening sacrifices, Sabbaths and feasts (v. 4). Which ordinary rhythms of worship in your life and church are easy to undervalue, and why might God treasure them?

Hiram said that God made Solomon king “because the LORD loves his people” (v. 11). How does it change the way you think of Jesus’ rule over your life to see it as an expression of God’s love for you?

The temple was built by foreign hands, many of them conscripted (vv. 13–18), yet God later called it a house of prayer for all peoples. Who are the outsiders around you, and how can your church welcome them as “fellow citizens with the saints” (Ephesians 2:19)?

3.title: He Began to Build
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to David his father, at the place that David had appointed, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.<sup>2</sup>He began to build in the second month of the fourth year of his reign.<sup>3</sup>These are Solomon's measurements for building the house of God: the length, in cubits of the old standard, was sixty cubits, and the breadth twenty cubits.<sup>4</sup>The vestibule in front of the nave of the house was twenty cubits long, equal to the width of the house, and its height was 120 cubits. He overlaid it on the inside with pure gold.<sup>5</sup>The nave he lined with cypress and covered it with fine gold and made palms and chains on it.<sup>6</sup>He adorned the house with settings of precious stones. The gold was gold of Parvaim.<sup>7</sup>So he lined the house with gold—its beams, its thresholds, its walls, and its doors— and he carved cherubim on the walls.<sup>8</sup>And he made the Most Holy Place. Its length, corresponding to the breadth of the house, was twenty cubits, and its breadth was twenty cubits. He overlaid it with 600 talents of fine gold.<sup>9</sup>The weight of gold for the nails was fifty shekels. And he overlaid the upper chambers with gold.<sup>10</sup>In the Most Holy Place he made two cherubim of wood and overlaid them with gold.<sup>11</sup>The wings of the cherubim together extended twenty cubits: one wing of the one, of five cubits, touched the wall of the house, and its other wing, of five cubits, touched the wing of the other cherub;<sup>12</sup>and of this cherub, one wing, of five cubits, touched the wall of the house, and the other wing, also of five cubits, was joined to the wing of the first cherub.<sup>13</sup>The wings of these cherubim extended twenty cubits. The cherubim stood on their feet, facing the nave.<sup>14</sup>And he made the veil of blue and purple and crimson fabrics and fine linen, and he worked cherubim on it.<sup>15</sup>In front of the house he made two pillars thirty-five cubits high, with a capital of five cubits on the top of each.<sup>16</sup>He made chains like a necklace and put them on the tops of the pillars, and he made a hundred pomegranates and put them on the chains.<sup>17</sup>He set up the pillars in front of the temple, one on the south, the other on the north; that on the south he called Jachin, and that on the north Boaz.
3.overview:
Where we are. The workers, timber and craftsman are ready (chapter 2). In the fourth year of his reign Solomon begins to build, and this chapter takes the house from its foundation to the golden inner room and the two pillars at its door.

The message. God’s house stands on ground where he had already provided a substitute, stopped his sword of judgment and accepted an offering paid for in full: Israel’s worship rested on grace. At its heart is a room of gold where God is enthroned between the cherubim, and yet a veil still shuts it off. God has come to dwell among his people, but the way into his presence is not yet open.

Why it was said. The first readers worshipped in a plain rebuilt temple on the same site (Ezra 5:15; 6:7; see the introduction). They needed to know that whatever their house lacked in gold, it stood where God had shown his mercy, and that the ground of their worship had never been the splendour of the building.

How the chapter makes its case. First the ground and the date: Mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared to David, on Ornan’s threshing floor (vv. 1–2). Then the measurements and the gold, from the walls and doors to the Most Holy Place and the nails (vv. 3–9). Then the heart of the house: two golden cherubim filling the inner room, and the veil embroidered with cherubim (vv. 10–14). Last, the two free-standing pillars at the door, named Jachin and Boaz (vv. 15–17).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and promise. On Moriah Abraham said, “God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son” (Genesis 22:8), and outside the walls of the same city “Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). The veil that barred the way was torn when he died (Matthew 27:51), so that we enter “by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:20). And the pillars at the door point to his promise: “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God” (Revelation 3:12).

For us. We come to God on ground of grace: a substitute provided, judgment turned aside, a price paid by Christ. So no believer stands outside the veil now; draw near with confidence. And since nothing in God’s house was too small for care, no faithful work done for him is wasted, however hidden.
3.theology:
Verse 1 ties three events into one piece of ground. A father climbed that hill with his son and a knife and came down with a ram provided in his son's place. A king stood on it while an angel held a drawn sword over the city, and offered on an altar God lit himself. And a farmer sold it for its full price to a man who would not bring God an offering that cost him nothing. A substitute provided, a judgment halted and a price paid: the altar of Israel stood on all three.

The New Testament gathers the three into one person. Abraham said God would provide for himself the lamb (Genesis 22:8), and John the Baptist pointed to the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). Paul echoes the same mountain when he says God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). Every sacrifice on this hill pointed to the one that would not need repeating, offered just outside the same city.

Inside, the veil carries the same embroidered guardians that hung in the wilderness, the reminder that the way in was still shut. It stayed shut until the veil was torn when Jesus died.
3.examples:
Fifty shekels of gold went on the nails, which nobody would ever look at, in a building whose visible surfaces were already covered. Nothing in that house was too small for care.

The two pillars hold nothing up; they exist to be walked between, and they carry names that every worshipper had to pass. Before anyone entered, the doorway told them who establishes and who gives strength.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The house rises on ground God had already marked with grace, and it is clothed in gold from its beams to its nails. Solomon begins to build on Mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared to David, on the threshing floor David bought from Ornan, in the second month of his fourth year (vv. 1–2). The measurements follow, in cubits of the old standard: sixty by twenty, with a porch across the front (vv. 3–4). Then the gold: the nave lined with cypress and covered with fine gold, adorned with palms, chains and precious stones, cherubim carved on the walls, six hundred talents on the Most Holy Place, and gold even for the nails and the upper rooms (vv. 5–9).
verseByVerse.theology: The temple is built on ground where God had already provided a substitute and shown mercy, and which had been bought at full price. Worship there began from grace, not from Israel's achievement.
verseByVerse.examples: A father's quiet preparation for something he would never see was finished by his son. Much faithful work is like that.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to David his father, at the place that David had appointed, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. He began to build in the second month of the fourth year of his reign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temple was built on the very ground where God had provided a substitute for Isaac, stopped the sword of judgment over Jerusalem, and accepted an offering paid for in full. Israel’s worship stood, quite literally, on grace.

On Mount Moriah. Everything 1 Chronicles was working towards is packed into this sentence, which identifies the ground three times. The name Moriah has been used once before, when Abraham was told to take his only son to the land of Moriah and offer him there; he lifted the knife, was stopped, and saw a ram caught in a thicket by its horns. “So Abraham called the name of that place, ‘The LORD will provide’” (Genesis 22:14). No other book calls the temple mount by that name.

Where the LORD had appeared to David his father. On that hill the angel of the LORD stood between earth and heaven with a drawn sword stretched out over Jerusalem, while seventy thousand had died of the plague. David built an altar in haste, God answered with fire from heaven, and the sword was put back into its sheath (1 Chronicles 21:14–27).

The threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. A farm on the high ground (see Threshing Floor and Winnowing), bought by a king who said, “I will not take for the LORD what is yours, nor offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing” (1 Chronicles 21:24). Samuel’s fifty shekels of silver bought the threshing floor and the oxen (2 Samuel 24:24); Chronicles’ six hundred shekels of gold bought “the site” (1 Chronicles 21:25), most likely the whole hilltop.

A substitute, a halted sword, a price paid. The house went up on top of all three, and every sacrifice there for nearly four centuries was offered on that hill. The second temple was rebuilt on the same site (Ezra 5:15), so whatever the Chronicler’s readers lacked in gold, they worshipped where God had shown that mercy.

The Lamb God provided. On Moriah God spared Abraham’s son. Outside the walls of the same city, centuries later, he did what he had spared Abraham: he “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). The substitute was provided, the sword fell on him and is sheathed for us, and the price was paid “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19).

A date left out. Kings dates the start from the exodus, in the four hundred and eightieth year (1 Kings 6:1); Chronicles leaves it out. Solomon’s fourth year was about 966 BC (see Regnal years).
verseByVerse.note: Outside this verse, the name Moriah appears in the Bible only in Genesis 22:2.

verseByVerse.quote: These are Solomon's measurements for building the house of God: the length, in cubits of the old standard, was sixty cubits, and the breadth twenty cubits. The vestibule in front of the nave of the house was twenty cubits long, equal to the width of the house, and its height was 120 cubits. He overlaid it on the inside with pure gold. The nave he lined with cypress and covered it with fine gold and made palms and chains on it. He adorned the house with settings of precious stones. The gold was gold of Parvaim. So he lined the house with gold—its beams, its thresholds, its walls, and its doors— and he carved cherubim on the walls. And he made the Most Holy Place. Its length, corresponding to the breadth of the house, was twenty cubits, and its breadth was twenty cubits. He overlaid it with 600 talents of fine gold. The weight of gold for the nails was fifty shekels. And he overlaid the upper chambers with gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house was modest in size but covered in gold, inside and out, down to its nails, because it was the dwelling place of the King of heaven. No part of God’s house was too small to deserve care.

Sixty cubits, and the breadth twenty cubits. About ninety feet by thirty (a cubit was about eighteen inches): not large, and exactly double the tabernacle on the ground. Like the tent before it, the house was the dwelling, not a hall for a congregation; Israel worshipped in the courts.

Its height was 120 cubits. The porch is given a height of a hundred and twenty cubits, four times the height Kings gives the whole building (1 Kings 6:2). No one can account for that figure with confidence (see the textual note below).

Covered it with fine gold. What is extraordinary is what went onto the surfaces: cypress lining, fine gold over beams, thresholds, walls and doors, carved palms and chains, settings of precious stones, cherubim carved on the walls, and six hundred talents of gold, more than twenty tons, on the Most Holy Place alone. The palms recall a garden and the cherubim the guardians of Eden (Genesis 3:24): the house is Eden remembered, the place where God dwells with his people again.

The weight of gold for the nails. Then, in the middle of the talents, the nails. David had laid up great quantities of iron “for nails for the doors of the gates” (1 Chronicles 22:3), for a building he would never enter. The son gilded them.

The city that needs no temple. In Kings the Most Holy Place is a perfect cube (1 Kings 6:20). The only other golden cube in Scripture is the new Jerusalem, whose “length and width and height are equal” (Revelation 21:16), a city of pure gold. John adds, “I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22). The shut room becomes the whole home of God’s people, because of the Lamb.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are obscure. “Cubits of the old standard” (v. 3) shows that the measure had changed by the Chronicler’s day; which standard is meant is not certain, but many think it is the older, longer cubit, a handbreadth more than the common one, which Ezekiel also uses (Ezekiel 40:5). And “gold of Parvaim” (v. 6) names a source no one has located, though Arabia is often suggested. The sense is plain: the best measure and the finest gold.

Textual note. Some ancient Greek and Syriac copies read twenty cubits for the height of the porch (v. 4), which may well be what was first written.
verseByVerse.note: A cubit was about 18 inches and a talent about 75 pounds (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Cherubim, Veil, and Two Pillars
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the heart of the house God is enthroned between golden cherubim, behind a veil that says the way in is still shut, and at its door two pillars proclaim his faithfulness. Two great cherubim of gilded wood fill the Most Holy Place from wall to wall, standing and facing the nave (vv. 10–13). The veil, worked in blue, purple and crimson with cherubim, follows the pattern of the tabernacle curtain (v. 14). Before the house stand two pillars with chains and a hundred pomegranates, named Jachin and Boaz, so that every worshipper entered between words about God (vv. 15–17).
verseByVerse.theology: The cherubim's new posture is noted below; it is wiser not to build a doctrine on it.
verseByVerse.examples: Pillars that carry no roof are a reminder that some things in worship are there not to be useful but to say something true.

verseByVerse.quote: In the Most Holy Place he made two cherubim of wood and overlaid them with gold. The wings of the cherubim together extended twenty cubits: one wing of the one, of five cubits, touched the wall of the house, and its other wing, of five cubits, touched the wing of the other cherub; and of this cherub, one wing, of five cubits, touched the wall of the house, and the other wing, also of five cubits, was joined to the wing of the first cherub. The wings of these cherubim extended twenty cubits. The cherubim stood on their feet, facing the nave. And he made the veil of blue and purple and crimson fabrics and fine linen, and he worked cherubim on it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the innermost room two golden cherubim spread their wings over the place of God’s throne, and a veil embroidered with cherubim shut that room off from all but the high priest. God was present among his people, and yet the way into his presence was still barred.

The wings of the cherubim. The arithmetic of the wings is given twice over: on each side one wing of five cubits touches the wall and the other touches the other cherub’s wing, so that the pair reach the full twenty cubits. The whole width of the room is under their wings, the throne room of the God who is “enthroned above the cherubim” (1 Chronicles 13:6).

Facing the nave. Then a detail no other account gives: they stood “facing the nave”. The two on the mercy seat in the wilderness faced each other, looking down at the place where the blood was sprinkled (Exodus 25:20). These stand upright and look outward, towards the room where the priests trimmed the lamps and set out the bread. The text does not say why, and it is wiser not to build on it.

He made the veil. The veil, which Chronicles alone mentions in this building, follows the tabernacle curtain given at Sinai item for item (Exodus 26:31). Only the high priest went in, once a year, with blood (Leviticus 16; see Day of Atonement). Cherubim were first posted at Eden to guard the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24); here they guard the way to God’s throne.

Torn from top to bottom. It hung there, or its successor did, until the Friday afternoon when Jesus died, when the curtain of the temple “was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51). The way the cherubim had guarded since Eden was opened from God’s side. So “we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:19–20).

Draw near. So “let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith” (Hebrews 10:22). The believer who prays with a troubled conscience is not outside the veil hoping to be noticed; he is invited in, by blood already accepted.

verseByVerse.quote: In front of the house he made two pillars thirty-five cubits high, with a capital of five cubits on the top of each. He made chains like a necklace and put them on the tops of the pillars, and he made a hundred pomegranates and put them on the chains. He set up the pillars in front of the temple, one on the south, the other on the north; that on the south he called Jachin, and that on the north Boaz.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two great bronze pillars stood free at the door of God’s house, bearing names that proclaimed his faithfulness, so that everyone who entered passed between them. They held nothing up; they existed to say something true about God.

Two pillars thirty-five cubits high. Kings gives eighteen cubits for each (1 Kings 7:15; Jeremiah 52:21). Perhaps Chronicles gives the pair as one rounded measurement, or a number was miscopied (see the introduction); it cannot be settled, and nothing depends on it.

Pillars that carry nothing. They stand free in front of the porch, carrying no roof: not architecture but a statement, planted where every worshipper walked between them, and named like persons. The pomegranates on their chains were also worked on the hem of the high priest’s robe (Exodus 28:33–34), fruit and beauty at the threshold of God’s house.

Jachin and Boaz. Jachin means “he will establish”, the verb God used in his promise to David: “I will establish his throne forever” (1 Chronicles 17:12). Boaz is the name of David’s ancestor (Ruth 4:21; see Boaz). Every priest going in to serve and every Israelite coming up to worship walked past a promise cast in bronze.

What became of them. Nearly four centuries later the Babylonians broke both pillars in pieces and carried the bronze to Babylon (2 Kings 25:13). Their names outlasted them, and so did the promise they proclaimed.

Pillars in the temple of God. The bronze is gone, but Christ makes a promise that outlasts it, and makes it to the weak: “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God. Never shall he go out of it” (Revelation 3:12). He said it to a church that had “but little power” (Revelation 3:8). In him God establishes his people, and in him is their strength.

Uncertain wording. Boaz is less clear than Jachin: “in him is strength” is a common suggestion but uncertain, and some think the two names were the opening words of inscriptions or prayers. The overall sense is plain: the pillars at the door spoke of God’s faithfulness and strength.

keyVerse.quote: Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to David his father, at the place that David had appointed, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
keyVerse.note: Before a single measurement, the Chronicler says where the house stood: on Moriah, where God provided a ram in Isaac’s place, and on the threshing floor where his sword of judgment was stopped and an altar was paid for in full. Israel’s worship rested on substitution, mercy and a price paid, and all three meet in the cross of Christ.

3.reflection:
The temple stood on ground where God had provided a substitute, stopped judgment and accepted an offering paid in full (v. 1). How does it steady your assurance to know that your access to God rests on what he has provided in Christ rather than on what you bring?

Gold went even on the nails and the hidden places (vv. 7–9). What unnoticed work is God calling you to do with care, and why does it matter to him even if no one else ever sees it?

The veil with its cherubim said that the way into God’s presence was shut, until it was torn when Jesus died (v. 14; Matthew 27:51). What keeps you from drawing near to God with confidence, and how does Hebrews 10:19–22 answer it?

Jachin and Boaz proclaimed that God establishes and gives strength, and Christ promises to make believers with “but little power” pillars in God’s temple (Revelation 3:8, 12). Where do you most need to rest on his strength rather than your own?

4.title: The Bronze Sea and the Golden Lampstands
4.text: <sup>1</sup>He made an altar of bronze, twenty cubits long and twenty cubits wide and ten cubits high.<sup>2</sup>Then he made the sea of cast metal. It was round, ten cubits from brim to brim, and five cubits high, and a line of thirty cubits measured its circumference.<sup>3</sup>Under it were figures of gourds, for ten cubits, compassing the sea all around. The gourds were in two rows, cast with it when it was cast.<sup>4</sup>It stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The sea was set on them, and all their rear parts were inward.<sup>5</sup>Its thickness was a handbreadth. And its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held 3,000 baths.<sup>6</sup>He also made ten basins in which to wash, and set five on the south side, and five on the north side. In these they were to rinse off what was used for the burnt offering, and the sea was for the priests to wash in.<sup>7</sup>And he made ten golden lampstands as prescribed, and set them in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north.<sup>8</sup>He also made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north.
