And he made a hundred basins of gold.<sup>9</sup>He made the court of the priests and the great court and doors for the court and overlaid their doors with bronze.<sup>10</sup>And he set the sea at the southeast corner of the house.<sup>11</sup>Hiram also made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Hiram finished the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of God:<sup>12</sup>the two pillars, the bowls, and the two capitals on the top of the pillars; and the two latticeworks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the top of the pillars;<sup>13</sup>and the 400 pomegranates for the two latticeworks, two rows of pomegranates for each latticework, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars.<sup>14</sup>He made the stands also, and the basins on the stands,<sup>15</sup>and the one sea, and the twelve oxen underneath it.<sup>16</sup>The pots, the shovels, the forks, and all the equipment for these Huram-abi made of burnished bronze for King Solomon for the house of the LORD.<sup>17</sup>In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah.<sup>18</sup>Solomon made all these things in great quantities, for the weight of the bronze was not sought.<sup>19</sup>So Solomon made all the vessels that were in the house of God: the golden altar, the tables for the bread of the Presence,<sup>20</sup>the lampstands and their lamps of pure gold to burn before the inner sanctuary, as prescribed;<sup>21</sup>the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of purest gold;<sup>22</sup>the snuffers, basins, dishes for incense, and fire pans, of pure gold, and the sockets of the temple, for the inner doors to the Most Holy Place and for the doors of the nave of the temple were of gold.
4.overview:
Where we are. The house stands, with its golden inner room and its two pillars (chapter 3). Now come the furnishings: the altar and the sea in the courts outside, the lampstands and tables in the holy place within, and the summing up of the craftsman’s work.

The message. God provided in his house everything sinful people needed in order to come near him: an altar for sacrifice, water for cleansing, light and bread in his presence. Everything follows the pattern God gave Moses, only on a greater scale. The very size of the altar and the sea says how much atonement and cleansing sinners need, and their daily use shows that the work was never finished.

Why it was said. The first readers had a rebuilt altar and temple but none of this splendour (Ezra 3:2–3; see the introduction). They needed to remember what the furnishings had been for: not display, but God’s appointed way for sinners to approach him, a way that still stood.

How the chapter makes its case. First the great bronze altar and the sea on its twelve oxen, with ten basins to rinse the offerings and the sea for the priests to wash in (vv. 1–6). Then ten golden lampstands, ten tables, a hundred golden basins and the two courts (vv. 7–10). Then Huram-abi’s bronze work is totalled, cast in the clay of the Jordan valley in quantities no one weighed (vv. 11–18). Last, the gold vessels of the holy place, down to the snuffers and the door sockets (vv. 19–22).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern. The priests stood at that altar day after day, “But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:12). The priests washed in the sea; Christ washes his people once for all and makes them priests to his God (John 13:10; Revelation 1:5–6). The lampstands point to the one who said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and the bread of the Presence to “the bread of life” (John 6:35).

For us. We come to God only by the way he has provided, and in Christ that way is complete: one sacrifice, a full cleansing, and open access for all his people. Bring him your daily sins and be washed again (1 John 1:9). And since nothing in his house was too ordinary or too hidden for gold, offer him your smallest service with care.
4.theology:
Verse 6 makes a division the whole sacrificial system depends on. The basins rinse the offering; the sea washes the men who bring it. A clean offering can be carried by unclean hands, and the house made far more provision for washing the men than for rinsing the offerings. Hebrews tells Christians to draw near with hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed with pure water, but it gives the reason first: we draw near by the blood of Jesus, through a great priest over the house of God (Hebrews 10:19–22). The sea had to be refilled every day; Christ cleanses his people once, and makes all of them priests.

And everything here is the tabernacle enlarged rather than replaced: what Israel could finally afford, it spent on doing exactly what it had been told in the wilderness, on a larger scale.
4.examples:
The foundry was in the Jordan valley because that is where the clay is, thirty miles away and three thousand feet below the site. Everything cast there had to be hauled uphill afterwards. The work that makes a thing possible is usually done a long way from where the thing will stand.

The snuffers were pure gold, and so were the door sockets, which disappeared under the doors the day they were hung. Nobody was going to see them. They were made of gold because of whose house it was.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Altar, the Sea, and the Lampstands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The great altar and the great sea say how much atonement and cleansing sinful worshippers need, and everything inside follows God’s pattern on a larger scale. Solomon makes a bronze altar twenty cubits square and ten high (v. 1), and the sea of cast metal, ten cubits across, standing on twelve oxen that face the four quarters, its brim like a lily (vv. 2–5). Ten basins rinse the parts of the burnt offering, while the sea is for the priests to wash in (v. 6). Ten golden lampstands and ten tables stand in the holy place, with a hundred golden basins (vv. 7–8); then come the court of the priests, the great court and doors covered with bronze (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: A huge altar and a huge basin say how much cleansing sinful worshippers need, and Hebrews says plainly that the blood of bulls and goats could never finish the work (Hebrews 10:4, 11–12).
verseByVerse.examples: When God gives plenty, faithfulness is not doing something new with it but doing what he asked more fully.

verseByVerse.quote: He made an altar of bronze, twenty cubits long and twenty cubits wide and ten cubits high. Then he made the sea of cast metal. It was round, ten cubits from brim to brim, and five cubits high, and a line of thirty cubits measured its circumference. Under it were figures of gourds, for ten cubits, compassing the sea all around. The gourds were in two rows, cast with it when it was cast. It stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The sea was set on them, and all their rear parts were inward. Its thickness was a handbreadth. And its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held 3,000 baths. He also made ten basins in which to wash, and set five on the south side, and five on the north side. In these they were to rinse off what was used for the burnt offering, and the sea was for the priests to wash in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon made a vast bronze altar for sacrifice and a vast basin for the priests to wash in, because sinful people can come near a holy God only by atonement and cleansing. The size of both says how much of each was needed.

An altar of bronze. The altar comes first, and it is enormous: twenty cubits square and ten high, about thirty feet by thirty and fifteen high. Kings never describes its making; only this book gives the dimensions. Bezalel’s altar at Gibeon, on which Solomon sacrificed in chapter 1, was five cubits square and three high (Exodus 27:1). The new one has sixteen times the surface. Everything about this house is the old pattern enlarged.

The sea of cast metal. Cast in one piece, ten cubits from brim to brim and five deep, thirty cubits round, a handbreadth thick, with two rows of gourds cast into it and a brim that flared “like the flower of a lily”. Nobody had seen so much standing water in a vessel, hence the name. Thirty cubits round for ten across is not exact (it should be a little over thirty-one), but the text gives round numbers, not geometry, and the flared rim may account for the difference.

It held 3,000 baths. Kings says two thousand baths (1 Kings 7:26). Some suggest one figure gives its full capacity and the other its usual filling; more likely a number was miscopied (see the introduction). Either way it held tens of thousands of litres.

It stood on twelve oxen. Three faced each quarter of the compass, with their hindquarters inward. Twelve probably recalls the tribes, and the four directions the whole earth. Two centuries later King Ahaz will take the sea down off them and set it on a stone pedestal (2 Kings 16:17).

The sea was for the priests to wash in. Verse 6 separates two things that are easy to confuse. The ten basins are for rinsing “what was used for the burnt offering”, the pieces of the sacrifice. The sea is for the priests themselves. At the tabernacle a small laver had served: Aaron and his sons were to wash their hands and feet before they ministered, “so that they may not die” (Exodus 30:21). In the permanent house the laver has become a sea. The men who handle holy things need cleansing as much as the offerings they carry.

Washed once, and washed daily. The night before he died, Jesus took a basin and washed his disciples’ feet. He told Peter, “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me”, and then, “The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean” (John 13:8, 10). The priests washed again every day; Christ cleanses his people once for all: he “freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom, priests to his God” (Revelation 1:5–6). What remains is the daily washing of the feet: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

Textual note. In verse 3 the Hebrew text of Chronicles reads “oxen” where Kings has “gourds” (1 Kings 7:24); the two words look alike in Hebrew. The ESV follows Kings, while some translations keep “bulls”. Nothing depends on it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he made ten golden lampstands as prescribed, and set them in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north. He also made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north. And he made a hundred basins of gold. He made the court of the priests and the great court and doors for the court and overlaid their doors with bronze. And he set the sea at the southeast corner of the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lampstands and tables of the tabernacle were multiplied tenfold but made “as prescribed”, and the courts were arranged so that every worshipper knew how near he might come. Abundance served faithfulness, not novelty.

Ten golden lampstands as prescribed. Moses was told to make one lampstand and one table (Exodus 25:23, 31); here each stands ten times over, in a nation that had spent centuries unable to afford any of it. It is not extravagance for its own sake: “as prescribed” says the pattern is kept. What has changed is the scale, not the design.

The light among the lampstands. The lamps burned in the holy place every night (see Oil Lamp), tended by priests. Jesus said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and John saw the risen Christ walking among golden lampstands, which, he was told, “are the seven churches” (Revelation 1:12–13, 20). The light of God’s house now burns in congregations of ordinary believers, and Christ walks among them still.

The court of the priests and the great court. One court for the priests and a great court outside it, with doors between. The building was arranged in degrees of nearness, and everyone who used it knew how far in he was allowed to go. That graded nearness is what the gospel undoes: those who were far off “have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter totals the work and shows that nothing in God’s house was too ordinary or too hidden for care. Huram-abi’s bronze is listed: pots, shovels and basins, the two pillars with their capitals, latticework and four hundred pomegranates, the stands, and the one sea on its twelve oxen (vv. 11–16). It was cast in the clay of the Jordan valley, in such quantity that the weight of the bronze was not sought (vv. 17–18). Then the gold vessels of the holy place: the incense altar, the tables for the bread of the Presence, the lampstands, and even the snuffers, fire pans and door sockets, all of gold (vv. 19–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The bronze in these verses was captured: David took it from two of Hadadezer's cities in a Syrian war a generation earlier (1 Chronicles 18:8). The sea the priests washed in was made from metal taken in war, and God turned the spoils of conflict into a means of cleansing.
verseByVerse.examples: There was so much bronze that nobody weighed it. God's provision for his house outran the counting.

verseByVerse.quote: Hiram also made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Hiram finished the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of God: the two pillars, the bowls, and the two capitals on the top of the pillars; and the two latticeworks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the top of the pillars; and the 400 pomegranates for the two latticeworks, two rows of pomegranates for each latticework, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars. He made the stands also, and the basins on the stands, and the one sea, and the twelve oxen underneath it. The pots, the shovels, the forks, and all the equipment for these Huram-abi made of burnished bronze for King Solomon for the house of the LORD. In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah. Solomon made all these things in great quantities, for the weight of the bronze was not sought.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Huram-abi finished all the bronze work for God’s house, cast in such quantity that no one even weighed it. David’s preparation and God’s provision overflowed what was needed.

So Hiram finished the work. The list runs back over everything he made (on his name, see the note on 2:13–16), and it puts ash pots and shovels in the same sentence as the pillars and the sea. Somebody had to clear out a fire that was never allowed to go out (Leviticus 6:13). Ordinary service in God’s house is counted with the grand.

In the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah. Casting bronze on that scale needs clay for the moulds, so the foundry was down in the Jordan valley where the clay is, and everything cast there had to be hauled up to Jerusalem afterwards.

The weight of the bronze was not sought. Nobody weighed it; they gave up. David had weighed out the gold and silver for each lampstand and each fork (1 Chronicles 28:14–17), and had said that the bronze and iron he gathered were “beyond weighing, for there is so much of it” (1 Chronicles 22:14). His son’s foundry proved it true.

Grace beyond weighing. The bronze that could not be weighed is a small picture of the God who supplied it. Paul speaks of “the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:7): God does not measure out his kindness grudgingly to those who come to him through his Son.

Uncertain wording. Succoth lay east of the Jordan, near the Jabbok. Zeredah, called Zarethan in Kings (1 Kings 7:46), has not been located with certainty, though it was clearly nearby in the same part of the valley.

verseByVerse.quote: So Solomon made all the vessels that were in the house of God: the golden altar, the tables for the bread of the Presence, the lampstands and their lamps of pure gold to burn before the inner sanctuary, as prescribed; the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of purest gold; the snuffers, basins, dishes for incense, and fire pans, of pure gold, and the sockets of the temple, for the inner doors to the Most Holy Place and for the doors of the nave of the temple were of gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every vessel used in the holy place was made of gold, down to the wick-trimmers and the hidden door sockets, because everything near God’s presence was to be fit for him.

Of pure gold. The list gets smaller as it goes. Snuffers were the little scissors for trimming a wick, made of pure gold because they would be used in a room where God had said he would dwell. The plan David received specified the weight of gold even for the forks (1 Chronicles 28:17); his son had them made.

The golden altar, the tables for the bread of the Presence. The small golden altar stood before the inner room for the burning of incense (Exodus 30:1–8), and the tables held the twelve loaves set out before the LORD each Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–8; see Bread). Incense was a picture of prayer rising to God: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you” (Psalm 141:2).

Bread and incense. Both find their meaning in Christ. He is “the bread of life” (John 6:35), and “he always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). In Solomon’s house the bread and incense were tended by priests behind a curtain; in Christ they are given to everyone who comes.

The sockets of the temple. The last item in the chapter is the least visible thing in the building: the sockets in which the inner doors and the doors of the nave turned, out of sight the moment the doors were hung. They were gold because of whose house it was.

keyVerse.quote: He also made ten basins in which to wash, and set five on the south side, and five on the north side. In these they were to rinse off what was used for the burnt offering, and the sea was for the priests to wash in.
keyVerse.note: This verse draws the line the whole system of sacrifice depended on: the offering had to be cleansed, and so did the men who brought it. A vast sea for the priests said how much cleansing those who serve God need. It points to Christ, who washes his people once for all and makes them priests to his God.

4.reflection:
The altar and the sea were enormous (vv. 1–6). What does their size say about how much atonement and cleansing sinners need, and how does Christ’s single sacrifice (Hebrews 10:11–12) answer that need?

The priests who handled holy things needed washing themselves (v. 6). Why is it easy for those who serve in a church to forget their own need of cleansing, and what does Jesus’ washing of his disciples’ feet (John 13:8–10) teach us?

The lampstands and tables were multiplied tenfold, yet made “as prescribed” (vv. 7–8, 20). When God gives a church more resources, how can it grow without drifting from what he has said?

Gold went even on snuffers and on door sockets no one would see (vv. 21–22). What small or hidden service in God’s house could you offer this week with the same care, and why does it matter to him?

5.title: The Glory of the LORD Filled the House
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus all the work that Solomon did for the house of the LORD was finished. And Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, and stored the silver, the gold, and all the vessels in the treasuries of the house of God.<sup>2</sup>Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel, in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David, which is Zion.<sup>3</sup>And all the men of Israel assembled before the king at the feast that is in the seventh month.<sup>4</sup>And all the elders of Israel came, and the Levites took up the ark.<sup>5</sup>And they brought up the ark, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent; the Levitical priests brought them up.<sup>6</sup>And King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel, who had assembled before him, were before the ark, sacrificing so many sheep and oxen that they could not be counted or numbered.<sup>7</sup>Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place, in the inner sanctuary of the house, in the Most Holy Place, underneath the wings of the cherubim.<sup>8</sup>The cherubim spread out their wings over the place of the ark, so that the cherubim made a covering above the ark and its poles.<sup>9</sup>And the poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the Holy Place before the inner sanctuary, but they could not be seen from outside. And they are there to this day.<sup>10</sup>There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets that Moses put there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel, when they came out of Egypt.<sup>11</sup>And when the priests came out of the Holy Place (for all the priests who were present had consecrated themselves, without regard to their divisions,<sup>12</sup>and all the Levitical singers, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, their sons and kinsmen, arrayed in fine linen, with cymbals, harps, and lyres, stood east of the altar with 120 priests who were trumpeters;<sup>13</sup>and it was the duty of the trumpeters and singers to make themselves heard in unison in praise and thanksgiving to the LORD), and when the song was raised, with trumpets and cymbals and other musical instruments, in praise to the LORD, "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever," the house, the house of the LORD, was filled with a cloud,<sup>14</sup>so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of God.
5.overview:
Where we are. The house stands on Moriah, finished and furnished (chapters 3–4). Seven years of work are over, and now the one thing the building was made for is carried in: the ark of the covenant, the sign of God’s presence among his people.

The message. The God who had shared Israel’s wanderings comes to dwell among them, and he comes in grace. At the centre of his house lies the law Israel had broken, covered by the place of atonement; and when his people sing of his goodness and his steadfast love, his glory fills the house so fully that no priest can stand. The house was never the point. He was.

Why it was said. The first readers had a rebuilt temple with an empty inner room: the ark had been lost when Babylon burned Jerusalem, and no cloud had filled the second house (see the introduction). They needed to know what the first house had been for and who had filled it, and that the song which brought the glory was still theirs to sing.

How the chapter makes its case. First the procession: the work finished, David’s gifts stored, and all Israel gathered at the Feast of Booths while the Levites carry the ark and the old tent of meeting up to the new house (vv. 1–6). Then the ark is set in the inner room beneath the cherubim, with its poles still in place and nothing inside but the two tablets of the covenant (vv. 7–10). Last, every priest and singer joins in one voice, “For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever”, and the cloud of glory fills the house (vv. 11–14).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern. The glory that filled Solomon’s house came to dwell in a man: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The lid over the broken law, where blood was sprinkled once a year, is the word Paul uses when he says that God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25). And the priests who could not stand in the glory point, by contrast, to the Saviour who brings sinners near and is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

For us. We do not need a cloud or a building to meet God; we come through Christ, in whom the glory dwells and the law’s demands are covered by his blood. So begin where Israel began, with the oldest song they had: he is good, and his steadfast love endures forever. And give to his work freely, as David did, even when you will not see it finished.
5.theology:
Verse 10 is the gospel laid out in furniture: the law inside the ark, and above it a gold lid where blood was put once a year. Paul says God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood (Romans 3:25), using the Greek Old Testament’s word for this very lid: his blood turns God’s just anger away.

And the cloud repeats what happened at the tabernacle in Moses' day. The Chronicler ties the song and the cloud together, and the song was one short line about God's own goodness: not a technique, and not the singers' fervour.
5.examples:
The people went into booths on the week God came indoors. The God who had shared their wandering now gave them a settled place to meet him.

For one day the rota of twenty-four priestly divisions was suspended and every priest in the country served at once. In a church as in a family, a rota is what makes work last; but there are days it cannot cope with, and somebody has to know which they are.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ark comes home to rest, and the whole nation gathers to bring it. The work is finished and David’s dedicated silver, gold and vessels are stored in the treasuries (v. 1). Solomon calls the elders and tribal heads to fetch the ark up from the city of David, and all Israel gathers at the feast of the seventh month, the Feast of Booths (vv. 2–3). The Levites take up the ark, as the law required, and bring the tent of meeting and its holy vessels with it, so that the old sanctuary and the new are joined at last (vv. 4–5). The sacrifices are past counting (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The old tent from Gibeon is carried in with the ark, and Israel's divided worship is in one building at last (see v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples: The Levites carry the ark this time, as the law says, because David learned from a fatal mistake. A failure repented of can become the way a people learns to obey.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus all the work that Solomon did for the house of the LORD was finished. And Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, and stored the silver, the gold, and all the vessels in the treasuries of the house of God. Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel, in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David, which is Zion. And all the men of Israel assembled before the king at the feast that is in the seventh month.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the house was finished, Solomon first brought in the gifts his father had set apart, and then gathered all Israel to bring up the ark at the feast that remembered their years without a home. The new house begins with an old man’s generosity and an old promise.

The things that David his father had dedicated. After seven years the first thing recorded once the last workman leaves is not an inspection but a delivery. The pile was made up of plunder from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Philistia and Amalek, set apart rather than spent (1 Chronicles 18:11); the gold of Ophir that David gave in his old age out of his own fortune (1 Chronicles 29:3–4); and the dedicated gifts kept under a Levite’s care with the givers’ names attached: Samuel, Saul, Abner and Joab (1 Chronicles 26:26–28). All of it goes into the treasuries of a building David never saw.

The ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David. For a generation the ark had rested in a tent David pitched for it on Zion, the old Jebusite stronghold (1 Chronicles 15:1). Now it moves a short way north and up, to the house on Moriah.

The feast that is in the seventh month. This is the Feast of Booths (Tabernacles), the week when every Israelite lived in a shelter of branches, “that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 23:43). So in the one week of the year when the whole nation camped out to remember that it once had no home, the ark is moved out of a tent into a house of stone and cedar. The God who had shared their wandering now gives them a settled place to meet him. That timing is by design.

Giving for what you will not see. David gave his best for a house he would never enter, and it was used. Faithful giving for a church building you will not live to see, for missionaries whose names you will forget, for a work that outlasts you, is never lost: the treasuries of God’s house keep the names.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the elders of Israel came, and the Levites took up the ark. And they brought up the ark, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent; the Levitical priests brought them up. And King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel, who had assembled before him, were before the ark, sacrificing so many sheep and oxen that they could not be counted or numbered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This time the ark was carried the way God commanded, and the two halves of Israel’s divided worship were brought together under one roof. The nation answered with more sacrifices than anyone could count.

The Levites took up the ark. A few words settle a question that had cost a life. The first time David moved the ark it went on a new cart, because nobody had checked the law; Uzzah put out his hand to steady it and died (1 Chronicles 13:9–10). David was angry, then afraid, and then he read the law, and the second time “the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded” (1 Chronicles 15:15). Kings says the priests took up the ark (1 Kings 8:3); Chronicles says the Levites, and in verse 5 calls them “the Levitical priests”. The priests were Levites (see Priests and Levites), and the Chronicler names the tribe the law had charged with carrying it.

The ark, the tent of meeting. Verse 5 closes something that had been open since the ark came to Jerusalem. The tabernacle Moses made had stood at Gibeon with the bronze altar, where the daily sacrifices were offered, while the ark sat in a different tent on Zion with the singers (1 Chronicles 16:37–40). Neither place had everything. Now the old tent is carried up into the new house, and the two halves are under one roof. David could not do it; every arrangement of his last years, the site, the gold, the courses of priests and singers, was aimed at this moment.

Could not be counted or numbered. These are words Scripture uses of the descendants promised to Abraham, “which cannot be numbered for multitude” (Genesis 32:12; compare 1 Kings 3:8). Here they describe a nation that had run out of ways to say thank you.

What it does not mean. Not that care over the forms of worship is legalism. Uzzah’s death taught Israel that God is to be approached in the way he has given, not the way that seems practical. The same God now gives us one way to himself, his Son (John 14:6), and it is a way of welcome, not of fear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — Two Tablets and Nothing Else
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the heart of God’s house lies his covenant law, sheltered beneath the cherubim. The priests set the ark in the Most Holy Place, under the outstretched wings of the great cherubim (vv. 7–8). Its poles are left in, as Moses commanded, long enough to be glimpsed from the Holy Place, “and they are there to this day”, a phrase the first readers knew was now history (v. 9). Then the reader is shown what is inside: the two tablets of stone from Horeb, and nothing else (v. 10). The covenant Israel had broken lies at the centre, under the lid where atoning blood was sprinkled.
verseByVerse.theology: The commandments that condemn are in the box; the place where blood is applied is its lid.
verseByVerse.examples: Even settled, the ark is ready to move, as though God would not have his people forget that he had spent centuries on the road with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place, in the inner sanctuary of the house, in the Most Holy Place, underneath the wings of the cherubim. The cherubim spread out their wings over the place of the ark, so that the cherubim made a covering above the ark and its poles. And the poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the Holy Place before the inner sanctuary, but they could not be seen from outside. And they are there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ark was set in the innermost room beneath the cherubim’s wings, with its carrying poles still in place, the sign of a God who had come to rest among his people yet was never confined to one place.

Underneath the wings of the cherubim. The ark goes into the inner room under the two great cherubim carved for it (3:10–13). It is the tabernacle arrangement enlarged: gold over acacia wood, a lid with its own small cherubim, and above it the larger pair whose wings fill the room, where God had promised to meet his people (Exodus 25:22).

The ends of the poles were seen. The poles were left in, as commanded at Sinai: “The poles shall remain in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it” (Exodus 25:15). It is a strange command for an object about to stop travelling. The ark is finally at rest on the hill God chose, and it is still rigged to be carried. A priest in the Holy Place could not see the ark, but he could see the ends of its poles, and so he could see that God’s presence was not tied down to a building.

And they are there to this day. These words have a shadow on them. Whoever first wrote them was writing while the poles were still there (1 Kings 8:8). The Chronicler, copying them, was not: by his time the house had been burned, the vessels carried to Babylon, and the ark itself lost without a word of explanation. He left the sentence standing. His readers, walking past a smaller temple with an empty room at its heart, read “to this day” and knew that the day it spoke of was long past.

The ark that was lost. What the first readers grieved was answered beyond what they could ask. Jeremiah had foretold a day when the ark would not be missed, for “Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the LORD” (Jeremiah 3:16–17). God’s throne among his people is now the risen Christ himself, and no fire can carry him off.

verseByVerse.quote: There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets that Moses put there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel, when they came out of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the very centre of God’s house lay nothing but the two tablets of the law, the covenant Israel had broken, and over them the lid where atoning blood was sprinkled. The law was not removed; it was covered.

Nothing in the ark except the two tablets. The jar of manna and Aaron’s staff that budded had been placed “before the testimony”, that is, in front of the tablets (Exodus 16:34; Numbers 17:10), and Hebrews lists them with the ark (Hebrews 9:4), describing the tabernacle as it was in Moses’ day. By Solomon’s day only the tablets remained. Inside the most sacred object in the nation were two slabs of stone with ten commandments cut into them.

The law at the centre. In the room nobody entered, inside a box nobody touched, lay the covenant Israel had broken before Moses got down the mountain (Exodus 32:19) and had gone on breaking ever since. The evidence against them was kept in the holiest place they had.

The covering is blood. On top of the box was a lid of solid gold, the mercy seat, and once a year on the Day of Atonement the high priest sprinkled blood on it, directly above the tablets (Leviticus 16:14–15). The law was not removed and not amended. It was covered, and the covering was blood.

The room is no longer shut. The Greek Old Testament’s word for that lid is the word Paul uses of a person: God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith” (Romans 3:25), a sacrifice that turns God’s just anger away. What was hidden in the dark of an inner room, above a broken covenant, with one man allowed near it one day a year, has been set out in the open where anyone may look. The law still stands, and the blood still covers it. But the room is no longer shut, and the law once written on stone God now writes on his people’s hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God’s people praise his goodness with one voice, he fills his house with his glory. Every priest present has consecrated himself, setting aside the usual rota (v. 11). The Levitical singers of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun stand east of the altar in fine linen with a hundred and twenty trumpeters, and their task is to sound as one (vv. 12–13). They sing the oldest line they have, “For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever”, and the house is filled with a cloud. The priests cannot stand to minister, “for the glory of the LORD filled the house of God” (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: On this day every priest in Israel is on duty at once, and the whole people sings as one voice.
verseByVerse.examples: The men who built the house were the first people it shut out. God's presence is a gift, never something his servants manage.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the priests came out of the Holy Place (for all the priests who were present had consecrated themselves, without regard to their divisions, and all the Levitical singers, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, their sons and kinsmen, arrayed in fine linen, with cymbals, harps, and lyres, stood east of the altar with 120 priests who were trumpeters; and it was the duty of the trumpeters and singers to make themselves heard in unison in praise and thanksgiving to the LORD), and when the song was raised, with trumpets and cymbals and other musical instruments, in praise to the LORD, "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever," the house, the house of the LORD, was filled with a cloud,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every priest and singer joined in one voice to praise God’s goodness and his steadfast love, and as they sang, God filled his house. The song was not about their longing but about his character.

Without regard to their divisions. David had arranged the priests in twenty-four courses, drawn by lot, so that every family had its week of service (1 Chronicles 24:1–19). On this day the fairest rota ever devised was set aside, and every priest in the country served at once. A rota is what makes work last, in a church as in a family; but there are days it cannot cope with, and somebody has to know which they are.

Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun. These were the three families David set over the music of God’s house (1 Chronicles 25:1), here in fine linen, east of the altar, with a hundred and twenty priests blowing trumpets.

To make themselves heard in unison. The Hebrew is plainer: to be as one. Not merely together in time, but one voice, so that a listener in the court could not tell the singers apart.

For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever. What they sang was one short line, the words David gave his singers on the day the ark came into Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:34, 41). It had been sung since then in all weathers. Now, with the house finished and the nation assembled, they reach for the sentence they already knew.

His steadfast love. Steadfast love translates the Hebrew hesed, and no single English word holds it. It is love that has bound itself by a promise. Ordinary affection rises and falls with how we are treated; hesed holds when the other side has stopped deserving it. That is why the line was worth singing every day: Israel’s story was full of broken promises, and none of them was God’s. We tend to measure God’s love by how well we have kept our side lately; the song measures it by him. See Steadfast Love in the Theological Dictionary.

Further than the singers could picture. At the cross this love went further than they could have imagined: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). So on the morning after you have failed again, start where they started: he is good, and his love has not run out.

Where Christians differ: should instruments be used in Christian worship? Some Reformed and other churches sing without instruments, holding that the temple’s trumpets and cymbals belonged to its ceremonial worship, fulfilled in Christ, and that the New Testament commands only singing. Most churches use instruments, seeing them as aids to singing that the Psalms themselves call for (Psalm 150). This commentary’s view: the New Testament neither commands nor forbids instruments, so churches may decide in good conscience; what it does require is singing with understanding, to one another and from the heart (Colossians 3:16), and here the instruments serve the words, not the other way round.

verseByVerse.quote: so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory of the LORD filled the house so completely that the priests could not stand to minister: the one it was built for had arrived.

The house, the house of the LORD. The text stutters at the end of verse 13, “the house, the house of the LORD”, as though the writer, having got there, cannot get the words out in one go.

The glory of the LORD filled the house of God. This had happened once before. When the tabernacle was finished, “the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting” (Exodus 40:34–35). Now the same thing happens to a courtyard full of consecrated priests who had spent years getting ready. There is no rebuke in it, no fire, nobody struck down. The room simply became unusable for its purpose, because the one it was built for had come.

A record, not a method. The Chronicler does not say that the priests prayed the cloud down. They sang a sentence about God’s character, and the glory came while they sang. It is a record of what happened when a nation did what it had been told, in the way it had been told, with one voice, not a technique for bringing God’s presence. Worship that tries to manufacture an atmosphere has misread this verse.

The glory came as a child. A thousand years later the glory came again, with no cloud and nobody shut out. It came as a child, wrapped in cloths and laid in a manger (Luke 2:7). John wrote, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14), and his word for “dwelt” means to pitch a tent. Solomon’s priests backed out of a room they could not stand in. Those who came to Jesus were not driven back: he sat them down and fed them. And one day “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3), with no temple in the city, “for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22).

keyVerse.quote: so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of God.
keyVerse.note: This is the moment the whole of 1 Chronicles and the first chapters of this book have been building towards: God himself comes to dwell among his people. The glory that overwhelmed the priests later came to dwell in Jesus, who brings sinners near instead of driving them back.

5.reflection:
David gave his wealth for a house he never saw, and his gifts were the first thing brought in (v. 1). What are you giving to, or working for, in God’s kingdom that you may never see completed, and why is it still worth it?

At the heart of the temple lay the law Israel had broken, covered by the place of atonement (v. 10). How does Romans 3:25 help you see what that arrangement was pointing to, and what difference does it make when your conscience accuses you?

The singers raised one simple line about God’s goodness and steadfast love, and the glory filled the house (v. 13). Why do you think God chose to answer that song, and how might the same truth shape your prayer on a hard day?

The priests could not stand in God’s glory, yet in Jesus the glory came near and welcomed sinners (John 1:14). How should that both humble us and give us confidence as we come to worship?

6.title: Toward This Place
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Solomon said, "The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness.<sup>2</sup>But I have built you an exalted house, a place for you to dwell in forever."<sup>3</sup>Then the king turned around and blessed all the assembly of Israel, while all the assembly of Israel stood.<sup>4</sup>And he said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth to David my father, saying,<sup>5</sup>'Since the day that I brought my people out of the land of Egypt, I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house, that my name might be there, and I chose no man as prince over my people Israel;<sup>6</sup>but I have chosen Jerusalem that my name may be there, and I have chosen David to be over my people Israel.'<sup>7</sup>Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>8</sup>But the LORD said to David my father, 'Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart.<sup>9</sup>Nevertheless, it is not you who shall build the house, but your son who shall be born to you shall build the house for my name.'<sup>10</sup>Now the LORD has fulfilled his promise that he made. For I have risen in the place of David my father and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and I have built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>11</sup>And there I have set the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that he made with the people of Israel."<sup>12</sup>Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in the presence of all the assembly of Israel and spread out his hands.<sup>13</sup>Solomon had made a bronze platform five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high, and had set it in the court, and he stood on it. 6.overview:
Where we are. The ark is in its place and the cloud of glory has filled the house so that the priests cannot stand (chapter 5). Into that silence Solomon speaks: first to explain what has happened, then to bless the people, and then, on his knees before the whole nation, to pray the longest prayer in the book.

The message. The God whom heaven cannot contain has bound himself by promise to hear his people, and above all to forgive them. The temple is not where God lives but where his people turn when they pray, and the prayer foresees every kind of trouble, sin, drought, plague, war and even exile, and asks the same thing each time: hear from heaven, and forgive. Because “there is no one who does not sin” (v. 36), the house of God must be a house of forgiveness, or it is no use at all.

Why it was said. The first readers knew that every disaster Solomon prayed about had happened, down to the last one: the people had sinned and been carried captive (see the introduction). This chapter told them that the way back had been prayed for on the day the temple opened, and that God, who had never listened from inside the building, still heard those who turned to him.

How the chapter makes its case. Solomon reads the cloud as the sign of God’s presence and blesses the people with a review of God’s faithfulness: what he promised David with his mouth he has fulfilled with his hand (vv. 1–11). Then he kneels on a bronze platform and praises the God who keeps covenant, asks him to keep his word to David, and confesses that no house can contain him (vv. 12–21). Seven petitions follow, each a case of trouble: a wrong between neighbours, defeat, drought, plague (vv. 22–31), the foreigner, war and exile (vv. 32–39). He ends with the words of Psalm 132, asking God to remember his steadfast love for David (vv. 40–42).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and pattern. Solomon asks, “will God indeed dwell with man on the earth?” (v. 18), and the answer came in Jesus, in whom “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The house toward which Israel prayed is fulfilled in the one through whom we now pray: “we have a great priest over the house of God” (Hebrews 10:21). The steadfast love for David with which the prayer ends was given in full when God raised Jesus from the dead (Acts 13:34). And the foreigner from a far country, heard by God, points to the gospel going to all nations.

For us. No sin, sorrow or distance puts you beyond the reach of this prayer, because you pray through Christ, who always lives to intercede for his people. Bring God the particular trouble only you know (v. 29), confess your sin plainly (v. 37), and expect him to hear and forgive. And like Solomon, begin your asking with what God has already promised and already done.
6.theology:
The prayer never confuses God's dwelling in heaven with the house a person prays toward, and that distinction is why it outlived the building (see vv. 18-21). Verse 18 asks the question the rest of Scripture answers: will God indeed dwell with man on the earth? And the king on his knees interceding for a nation of sinners is a picture the gospel completes: the greater Son of David always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and he is heard.

Verse 8 holds two things most people cannot hold at once: God refuses David and says you did well that it was in your heart. God’s no settled which man would build. It did not condemn David for wanting to.
6.examples:
The greatest day of Solomon's reign found him on his knees in public. Success is the moment when kneeling is hardest and most needed.

No trouble is too small for this prayer: it begins with a quarrel between neighbours, before famine, war and exile. A believer need not wait until things are desperate to bring them to God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — He Spoke With His Mouth and Fulfilled With His Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has kept his word to David, and the finished house is the proof. With the cloud still in the room, Solomon reads it from Scripture: the LORD dwells in thick darkness, and yet here is a house built for him (vv. 1–2). He turns to bless the whole standing assembly and rehearses God’s promise: no city and no king had been chosen since the Exodus, but now God has chosen both Jerusalem and David (vv. 3–6). David’s longing to build was refused and yet commended, and the son born afterwards has built it (vv. 7–9). So the promise is kept, and the ark with its covenant tablets is in its place (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: On the day the house is finished, the son repeats aloud the commendation God gave his father when he refused him.
verseByVerse.examples: The building is offered not as Solomon's achievement but as evidence that God keeps his word.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon said, "The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness. But I have built you an exalted house, a place for you to dwell in forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon reads the cloud from Scripture: the God who hides himself in thick darkness has come to dwell in the house built for him. The darkness is not a disaster but God’s signature.

He would dwell in thick darkness. The cloud is still in the building, the priests have backed out, the singers have stopped, and into that silence the king explains what has just happened from Scripture. At Sinai “the people stood far off, while Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was” (Exodus 20:21), and the mountain “burned with fire to the heart of heaven, wrapped in darkness, cloud, and gloom” (Deuteronomy 4:11). A psalm says, “He made darkness his covering, his canopy around him” (Psalm 18:11); another, “Clouds and thick darkness are all around him” (Psalm 97:2).

Hidden out of mercy. So the cloud is not an accident of weather. The God of Israel has always come in a darkness thick enough to hide him, and he hides himself out of mercy, not to keep people away: “man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20). Solomon looks at a room nobody can enter and concludes that God has moved in.

But I have built you an exalted house. A God who hides in thick darkness, and a building of gold and cedar that bears his name: Solomon puts the two side by side without resolving them, and the rest of his prayer keeps both in view. The resolution came in a person. The God no one has ever seen has been made known by “God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side” (John 1:18), and in Jesus’ face we see the glory that the cloud concealed (2 Corinthians 4:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king turned around and blessed all the assembly of Israel, while all the assembly of Israel stood. And he said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth to David my father, saying, 'Since the day that I brought my people out of the land of Egypt, I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house, that my name might be there, and I chose no man as prince over my people Israel; but I have chosen Jerusalem that my name may be there, and I have chosen David to be over my people Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon blesses God before the people for keeping his word: what God promised David with his mouth, he has fulfilled with his hand, by choosing both a city and a king.

The king turned around and blessed all the assembly. He had been facing the house; now he turns his back on it to face the people. The first thing he does on the greatest day of his reign is bless the congregation, as his father did when the ark came home (1 Chronicles 16:2) and as Aaron’s sons were commissioned to do (Numbers 6:23–27). The whole nation is standing.

Who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth. The blessing is not a wish but a recital of what God has said and done, and the two are joined. It is the plainest definition of faithfulness anyone has given: what God says with the one, he does with the other, and the building they are standing in is the evidence. “All the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20), Paul writes of Christ; Solomon is standing in one of the early instalments.

I have chosen Jerusalem … and I have chosen David. From the Exodus to David’s day God had picked no capital and no dynasty. The ark moved from Gilgal to Shiloh, into Philistine captivity and on to Kiriath-jearim; leadership passed from judge to judge with gaps in between. Then two choices, made together: a place and a person, a city for the name and a man for the throne. The temple and the covenant with David belong together, and both find their goal in one man, the Son of David who called his own body the temple (John 2:19–21).

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. But the LORD said to David my father, 'Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart. Nevertheless, it is not you who shall build the house, but your son who shall be born to you shall build the house for my name.' Now the LORD has fulfilled his promise that he made. For I have risen in the place of David my father and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and I have built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. And there I have set the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that he made with the people of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God refused David’s wish to build the temple and yet commended him for wanting to, and he kept his promise through the son born afterwards. A desire can be good and the answer still be no.

You did well that it was in your heart. Solomon tells the assembly plainly about his father’s disappointment (1 Chronicles 17:1–4; 22:8), and then comes the clause that repays a long look. God refused him and commended him in one breath. He did not say that David’s motives were mixed or that he should have asked first; the wanting itself is approved, on the record, by the one who said no to it.

Refusal without rebuke. The two are harder to hold together than either on its own. A refusal usually feels like a judgment on the desire behind it, so a man who is turned down concludes either that he was wrong to want it or that God was unkind to withhold it. Here is a third possibility, stated by God himself: the desire was good, the answer is no, and both are final. A believer whose prayer for a ministry, a marriage or a child has been answered no may hear this: wanting it was not wrong.

Your son who shall be born to you. When God refused David, the man who would do the work did not yet exist. David spent the rest of his life buying the site, stockpiling gold and iron, drawing plans and organising priests and singers for a son not yet born and a building he would never enter. A man who believes his refused ambition was still good can spend his life serving it.

The LORD has fulfilled his promise. Solomon sums up (vv. 10–11). Everything he lists is God’s doing except setting the ark in its place, and even that was only putting the covenant tablets where God said to put them. The greater promise to David, of a son whose throne would last forever (1 Chronicles 17:11–14), was still waiting; it is kept in Jesus, “the son of David” (Matthew 1:1).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king kneels before the whole nation to ask the God whom heaven cannot contain to watch over this house and forgive. On a bronze platform in the court, Solomon kneels and spreads his hands toward heaven (vv. 12–13). He praises the God who has no equal and who keeps covenant and steadfast love (vv. 14–15), and asks him to keep his promise to David, with its condition (vv. 16–17). Then he says what no temple can be: “heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you, how much less this house” (v. 18). He asks only that God’s eyes be open toward it, that he listen from heaven, and that when he hears, he forgive (vv. 19–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Solomon has built the most expensive building in the nation's history and spends the dedication saying what it is not.
verseByVerse.examples: Kneeling is not only for the private room. A leader on his knees in front of those he leads teaches them more than a speech.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in the presence of all the assembly of Israel and spread out his hands. Solomon had made a bronze platform five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high, and had set it in the court, and he stood on it. Then he knelt on his knees in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven,
verseByVerse.commentary:
On a platform built so that the whole nation could see him, the king knelt down and spread out his hands to pray. Israel’s greatest king is shown on his knees.

A bronze platform. Only Chronicles mentions it. Its measurements, five cubits by five by three, are the same as those of the bronze altar Bezalel made in the wilderness (Exodus 27:1), on which Solomon sacrificed at Gibeon in chapter 1. Whether that was deliberate cannot be known, and the text does not say; but the king stands in the temple court on a bronze structure the size of an altar, and what he is about to offer on it is prayer.

He knelt on his knees. Kings has him stand before the altar to pray and mentions the kneeling only at the end, in a passing clause (1 Kings 8:22, 54). Chronicles puts it in the middle of the sentence, in front of everybody. Israel watched its wealthiest and wisest king kneel in public on the day his greatest work was finished, and the writer thought that was the detail to keep. The posture does not make prayer heard, but it tells the truth about who is great.

A greater king on his knees. A greater Son of David knelt too, alone in a garden, and prayed not for a building but for the people his Father had given him, and then gave himself for them (Luke 22:41; John 17:9). Solomon prayed once for his nation; Christ “always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25).
verseByVerse.note: A cubit was about 18 inches (ESV note): the platform was about 7½ feet square and 4½ feet high.

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven or on earth, keeping covenant and showing steadfast love to your servants who walk before you with all their heart, who have kept with your servant David my father what you declared to him. You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand have fulfilled it this day. Now therefore, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for your servant David my father what you have promised him, saying, 'You shall not lack a man to sit before me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk in my law as you have walked before me.' Now therefore, O LORD, God of Israel, let your word be confirmed, which you have spoken to your servant David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon praises the God who has no equal and who keeps his covenant with steadfast love, and on that ground asks him to keep his word to David’s house.

There is no God like you, in heaven or on earth. The prayer opens with a comparison and finds nothing to compare. Not the best of the gods; there is no other in either place.

Keeping covenant and showing steadfast love. Covenant and steadfast love are held together, the legal word and the warm one (see Steadfast Love). God has bound himself by his promise, and he keeps it gladly. The evidence is in the room: “You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand have fulfilled it this day” (v. 15). Solomon returns to it because it is the only argument he has, and it is enough. The surest prayers begin with what God has already said.

If only your sons pay close attention. The condition stands out, because this book has been leaving such conditions out. When Nathan brought God’s promise to David, Chronicles omitted the warning that God would discipline David’s son when he sinned (compare 1 Chronicles 17:13 with 2 Samuel 7:14). When God granted wisdom at Gibeon, Chronicles left out the condition that Kings attaches (1 Kings 3:14). Here at last the condition is stated, and by the king himself, in prayer, about his own sons. Kings has “to walk before me”; Chronicles has “to walk in my law” (1 Kings 8:25), naming the standard. The Chronicler does not use it as a threat. He lets Solomon say it as a request.

Let your word be confirmed. Verse 17 is the shortest request in the prayer. He is not asking God to add anything, but to stand by a sentence already spoken, as he asked at Gibeon (1:9). No son of David met the condition except one. Jesus walked in God’s law perfectly, and because he did, the promise to David stands for everyone who belongs to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "But will God indeed dwell with man on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built! Yet have regard to the prayer of your servant and to his plea, O LORD my God, listening to the cry and to the prayer that your servant prays before you, that your eyes may be open day and night toward this house, the place where you have promised to set your name, that you may listen to the prayer that your servant offers toward this place. And listen to the pleas of your servant and of your people Israel, when they pray toward this place. And listen from heaven your dwelling place, and when you hear, forgive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No house can contain the God of heaven, so Solomon asks only that God would watch over this one, listen from heaven to prayer made toward it, and forgive.

But will God indeed dwell with man on the earth? In the middle of the dedication of the building he spent seven years raising, Solomon asks the question the whole Bible is answering, and answers it at once: “Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built!” He had said it in his letter to Hiram (2:6), and he says it again with the gold on the walls and the cloud in the room. The house is a marvel, the house is not the point, and its builder is the one insisting on it.

The answer to Solomon’s question. Centuries later John, who had touched the answer with his own hands (1 John 1:1), wrote, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The God whom heaven cannot contain was contained in a womb, laid in a manger and nailed to a cross, without ceasing to be God. And near the end of Scripture a voice from the throne says, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

That your eyes may be open day and night toward this house. What Solomon asks for is attention: not that God would live in the house, but that he would look at it. Verse 19 piles up four words for asking in one sentence, prayer, plea, cry and prayer again. A man about to describe famine, siege and captivity is reaching for every word his language has for a person trying to get God’s attention.

Listen from heaven your dwelling place. The prayer keeps the two places distinct all the way through. God’s address is heaven; the house is what a person turns toward. The refrain “hear from heaven” runs through every petition to verse 39, and four times it adds “your dwelling place”. In a building that had cost more gold than anyone could weigh, the king points away from it and upward. That is why the prayer outlived the building: a man in Babylon could face that direction and be heard, because the hearing had never been done from there.

And when you hear, forgive. Not act, answer or intervene, but forgive, and it is asked five times before the prayer is done (vv. 21, 25, 27, 30, 39). Solomon has worked out what his nation will mostly need. Every Christian who prays still needs it first (Luke 11:4).

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should face Jerusalem, or any building, to pray. Jesus said the hour had come when “the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4:23). We pray through Christ, the true temple, and so “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16) from a kitchen, a hospital bed or a prison cell.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Whatever trouble comes, from a private wrong to a national disaster, God’s people may turn to him and ask him to hear, judge rightly and forgive. The first case is an oath at the altar over a wrong between neighbours (vv. 22–23). The second is defeat in battle because of sin (vv. 24–25). The third is drought, sent until the people turn, when God will teach them the good way (vv. 26–27). The fourth gathers every plague and siege and then narrows to each person, “each knowing his own affliction and his own sorrow” (vv. 28–29). The ground of the asking is that God alone knows the heart, and the goal is that his people fear him (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 30 makes the claim the whole prayer rests on: you, you only, know the hearts of the children of mankind. When David handed over the kingdom he told Solomon that the LORD searches all hearts (1 Chronicles 28:9). Solomon now prays that truth back to God.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone whose private grief feels lost inside a larger disaster may take heart: Solomon's prayer stops to name the single person with his own sorrow, and God sees him.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man sins against his neighbor and is made to take an oath and comes and swears his oath before your altar in this house, then hear from heaven and act and judge your servants, repaying the guilty by bringing his conduct on his own head, and vindicating the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness. "If your people Israel are defeated before the enemy because they have sinned against you, and they turn again and acknowledge your name and pray and plead with you in this house, then hear from heaven and forgive the sin of your people Israel and bring them again to the land that you gave to them and to their fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon’s first cases are a private wrong between neighbours and a national defeat caused by sin: in both he asks God to hear, judge rightly and forgive those who turn back to him.

Seven cases. Now the requests, and they are cases rather than themes: seven of them, each beginning with an “if” or a “when”.

If a man sins against his neighbor. The first is the smallest, and it is domestic: two men in a village, a dispute nobody can settle, and a procedure in which the accused swears his innocence at the altar (compare Exodus 22:10–11). God is asked to sort out who is lying, “repaying the guilty by bringing his conduct on his own head, and vindicating the righteous”. The most magnificent building in Israel is put at the disposal of a quarrel between neighbours, and that case is listed before the armies, the famines and the exile. No wrong is too small for God’s justice.

Defeated before the enemy because they have sinned. The second case is national, and the diagnosis is blunt: the cause is named in advance, and it is not the enemy’s strength. What the people do about it has three verbs: they “turn again and acknowledge your name and pray”. Turning first, then confessing again the God they had abandoned, then asking. Solomon requests that God “bring them again to the land”: the first hint in the prayer that being out of it is possible.

The judge who took the verdict. Solomon asks God to bring the guilty man’s conduct on his own head. The gospel goes further than his prayer could: God brought our conduct on the head of his innocent Son, “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

verseByVerse.quote: "When heaven is shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, if they pray toward this place and acknowledge your name and turn from their sin, when you afflict them, then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel, when you teach them the good way in which they should walk, and grant rain upon your land, which you have given to your people as an inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God shuts the sky because of sin, he does it to turn his people back, and Solomon asks him not only to forgive and send rain but to teach them the good way to walk.

When heaven is shut up. The first two cases began with “if”; this one begins with “when”. In a country farming rain-fed hills with no great river, drought is not a remote possibility but a matter of time, and Solomon prays about it as a certainty. The covenant itself had warned that disobedience would close the sky (Deuteronomy 11:16–17).

When you afflict them. The remedy has the same shape: pray toward the place, acknowledge the name, turn from the sin. Then comes a clause easy to miss: they turn “when you afflict them”. The affliction is God’s, and it is aimed at producing the turning. The shut sky is not God losing interest but God getting their attention in the one way a farming nation cannot ignore.

When you teach them the good way in which they should walk. The request joins things most people would not put together: forgive, teach, and send rain. Solomon does not ask for the weather to change and leave it there. He asks for instruction in the middle of the drought, as though the point of the whole episode were that they should learn to walk somewhere better. “Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word” (Psalm 119:67).

What it does not mean. Not that every hardship a Christian faces is punishment for a particular sin; Jesus refused to read suffering that way (John 9:2–3; see the note on 7:13–14). But every hardship is an occasion to ask what God may be teaching, and to pray for the lesson as well as the relief.

verseByVerse.quote: "If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence or blight or mildew or locust or caterpillar, if their enemies besiege them in the land at their gates, whatever plague, whatever sickness there is, whatever prayer, whatever plea is made by any man or by all your people Israel, each knowing his own affliction and his own sorrow and stretching out his hands toward this house, then hear from heaven your dwelling place and forgive and render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways, for you, you only, know the hearts of the children of mankind, that they may fear you and walk in your ways all the days that they live in the land that you gave to our fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever calamity strikes, God knows each sufferer’s own sorrow and each heart, and Solomon asks him to hear each one, so that his people may learn to fear him and walk in his ways.

Whatever plague, whatever sickness. Seven named disasters, famine, pestilence, blight, mildew, locust, caterpillar and siege, then two open categories to catch anything forgotten. Solomon is trying to build a prayer with no gaps in it, because he is praying for four centuries of a nation he will not live to see.

Each knowing his own affliction and his own sorrow. Halfway through the list the prayer narrows to one person: the plea may be made “by any man or by all your people Israel”. The phrase is one only somebody who has watched people suffer would write. A national calamity is a single word in a chronicle and a thousand separate rooms at the time. The locust took everybody’s crop, and each family sat with its own version of the loss. Solomon prays for the whole nation and then insists on each person inside it. God does not deal with his people in bulk; there is a word here for the one whose grief no one else understands.

You, you only, know the hearts. Solomon turns his father’s sentence, “the LORD searches all hearts” (1 Chronicles 28:9), into the reason God can be trusted with a nation’s grief. Nobody else can tell the man who is sorry from the man who is only frightened. God can, and that is why Solomon is willing to ask him to “render to each”.

That they may fear you and walk in your ways. Verse 31 gives the point of the whole exercise, and it is not relief. The rain, the healing and the lifted siege are not the goal; Solomon asks not for a comfortable nation but for one that has learned something and kept it. That is no glib verdict on anyone’s suffering. It is a prayer that God would not waste it.

A high priest who knows. The God who knows each heart has also learned each sorrow from the inside. In Christ “we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15). The sufferer who stretches out his hands to God now stretches them to one who has borne griefs and carried sorrows (Isaiah 53:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–39 — The Foreigner, and the Exile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s house is to be a place of prayer for all nations and a hope even for the people he has sent away for their sin. The fifth petition is for the foreigner who comes from far because he has heard of God’s great name; Solomon asks God to grant all he asks, so that all peoples may know and fear him (vv. 32–33). The sixth is for armies God sends out (vv. 34–35). The last and longest is for exile: “there is no one who does not sin”, and if the captives turn, confess and pray toward their land, God is asked to hear and forgive (vv. 36–39).
verseByVerse.theology: The widest petition in the prayer is made for an outsider, so that the whole earth may learn the name.
verseByVerse.examples: The people who first read this book were living inside verse 38, praying toward a city they had been carried away from. No distance from God, even one a person has caused, is beyond this prayer's reach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Likewise, when a foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, comes from a far country for the sake of your great name and your mighty hand and your outstretched arm, when he comes and prays toward this house, hear from heaven your dwelling place and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you, in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name and fear you, as do your people Israel, and that they may know that this house that I have built is called by your name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon asks God to answer the foreigner who comes from afar because of his great name, so that all the peoples of the earth may come to know and fear him. The temple was meant to be a witness to the nations.

When a foreigner … comes from a far country. The fifth petition is the one nobody would have predicted. This is not one of the resident foreigners quarrying stone in the hills (2:17–18), but somebody from a far country who has heard something and travelled. What he has heard is not that Israel is prosperous or its temple a spectacle, but of “your great name and your mighty hand and your outstretched arm”, the language of the Exodus, the story of what this God did for slaves.

Do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you. For Israel Solomon has asked forgiveness and restoration. For the foreigner he asks that God grant all he asks, with no condition. The king of Israel stands in the court of the temple on the day of its dedication and asks God to give a Gentile whatever he asks for. Within a few chapters a foreign queen will come from far away, having heard of Solomon’s fame “concerning the name of the LORD” (9:1; 1 Kings 10:1).

That all the peoples of the earth may know your name. The reason is not politeness. The point of answering the outsider is that the news should travel: a foreigner who goes home with his prayer answered is a witness in a country the temple will never reach. God’s promise that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham (Genesis 12:3) is still in view.

A house of prayer for all peoples. Isaiah heard God say the same thing centuries later, and more sharply: foreigners who joined themselves to the LORD would be brought to his holy mountain, “for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples” (Isaiah 56:7). In the last week of his life the Son of David walked into the temple court, found it filled with traders’ tables, and drove the traders out quoting that verse (Mark 11:17), most likely because they had set up in the outer court, the one part of that later temple where a foreigner like this one was allowed to stand. Now the dividing wall is gone, and Gentiles who were far off “have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "If your people go out to battle against their enemies, by whatever way you shall send them, and they pray to you toward this city that you have chosen and the house that I have built for your name, then hear from heaven their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God sends his people out to battle, Solomon asks him to hear their prayer and uphold their just cause.

By whatever way you shall send them. The sixth case is the only one in which the nation has done nothing wrong, and the clause in the middle is the whole condition. The prayer covers armies God has sent, and says nothing about the others. Soldiers a hundred miles from Jerusalem turn to face a building and pray.

Maintain their cause. A courtroom phrase rather than a battlefield one: uphold their right. Solomon wants the verdict to be just more than he wants the fight to be won.
