Does this bless a nation’s wars today? It was prayed for Israel, a nation God governed directly and sometimes sent to battle. The church is not that nation; its King said, “My kingdom is not of this world”, which is why his servants do not fight for it (John 18:36). Christians still pray for just causes and for those who serve, but “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4): the weapons of the kingdom are the word and prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: "If they sin against you— for there is no one who does not sin—and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy, so that they are carried away captive to a land far or near, yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive, and repent and plead with you in the land of their captivity, saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly,' if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their captivity to which they were carried captive, and pray toward their land, which you gave to their fathers, the city that you have chosen and the house that I have built for your name, then hear from heaven your dwelling place their prayer and their pleas, and maintain their cause and forgive your people who have sinned against you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because everyone sins, Solomon prays even for the exile that will follow the people’s unfaithfulness: if they repent in the land of their captivity and pray toward home, he asks God to hear and forgive.

For there is no one who does not sin. The seventh case is the longest, and the one the first readers of this book had lived through. The parenthesis stops the sentence dead (compare Ecclesiastes 7:20; Romans 3:23). It is why the case has to be prayed for at all. The thing that will eventually destroy the nation is already present in every person in the courtyard, including the man on the platform, whose own heart would turn in old age (1 Kings 11:4). So on the day the temple opens, its dedication includes a petition for the generation that will watch it burn.

We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly. Solomon even supplies the exiles’ words of confession. They were used: in Babylon Daniel prayed, “we have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly and rebelled” (Daniel 9:5), and his prayer was heard.

And pray toward their land. About four centuries later Daniel, a high official in Babylon, “had windows in his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem. He got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God” (Daniel 6:10), and went on doing it after it had been made a capital offence. He was doing what this verse told him, in a city a desert’s width away, facing a hill with a ruin on it.

Forgive your people who have sinned against you. The petition is the one that has run through the whole prayer: hear, and forgive. The house may be gone; the direction still works, because God was never listening from inside it. It works too for those who have never obeyed as they should: the way back is to turn and confess to the God who has promised to forgive (1 John 1:9), because the Son of David obeyed in their place and his righteousness is counted as theirs (Romans 5:19). No one has wandered so far that this prayer does not reach them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–42 — Arise, O LORD, to Your Resting Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer ends by resting everything on God’s steadfast love for David. Solomon gathers his requests into one line, that God’s eyes be open and his ears attentive to prayer made in this place (v. 40). Then he borrows the words of Psalm 132, the song of David’s vow to find a home for the ark: he asks God to arise to his resting place, to clothe his priests with salvation and to make his saints rejoice (v. 41). He ends not with the building but with a plea: do not turn away from your anointed king; remember your steadfast love for David (v. 42).
verseByVerse.theology: The son finishes his father's psalm on the day his father's project is opened.
verseByVerse.examples: The prayer ends not on what Solomon has built but on what God has promised. That is the safest place for any prayer to end.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, O my God, let your eyes be open and your ears attentive to the prayer of this place. "And now arise, O LORD God, and go to your resting place, you and the ark of your might. Let your priests, O LORD God, be clothed with salvation, and let your saints rejoice in your goodness. O LORD God, do not turn away the face of your anointed one! Remember your steadfast love for David your servant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon ends his prayer in the words of Psalm 132, asking God to take up his rest among his people and to remember his steadfast love for David. He rests everything not on the building but on God’s promise.

Let your eyes be open and your ears attentive. Eyes and ears, the two things he has asked for since verse 20, are gathered into one line. Then the prayer ends with words that are not Solomon’s own, and here Chronicles differs from Kings. In Kings the prayer closes on the Exodus and on Moses (1 Kings 8:51–53). Here it closes with Psalm 132, the psalm of David’s vow, “I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids” (Psalm 132:4), until he found a place for the LORD. The son ends the dedication by quoting the song about the vow, on the day the vow is fulfilled.

Go to your resting place. The word is the one David used when he said, “I had it in my heart to build a house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the LORD” (1 Chronicles 28:2). Everything since has been about giving the ark, which had moved from tent to tent for centuries, a settled home.

Let your priests, O LORD God, be clothed with salvation. The psalm prays, “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 132:9), and later gives God’s answer: “Her priests I will clothe with salvation” (Psalm 132:16). Solomon prays with the words of the answer. He asks for what God has already promised.

Do not turn away the face of your anointed one. The anointed one is Solomon, the king anointed with oil. But the Hebrew word is mashiach, Messiah, and the line of anointed kings was always leading to the Anointed One, the Christ.

Remember your steadfast love for David your servant. He does not end on the building but on a promise made to his father. Isaiah later told people who had nothing to come and buy without money: “I will make with you an everlasting covenant, my steadfast, sure love for David” (Isaiah 55:3). And Paul, preaching in a synagogue in Antioch, said that God fulfilled it by raising Jesus from the dead, “no more to return to corruption”: “I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David” (Acts 13:34). The house Solomon dedicated stood nearly four hundred years and was burned. The steadfast love promised to David was given in full on the third day, and it does not depend on any building.

keyVerse.quote: But will God indeed dwell with man on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built!
keyVerse.note: At the height of the temple’s glory its builder confesses that no house can hold God, and so the whole prayer asks him to hear from heaven. Solomon’s question is the one the whole Bible answers: God did come to dwell with man on the earth, in Jesus Christ, and will dwell with his people forever in the new creation.

6.reflection:
Solomon begins with what God has promised and already done: “You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand have fulfilled it this day” (v. 15). How might beginning your prayers with God’s promises and past faithfulness change the way you pray?

God refused David’s wish to build the temple yet said, “you did well that it was in your heart” (v. 8). Have you known a good desire that God answered with no? How does this verse help you think about it?

The word “forgive” runs all through the prayer, and verse 36 explains why: “there is no one who does not sin”. Why is forgiveness the thing God’s people most need from him, and how does Christ make it certain for us?

Solomon prays for the foreigner from a far country so that “all the peoples of the earth may know your name” (v. 33). How does this shape the way your church welcomes outsiders and supports mission?

7.title: If My People
7.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as Solomon finished his prayer, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple.<sup>2</sup>And the priests could not enter the house of the LORD, because the glory of the LORD filled the LORD's house.<sup>3</sup>When all the people of Israel saw the fire come down and the glory of the LORD on the temple, they bowed down with their faces to the ground on the pavement and worshiped and gave thanks to the LORD, saying, "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever."<sup>4</sup>Then the king and all the people offered sacrifice before the LORD.<sup>5</sup>King Solomon offered as a sacrifice 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. So the king and all the people dedicated the house of God.<sup>6</sup>The priests stood at their posts; the Levites also, with the instruments for music to the LORD that King David had made for giving thanks to the LORD— for his steadfast love endures forever—whenever David offered praises by their ministry; opposite them the priests sounded trumpets, and all Israel stood.<sup>7</sup>And Solomon consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of the LORD, for there he offered the burnt offering and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar Solomon had made could not hold the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat.<sup>8</sup>At that time Solomon held the feast for seven days, and all Israel with him, a very great assembly, from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt.<sup>9</sup>And on the eighth day they held a solemn assembly, for they had kept the dedication of the altar seven days and the feast seven days.<sup>10</sup>On the twenty-third day of the seventh month he sent the people away to their homes, joyful and glad of heart for the prosperity that the LORD had granted to David and to Solomon and to Israel his people.<sup>11</sup>Thus Solomon finished the house of the LORD and the king's house. All that Solomon had planned to do in the house of the LORD and in his own house he successfully accomplished.<sup>12</sup>Then the LORD appeared to Solomon in the night and said to him: "I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice.<sup>13</sup>When I shut up the heavens so that there is no rain, or command the locust to devour the land, or send pestilence among my people,<sup>14</sup>if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land.<sup>15</sup>Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer that is made in this place.<sup>16</sup>For now I have chosen and consecrated this house that my name may be there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time.<sup>17</sup>And as for you, if you will walk before me as David your father walked, doing according to all that I have commanded you and keeping my statutes and my rules,<sup>18</sup>then I will establish your royal throne, as I covenanted with David your father, saying, 'You shall not lack a man to rule Israel.'<sup>19</sup>"But if you turn aside and forsake my statutes and my commandments that I have set before you, and go and serve other gods and worship them,<sup>20</sup>then I will pluck you up from my land that I have given you, and this house that I have consecrated for my name, I will cast out of my sight, and I will make it a proverb and a byword among all peoples.<sup>21</sup>And at this house, which was exalted, everyone passing by will be astonished and say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?'<sup>22</sup>Then they will say, 'Because they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers who brought them out of the land of Egypt, and laid hold on other gods and worshiped them and served them. Therefore he has brought all this disaster on them.'"
7.overview:
Where we are. Solomon has just finished his great prayer of dedication, asking again and again that God would hear from heaven and forgive (chapter 6). This chapter gives God’s answer: first in fire and glory before the whole nation, then in words spoken to the king by night.

The message. God hears. He accepts the sacrifice, fills his house with glory, and promises that when his people humble themselves, pray, seek his face and turn from their wicked ways, he will hear, forgive and heal. But the same voice that gives the promise gives the warning: if they forsake him for other gods, the land will be lost and this splendid house will become a byword. His grace is free, but it is not to be presumed on.

Why it was said. The first readers had lived through both halves of God’s answer: the ruin of verses 19–22, and the mercy of verse 14 that brought them home (see the introduction). This chapter, with its verse 14, is the key to the whole book that follows, and it told them that the way to go on living in the land God had given back was the same four verbs.

How the chapter makes its case. Fire falls from heaven the moment Solomon stops praying, the glory fills the house, and the people fall on their faces singing that God is good (vv. 1–3). Sacrifices beyond counting follow, so many that the court itself must be consecrated (vv. 4–7). Two weeks of feasting end with the people sent home glad (vv. 8–11). Then God appears to Solomon by night: he has heard, he names the building a house of sacrifice, and he gives the promise of verse 14 (vv. 12–16). Last comes the condition for the king and the warning for the nation, with its epitaph already written (vv. 17–22).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. The house of sacrifice, where offerings were repeated for centuries, gives way to the one sacrifice by which Christ “sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:12), and the fire that fell on the altar fell in judgment on him in our place. The promise to hear and forgive those who humble themselves is kept through the Son of David who “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death” (Philippians 2:8). And the warning of a house cast out of God’s sight was fulfilled twice, under Babylon and again under Rome, for Jesus wept over it (Luke 19:41–44): the people needed more than a temple. They needed a new heart and a Saviour.

For us. God still hears those over whom his name is called, the church of Jesus Christ, when they humble themselves, pray, seek his face and turn. Come to him that way, not with a bargain but with confession, sure that “if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). And do not presume on his kindness: the privilege of being near him is a call to faithfulness.
7.theology:
Verse 14 is the sentence the whole book is built on, and verse 13 is the half people leave off when they quote it: the one who offers the remedy is the one who sent the trouble. Four things are asked of the people (humble themselves, pray, seek my face, turn), and the fourth keeps the first three from becoming a mere method. God promises three: to hear, to forgive and to heal, with the land last.

Who may claim the promise today is taken up at verse 14 below. And the warning is spoken the same night: the house he has just consecrated can be cast out of his sight, and the reason is supplied in advance.
7.examples:
God gave more than Solomon dared to ask: he asked for eyes and ears and was given God's heart as well.

The people lying on the pavement already knew the words, because the Levites had sung that one line morning and evening for a generation. The words of worship learned in ordinary weeks are the ones that come when the great day, or the hard one, arrives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Fire, and an Altar Too Small
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers Solomon’s prayer at once with fire and glory, and his people fall down and praise him. As soon as the prayer ends, fire comes down from heaven and consumes the offerings, and the glory of the LORD fills the house, so that once again the priests cannot enter (vv. 1–2). The people see it, bow with their faces to the pavement, and give thanks in the singers’ words: “For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever” (v. 3). Twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep are offered (vv. 4–5), the Levites play David’s instruments (v. 6), and the middle of the court is consecrated because the great bronze altar cannot hold all that is brought (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Fire from heaven is how God marks a place as his own, and here he answers the moment Solomon finishes praying.
verseByVerse.examples: Everything about that house was built at the limit of what a nation could manage, and the first thing it did was overflow.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Solomon finished his prayer, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple. And the priests could not enter the house of the LORD, because the glory of the LORD filled the LORD's house. When all the people of Israel saw the fire come down and the glory of the LORD on the temple, they bowed down with their faces to the ground on the pavement and worshiped and gave thanks to the LORD, saying, "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answered Solomon’s prayer at once with fire from heaven and the glory of his presence, and the whole people fell on their faces and praised his goodness.

As soon as Solomon finished his prayer. Not that night, not the following week: the last word had barely left his mouth. The prayer had asked God to hear; the fire says he has.

Fire came down from heaven. Kings has no fire in its account of this day (1 Kings 8:54–64); only Chronicles records it. It had happened twice before. When Aaron made the first offerings at the tabernacle, “fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the pieces of fat on the altar, and when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces” (Leviticus 9:24). And on this very hill, on the threshing floor David bought after the plague, “the LORD answered him with fire from heaven upon the altar of burnt offering” (1 Chronicles 21:26). The fire is God’s acceptance: he receives the offering and the house, and the worship offered there is his own appointing.

The priests could not enter. For the second time in three chapters (5:14), the glory fills the house and the priests cannot get in.

They bowed down with their faces to the ground on the pavement. Farmers and soldiers lying face-down on paving stones say the choir’s line: “For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever.” What the Levites sang in chapter 5 the whole nation now says. When God shows himself, the right response is not only awe but thanksgiving, because the God of fire is good.

The fire that fell on Christ. Fire from heaven fell on the sacrifice, not on the people. That is the gospel in picture: the judgment that sinners deserve falls on a substitute. At the cross it fell on God’s own Son, “who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32), and those who shelter in him can say, without fear, that God is good.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king and all the people offered sacrifice before the LORD. King Solomon offered as a sacrifice 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. So the king and all the people dedicated the house of God. The priests stood at their posts; the Levites also, with the instruments for music to the LORD that King David had made for giving thanks to the LORD— for his steadfast love endures forever—whenever David offered praises by their ministry; opposite them the priests sounded trumpets, and all Israel stood. And Solomon consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of the LORD, for there he offered the burnt offering and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar Solomon had made could not hold the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king and the people dedicated God’s house with sacrifices so many that even the great altar could not hold them. No altar was ever going to be large enough for the thanks God is owed.

22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. The figures are hard to take in. At that scale it is not an event but weeks of work, with the whole priesthood on duty. Kings calls them peace offerings (1 Kings 8:63), of which the worshippers ate, so the dedication was also a vast feast shared by the nation before God.

Could so many animals be sacrificed? The celebration lasted fourteen days (v. 9), and the courtyard was consecrated for the overflow (v. 7). The numbers may be taken as they stand; either way the point is lavish worship. Kings gives the same figures (1 Kings 8:63), so this is not one of the places where the two books differ.

The instruments for music to the LORD that King David had made. The Levites are at their posts with David’s instruments, and the refrain is quoted again in the middle of the sentence, as though the writer cannot mention the instruments without the words that went with them. David made them for a house he was told he would not build. Now they are being played in it.

Solomon consecrated the middle of the court. The bronze altar, sixteen times the area of the one Bezalel made for the tabernacle (4:1; Exodus 27:1), was not big enough on its first working day, so the paving around it was consecrated for the overflow.

One sacrifice, enough. All those animals could not take away one sin (Hebrews 10:4); they were thanks and pictures, not payment. The sacrifice that was enough was a single one: Christ “offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins” (Hebrews 10:12). Our thanks can never be large enough, but our forgiveness does not depend on its size.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — Seven Days, and Seven More
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The nation rejoices together in what God has done and goes home glad. Solomon keeps the feast with a vast assembly gathered from the far north to the border of Egypt: seven days for the dedication of the altar and seven for the Feast of Booths, with a solemn assembly on the eighth day (vv. 8–9). On the twenty-third day of the seventh month he sends the people home “joyful and glad of heart” for the goodness the LORD had shown to David, to Solomon and to Israel (v. 10). The two houses, God’s and the king’s, are finished (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The gladness in verse 10 is credited to what the LORD granted to David, Solomon and Israel together.
verseByVerse.examples: Nobody was in a hurry: two weeks of worship, and the people went home glad. Joy is the fitting end of meeting with God.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Solomon held the feast for seven days, and all Israel with him, a very great assembly, from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt. And on the eighth day they held a solemn assembly, for they had kept the dedication of the altar seven days and the feast seven days. On the twenty-third day of the seventh month he sent the people away to their homes, joyful and glad of heart for the prosperity that the LORD had granted to David and to Solomon and to Israel his people. Thus Solomon finished the house of the LORD and the king's house. All that Solomon had planned to do in the house of the LORD and in his own house he successfully accomplished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All Israel feasted for two weeks and went home joyful and glad of heart for God’s goodness to David, to Solomon and to his people. Gladness is the right ending to worship.

From Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt. The assembly is described by its edges, Lebo-hamath in the far north and the Brook of Egypt in the south: the whole land, the same span the Chronicler used when David first went to fetch the ark (1 Chronicles 13:5).

The dedication of the altar seven days and the feast seven days. Seven days for the dedication, seven for the Feast of Booths, and on the eighth day of the feast a solemn assembly to close it (Leviticus 23:36).

On the twenty-third day of the seventh month. Kings says he sent the people away “on the eighth day” (1 Kings 8:66), and Chronicles dates it to the twenty-third. The feast began on the fifteenth (Leviticus 23:34), so its eighth day fell on the twenty-second; the most natural reading is that the closing assembly was held that day and the people left the next morning.

Joyful and glad of heart. The people go home not exhausted or burdened but glad, and the reason is “the prosperity that the LORD had granted” (the word is goodness). There are three names in verse 10. Kings mentions David and Israel; Chronicles adds Solomon. And the first name, David, belongs to a man dead for years: the one who bought the ground, gathered the gold and drew the plans is named first at the dedication he never saw.

Thus Solomon finished the house of the LORD and the king’s house. The project is signed off, God’s house and the king’s together, as they were announced together in 2:1. All that Solomon had planned, he accomplished. The Chronicler does not comment; the next words are God’s.
verseByVerse.note: Lebo-hamath (“the entrance of Hamath”) in the far north to the Brook of Egypt in the south: the whole land.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God promises to hear, forgive and heal his people when they humble themselves and turn back to him. He appears to Solomon by night: he has heard the prayer and chosen the place as “a house of sacrifice” (v. 12). He claims as his own the drought, locust and pestilence Solomon had prayed about (v. 13), and gives the sentence on which the whole book turns: “if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land” (v. 14). He grants what Solomon asked, his eyes and ears open to this place, and adds what Solomon did not dare to ask: his heart (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Before the promise there is a claim: the drought and the locust and the plague are named in the first person as God's own doing.
verseByVerse.examples: The God who could have answered with a warning answers first with his heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD appeared to Solomon in the night and said to him: "I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answered Solomon by night: he had heard his prayer and chosen this place as a house of sacrifice. The heart of the temple was not its gold but its altar.

Then the LORD appeared to Solomon in the night. Twice God came to this man at night: once at Gibeon before anything was built, and now with the building full of smoke. The first time he asked a question, “Ask what I shall give you” (1:7); this time he answers one. Solomon had asked again and again that God would hear; the reply uses his own word: “I have heard your prayer”.

A house of sacrifice. God names the building: not a palace or a sanctuary or a dwelling, but “a house of sacrifice”. Solomon had said the same in his letter to Hiram, a place “to make offerings before him” (2:6), and God confirms it. That is what this hill, Moriah, had been from the beginning: the ram God provided for Abraham in place of Isaac (Genesis 22:13–14; see 3:1), and the offering that stopped the plague at David’s threshing floor (1 Chronicles 21:26–27). Now a house stood over the spot with an altar too small for its first day’s work.

A single sacrifice, and he sat down. The house of sacrifice was never meant to be the last word. Its offerings were repeated morning and evening for centuries because none of them could finish the work, whereas Christ “offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins” and sat down (Hebrews 10:12). The place where God now meets sinners is the risen Christ himself, the temple his enemies destroyed and he raised in three days (John 2:19–21). “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29).

verseByVerse.quote: When I shut up the heavens so that there is no rain, or command the locust to devour the land, or send pestilence among my people, if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God sends drought, locust or plague on his covenant people, and they humble themselves, pray, seek his face and turn from their sin, he promises to hear, forgive and heal their land. This is the promise on which the whole of 2 Chronicles turns.

When I shut up the heavens. Three disasters, and God claims all three in the first person: I shut up, I command, I send. The drought is not bad luck, nor the locust a natural cycle God happens to be able to work with. And the three are not chosen at random: Solomon’s third case was drought and his fourth famine, locust and pestilence (6:26–28). God answers Solomon in Solomon’s own words.

If my people who are called by my name. Literally, those over whom my name has been called: the people God has claimed as his own. They are “my people” before anything is asked of them, so the turning is not a price paid for the hearing but the response of those who already belong to him.

Humble themselves. This comes first, and the book will not let go of it. It is used of Rehoboam and his princes when the Egyptians come (12:6–7), of Hezekiah after his heart was proud (32:26), of Josiah when the book of the law was read to him (34:27), and, most astonishingly, of Manasseh, in chains in Babylon after filling Jerusalem with innocent blood, who “humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers” and was heard (33:12–13). It is used too of the last king of Judah, who “did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet” (36:12). From here to the exile, each king is measured by whether he humbled himself. “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

And pray and seek my face. Not help, or an outcome, but my face: God himself. It is what David told the nation on the day the ark came home: “Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually!” (1 Chronicles 16:11), where “presence” is literally “face”.

And turn from their wicked ways. The fourth verb keeps the other three honest. It is possible to be humbled by circumstances, to pray hard and to want God very much, and to change nothing. For the Christian, the Spirit who lives in him works that turning, giving the new heart God promised (Ezekiel 36:26–27).

Then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land. Then God’s three: hear, forgive, heal. Solomon had asked for rain; God says he will deal with the sin first and the land afterwards. The Chronicler’s first readers had seen both halves of this: the land lost for sin, and then a people who confessed in exile heard and brought home (Daniel 9:3–19; Ezra 1:1–4). The book holds the promise up to them as the way to go on living in the land given back to them.

The one who humbled himself. No king of Judah humbled himself fully or turned for good. The Son of David did: “he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8), and because of his humbling God hears from heaven, forgives his people’s sin, and will one day heal not one land but the whole creation (Romans 8:19–21).

Does every drought or epidemic mean God is punishing a particular sin? No. Verse 13 says God sends such things, and under the old covenant he used them to call Israel back. But Jesus refused to read disasters as proof that the victims were worse sinners (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:2–3). What a calamity says to everyone is what verse 14 says: turn, and seek his face. The sufferer who has done that is not under wrath, whatever the weather does.

Where Christians differ: does this verse promise to heal a nation today? Many Christians claim it for their own country, praying that if its believers repent, God will heal the nation. Others hold that it was spoken only to Israel under the old covenant and has no direct use today. This commentary’s view (see the introduction): “my people who are called by my name” were the covenant people, at a temple God had just chosen, in a land he had given them by oath, and the drought and plague were the covenant’s warnings on that land; no nation now stands in Israel’s place. What carries over is the people over whom his name is now called, the church of Jesus Christ, and the four verbs. When the church humbles itself, prays, seeks his face and turns, it is promised God’s ear and his pardon, through the high priest who is in heaven for us. A Christian may rightly plead for his own country, as Nineveh’s repentance shows that God hears any people who turn (Jonah 3); but the church is not promised a national revival on a timetable, and the full healing of the land waits for the new creation (Revelation 22:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer that is made in this place. For now I have chosen and consecrated this house that my name may be there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promised that his eyes and ears would be open to prayer in this place, and added what Solomon had not dared to ask: his heart would be there too.

My eyes will be open and my ears attentive. Solomon’s last request before the psalm was that God’s eyes be open and his ears attentive to the prayer of this place (6:40). God gives it back to him word for word.

My eyes and my heart will be there for all time. Then God adds something. Solomon asked for eyes and ears; God says eyes and heart. Eyes and ears are as much as a man drafting a petition can decently request. Nobody asks a king for his heart; God volunteers it. He will not merely watch over the building; his love will rest on it. The words he uses of the house, my name, my eyes, my heart, are the language of someone describing where he has left something precious.

If God said “forever”, why was the temple destroyed? The promise of verse 16 was given within the covenant, and the next verses spell out its condition: if the people forsook him, this very house would be cast out of his sight (vv. 19–20). And God did not take back his heart when the house fell. His name, his eyes and his heart came to rest on the true temple, his Son (John 2:21), and through him on his people, who “are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22). The New Testament does not look for a rebuilt temple; in the new Jerusalem there is none, “for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22).

Where his heart is now. If God’s heart rested on a building of stone and gold, it rests far more on the people his Son bought with his blood. A believer who feels forgotten can know that God’s eyes are open to his prayer and his heart is set on him, for all time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — The Epitaph, Written in Advance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s blessing calls for faithfulness, and the house he has filled will not protect a people who forsake him. If Solomon walks as David walked, God will establish his throne as he promised (vv. 17–18). But if the people turn aside to serve other gods, God will uproot them from his land and cast this consecrated house out of his sight, making it a byword among the nations (vv. 19–20). Passers-by will ask why, and God supplies the answer in advance: “Because they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers” (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: On the day the temple is dedicated God describes its ruin and writes the inscription for it.
verseByVerse.examples: The charge in verse 22 runs through the whole book: Azariah will warn Asa against forsaking him, Zechariah will say Joash's generation has, and the Chronicler will say it of Judah at the end.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for you, if you will walk before me as David your father walked, doing according to all that I have commanded you and keeping my statutes and my rules, then I will establish your royal throne, as I covenanted with David your father, saying, 'You shall not lack a man to rule Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promised Solomon that if he walked as David walked, his throne would stand, as God had covenanted with David.

As David your father walked. The standard held up to Solomon is his father, and it must be understood exactly, because David’s record in this book includes a census that cost seventy thousand lives. The standard is not a life without sin but a life turned toward God: a man who sought God, sinned, was told so, said “I have sinned greatly in what I have done” (1 Chronicles 21:8) without being asked twice, and put it right.

You shall not lack a man to rule Israel. The promise attached is the one God gave David through Nathan (1 Chronicles 17:11–14). Solomon had quoted it in his prayer with the condition attached (6:16), and God repeats it with the condition attached, so that nobody could say afterwards that it was not made clear.

The son who walked perfectly. No son of David walked that way without fault, and Solomon himself did not (1 Kings 11:4), except one. Jesus kept every command of his Father, and it is his obedience, not ours, that is counted to those who are his (Romans 5:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Through him the throne of David is established forever (Luke 1:32–33).

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you turn aside and forsake my statutes and my commandments that I have set before you, and go and serve other gods and worship them, then I will pluck you up from my land that I have given you, and this house that I have consecrated for my name, I will cast out of my sight, and I will make it a proverb and a byword among all peoples. And at this house, which was exalted, everyone passing by will be astonished and say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?' Then they will say, 'Because they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers who brought them out of the land of Egypt, and laid hold on other gods and worshiped them and served them. Therefore he has brought all this disaster on them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the very day of the temple’s glory, God warned that if his people forsook him for other gods, he would uproot them from his land and cast this house out of his sight. Privilege is no protection for those who abandon him.

But if you turn aside. The “you” is now plural: the whole people, not only the king. At the end of the greatest day in Israel’s history, God describes the ruin.

I will pluck you up from my land that I have given you. The land is “my land”: not theirs to keep, but God’s, given to them. The throne is the LORD’s, the ground is his, and so is the house he has just filled with fire and glory. And the house is not spared: God says he will cast out of his sight the building he has just consecrated, and make it “a proverb and a byword among all peoples”. The covenant had said as much from the beginning (Deuteronomy 28:37).

Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house? God supplies both the passer-by’s question and the answer, as Moses had foretold: the nations will ask, and be told, “It is because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 29:24–25). On the day of the dedication the epitaph is already cut. Nearly four hundred years later the last chapter of this book reports what happened in almost the same terms: they kept mocking God’s messengers “until there was no remedy”, and the Chaldeans burned the house (36:16–19). Nobody who had this chapter could say they had not been told.

The promise and the warning. So the high point of the book contains its ending, and the promise and the warning were spoken the same night by the same voice. The house that could be cast out of God’s sight was never the thing that would last. What lasts is verse 14, and it needs no building: four verbs from a people over whom his name is called, and three from a God who hears, forgives and heals.

Jesus and the second house. The warning came true twice. The rebuilt temple, enlarged by Herod, stood in Jesus’ day, and he wept over Jerusalem and said, “See, your house is left to you desolate” (Matthew 23:38), and that “there will not be left here one stone upon another” (Matthew 24:2). In AD 70 it fell to Rome. Jesus took the desolation of God’s rejected house into himself on the cross, forsaken so that those who trust him might never be cast out of God’s sight (Matthew 27:46; John 6:37).

What it does not mean. Not that a believer who falls into sin loses his place with God. The warning is for those who abandon the LORD and give themselves to other gods. But nor may anyone treat God’s nearness as a guarantee while he turns away: churches, like temples, can become empty shells (Revelation 2:5). The remedy is the one verse 14 gives.

keyVerse.quote: if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land.
keyVerse.note: This is the verse on which the whole of 2 Chronicles turns: every king that follows is measured by whether he humbled himself and sought God. It was spoken to Israel about its covenant land, but its four verbs and three promises still describe how God deals with the people called by his name, who now come to him through Christ for forgiveness.

7.reflection:
When the fire fell and the glory filled the house, the people fell on their faces and said, “For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever” (v. 3). Why is thanksgiving the right response to God’s holiness, and how does the cross make it possible for us?

God calls the temple “a house of sacrifice” (v. 12). How does Hebrews 10:11–12 show what all those sacrifices were pointing to, and what does it mean for your assurance that Christ’s sacrifice was offered once for all?

Verse 14 has four verbs for God’s people: humble themselves, pray, seek his face, turn from their wicked ways. Which of these do you find hardest, and what would each look like in your life and in your church this month?

On the very night of his promise God also warned of ruin (vv. 19–22). How do we hold together the assurance of God’s grace and the seriousness of his warnings without falling into either fear or presumption?

8.title: All That Solomon Planned to Do
8.text: <sup>1</sup>At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the house of the LORD and his own house,<sup>2</sup>Solomon rebuilt the cities that Hiram had given to him, and settled the people of Israel in them.<sup>3</sup>And Solomon went to Hamath-zobah and took it.<sup>4</sup>He built Tadmor in the wilderness and all the store cities that he built in Hamath.<sup>5</sup>He also built Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon, fortified cities with walls, gates, and bars,<sup>6</sup>and Baalath, and all the store cities that Solomon had and all the cities for his chariots and the cities for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.<sup>7</sup>All the people who were left of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of Israel,<sup>8</sup>from their descendants who were left after them in the land, whom the people of Israel had not destroyed—these Solomon drafted as forced labor, and so they are to this day.<sup>9</sup>But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves for his work; they were soldiers, and his officers, the commanders of his chariots, and his horsemen.<sup>10</sup>And these were the chief officers of King Solomon, 250, who exercised authority over the people.<sup>11</sup>Solomon brought Pharaoh's daughter up from the city of David to the house that he had built for her, for he said, "My wife shall not live in the house of David king of Israel, for the places to which the ark of the LORD has come are holy."<sup>12</sup>Then Solomon offered up burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar of the LORD that he had built before the vestibule,<sup>13</sup>as the duty of each day required, offering according to the commandment of Moses for the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the three annual feasts—the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Booths.<sup>14</sup>According to the ruling of David his father, he appointed the divisions of the priests for their service, and the Levites for their offices of praise and ministry before the priests as the duty of each day required, and the gatekeepers in their divisions at each gate, for so David the man of God had commanded.<sup>15</sup>And they did not turn aside from what the king had commanded the priests and Levites concerning any matter and concerning the treasuries.<sup>16</sup>Thus was accomplished all the work of Solomon from the day the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid until it was finished. So the house of the LORD was completed.<sup>17</sup>Then Solomon went to Ezion-geber and Eloth on the shore of the sea, in the land of Edom.<sup>18</sup>And Hiram sent to him by the hand of his servants ships and servants familiar with the sea, and they went to Ophir together with the servants of Solomon and brought from there 450 talents of gold and brought it to King Solomon.
8.overview:
Where we are. The temple has been dedicated, the fire has fallen, and God has answered by night with promise and warning (chapter 7). Now the Chronicler surveys the rest of Solomon’s twenty years of building, the ordering of worship in the new house, and the gold that came by sea, before the queen of Sheba arrives in chapter 9.

The message. God kept his word to Solomon: his kingdom was secure, his building finished, and above all the worship of God set running exactly as God’s word required, “according to the commandment of Moses” and the arrangements of David. Yet the chapter also lets cracks show, a subject people pressed into forced labour and a foreign marriage the law had forbidden, so that even at its height the kingdom is not the kingdom God’s people were waiting for.

Why it was said. The first readers had little power and no gold, but they did have an altar and the law of Moses, and they had rebuilt their worship on the same double pattern, Moses for what was offered and David for who served (Ezra 3:2, 10; see the introduction). The chapter told them that the lasting achievement of Solomon’s reign was not the cities or the fleet, but the faithful worship they still had.

How the chapter makes its case. First the building beyond the temple: cities rebuilt and settled, a campaign in the north, store cities and chariot cities, and Beth-horon fortified (vv. 1–6). Then the workforce: the Canaanite remnant pressed into forced labour, while Israelites served as soldiers and officers (vv. 7–10). Then Pharaoh’s daughter moved out of David’s city because the places the ark had been were holy (v. 11). Then the heart of the chapter: daily, weekly, monthly and yearly offerings according to Moses, and priests, Levites and gatekeepers according to David, with nobody turning aside (vv. 12–16). Last, a fleet crewed with Hiram’s sailors brings gold from Ophir (vv. 17–18).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. Solomon’s kingdom stood on a heavy yoke, and his son would lose ten tribes over it (10:4). The greater Son of David “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), and says, “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). Solomon’s marriage to Pharaoh’s daughter would help turn his heart away; Christ loved his bride, the church, and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). And the worship ordered by Moses and David finds its fulfilment in him, the priest and sacrifice to whom every offering pointed.

For us. The most lasting thing a generation can build is not wealth or influence but faithful worship that keeps on after the builders are gone. Order your life and your church by God’s word, not by fashion. And watch the place where, like Solomon, you are careful about outward holiness while compromising where it matters most.
8.theology:
Verses 13 and 14 name two authorities and rank neither: the commandment of Moses governs what is offered, the ruling of David who offers it. God revealed the one, David worked out the other in obedience to it, and the Chronicler treats both as binding.

And verse 11 shows devotion applied at the wrong point. Solomon is careful about where his Egyptian wife lives, but care in that small matter is no protection when the large one, the marriage itself, was already wrong.

The two authorities of verses 13 and 14 meet in one person. Christ is the prophet like Moses (Acts 3:22) and the Son of David, and he is the high priest whose single offering ended the daily round of verse 13 (Hebrews 10:11–14). The worship Moses ordered and David staffed was a copy and shadow of the heavenly things (Hebrews 8:5), and he is the reality it copied.
8.examples:
The richest king in the nation's history walled towns a woman named Sheerah had founded generations before. Most of what any of us build stands on someone else's forgotten work.

Keeping a good arrangement running for a generation is harder than setting it up, and far less interesting to write about. Verse 15 thinks it worth recording, and so should any church that has faithful people turning up in the right week, year after year.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Twenty Years, and What He Built
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gave Solomon a secure and prosperous kingdom, yet the record shows its cost and one fault that would grow. After twenty years spent on the two houses (v. 1), he rebuilds the cities Hiram had given and settles Israelites there (v. 2), takes Hamath-zobah, and builds Tadmor in the wilderness and the store cities in Hamath (vv. 3–4). He fortifies Upper and Lower Beth-horon and builds store cities, chariot cities and “whatever Solomon desired to build” (vv. 5–6). The Canaanite remnant is drafted as forced labour, while no Israelite is made a slave (vv. 7–10). And Pharaoh’s daughter is moved out of David’s city, because the places the ark had come to are holy (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 11 is the only place the Chronicler lets us hear Solomon reason about his Egyptian wife, and what he reasons about is her address, not the marriage.
verseByVerse.examples: The chief officers were Israelites; the burden fell on others, and the next reign will show how heavily it was felt.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the house of the LORD and his own house, Solomon rebuilt the cities that Hiram had given to him, and settled the people of Israel in them. And Solomon went to Hamath-zobah and took it. He built Tadmor in the wilderness and all the store cities that he built in Hamath. He also built Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon, fortified cities with walls, gates, and bars, and Baalath, and all the store cities that Solomon had and all the cities for his chariots and the cities for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having finished God’s house and his own, Solomon built and fortified cities throughout his kingdom, securing its borders and its trade. God’s promise of peace and prosperity (1:12) was being kept.

At the end of twenty years. Kings divides the total: seven years on God’s house and thirteen on his own (1 Kings 6:38; 7:1). Chronicles gives the sum and does not do the subtraction for anybody.

The cities that Hiram had given to him. This reads oddly beside Kings, where Solomon gives Hiram twenty towns in Galilee and Hiram, unimpressed, calls the district Cabul (1 Kings 9:11–13). The likeliest explanation is that Hiram handed them back, and that Chronicles describes what Solomon did with them afterwards: he rebuilt them and settled Israelites there. It cannot be proved, and nothing turns on it.

Hamath-zobah … Tadmor in the wilderness. This is the only military campaign recorded in Solomon’s reign, in the far north, in the region of the Aramean kingdoms David had subdued (1 Chronicles 18:3). The building list is that of a man securing a trade empire: Tadmor in the desert on the caravan road, store cities in Hamath, chariot cities, and “whatever Solomon desired to build”.

Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon. The two Beth-horons already existed, and 1 Chronicles says who founded them: “His daughter was Sheerah, who built both Lower and Upper Beth-horon” (1 Chronicles 7:24), a woman of the tribe of Ephraim and one of the very few people in nine chapters of genealogy credited with building anything. She put them on the ridge guarding the pass up from the coastal plain, and centuries later the wealthiest king Israel ever had walled what she started, because she had chosen the right hill. Faithful work done long ago, by people history barely names, is still holding up what God’s people build today.

A kingdom at rest. Solomon’s name means peace, and his reign was the high point of Israel’s power. But the peace rested on fortresses and chariot cities. The Son of David whose kingdom has no end is the “Prince of Peace”, and “of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end” (Isaiah 9:6–7); his peace rests not on walls but on his blood (Colossians 1:20).

Uncertain wording. Where Chronicles has Tadmor, the Hebrew text of Kings reads Tamar, and adds “in the land of Judah” (1 Kings 9:18). Tadmor is the great desert oasis later called Palmyra, far to the north-east of Damascus; Tamar was a place in the south of Judah. The names are very similar, and either Chronicles names a different, more northerly city, or one name has been read for the other. “Hamath-zobah” occurs only here and probably names the territory where the old kingdoms of Hamath and Zobah met.

verseByVerse.quote: All the people who were left of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of Israel, from their descendants who were left after them in the land, whom the people of Israel had not destroyed—these Solomon drafted as forced labor, and so they are to this day. But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves for his work; they were soldiers, and his officers, the commanders of his chariots, and his horsemen. And these were the chief officers of King Solomon, 250, who exercised authority over the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon put the surviving Canaanite peoples to forced labour, but made no Israelites slaves; Israelites served as his soldiers and officers. The Chronicler records it as a fact of the reign, not as a policy he defends.

Drafted as forced labor, and so they are to this day. The remnant of the Canaanite peoples, whom Israel had not driven out, were conscripted, a subject population put to work, described without apology and still the case when the source was written. Israelites commanded; the residents who were not Israelites carried.

But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves. There is a difficulty here, and it should be named. Kings says Solomon “drafted forced labor out of all Israel, and the draft numbered 30,000 men”, sent to Lebanon in shifts, a month away and two months at home (1 Kings 5:13–14). The usual reading is that this was a rotating obligation of a few months a year, not the permanent servitude the Canaanites were put under. The reader troubled by it is not being unreasonable, and should know that when Solomon’s son comes to the throne the northern tribes will say, “Your father made our yoke heavy”, and the man in charge of the forced labour will be stoned to death (10:4, 18).

250, who exercised authority over the people. Kings gives 550 chief officers (1 Kings 9:23). But Kings also counts 3,300 foremen (1 Kings 5:16) where Chronicles counts 3,600 (2:18), and both totals come to 3,850. The two books seem to divide the same body of supervisors differently, perhaps Israelite and Canaanite officers, and the agreement of the totals suggests careful records behind both.

A different yoke. Even Israel’s best king built his kingdom on other men’s backs. The King whose kingdom lasts carried the load himself: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). His invitation to the weary is the opposite of Solomon’s levy: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29).

For those who lead. Anyone with authority, in a business, a family or a church, can get great things done by laying heavy burdens on others. The Chronicler does not hide what it cost Solomon’s house. Christian leaders are to lead as servants (Mark 10:42–44), and to ask not only what got built but what it cost the people who built it.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon brought Pharaoh's daughter up from the city of David to the house that he had built for her, for he said, "My wife shall not live in the house of David king of Israel, for the places to which the ark of the LORD has come are holy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon moved his Egyptian wife out of David’s city because the places the ark had been were holy: careful about holiness at the one point where care could not help him.

Solomon brought Pharaoh’s daughter up from the city of David. Kings records the move in half a sentence (1 Kings 9:24; compare 3:1). Chronicles gives the reasoning, and it is scrupulous: ground the ark has occupied is holy, so his Egyptian wife will live somewhere else. He has thought about it carefully, and missed the point.

The real question. The question the verse raises is not where she should live. Israel’s law had warned against marriages with the surrounding nations and forbidden a king to multiply wives, “lest his heart turn away” (Deuteronomy 7:3–4; 17:17), because they would turn his heart to other gods. The devout care in this verse is being exercised about a marriage that should not have existed.

What this book leaves out. Here is the largest thing the Chronicler omits. He has nothing from 1 Kings 11: no seven hundred wives, no high places for Chemosh and Molech, no sentence that the kingdom would be torn away; he ends Solomon’s reign with him sleeping with his fathers (9:31). He does not conceal it. In the next chapters he names “the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite” and says the division was “brought about by God” to fulfil that word (9:29; 10:15), and any reader who wants to know why Ahijah said it must open the other book (see the introduction). His subject is the temple and the throne rather than the man, and this verse gives one glimpse of the trouble.

A bride made holy. Solomon kept his foreign wife at a distance from the holy places because she could not be made fit for them. Christ does the opposite with his bride: he takes a people from every nation, unfit by nature, and makes them holy by his own self-giving, “that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27).

What it does not mean. Not that Egyptians, or any foreigners, are unclean; Solomon has just prayed for the foreigner (6:32–33), and Ruth the Moabitess was David’s great-grandmother. The law’s concern was faith, not race: marriage to someone who served other gods would turn the heart (1 Kings 11:2). Christians are likewise to marry “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). And the warning is wider: it is possible to be scrupulous about outward holiness while making peace with the very thing that is drawing the heart away.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–18 — According to Moses, According to David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The crowning work of Solomon’s reign was worship ordered by God’s word and kept faithfully. He offers burnt offerings on the altar he built, as each day, Sabbath, new moon and annual feast required “according to the commandment of Moses” (vv. 12–13). He appoints the priests, Levites and gatekeepers in their divisions “according to the ruling of David his father”, “the man of God” (v. 14), and nobody turns aside from what the king commanded (v. 15). So the work on the house of the LORD is completed (v. 16). Last, Solomon goes to Ezion-geber on the Red Sea, and with ships and sailors sent by Hiram brings 450 talents of gold from Ophir (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: David is called by a title Scripture otherwise gives to Moses, the man of God, because his ordering of worship served what Moses had received.
verseByVerse.examples: Steady faithfulness in ordinary duties is not dull. Verse 15 treats it as a triumph.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon offered up burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar of the LORD that he had built before the vestibule, as the duty of each day required, offering according to the commandment of Moses for the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the three annual feasts—the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Booths. According to the ruling of David his father, he appointed the divisions of the priests for their service, and the Levites for their offices of praise and ministry before the priests as the duty of each day required, and the gatekeepers in their divisions at each gate, for so David the man of God had commanded. And they did not turn aside from what the king had commanded the priests and Levites concerning any matter and concerning the treasuries. Thus was accomplished all the work of Solomon from the day the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid until it was finished. So the house of the LORD was completed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon set the temple’s worship running as God’s word required: the offerings according to Moses, and the priests, Levites and gatekeepers according to David, and nobody turned aside. This, not the cities or the gold, was his lasting work.

As the duty of each day required. The burnt offerings follow the law’s calendar: every day, on Sabbaths and new moons, and at the three pilgrim feasts, the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of Booths (Exodus 23:14–17; Numbers 28–29). What is offered, and when, comes from the law of Moses. Nothing here is Solomon’s invention.

According to the ruling of David his father. The rotas are David’s: twenty-four divisions of priests, twenty-four of singers, and the gatekeepers whose gates were assigned by lot, “small and great alike” (1 Chronicles 26:13), all set up by an old man for a building he never entered, and all of it running. Here alone in Chronicles David is called “the man of God”, a title usually given to prophets and to Moses: his ordering of worship carried God’s authority (1 Chronicles 28:19).

The same pattern after the exile. The Chronicler’s readers knew this double pattern because it was theirs. When the exiles rebuilt the altar, they offered burnt offerings “as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God” (Ezra 3:2), and when the foundation was laid the priests and Levites took their places “according to the directions of David king of Israel” (Ezra 3:10).

They did not turn aside. Verse 15 is a small sentence about a large achievement. Nobody drifted. Years after the lots were drawn, the men were still turning up in the right week, and the treasuries were still being kept. Faithfulness in worship is mostly showing up, again and again, doing what God has asked. That is why the Chronicler mentions it.

The end of the daily offering. The sacrifices Solomon set running were offered every day because none of them could finish the work. They pointed to Christ, who “has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily” but did this “once for all when he offered up himself” (Hebrews 7:27). The Christian’s daily offering now is not a burnt offering but thanks and a life given back to God (Romans 12:1; Hebrews 13:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon went to Ezion-geber and Eloth on the shore of the sea, in the land of Edom. And Hiram sent to him by the hand of his servants ships and servants familiar with the sea, and they went to Ophir together with the servants of Solomon and brought from there 450 talents of gold and brought it to King Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With ships and sailors sent by Hiram, Solomon’s men sailed from Ezion-geber to Ophir and brought back a great fortune in gold. God’s promise of riches (1:12) was being kept, and the next chapter shows what so much gold could do.

Ezion-geber and Eloth on the shore of the sea. The chapter ends at sea. Ezion-geber lay at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, the arm of the Red Sea, in Edomite territory that David had conquered, and gave Israel a harbour opening on the trade routes to Arabia and beyond. A later king of Judah would build ships there too, and see them wrecked (20:36–37).

Hiram sent to him … ships and servants familiar with the sea. Israel was not a seafaring people, and the arrangement is the same as with the timber: the Phoenicians knew how, and Solomon hired them and sent his own men along to learn. Kings says Solomon built the fleet at Ezion-geber and Hiram sent the seamen (1 Kings 9:26–27); Chronicles says Hiram sent ships. Hiram may have supplied ships’ timbers and shipwrights, or vessels taken overland in sections; either way the skill was Phoenician.

450 talents of gold. Kings says 420 (1 Kings 9:28), perhaps a copying slip in one of them, since numbers were easily miscopied (see the introduction); no one can be sure. Either way it was an enormous sum, many tonnes of gold (see Talent) arriving from a single voyage, and the next chapter is about what happens to a kingdom when gold starts coming in faster than anybody can count it.

Gold of Ophir. Ophir’s gold was proverbial (Job 28:16). A royal wedding psalm pictures the king’s bride standing at his right hand “in gold of Ophir” (Psalm 45:9), and Hebrews applies that psalm to the Son of God: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever” (Hebrews 1:8). Solomon’s gold is gone; the bride of Christ will be clothed in splendour that does not tarnish (Revelation 19:7–8). So “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys” (Matthew 6:20).

Uncertain wording. Where Ophir was is not known. Southern Arabia, the Horn of Africa and India have all been proposed. What is certain is that it was far away, reached by sea from the Red Sea, and famous for its gold.
verseByVerse.note: Ezion-geber and Eloth lay at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba. A talent was about 75 pounds (ESV note).

keyVerse.quote: According to the ruling of David his father, he appointed the divisions of the priests for their service, and the Levites for their offices of praise and ministry before the priests as the duty of each day required, and the gatekeepers in their divisions at each gate, for so David the man of God had commanded.
keyVerse.note: For the Chronicler the crowning work of Solomon’s reign was not his cities or his gold but worship set running as God had directed, through Moses and through David. It was this pattern that the returned exiles rebuilt, and it points to Christ, the priest and sacrifice in whom all that worship was fulfilled.

8.reflection:
Solomon’s twenty years of building included fortresses, store cities and a fleet, yet the Chronicler gives most weight to the ordering of worship (vv. 12–16). What do you think God counts as the lasting achievements of a life or of a church?

Solomon’s kingdom rested partly on forced labour, and it later cost his son ten tribes (vv. 7–10; 10:4). How does Jesus’ way of leading (Mark 10:42–45; Matthew 11:28–30) challenge the way we use authority at home, at work or in church?

Solomon was careful to keep Pharaoh’s daughter away from the holy places, but the marriage itself went against God’s law (v. 11). Where might we be careful about outward religion while compromising in something that is drawing our hearts away?

“They did not turn aside” (v. 15): the worship went on faithfully, week after week. What helps you keep going in the ordinary, repeated work of following Christ and serving his church when it is unspectacular?

9.title: Something Greater Than Solomon Is Here
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon, she came to Jerusalem to test him with hard questions, having a very great retinue and camels bearing spices and very much gold and precious stones. And when she came to Solomon, she told him all that was on her mind.<sup>2</sup>And Solomon answered all her questions. There was nothing hidden from Solomon that he could not explain to her.<sup>3</sup>And when the queen of Sheba had seen the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built,<sup>4</sup>the food of his table, the seating of his officials, and the attendance of his servants, and their clothing, his cupbearers, and their clothing, and his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of the LORD, there was no more breath in her.<sup>5</sup>And she said to the king, "The report was true that I heard in my own land of your words and of your wisdom,<sup>6</sup>but I did not believe the reports until I came and my own eyes had seen it. And behold, half the greatness of your wisdom was not told me; you surpass the report that I heard.<sup>7</sup>Happy are your men! Happy are these your servants, who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom!<sup>8</sup>Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on his throne as king for the LORD your God! Because your God loved Israel and would establish them forever, he has made you king over them, that you may execute justice and righteousness."<sup>9</sup>Then she gave the king 120 talents of gold, and a very great quantity of spices, and precious stones. There were no spices such as those that the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.<sup>10</sup>Moreover, the servants of Hiram and the servants of Solomon, who brought gold from Ophir, brought algum wood and precious stones.<sup>11</sup>And the king made from the algum wood supports for the house of the LORD and for the king's house, lyres also and harps for the singers. There never was seen the like of them before in the land of Judah.<sup>12</sup>And King Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all that she desired, whatever she asked besides what she had brought to the king. So she turned and went back to her own land with her servants.<sup>13</sup>Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold,<sup>14</sup>besides that which the explorers and merchants brought. And all the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land brought gold and silver to Solomon.<sup>15</sup>King Solomon made 200 large shields of beaten gold; 600 shekels of beaten gold went into each shield.<sup>16</sup>And he made 300 shields of beaten gold; 300 shekels of gold went into each shield; and the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.<sup>17</sup>The king also made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with pure gold.<sup>18</sup>The throne had six steps and a footstool of gold, which were attached to the throne, and on each side of the seat were armrests and two lions standing beside the armrests,<sup>19</sup>while twelve lions stood there, one on each end of a step on the six steps. Nothing like it was ever made for any kingdom.<sup>20</sup>All King Solomon's drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. Silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon.<sup>21</sup>For the king's ships went to Tarshish with the servants of Hiram. Once every three years the ships of Tarshish used to come bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.<sup>22</sup>Thus King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom.<sup>23</sup>And all the kings of the earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom, which God had put into his mind.<sup>24</sup>Every one of them brought his present, articles of silver and of gold, garments, myrrh, spices, horses, and mules, so much year by year.<sup>25</sup>And Solomon had 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots, and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.<sup>26</sup>And he ruled over all the kings from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt.<sup>27</sup>And the king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah.<sup>28</sup>And horses were imported for Solomon from Egypt and from all lands.<sup>29</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, from first to last, are they not written in the history of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam the son of Nebat?<sup>30</sup>Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years.<sup>31</sup>And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father, and Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.
9.overview:
Where we are. The temple stands, filled with glory, and God has answered Solomon’s prayer with the promise of 7:14 and a warning about what forsaking him would cost (7:17–22). Chapter 8 recorded the rest of Solomon’s building and trade. This chapter closes his reign and the first part of the book (chapters 1–9).

The message. God made Solomon’s kingdom a window through which the nations could see the God of Israel: a foreign queen looks through it and blesses the LORD who loves his people and gave them a king to do justice. Yet the same chapter quietly lets the reader watch the gifts turn into hoards of gold, wives and Egyptian horses, the three things the law told a king not to multiply. The glory was real, and it was not final. Israel still needed a better king.

Why it was said. The first readers were few, poor and ruled by Persia, with a plain temple and no king (see the introduction). This chapter reminds them what God once did through David’s son, that their God can be known and praised far beyond their small province, and that wealth was never the measure of his blessing.

How the chapter makes its case. First the queen of Sheba (vv. 1–12): she comes to test Solomon, is answered, is left breathless by his worship, and confesses that God set him on his throne because he loved Israel. Then the gold (vv. 13–21): 666 talents a year, golden shields, an ivory throne guarded by lions, and silver counted as nothing. Last the summary (vv. 22–31): kings from everywhere seek his wisdom, the reign ends with the same horses from Egypt it began with, and Solomon is buried without a verdict, while the sources point to the prophet who would give ten tribes to Jeroboam.

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. Jesus said that the queen of the South “came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). Wise men from the east would bring him gold and myrrh as a child (Matthew 2:11), and the nations will bring their glory into his city (Revelation 21:24). But where Solomon gathered riches for himself, Christ “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9), and the Lion of Judah takes his throne as a Lamb that was slain (Revelation 5:5–6).

For us. The queen travelled fifteen hundred miles on a rumour; we have the King himself in the gospel, and on the day we see him we will say that the half was not told us. Meanwhile Solomon warns every believer that blessing can be received gratefully and then quietly hoarded. Hold God’s gifts with open hands, and let the people who watch your life see, last of all and above all, your worship.
9.theology:
The law of the king in Deuteronomy 17 forbids a king to pile up three things, horses, wives, and silver and gold, and this chapter reports the third as splendour (see vv. 13-16). Against that stands verse 8, where a foreign queen states Israel's monarchy correctly. Twice in this book the meaning of the throne is put most clearly by outsiders.

Against all three stands the King who kept the law of the king. He had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), refused the kingdoms of the world when they were offered (Matthew 4:8–10), and came to his city humble and mounted on a donkey rather than a chariot (Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 21:5). Isaiah saw the nations streaming to Zion, all those from Sheba shall come. They shall bring gold and frankincense (Isaiah 60:6), and many Christians have seen a first glimpse of it in the magi who knelt before the child in Bethlehem with gold and frankincense (Matthew 2:11).
9.examples:
The queen envied the servants rather than the king. The people nearest a good thing are usually the last to notice they have it, and that is as true of a church's ordinary members as of Solomon's servants.

Five hundred shields of beaten gold hung in a hall built to display them, and within a few years of his death an Egyptian army carried them off. What is stored up for display is the easiest thing to lose (Matthew 6:19–20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon’s God-given wisdom draws a foreign queen to Jerusalem, and she leaves blessing the LORD. She comes with camels, spices and gold to test him with hard questions, and nothing is hidden from him (vv. 1–2). Then she looks, from the wisdom and the house to the cupbearers and, last of all, the burnt offerings, and there is no more breath in her (vv. 3–4). She admits that the half had not been told her (vv. 5–7) and blesses Israel’s God, who set Solomon on his throne because he loved Israel (v. 8). She gives 120 talents of gold and spices, Solomon turns the trade in rare wood into music for the temple, and she goes home with all she desired (vv. 9–12).
verseByVerse.theology: She had come to test a reputation for cleverness, and what took her breath away was watching him worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Outsiders sometimes see what insiders have stopped noticing. A foreign monarch, for the second time in this book, describes Israel's throne better than most Israelites did.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon, she came to Jerusalem to test him with hard questions, having a very great retinue and camels bearing spices and very much gold and precious stones. And when she came to Solomon, she told him all that was on her mind. And Solomon answered all her questions. There was nothing hidden from Solomon that he could not explain to her. And when the queen of Sheba had seen the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built, the food of his table, the seating of his officials, and the attendance of his servants, and their clothing, his cupbearers, and their clothing, and his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of the LORD, there was no more breath in her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A foreign queen came to test Solomon’s fame, had every question answered, and was left breathless, last of all, by his worship.
