To test him with hard questions. Sheba lay in south-west Arabia, some fifteen hundred miles away. The word for hard questions is the one used for riddles: a contest of the kind courts held, to find out whether a rival’s reputation was exaggerated.

Had seen the wisdom of Solomon. Then she stops asking and starts looking, and the Chronicler lists what she saw, in order, down to the cupbearers’ clothing.

There was no more breath in her. The last item is worship, and there the sentence breaks off. The buildings and uniforms impressed her; the king going up to the house of God left her breathless. The best thing a believer’s life can show a curious visitor is not its comforts but its God.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 4 can be read as his burnt offerings that he offered or as the ascent by which he went up to the house of the LORD, perhaps a stairway from palace to temple. The ESV takes the first, as in 1 Kings 10:5. Either way the list ends with the king at the house of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And she said to the king, "The report was true that I heard in my own land of your words and of your wisdom, but I did not believe the reports until I came and my own eyes had seen it. And behold, half the greatness of your wisdom was not told me; you surpass the report that I heard. Happy are your men! Happy are these your servants, who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom! Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on his throne as king for the LORD your God! Because your God loved Israel and would establish them forever, he has made you king over them, that you may execute justice and righteousness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The queen confessed that the report fell short of the truth, and then said what Israel’s kings were for better than most Israelites did: the throne was God’s, given out of love for his people, for justice. She came to catch out an exaggeration and found an understatement.

Happy are these your servants. She calls happy not the king but those who stand in his room every day and listen: the real privilege is to be near wisdom.

Set you on his throne. His throne: not Solomon’s; the chair belongs to God, as the previous book said when Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD (1 Chronicles 29:23). As king for the LORD: held on someone else’s behalf. Because your God loved Israel: the king exists because of God’s affection for the people, as Hiram of Tyre had written (2:11). And that you may execute justice and righteousness: the pair that measured David and will measure every king after him.

A pagan queen’s theology. A queen from the far end of Arabia states the theology of Israel’s monarchy in one sentence. Readers under a Persian governor, wondering whether their God was known beyond their province, are shown that he can be.

Something greater than Solomon. Centuries later Jesus told a crowd, “The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). She crossed a desert on a report; they had wisdom itself in front of them and would not cross the street. The truly happy servants are those who hear Christ’s words, and when “your eyes will behold the king in his beauty” (Isaiah 33:17), their verdict will be hers: the half was not told me.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she gave the king 120 talents of gold, and a very great quantity of spices, and precious stones. There were no spices such as those that the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon. Moreover, the servants of Hiram and the servants of Solomon, who brought gold from Ophir, brought algum wood and precious stones. And the king made from the algum wood supports for the house of the LORD and for the king's house, lyres also and harps for the singers. There never was seen the like of them before in the land of Judah. And King Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all that she desired, whatever she asked besides what she had brought to the king. So she turned and went back to her own land with her servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gifts flowed both ways: trade became music for God’s house, and the queen went home with all she asked, as Solomon had prayed God would do for the foreigner.

120 talents of gold. A hundred and twenty talents of gold and unmatched spices: trade between Jerusalem and southern Arabia is being opened, and both parties know it.

Lyres also and harps for the singers. Solomon makes the rare algum wood into instruments: the trade empire feeds the temple’s music. His father had made instruments for the same purpose (1 Chronicles 23:5); the son buys the wood by the shipload.

All that she desired. She gave much and received more, which is exactly what Solomon had prayed at the dedication that God would do for any foreigner who came from a far country for the sake of his name (6:32–33).

Uncertain wording. No one now knows what tree algum was (1 Kings 10:11–12 spells it almug; 2:8 has it from Lebanon). Suggestions include red sandalwood and juniper. It was clearly rare, costly and fine enough for instruments.
verseByVerse.note: 120 talents of gold is about 4½ tons (a talent was about 75 pounds, ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Gold, and the Law of the King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon’s wealth outstrips every kingdom, and readers who know the law of the king will see what the Chronicler does not need to say. The annual revenue is 666 talents of gold, besides trade and tribute (vv. 13–14). Five hundred shields of beaten gold hang in the House of the Forest of Lebanon, ornaments an Egyptian army will one day carry off (vv. 15–16). An ivory throne with six steps and twelve lions is built, and nothing like it was made for any kingdom (vv. 17–19). Silver is counted as nothing, and every three years the fleet returns with gold, ivory, apes and peacocks (vv. 20–21). Deuteronomy 17 had told a king not to multiply gold.
verseByVerse.theology: The splendour is real, and so is the warning in Deuteronomy that a king should not heap up silver and gold.
verseByVerse.examples: Three chapters from now Rehoboam will replace these gold shields with bronze replicas and put a guard on them: the outward show kept up after the substance has gone.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold, besides that which the explorers and merchants brought. And all the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land brought gold and silver to Solomon. King Solomon made 200 large shields of beaten gold; 600 shekels of beaten gold went into each shield. And he made 300 shields of beaten gold; 300 shekels of gold went into each shield; and the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gold poured in beyond counting, and the Chronicler lets readers who knew the law of the king notice that this was one of the things a king must not heap up.

666 talents of gold. About twenty-five tons of gold a year, before trade income. Readers have long linked the number with Revelation 13:18, but nothing in either passage connects them beyond the number.

What the law forbade. A king of Israel was not to pile up three things: horses, especially by sending the people back to Egypt for them; wives, lest his heart turn away; and silver and gold (Deuteronomy 17:16–17). Chapter 1 ended with the Egyptian horses (1:16–17); the wives are in Kings (1 Kings 11:1–8); here, closing the reign, is the gold. The Chronicler adds no comment, assuming his reader has Deuteronomy. He shows a man who received wisdom as a gift and riches as a bonus (1:11–12), piling up the very three things the law had named.

200 large shields of beaten gold. Ceremonial shields, since gold is too soft to fight with. In the fifth year of Solomon’s son an Egyptian army will take every one of them (12:9).

When gifts become hoards. The riches were God’s good gift; the danger lay in what a heart does with more than enough. Plenty tests us more quietly than want, which is why the wise man prayed, “give me neither poverty nor riches” (Proverbs 30:8).

verseByVerse.quote: The king also made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with pure gold. The throne had six steps and a footstool of gold, which were attached to the throne, and on each side of the seat were armrests and two lions standing beside the armrests, while twelve lions stood there, one on each end of a step on the six steps. Nothing like it was ever made for any kingdom. All King Solomon's drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. Silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon. For the king's ships went to Tarshish with the servants of Hiram. Once every three years the ships of Tarshish used to come bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The throne guarded by lions and a court where silver counted for nothing told every visitor who ruled here.

The lions of Judah. The throne gets more detail than anything else Solomon owned: ivory and gold, six steps, and fourteen lions, with a man climbing above them. The lion is Judah’s animal (Jacob called Judah a lion’s cub and said the sceptre would not depart from him, Genesis 49:9–10), and the arrangement says what a throne room is for: everyone who came in had to look up. The New Testament gives the lion’s title to one king only, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, who turns out, when John looks, to be a Lamb that had been slain (Revelation 5:5–6). Solomon climbed to his throne; Christ reached his by going down.

Silver was not considered as anything. Silver, other nations’ money, was beneath notice in Jerusalem.

Ivory, apes, and peacocks. These cargoes are curiosities, what a court buys when it has nothing left to want.

Uncertain wording. The word translated peacocks occurs only here and in 1 Kings 10:22. Older translations took it as peacocks; some scholars suggest baboons. Either way they are rare animals for display.
verseByVerse.note: Ships of Tarshish were large ocean-going vessels. Kings speaks of ships of Tarshish; Chronicles says the ships went to Tarshish, probably using the name loosely for distant voyages.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–31 — The Reign Ends Where It Began
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The greatest reign in Israel’s history closes with its gifts intact and its dangers unchanged. Solomon excels all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom, and they come to hear the wisdom God put into his mind, bringing tribute that includes horses (vv. 22–24). Then the paragraph of chapter 1 returns almost word for word: the stables and horsemen, dominion from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt, silver as common as stone, and horses from Egypt (vv. 25–28). The sources are named, two of them about Jeroboam, and forty years end with a burial and no verdict (vv. 29–31).
verseByVerse.theology: God gave Solomon wisdom first and riches as an addition. Verse 22 names riches first: the gifts God gives can quietly change places in a life without anyone saying so.
verseByVerse.examples: The Chronicler's silence over Solomon's grave is not cruelty; it leaves judgment to God and sends the reader to what God has promised David's line.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom. And all the kings of the earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom, which God had put into his mind. Every one of them brought his present, articles of silver and of gold, garments, myrrh, spices, horses, and mules, so much year by year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every king on earth came to hear Solomon, but the summary now names his riches before his wisdom, and the tribute includes horses.

In riches and in wisdom. At Gibeon God gave wisdom first and riches added (1:12). Here riches come first. The Chronicler makes no accusation, and the order may mean nothing. But the two nouns have swapped places, and the man God commended for not asking for wealth is now summed up by it.

Which God had put into his mind. All the kings of the earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom, which God had put into his mind: even in a verse about his fame, the wisdom is God’s gift.

Horses, and mules. Horses arrive every year, though the law told the king not to multiply them.

Even Solomon in all his glory. Jesus set this splendour beside a wild flower, “even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these” (Matthew 6:29), to free his hearers from anxious striving: seek first the kingdom, and these things will be added (Matthew 6:33), the order God set before Solomon at Gibeon.

verseByVerse.quote: And Solomon had 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots, and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem. And he ruled over all the kings from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt. And the king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah. And horses were imported for Solomon from Egypt and from all lands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reign ends where it began, with horses from Egypt, and with Israel holding, for the only time, the whole land promised to Abraham.

The same paragraph twice. These verses repeat 1:14–17 almost word for word. Forty years lie between: a temple filled with fire, a queen answered, tribute from every court. Yet the horses were still coming from Egypt.

From the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines. In between sits verse 26: he ruled over all the kings from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt. That is the territory God described to Abraham (Genesis 15:18). Israel held it once, under this man, and never again; the next chapter shows how quickly a kingdom can lose what God has given.

4,000 stalls for horses. Chronicles has 4,000 stalls; 1 Kings 4:26 has 40,000, most likely a copying slip there (see the introduction).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, from first to last, are they not written in the history of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam the son of Nebat? Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years. And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father, and Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon is buried with no verdict spoken, and the sources named include two that tell of the man who will take ten tribes from his son.

The prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite. Ahijah is the prophet who met Jeroboam on a road outside Jerusalem, tore a new cloak into twelve pieces and told him to take ten, because Solomon had forsaken God and bowed down to Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom (1 Kings 11:29–33). Iddo’s visions concern Jeroboam by name. The Chronicler knows the story; he tells you where it is written down.

No verdict on Solomon. This book explained Saul’s death and gave David a good old age, but says nothing in assessment of the temple builder. The silence is neither neutral nor an attack: it is what a careful historian does when the full account is in another book. The house stands, the promise of chapter 7 has been given with its condition attached, and the man is buried without a word said over him.

Waiting for a greater son. Solomon came closer than any king to what God promised David, yet he died and his kingdom split. The throne established forever (1 Chronicles 17:12–14) waited for the Son of David whom death could not hold, of whom Peter said that David “foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ” (Acts 2:31).

Are the histories of Nathan, Ahijah and Iddo lost Scripture? They were prophets’ records the inspired writer drew on (the first names Nathan), as Luke drew on earlier accounts (Luke 1:1–3). Not every writing of a prophet was given to be Scripture, and God has preserved all of his word that he meant the church to have (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

Was Solomon saved? Chronicles is silent about his later sins; Kings says his heart was turned away (1 Kings 11:4). Scripture does not say whether he repented, and we should not claim more than it says.

keyVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on his throne as king for the LORD your God! Because your God loved Israel and would establish them forever, he has made you king over them, that you may execute justice and righteousness.
keyVerse.note: A foreign queen states the meaning of Israel’s kingship more clearly than anyone in the chapter: the throne is God’s, the king rules on his behalf, he is given out of God’s love for his people, and his task is justice. Every king after Solomon will be measured by this, and only the Son of David who reigns forever fills it completely.

9.reflection:
The queen of Sheba came a very long way to test what she had heard, and what finally took her breath away was Solomon’s worship (v. 4). What do visitors to your home or your church see last and most? What would you want them to see?

She called happy the servants who stood before Solomon every day and heard his wisdom (v. 7). Jesus said that something greater than Solomon is here (Matthew 12:42). How do you value the daily privilege of hearing Christ’s word, and what tends to crowd it out?

The chapter quietly shows Solomon multiplying gold and horses, the things Deuteronomy 17:16–17 warned a king against. Why is prosperity often more dangerous to faith than hardship? Where might God’s good gifts be turning into hoards in your life?

Solomon is buried without a verdict, and his kingdom splits in the next chapter. How does his story make you long for a better king, and what does Christ’s becoming poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9) show about how he is better?

10.title: The Folly of Rehoboam
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king.<sup>2</sup>And as soon as Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon), then Jeroboam returned from Egypt.<sup>3</sup>And they sent and called him. And Jeroboam and all Israel came and said to Rehoboam,<sup>4</sup>"Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you."<sup>5</sup>He said to them, "Come to me again in three days." So the people went away.<sup>6</sup>Then King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men, who had stood before Solomon his father while he was yet alive, saying, "How do you advise me to answer this people?"<sup>7</sup>And they said to him, "If you will be good to this people and please them and speak good words to them, then they will be your servants forever."<sup>8</sup>But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him, and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him and stood before him.<sup>9</sup>And he said to them, "What do you advise that we answer this people who have said to me, 'Lighten the yoke that your father put on us'?"<sup>10</sup>And the young men who had grown up with him said to him, "Thus shall you speak to the people who said to you, 'Your father made our yoke heavy, but you lighten it for us'; thus shall you say to them, 'My little finger is thicker than my father's thighs.<sup>11</sup>And now, whereas my father laid on you a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.'"<sup>12</sup>So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king said, "Come to me again the third day."<sup>13</sup>And the king answered them harshly; and forsaking the counsel of the old men,<sup>14</sup>King Rehoboam spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, "My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to it. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions."<sup>15</sup>So the king did not listen to the people, for it was a turn of affairs brought about by God that the LORD might fulfill his word, which he spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.<sup>16</sup>And when all Israel saw that the king did not listen to them, the people answered the king, "What portion have we in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. Each of you to your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, David." So all Israel went to their tents.<sup>17</sup>But Rehoboam reigned over the people of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah.<sup>18</sup>Then King Rehoboam sent Hadoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and the people of Israel stoned him to death with stones. And King Rehoboam quickly mounted his chariot to flee to Jerusalem.<sup>19</sup>So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day.
10.overview:
Where we are. Solomon has been buried without a verdict, and the sources named at his death pointed to Ahijah’s prophecy about Jeroboam (9:29–31). Now the second and longer part of the book begins: the kings of Judah, from the split of the kingdom to the exile (chapters 10–36).

The message. A king who will not serve loses the people he wants to rule. Rehoboam is told that if he will be good to his people they will serve him forever, and he chooses threats instead. Yet the Chronicler adds that this was “a turn of affairs brought about by God”: the young king is wholly to blame, and God is wholly in charge, keeping the word he had spoken.

Why it was said. The first readers lived with the long result of this day. The northern kingdom had been gone for three centuries, and the people of God were a small remnant around Jerusalem (see the introduction). They needed to know how the twelve tribes came apart, that it was not an accident of history, and that God’s promise to David had not failed when most of David’s kingdom walked away.

How the chapter makes its case. At Shechem the tribes, with Jeroboam back from Egypt, offer to serve if the yoke is lightened (vv. 1–4). Rehoboam asks two councils: the old men say serve the people and win them for life; his friends supply a slogan about little fingers and scorpions, and he takes it (vv. 5–11). He answers harshly, and the Chronicler names God’s hand behind it (vv. 12–15). Israel walks out with an old rebel’s cry, stones the taskmaster, and is in rebellion against David’s house “to this day” (vv. 16–19).

Where it leads. To Christ by contrast and by promise. The old men’s counsel, “be a servant to this people” (1 Kings 12:7), describes the Son of David who “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), and who says, “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). And the tear in David’s kingdom was not the last word: God promised that “one king shall be king over them all” (Ezekiel 37:22), and Jesus gathers his scattered people so that “there will be one flock, one shepherd” (John 10:16).

For us. Anyone with authority, at home, at work or in the church, faces Rehoboam’s choice: to serve or to be served. Listen to wise counsel, especially when it is not what you want to hear, and lead as Christ leads. And take comfort that God rules even through human folly; no foolish decision, ours or anyone else’s, has ever slipped out of his hands.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rehoboam is offered loyalty at the price of mercy, and he listens to the wrong voices. He goes to Shechem, where all Israel has come to make him king, and Jeroboam returns from Egypt (vv. 1–3). The demand is specific: lighten the yoke, and we will serve you (v. 4). The old men who had served Solomon tell him to be good to the people, and they will serve him forever (vv. 5–7). He abandons their counsel and turns to the men he grew up with, who give him a boast about his little finger and a threat of scorpions (vv. 8–11). Authority that will not serve is about to lose what it holds.
verseByVerse.theology: The old men’s advice is about serving: a king who wants to be served must serve first.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone facing a hard decision does well to ask who they are really consulting: people who will tell them the truth, or people who will tell them what they want to hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king. And as soon as Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon), then Jeroboam returned from Egypt. And they sent and called him. And Jeroboam and all Israel came and said to Rehoboam, "Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Shechem the northern tribes, with Jeroboam back from Egypt, offered to serve Solomon’s son on one condition: that he lighten his father’s heavy yoke.

Rehoboam went to Shechem. Rehoboam goes to them. The coronation is not in Jerusalem but some thirty miles north, where the northern tribes have assembled; they have not offered to travel. Joshua gathered the tribes there and told them to choose whom they would serve (Joshua 24:1, 15); Abimelech had himself made king there after killing seventy of his brothers (Judges 9:1–6). Israel has chosen its rulers on that ground before, once well and once badly.

Jeroboam returned from Egypt. The Chronicler says Jeroboam had fled from Solomon and never says why. The reader has to go to Kings, where the prophet Ahijah tore a cloak into twelve pieces on a road and gave him ten, and Solomon tried to have him killed (1 Kings 11:29–40).

Lighten the hard service. The labour levy had built the temple, the palace and the store cities. This book has been careful to say that Israelites were not made slaves (8:9), but the men at Shechem plainly felt their service as a heavy yoke.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Come to me again in three days." So the people went away. Then King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men, who had stood before Solomon his father while he was yet alive, saying, "How do you advise me to answer this people?" And they said to him, "If you will be good to this people and please them and speak good words to them, then they will be your servants forever." But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him, and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him and stood before him. And he said to them, "What do you advise that we answer this people who have said to me, 'Lighten the yoke that your father put on us'?" And the young men who had grown up with him said to him, "Thus shall you speak to the people who said to you, 'Your father made our yoke heavy, but you lighten it for us'; thus shall you say to them, 'My little finger is thicker than my father's thighs. And now, whereas my father laid on you a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The old men counselled Rehoboam to serve the people and win them for life; he abandoned them for the swaggering threats of his friends. He had asked for three days, which was sensible, and consulted his father’s counsellors first, which was better.

If you will be good to this people. Every verb in their answer is about giving way. Men who had watched a kingdom run for four decades knew that authority is not held by asserting it. Kings records it more bluntly: If you will be a servant to this people today (1 Kings 12:7).

But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him. The verb is the one this book uses when Israel forsakes the LORD, the one God used at the dedication when he said why the house would be ruined: Because they abandoned the LORD (7:22). Forsaking God has a smaller form, and it looks like a young man walking out of a room full of grey heads.

The young men who had grown up with him. One word changes between the two consultations. To the old men he said advise me; to his friends, what do you advise that we answer. In the first room he was a king asking for counsel; in the second he is one of the group, and his we gives him away before anybody has spoken.

My little finger is thicker than my father’s thighs. They give him not advice but a slogan. They do not weigh the grievance or ask what the north might do; they tell the king what he will enjoy saying, and he takes it.

Feared or loved? The young men’s theory of power has never lacked defenders. Machiavelli put it plainly in The Prince: if a ruler cannot be both, it is much safer to be feared than loved, and much modern leadership advice says a softer version of the same. The old men knew what the theory leaves out. Fear can make people comply, but not stay, and the northern tribes walked away in a single day. The surprise of the gospel is that this is how God himself rules. Rehoboam said, “I will add to your yoke.” The Son of David said, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart,” and “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:29–30). He did not win his people by being feared. He won them by being lifted up on a cross, and they have followed him ever since without being made to.

Uncertain wording. Scorpions is the ordinary word for the creature, and no whip of that name is described elsewhere. It probably names a crueller whip, perhaps barbed or weighted; some take it as a figure for stinging pain. Either way: worse than his father.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — Each of You to Your Tents
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A proud answer splits the kingdom, and God stands behind the event without excusing the man. On the third day the king answers harshly, in the young men’s words (vv. 12–14), and the Chronicler names a second cause: a turn of affairs brought about by God, to fulfil the word spoken through Ahijah (v. 15). Israel answers with an old rebel’s slogan, “Each of you to your tents, O Israel!” (v. 16). Rehoboam is left with Judah, sends his taskmaster, who is stoned, and flees to Jerusalem in his chariot (vv. 17–18). Israel has been in rebellion against David’s house “to this day” (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: A young king's contempt tore the nation in half, and it was a turn of affairs brought about by God. Neither statement cancels the other.
verseByVerse.examples: When people are hurting, sending the very person they hold responsible to deal with them is not leadership. Rehoboam learned that when Hadoram was stoned.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king said, "Come to me again the third day." And the king answered them harshly; and forsaking the counsel of the old men, King Rehoboam spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, "My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to it. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions." So the king did not listen to the people, for it was a turn of affairs brought about by God that the LORD might fulfill his word, which he spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rehoboam answered harshly and lost the kingdom by his own folly, yet the Chronicler says it was God’s doing, to keep the word he had spoken through Ahijah.

Forsaking the counsel of the old men. The Chronicler repeats the whole slogan, so that we hear it twice, and the verb: forsaking the counsel of the old men.

A turn of affairs brought about by God. Verse 15 is the hinge of the chapter. A spoiled young man preferred flattery to counsel and split a nation, and it was God’s doing, to keep a prophet’s word. Nothing in verse 15 excuses Rehoboam; nothing in the ten verses before it puts the outcome beyond God’s ordering.

That the LORD might fulfill his word. Consider which word God is keeping. Ahijah’s prophecy was given because Solomon had gone after other gods (1 Kings 11:31–33), which this book does not record. The Chronicler names the prophet and the word, and leaves the reason in Kings, as he did in chapter 9. The same word kept a lamp for David in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:36).

Did God make Rehoboam act foolishly? No. Rehoboam chose freely and is blamed for it, and God was not the author of his sin. Yet God so ruled over the choice that it served his purpose, as he did at the cross, where wicked men did what his hand had planned (Acts 4:27–28). The Westminster Confession of Faith puts it this way: God ordains whatever comes to pass, yet so, as thereby neither is God the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures (Westminster 3.1), and the 1689 London Baptist Confession says the same.

verseByVerse.quote: And when all Israel saw that the king did not listen to them, the people answered the king, "What portion have we in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. Each of you to your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, David." So all Israel went to their tents. But Rehoboam reigned over the people of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah. Then King Rehoboam sent Hadoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and the people of Israel stoned him to death with stones. And King Rehoboam quickly mounted his chariot to flee to Jerusalem. So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribes walked away with an old rebel’s cry, stoned the king’s taskmaster and left David’s house with Judah alone, a split never healed in Israel’s history.

What portion have we in David? The cry is not new. In David’s day a worthless man of Benjamin named Sheba (not the queen’s country) blew a trumpet and shouted almost the same lines (2 Samuel 20:1), and it took Joab, a siege and Sheba’s head thrown over a wall to end it. The words had waited two generations for an occasion.

No inheritance in the son of Jesse. To dismiss the dynasty they reach for the son of Jesse. Saul used it when he would not say David’s name (1 Samuel 20:27); Nabal used it to refuse a fugitive food (1 Samuel 25:10). Here it is a whole nation’s way of saying the family is nobody.

The people of Israel stoned him to death. The king sends Hadoram (Adoram in 1 Kings 12:18), the man in charge of the forced labour, of all people, to deal with them. They stone him, and Rehoboam runs for his life from his own coronation.

In rebellion against the house of David to this day. The man who first wrote to this day was living while the northern kingdom still stood. When the Chronicler copied it, that kingdom had been gone three hundred years. Yet he still calls the northern tribes Israel, and Hezekiah will invite them back to the LORD’s house (30:1–9).

Look now to your own house, David. It was meant as a sneer, and God answered it by looking to David’s house. He promised that “one king shall be king over them all” and that “they shall all have one shepherd” (Ezekiel 37:22, 24). The Son of David gathers the scattered, Israel and the nations alike, so that “there will be one flock, one shepherd” (John 10:16).

10.theology:
Verse 15 puts two causes behind one event, as this history did over David's census, where one account names Satan and the other the LORD and the king says twice that the sin was his. Ten verses show how Rehoboam earned the outcome; one says God ordered it. Neither is withdrawn.

The tribes asked for a lighter yoke, and the son of Solomon promised a heavier one. A greater Son of David answered the same longing the other way: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart ... For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Matthew 11:29–30). He took the old men's advice further than they meant it, for he came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). And the split that opened at Shechem is one the prophets promised would be healed under one shepherd, my servant David (Ezekiel 37:22–24), the shepherd who gathers one flock (John 10:16).
10.examples:
Authority is not held by asserting it. In a home, a church or a business, those in charge are followed longest when they serve first, as the old men told Rehoboam.

Friends who tell us only what we enjoy hearing are no friends in a crisis. The young men gave Rehoboam a slogan, and it cost him ten tribes.

keyVerse.quote: If you will be good to this people and please them and speak good words to them, then they will be your servants forever.
keyVerse.note: This is the road Rehoboam did not take, and the whole chapter turns on his refusal. The old men understood that authority which serves first is the kind people follow, and their counsel describes the one Son of David who never refused it: he came not to be served but to serve. Verse 15 adds that God ruled over the refusal, but it never makes the refusal right.

10.reflection:
The old men advised Rehoboam to serve the people, and his friends told him what he wanted to hear (vv. 6–11). Whose counsel do you most readily listen to, and how can you tell good advice from flattering advice?

Rehoboam chose to rule by fear rather than by service. Where are you tempted to use whatever authority you have, at home, at work or in church, to be served rather than to serve? What would serving first look like this week?

Verse 15 says the split was “a turn of affairs brought about by God”, yet Rehoboam is fully to blame. How do you hold together God’s rule over events and our responsibility for our choices? How might that truth comfort someone hurt by another’s foolish decision?

Jesus says, “Take my yoke upon you… my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:29–30). How is his rule different from Rehoboam’s, and what burdens are you carrying that he has not laid on you?

11.title: He Walked in the Way of David and Solomon
11.text: <sup>1</sup>When Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, he assembled the house of Judah and Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors, to fight against Israel, to restore the kingdom to Rehoboam.<sup>2</sup>But the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah the man of God:<sup>3</sup>"Say to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all Israel in Judah and Benjamin,<sup>4</sup>'Thus says the LORD, You shall not go up or fight against your relatives. Return every man to his home, for this thing is from me.'" So they listened to the word of the LORD and returned and did not go against Jeroboam.<sup>5</sup>Rehoboam lived in Jerusalem, and he built cities for defense in Judah.<sup>6</sup>He built Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa,<sup>7</sup>Beth-zur, Soco, Adullam,<sup>8</sup>Gath, Mareshah, Ziph,<sup>9</sup>Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah,<sup>10</sup>Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron, fortified cities that are in Judah and in Benjamin.<sup>11</sup>He made the fortresses strong, and put commanders in them, and stores of food, oil, and wine.<sup>12</sup>And he put shields and spears in all the cities and made them very strong. So he held Judah and Benjamin.<sup>13</sup>And the priests and the Levites who were in all Israel presented themselves to him from all places where they lived.<sup>14</sup>For the Levites left their common lands and their holdings and came to Judah and Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his sons cast them out from serving as priests of the LORD,<sup>15</sup>and he appointed his own priests for the high places and for the goat idols and for the calves that he had made.<sup>16</sup>And those who had set their hearts to seek the LORD God of Israel came after them from all the tribes of Israel to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their fathers.<sup>17</sup>They strengthened the kingdom of Judah, and for three years they made Rehoboam the son of Solomon secure, for they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon.<sup>18</sup>Rehoboam took as wife Mahalath the daughter of Jerimoth the son of David, and of Abihail the daughter of Eliab the son of Jesse,<sup>19</sup>and she bore him sons, Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham.<sup>20</sup>After her he took Maacah the daughter of Absalom, who bore him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith.<sup>21</sup>Rehoboam loved Maacah the daughter of Absalom above all his wives and concubines (he took eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and fathered twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters).<sup>22</sup>And Rehoboam appointed Abijah the son of Maacah as chief prince among his brothers, for he intended to make him king.<sup>23</sup>And he dealt wisely and distributed some of his sons through all the districts of Judah and Benjamin, in all the fortified cities, and he gave them abundant provisions and procured wives for them.
11.overview:
Where we are. The kingdom has split. Rehoboam has fled his own coronation at Shechem, and ten tribes have gone with Jeroboam (chapter 10). Back in Jerusalem, he is king of Judah and Benjamin only.

The message. When God’s people listen to his word, he makes them strong, and the true Israel is found wherever hearts are set to seek the LORD. A king obeys a prophet and calls off a war; priests, Levites and ordinary families from every tribe leave their homes to worship at the place God chose; and for three years, while Judah walks in the way of David and Solomon, the kingdom is secure.

Why it was said. The first readers were a small community around a rebuilt temple, many of them descended from people who had given up much to come back (see the introduction). This chapter tells them that Israel had always been defined less by borders than by seeking the LORD, that people from every tribe had belonged to Jerusalem, and that blessing follows obedience to God’s word.

How the chapter makes its case. First the war that did not happen: 180,000 men are mustered, and one word from Shemaiah sends them home (vv. 1–4). Then Rehoboam fortifies fifteen cities, mostly facing south and west (vv. 5–12). At the centre, Jeroboam drives out the LORD’s priests, and the Levites and all who seek the LORD come south and strengthen Judah, for three years (vv. 13–17). Last, the king’s household: eighteen wives, a favourite, and an heir chosen (vv. 18–23).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern. The people who left their lands to worship where God had put his name are a picture of the many Jesus draws to himself: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (John 12:32). He is the true temple (John 2:19–21), and he promised that no one who has left “house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands” for his sake will fail to receive far more (Mark 10:29–30). And the first fortress on Rehoboam’s list, Bethlehem, was the town from which a far greater son of David would come (Micah 5:2).

For us. Obey God’s word even when it costs face, as Rehoboam’s army did. Set your heart to seek the LORD, whatever it costs, and know that you are part of a people gathered from everywhere around Christ. And watch the good years, because the next chapter shows how quickly security can turn a heart away.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The War That Did Not Happen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah is made secure first by obeying God’s word, and then by good work. Rehoboam musters 180,000 chosen warriors from Judah and Benjamin to restore the kingdom (v. 1), but the word of the LORD comes through Shemaiah: do not fight against your relatives, “for this thing is from me” (vv. 2–4). They listen and go home. Rehoboam then fortifies fifteen cities, among them Bethlehem, Tekoa, Adullam, Lachish and Hebron, puts commanders in them with stores of food, oil and wine, and arms them with shields and spears (vv. 5–12). Most face south and west, towards the Philistine plain and Egypt.
verseByVerse.theology: Rehoboam is not told that he was wronged and must forgive; he is told that the thing he wants to undo came from God, and to go home.
verseByVerse.examples: The man who would not listen at Shechem listens now. One bad decision need not be followed by another, and it is never too late to heed God's word.

verseByVerse.quote: When Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, he assembled the house of Judah and Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors, to fight against Israel, to restore the kingdom to Rehoboam. But the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah the man of God: "Say to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all Israel in Judah and Benjamin, 'Thus says the LORD, You shall not go up or fight against your relatives. Return every man to his home, for this thing is from me.'" So they listened to the word of the LORD and returned and did not go against Jeroboam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rehoboam raised an army to win back the north, but when God’s prophet called the split God’s doing, king and army obeyed and went home.

180,000 chosen warriors. It is the obvious response, and a prophet nobody has heard of stops it with a few words.

Fight against your relatives. First, the enemy is renamed: not rebels or Jeroboam’s faction, but your relatives, literally “your brothers”. Second: this thing is from me. The Chronicler said it as narrator (10:15); now God says it to Rehoboam directly.

So they listened. An army mustered, a king with a legitimate claim, one unknown prophet with a sentence, and the army went home: the last thing anyone expected from the man in the previous chapter, and to his credit. Obeying God when it costs face is often harder than when it costs effort. The peace was partial: the next chapter adds that there were continual wars between Rehoboam and Jeroboam (12:15; 1 Kings 14:30), probably border fighting rather than the full campaign Shemaiah stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: Rehoboam lived in Jerusalem, and he built cities for defense in Judah. He built Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa, Beth-zur, Soco, Adullam, Gath, Mareshah, Ziph, Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah, Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron, fortified cities that are in Judah and in Benjamin. He made the fortresses strong, and put commanders in them, and stores of food, oil, and wine. And he put shields and spears in all the cities and made them very strong. So he held Judah and Benjamin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rehoboam made Judah strong with a ring of fortified cities, good work thoroughly done, though walls were never Judah’s real defence.

The names on the list. Fifteen cities, and the list opens with Bethlehem, David’s town, from which, Micah would say, “one who is to be ruler in Israel” would come (Micah 5:2). Then Etam and Tekoa, where the shepherd Amos would be called to prophesy; Beth-zur, Soco, and Adullam, where David hid in a cave with four hundred men in debt and distress (1 Samuel 22:1–2); Gath, Mareshah, Ziph, whose people twice betrayed David’s hiding place to Saul; Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah, Zorah, Aijalon and Hebron.

Facing south and west. The Chronicler records good work as good work, with commanders, stores and weapons in each. But look at the map. Almost every one of these towns lies south or west of Jerusalem, along the approaches from the Philistine plain and the road up from Egypt. He is not fortifying against the north at all. He seems to have believed the word about his brothers enough to build his defences facing the other way.

Why the wall failed. The wall faced the right direction, and Egypt came through it anyway (12:4), because by then Judah had abandoned the LORD. “Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman stays awake in vain” (Psalm 127:1).

Uncertain wording. Which Gath is meant is uncertain: the Philistine city, then under Judah’s control, or perhaps Moresheth-gath (Micah 1:14), near Mareshah, the next name on the list.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The faithful from every tribe gather to Jerusalem, and while they walk in God’s way the kingdom is strong. Jeroboam throws out the Levites and appoints his own priests for the high places, the goat idols and the calves, so the priests and Levites leave their lands and come to Judah (vv. 13–15). With them come all from every tribe who had set their hearts to seek the LORD, and for three years they make the kingdom secure (vv. 16–17). The chapter closes on the king’s household: many wives, a favourite son made heir, and princes posted wisely through the fortified cities (vv. 18–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 16 is a migration of ordinary worshippers, willing to leave a country to keep seeking the LORD.
verseByVerse.examples: Faithfulness sometimes costs a home or a livelihood. The Levites paid that price, and Judah was strengthened by it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the priests and the Levites who were in all Israel presented themselves to him from all places where they lived. For the Levites left their common lands and their holdings and came to Judah and Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his sons cast them out from serving as priests of the LORD, and he appointed his own priests for the high places and for the goat idols and for the calves that he had made. And those who had set their hearts to seek the LORD God of Israel came after them from all the tribes of Israel to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their fathers. They strengthened the kingdom of Judah, and for three years they made Rehoboam the son of Solomon secure, for they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jeroboam replaced the LORD’s priests, the Levites gave up their lands to come south, followed by all from every tribe who had set their hearts to seek the LORD, and while they walked in God’s way Judah was strong.

Jeroboam and his sons cast them out. Jeroboam had a political problem: if his people kept going up to Jerusalem three times a year, the northern kingdom would not last a generation (1 Kings 12:26–27). So he set up his own shrines, calves and clergy.

The Levites left their common lands. The law had given Levi no territory, only pasturelands attached to their towns (Numbers 35:2–5), and rather than serve at a golden calf the priests and Levites walked away from them and turned up in Judah with nothing.

Those who had set their hearts to seek the LORD. Verse 16 is the sentence to remember from this chapter. These are farmers, traders and families from every northern tribe, whose living did not depend on the temple; they moved because worship had been moved somewhere they could not follow. Seeking the LORD is what Saul failed to do (1 Chronicles 10:14), what David charged Solomon to do (1 Chronicles 28:9), and what the promise in chapter 7 asks (7:14), and here it describes ordinary people packing up a house.

Drawn to the place of his name. These pilgrims picture what Christ does. Worship is no longer tied to Jerusalem (John 4:21–24), because he is where God dwells with his people, and he draws them from every nation to himself. Following him still costs some believers homes and lands, and he promised that none of it would be lost (Mark 10:29–30).

For three years. Three years, said twice in one verse. The Chronicler is timing a reign: the next chapter opens when the rule of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he abandoned the law of the LORD. Notice too the way of David and Solomon: both are held up as the pattern, Solomon for the house he built rather than his later failings.

Uncertain wording. The goat idols are literally “hairy ones”, the word the ESV renders goat demons in Leviticus 17:7. They were probably demons worshipped in goat form; whether Jeroboam made goat-shaped images is not clear.
verseByVerse.note: Jeroboam's calves stood at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28–29).

verseByVerse.quote: Rehoboam took as wife Mahalath the daughter of Jerimoth the son of David, and of Abihail the daughter of Eliab the son of Jesse, and she bore him sons, Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham. After her he took Maacah the daughter of Absalom, who bore him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith. Rehoboam loved Maacah the daughter of Absalom above all his wives and concubines (he took eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and fathered twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters). And Rehoboam appointed Abijah the son of Maacah as chief prince among his brothers, for he intended to make him king. And he dealt wisely and distributed some of his sons through all the districts of Judah and Benjamin, in all the fortified cities, and he gave them abundant provisions and procured wives for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rehoboam made his favourite wife’s son heir and wisely spread his sons through the fortified cities, but he repeated his father’s sin of multiplying wives.

Eighteen wives and sixty concubines. The law of the king forbade multiplying wives (Deuteronomy 17:17); the Chronicler simply gives the numbers.

Maacah the daughter of Absalom. One name stands out: Maacah, whom Rehoboam loved above all his wives, a descendant of Absalom, the son who seized David’s throne for a time. David’s house is marrying into the family of its own rebel.

Abijah the son of Maacah as chief prince. Her son Abijah is made chief prince, though Jeush, by another wife, is named first three verses earlier. The Chronicler notes it without comment, as an earlier list noted the gatekeeper Hosah making a younger son chief (1 Chronicles 26:10).

He dealt wisely. Scattering the princes keeps any one from building a base at court and ties every garrison to the family. The man is capable; what the next chapter reports is not incompetence.

Did God approve of polygamy? No. Scripture records much it does not approve, and the stories show polygamy’s fruit: rivalry, favouritism and divided hearts. God’s pattern from the beginning was one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24), and Jesus held his hearers to it (Matthew 19:4–6). The law tolerated what it did not commend.

Uncertain wording. Daughter can mean granddaughter. Absalom’s only named daughter was Tamar (2 Samuel 14:27), and 13:2 calls Abijah’s mother Micaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah; a common explanation is that Tamar married Uriel, and Micaiah is a variant of Maacah. In verse 18, Abihail is probably Mahalath’s mother rather than a second wife.

11.theology:
God tells the man who lost by the division, to his face, that it came from him, and calls the men on the other side your relatives before a sword is drawn.

Verse 16 puts the book’s key word, seek, into the lives of ordinary people. They left land to stay near the place God had chosen for his name. Jesus told a Samaritan woman that the hour had come when the Father would be worshipped neither on her mountain nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and truth (John 4:21–24), because the meeting place would be himself. And he promised that no one who leaves house or lands for his sake and the gospel's will fail to receive a hundredfold, with persecutions, and eternal life (Mark 10:29–30).
11.examples: Rehoboam fortified well, governed shrewdly, and disbanded an army because a prophet told him to. What follows in the next chapter is not the collapse of an incompetent man but what happened to a capable one once he was secure. Security, not hardship, is often when faith grows careless.

keyVerse.quote: And those who had set their hearts to seek the LORD God of Israel came after them from all the tribes of Israel to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their fathers.
keyVerse.note: This is the Chronicler’s definition of the true Israel: not a territory but people from every tribe who set their hearts to seek the LORD, and pay what it costs to worship where he has put his name. The same words become the verdict on Rehoboam in 12:14, by their absence. They describe everyone Christ draws to himself.

11.reflection:
Rehoboam and 180,000 armed men turned back at one word from a prophet (vv. 1–4). When has obeying God cost you face or a plan you had set your heart on? What helps you obey when it does?

Rehoboam fortified his cities well, and the next chapter shows they could not save him (Psalm 127:1). What “fortified cities” do you rely on for security, and how do you hold them alongside trusting God?

Ordinary people from every tribe left their homes because they “had set their hearts to seek the LORD” (v. 16). What does it look like to set your heart to seek the LORD in your circumstances? What might it cost you?

The good years lasted exactly three years (v. 17). Why do comfort and success so often weaken our seeking of God? How can a church help its members keep seeking him when life goes well?

12.title: He Abandoned the Law of the LORD
12.text: <sup>1</sup>When the rule of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he abandoned the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him.<sup>2</sup>In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, because they had been unfaithful to the LORD, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem<sup>3</sup>with 1,200 chariots and 60,000 horsemen. And the people were without number who came with him from Egypt— Libyans, Sukkiim, and Ethiopians.<sup>4</sup>And he took the fortified cities of Judah and came as far as Jerusalem.<sup>5</sup>Then Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and to the princes of Judah, who had gathered at Jerusalem because of Shishak, and said to them, "Thus says the LORD, 'You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you to the hand of Shishak.'"<sup>6</sup>Then the princes of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, "The LORD is righteous."<sup>7</sup>When the LORD saw that they humbled themselves, the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah: "They have humbled themselves. I will not destroy them, but I will grant them some deliverance, and my wrath shall not be poured out on Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak.<sup>8</sup>Nevertheless, they shall be servants to him, that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms of the countries."<sup>9</sup>So Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem. He took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house. He took away everything. He also took away the shields of gold that Solomon had made,<sup>10</sup>and King Rehoboam made in their place shields of bronze and committed them to the hands of the officers of the guard, who kept the door of the king's house.<sup>11</sup>And as often as the king went into the house of the LORD, the guard came and carried them and brought them back to the guardroom.<sup>12</sup>And when he humbled himself the wrath of the LORD turned from him, so as not to make a complete destruction. Moreover, conditions were good in Judah.<sup>13</sup>So King Rehoboam grew strong in Jerusalem and reigned. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite.<sup>14</sup>And he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.<sup>15</sup>Now the acts of Rehoboam, from first to last, are they not written in the chronicles of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer? There were continual wars between Rehoboam and Jeroboam.<sup>16</sup>And Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, and Abijah his son reigned in his place.
12.overview:
Where we are. For three years Judah walked in the way of David and Solomon, strengthened by the Levites and the faithful who came south (11:17). Rehoboam’s cities are fortified and his sons posted through the land. Now the kingdom is established and strong.

The message. Security tempts the heart to forsake God, and God answers forsaking with forsaking. Yet the moment his people humble themselves and confess that he is righteous, he turns his wrath aside: this is the first test of the promise of 7:14, and it holds. Mercy is real, though some consequences remain to teach; and humbling oneself in a crisis is not the same as a heart set to seek the LORD.

Why it was said. The first readers were themselves servants of a foreign empire because of their fathers’ sins (Nehemiah 9:36–37), with a temple long since stripped (see the introduction). This chapter tells them why such things happen, that humbling themselves before God still brings mercy, and that serving God is far better than serving the kingdoms of the earth.

How the chapter makes its case. Strong and secure, Rehoboam abandons the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him; in the fifth year Shishak of Egypt sweeps through the fortresses to Jerusalem (vv. 1–4). Shemaiah announces, “You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you”; king and princes humble themselves, and God grants some deliverance, leaving them to learn what serving Shishak is like (vv. 5–8). The treasures go, and Solomon’s gold shields are replaced with bronze (vv. 9–11). Conditions improve, but the verdict is that Rehoboam did not set his heart to seek the LORD (vv. 12–16).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by God’s character revealed in him. “You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you” is the just sentence on every heart that forsakes God. On the cross Jesus took that sentence: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). Because he was forsaken, God says to all who trust him, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). Rehoboam humbled himself only when an army was at the gate; Christ “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death” (Philippians 2:8), and his whole-hearted obedience is counted to those who have none of their own (Romans 5:19).

For us. Watch the good years, because comfort, not hardship, is where hearts most often drift from God. When his discipline comes, do what Rehoboam’s princes did: agree with God, say “The LORD is righteous”, and find that he is quick to show mercy. But do not settle for a crisis humility. Set your heart to seek the LORD, every day, in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Established, and Strong, and Gone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Forsaking God brings his discipline, and humbling oneself before him brings mercy. Established and strong, Rehoboam abandons the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him (v. 1). In the fifth year, because they had been unfaithful, Shishak of Egypt takes the fortified cities and reaches Jerusalem (vv. 2–4). Shemaiah brings the sentence: “You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you to the hand of Shishak” (v. 5). The princes and the king humble themselves and say, “The LORD is righteous” (v. 6), and God grants some deliverance, but leaves them as Shishak’s servants, to learn the difference between serving him and serving the kingdoms of the earth (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: For the first time someone does what 7:14 asked, and God moves at once.
verseByVerse.examples: Honest repentance is never wasted, even when some consequences remain. God still answered, and the city still stood.

verseByVerse.quote: When the rule of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he abandoned the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him. In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, because they had been unfaithful to the LORD, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem with 1,200 chariots and 60,000 horsemen. And the people were without number who came with him from Egypt— Libyans, Sukkiim, and Ethiopians. And he took the fortified cities of Judah and came as far as Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once secure, Rehoboam abandoned the law of the LORD, and the nation with him, and in his fifth year Egypt’s army swept through his fortresses to Jerusalem.

When the rule of Rehoboam was established. The three years of 11:17 were counting to this: the good period lasted exactly as long as the insecurity. Two words trigger the fall: established, and strong. While the throne was shaky Rehoboam listened to a prophet and welcomed refugee Levites; the moment nothing threatened him he abandoned the law, as Moses had warned that full stomachs and multiplied silver would tempt Israel to forget the LORD (Deuteronomy 8:11–14).

And all Israel with him. Whatever a king stops doing, a nation stops doing. Those who lead, in a home, a church or a nation, never sin alone.

Because they had been unfaithful to the LORD. Verse 2 gives the reason in one word: unfaithful, the charge the previous book laid against Saul, who died for his breach of faith (1 Chronicles 10:13), now used of a son of David, and the word that will finally explain the exile (36:14).

He took the fortified cities of Judah. The fortresses of chapter 11 fall. Rehoboam had walled the right frontier, and it made no difference.

Shishak king of Egypt. Here the Bible’s history meets Egypt’s. Shishak is almost certainly Pharaoh Shoshenq I, and a relief he carved at Karnak lists towns he claimed in Israel and Judah around 925 BC. The surviving list does not name Jerusalem, which may fit a city that bought him off with its treasures rather than one he stormed.

Uncertain wording. The Sukkiim appear nowhere else in the Bible, and who they were is unknown; perhaps a desert people serving in Egypt’s army, alongside Libyans and Ethiopians (Cushites from the upper Nile).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and to the princes of Judah, who had gathered at Jerusalem because of Shishak, and said to them, "Thus says the LORD, 'You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you to the hand of Shishak.'" Then the princes of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, "The LORD is righteous." When the LORD saw that they humbled themselves, the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah: "They have humbled themselves. I will not destroy them, but I will grant them some deliverance, and my wrath shall not be poured out on Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak. Nevertheless, they shall be servants to him, that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms of the countries."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God told Judah that their forsaking had brought his; when they humbled themselves and confessed him righteous, he spared the city at once, yet left them under Shishak to learn how much better his service is.

Shemaiah the prophet came. Shemaiah, who stopped a civil war in chapter 11, faces king and princes gathered with an Egyptian army outside: You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you. It is the verb of verse 1, turned round and handed back.

The LORD is righteous. Then they humble themselves, the first verb of the promise in chapter 7 (7:14), appearing for the first time since God spoke it. They do not plead for mercy or even say they are sorry. They say, The LORD is righteous: the guilty declare that the judge is right, and never get round to asking for anything at all.

When the LORD saw. God moves immediately; he is watching for it. The next clause is the honest part: some deliverance. The city will not fall, and still Shishak carries off its treasures. The consequence is reduced rather than cancelled.

That they may know my service. Judah had begun to think God’s service a burden; a season under Egyptian taxation will teach the difference between the two masters faster than a sermon. It is not punishment left over but a lesson, one the Chronicler’s readers knew from the inside. Under Persian rule they confessed, “Behold, we are slaves this day”, with the land’s rich yield going to the kings God had set over them because of their sins (Nehemiah 9:36–37).

The sentence Christ bore. This sentence is the just answer to every heart that forsakes God. At the cross Jesus, who had never forsaken his Father, cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). He was abandoned in the place of those who had abandoned God, so that to everyone who trusts him God now says, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

Living with consequences. For a believer living with the results of past sin, verse 8 is honest and kind. Forgiveness is full the moment a sinner humbles himself, as David heard (2 Samuel 12:13). Some consequences may remain, and God uses them as a Father’s discipline, “for our good, that we may share his holiness” (Hebrews 12:10). They are not a sign that the pardon was partial.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rehoboam is spared, but his reign ends with the forms of glory kept and the heart of faith missing. Shishak takes away everything, including Solomon’s gold shields, and Rehoboam makes bronze ones, kept in the guardroom and carried out whenever the king goes to the house of the LORD (vv. 9–11). Because he humbled himself the wrath turns away, and conditions are good in Judah (v. 12). He reigns seventeen years in the city the LORD chose; his mother was Naamah the Ammonite (v. 13). The verdict: “he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the LORD” (v. 14). The sources are named, the wars with Jeroboam never stop, and Abijah succeeds him (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: In 11:16 ordinary people set their hearts to seek the LORD. Verse 14 says the king did not, and that is the whole charge against him.
verseByVerse.examples: A church or a life can keep every outward form while the substance has quietly gone. The question worth asking is not whether the procession still runs but what it is carrying.

verseByVerse.quote: So Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem. He took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house. He took away everything. He also took away the shields of gold that Solomon had made, and King Rehoboam made in their place shields of bronze and committed them to the hands of the officers of the guard, who kept the door of the king's house. And as often as the king went into the house of the LORD, the guard came and carried them and brought them back to the guardroom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shishak stripped the temple and palace of their treasures, and Rehoboam replaced Solomon’s gold shields with bronze ones kept under guard: the ceremony went on, while the glory had gone.

He took away everything. Five years after Solomon’s death everything is carried out of the gate by an Egyptian, and the Chronicler dwells on one detail.

Shields of bronze. Five hundred shields of beaten gold had hung in the House of the Forest of Lebanon, made to be looked at (9:15–16). The replacements are bronze, kept locked up, fetched out for ceremonies and taken straight back to the guardroom afterwards.

A picture of decline. It is an exact picture of decline, made out of an administrative arrangement. The form is kept perfectly. The procession still goes up. What is being carried has been quietly substituted, and everyone has agreed not to mention it. Churches can do the same, like the one told, “You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead” (Revelation 3:1). The remedy is not better bronze but a return to the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he humbled himself the wrath of the LORD turned from him, so as not to make a complete destruction. Moreover, conditions were good in Judah. So King Rehoboam grew strong in Jerusalem and reigned. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite. And he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the LORD. Now the acts of Rehoboam, from first to last, are they not written in the chronicles of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer? There were continual wars between Rehoboam and Jeroboam. And Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, and Abijah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Rehoboam humbled himself, God turned his wrath aside and Judah recovered, but the final verdict on his seventeen years is that he did evil, because he never set his heart to seek the LORD.

Conditions were good in Judah. Told the truth, he agreed with it, and the country recovered. The promise of 7:14 has been tested for the first time, and it held.

His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonite. Seventeen years in the city the LORD had chosen, and a mother who was an Ammonite: Solomon’s foreign marriages are not narrated in this book, and here is one producing the next king of Judah. The Chronicler does not connect the two clauses; he puts them in the same verse.

He did not set his heart to seek the LORD. The verdict cuts. One chapter back, people came south from every tribe with no office to lose, because they had set their hearts to seek the LORD (11:16). They put themselves under a king who did not. Same words, opposite subjects, one chapter apart. The charge is not that he worshipped other gods or robbed the temple, but something left undone. He humbled himself when the Egyptians came, and still went to his grave without ever turning his whole heart toward God.

Judged for what he never did. Most of us measure goodness by what we have not done. I have not stolen, betrayed my marriage or hurt anyone on purpose, so I think of myself as a reasonably good person. The verdict on Rehoboam is about an absence. The law’s great command is not a prohibition but a love, “You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart” (Deuteronomy 6:5), and by that measure a life with nothing on the charge sheet can still be a life turned away from God. Jesus told stories in which the condemned had done nothing: the servant who buried his talent, the people who walked past the hungry. That is uncomfortable, but it is also the door to the gospel. Christ did not merely refrain from sin. He loved his Father with all his heart every hour of his life, and that whole-hearted obedience is counted to those who have none of their own to offer (Romans 5:19).

Are the records of Shemaiah and Iddo lost Scripture? They were prophets’ histories and genealogies the inspired writer drew on, as Luke drew on earlier accounts (Luke 1:1–3). Not every writing of a prophet was given to be Scripture, and God has preserved all of his word that he meant the church to have (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

12.theology:
Verse 6 is the first time in this book that anyone does what 7:14 asked. They humble themselves, the test by which every king from here to the exile is measured, and God answers at once, honestly but within limits: some deliverance, and a season under another master so that Judah can compare the two kinds of service.

The charge in verse 14 is not idolatry or violence but something left undone: he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.

Rehoboam humbled himself under pressure and received some deliverance. The gospel tells of a Son of David who humbled himself with no sin of his own to confess, by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). Because he did, those who humble themselves before God through him receive not some deliverance but all of it: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).
12.examples:
Comfortable seasons need watching more than hard ones. Rehoboam obeyed while the throne was shaky and abandoned the law once he was established and strong.

He humbled himself and God turned the wrath away, and the epitaph still reads that he did evil. A person can respond rightly to a crisis and never set his heart in the direction it pointed. The heart that seeks God is his gift before it is our act: the Spirit who now lives in believers is the one who turns it and keeps it turned (Galatians 5:16).

keyVerse.quote: And when he humbled himself the wrath of the LORD turned from him, so as not to make a complete destruction. Moreover, conditions were good in Judah.
keyVerse.note: This is the first time the promise of 7:14 is put to the test, and it holds: a king who has forsaken God humbles himself, and God turns his wrath aside. Two verses later comes the sober other half, that he never set his heart to seek the LORD. God’s mercy is swift, but a moment of humility is not yet a heart given to him.

12.reflection:
Rehoboam abandoned the law of the LORD when his rule “was established and he was strong” (v. 1). Why is security often more dangerous to faith than trouble? Where in your life are you most at risk of drifting because things are going well?

The king and princes humbled themselves and simply said, “The LORD is righteous” (v. 6). What does it look like to agree with God about our sin rather than excuse it? How does Christ, forsaken in our place, make that kind of honesty safe?

God forgave Judah but left some consequences “that they may know my service” (v. 8). How can a forgiven believer live with the lasting results of past sin without doubting God’s pardon?

The bronze shields kept the ceremony going after the gold had gone (vv. 9–11), and the final verdict was that Rehoboam “did not set his heart to seek the LORD” (v. 14). Where might we be keeping the outward forms of faith while the heart is elsewhere? What would it mean to set our hearts to seek him?

13.title: We Have Not Abandoned the LORD
13.text: <sup>1</sup>In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam, Abijah began to reign over Judah.<sup>2</sup>He reigned for three years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Micaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. Now there was war between Abijah and Jeroboam.<sup>3</sup>Abijah went out to battle, having an army of valiant men of war, 400,000 chosen men. And Jeroboam drew up his line of battle against him with 800,000 chosen mighty warriors.<sup>4</sup>Then Abijah stood up on Mount Zemaraim that is in the hill country of Ephraim and said, "Hear me, O Jeroboam and all Israel!<sup>5</sup>Ought you not to know that the LORD God of Israel gave the kingship over Israel forever to David and his sons by a covenant of salt?<sup>6</sup>Yet Jeroboam the son of Nebat, a servant of Solomon the son of David, rose up and rebelled against his lord,<sup>7</sup>and certain worthless scoundrels gathered about him and defied Rehoboam the son of Solomon, when Rehoboam was young and irresolute and could not withstand them.<sup>8</sup>"And now you think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David, because you are a great multitude and have with you the golden calves that Jeroboam made you for gods.<sup>9</sup>Have you not driven out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and made priests for yourselves like the peoples of other lands? Whoever comes for ordination with a young bull or seven rams becomes a priest of what are not gods.<sup>10</sup>But as for us, the LORD is our God, and we have not forsaken him. We have priests ministering to the LORD who are sons of Aaron, and Levites for their service.<sup>11</sup>They offer to the LORD every morning and every evening burnt offerings and incense of sweet spices, set out the showbread on the table of pure gold, and care for the golden lampstand that its lamps may burn every evening. For we keep the charge of the LORD our God, but you have forsaken him.<sup>12</sup>Behold, God is with us at our head, and his priests with their battle trumpets to sound the call to battle against you. O sons of Israel, do not fight against the LORD, the God of your fathers, for you cannot succeed."<sup>13</sup>Jeroboam had sent an ambush around to come upon them from behind. Thus his troops were in front of Judah, and the ambush was behind them.<sup>14</sup>And when Judah looked, behold, the battle was in front of and behind them. And they cried to the LORD, and the priests blew the trumpets.<sup>15</sup>Then the men of Judah raised the battle shout.
