And when the men of Judah shouted, God defeated Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah.<sup>16</sup>The men of Israel fled before Judah, and God gave them into their hand.<sup>17</sup>Abijah and his people struck them with great force, so there fell slain of Israel 500,000 chosen men.<sup>18</sup>Thus the men of Israel were subdued at that time, and the men of Judah prevailed, because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers.<sup>19</sup>And Abijah pursued Jeroboam and took cities from him, Bethel with its villages and Jeshanah with its villages and Ephron with its villages.<sup>20</sup>Jeroboam did not recover his power in the days of Abijah. And the LORD struck him down, and he died.<sup>21</sup>But Abijah grew mighty. And he took fourteen wives and had twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.<sup>22</sup>The rest of the acts of Abijah, his ways and his sayings, are written in the story of the prophet Iddo.
13.overview:
Where we are. Rehoboam’s reign has ended (chapter 12), with the kingdom torn in two and the temple stripped by Shishak. His son Abijah inherits a small kingdom and the border war with Jeroboam’s Israel that had run all through his father’s days (12:15).

The message. The kingdom of the LORD does not stand on numbers, strategy or a king’s character. It stands on what God has promised to David’s house and on worship offered the way God appointed, and those who rely on him are not abandoned, even when surrounded. And God is greater than the man who speaks for him: Abijah preached the truth better than he lived it, and God honoured the truth.

Why it was said. The first readers were few, had no king and no army, but they had a rebuilt temple and its daily service (see the introduction). Abijah’s sermon told them that faithful worship was what had always marked out God’s people, and that God’s promise to David had not gone stale.

How the chapter makes its case. Outnumbered two to one, Abijah climbs a hill in enemy territory and preaches to the opposing army (vv. 1–4). God gave the kingdom to David’s sons by a covenant of salt; Jeroboam rebelled, and the north now fights God’s kingdom with a multitude, golden calves and a priesthood anyone can buy (vv. 5–9). Judah has the LORD and the worship he appointed, so do not fight against God (vv. 10–12). Surrounded by an ambush, Judah cries to the LORD, the priests sound the trumpets, and God defeats Israel (vv. 13–16), because Judah relied on him (vv. 17–18). Jeroboam never recovers, and Abijah grows strong and takes fourteen wives (vv. 19–22).

Where it leads. To Christ first by promise. The covenant of salt gave the kingdom to David’s sons “forever” (v. 5), and that forever reaches Jesus, of whose kingdom “there will be no end” (Luke 1:33). It leads by pattern: the true priest is not one who buys the office with a bull and seven rams, for “no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God” (Hebrews 5:4), And it leads by the need it exposes. Abijah’s sermon outran his life; Kings says his heart “was not wholly true to the LORD his God” (1 Kings 15:3). Only one Son of David ever preached the truth about God and lived every word of it.

For us. A church is not strong because it is large, or weak because it is small. It is strong when the Lord is its God and it has not forsaken him. When you are surrounded, cry out; and when you speak truly about God, ask him to make your life match it, resting meanwhile on the Son of David whose life always did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — A Sermon on a Mountain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abijah’s case is that the throne belongs to God, and God has given it to David’s sons, so an army fighting Judah is fighting him. Outnumbered two to one (vv. 1–3), he climbs Mount Zemaraim and preaches. The kingship was given to David’s line by a covenant of salt (vv. 4–5); Jeroboam was a rebel who exploited a weak king (vv. 6–7); and the north now sets a great multitude and two golden calves against “the kingdom of the LORD” (v. 8), served by priests anyone can buy (v. 9). Judah’s evidence is not its army but its worship: the LORD is our God, his priests serve, the lamps burn (vv. 10–11). So the sermon ends with an appeal, not a threat: do not fight against God, “for you cannot succeed” (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Abijah bases Judah’s claim to be God’s kingdom not on its army or its king but on its worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Abijah's courage is worth copying: outnumbered and on hostile ground, he spoke to his enemies as brothers and pleaded with them to stop.

verseByVerse.quote: In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam, Abijah began to reign over Judah. He reigned for three years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Micaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. Now there was war between Abijah and Jeroboam. Abijah went out to battle, having an army of valiant men of war, 400,000 chosen men. And Jeroboam drew up his line of battle against him with 800,000 chosen mighty warriors. Then Abijah stood up on Mount Zemaraim that is in the hill country of Ephraim and said, "Hear me, O Jeroboam and all Israel!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abijah, outnumbered two to one, does what no other king in this book does: he stands on a hill in enemy territory and preaches to the army that has come to fight him.

Micaiah the daughter of Uriel. Chapter 11 called his mother Maacah the daughter of Absalom (11:20). The usual explanation is that she was Absalom’s granddaughter through his daughter Tamar, who married Uriel, and that Micaiah is a form of Maacah. It cannot be settled, and nothing depends on it.

800,000 chosen mighty warriors. Whatever the figures represent, the ratio is the point: Judah is outnumbered two to one, and both sides know it.

Abijah stood up on Mount Zemaraim. Zemaraim was a town of Benjamin listed beside Bethel (Joshua 18:22), so this was border ground Jeroboam held. Instead of a battle speech to his own men, Abijah preaches at the enemy: eight verses of theology delivered across a valley to people who have come to kill him.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, since they were often written with letters or abbreviations, and parallel accounts sometimes count different things. Some also think the Hebrew word for thousand can mean a military unit, which would make the armies far smaller. Neither touches what the passage teaches; this commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as first given is without error, though not every such difference can now be settled.
verseByVerse.note: Abijah is called Abijam in Kings.

verseByVerse.quote: Ought you not to know that the LORD God of Israel gave the kingship over Israel forever to David and his sons by a covenant of salt? Yet Jeroboam the son of Nebat, a servant of Solomon the son of David, rose up and rebelled against his lord, and certain worthless scoundrels gathered about him and defied Rehoboam the son of Solomon, when Rehoboam was young and irresolute and could not withstand them. "And now you think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David, because you are a great multitude and have with you the golden calves that Jeroboam made you for gods. Have you not driven out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and made priests for yourselves like the peoples of other lands? Whoever comes for ordination with a young bull or seven rams becomes a priest of what are not gods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abijah tells the north whose throne they are attacking: God gave the kingdom to David’s sons by a lasting covenant, and they have exchanged him for calves and a priesthood for sale.

By a covenant of salt. The phrase comes from the law, used of the priests’ portion, “a covenant of salt forever before the LORD” (Numbers 18:19), and of the salt on the grain offering (Leviticus 2:13). Abijah is not claiming that his family deserves the throne. He is claiming that God said something, and that the saying has not gone stale.

Rose up and rebelled against his lord. The history is partisan but not false. Jeroboam was Solomon’s servant, and worthless men gathered round him when Rehoboam was “young and irresolute”. Rehoboam was forty-one at the time (12:13), so “young” is kind to him; “irresolute” is not. Abijah does not mention that God himself had given Jeroboam the ten tribes (11:4), but that gift was never a licence to set up other gods.

The kingdom of the LORD. This is what 1 Chronicles called David’s throne (1 Chronicles 17:14; 28:5), and here a king of Judah says it aloud to an opposing army. He is not defending a dynasty. He is telling them whose throne they are attacking.

The golden calves. Against it the north has two assets, and Abijah names both with contempt: a great multitude, and “the golden calves that Jeroboam made you for gods”. Large numbers, and gods somebody made.

A priest of what are not gods. Jeroboam had driven out the priests and Levites and appointed his own (11:14–15); Kings adds that anyone who wished could be ordained (1 Kings 13:33). A young bull and seven rams buys the office: a real fee, a real ceremony, a real title, and nothing at the other end of it.

A priest no one could buy. The priesthood was never for sale, because a priest stands before God for others, and only God can say who may: “no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was” (Hebrews 5:4). Christ was appointed with an oath, “You are a priest forever” (Hebrews 7:21), and offered not a bull and seven rams but himself. Behind him stands a God who truly is God, and so a priest who truly gets through.

Uncertain wording. The picture behind “covenant of salt” is not certain. Salt preserves, so it may mean a covenant that does not decay, and Numbers 18:19 joins it with “forever”. Salt was also shared at meals that sealed agreements, so it may picture a bond sealed in fellowship. Either way the sense is a covenant meant to last.
verseByVerse.note: The phrase appears in the law at Numbers 18:19 and Leviticus 2:13.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for us, the LORD is our God, and we have not forsaken him. We have priests ministering to the LORD who are sons of Aaron, and Levites for their service. They offer to the LORD every morning and every evening burnt offerings and incense of sweet spices, set out the showbread on the table of pure gold, and care for the golden lampstand that its lamps may burn every evening. For we keep the charge of the LORD our God, but you have forsaken him. Behold, God is with us at our head, and his priests with their battle trumpets to sound the call to battle against you. O sons of Israel, do not fight against the LORD, the God of your fathers, for you cannot succeed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s proof that it belongs to God is not its army but faithful worship, and Abijah ends with a plea to his kinsmen not to fight against God.

We have priests ministering to the LORD. A reader braced for boasting about armies or the temple’s splendour gets none of it. The right men are doing the right things at the right hours: the lamps lit every evening, fresh bread on the table, the sacrifice at dawn and at dusk, yesterday and tomorrow. It echoes what the Chronicler said of Solomon’s day: “they did not turn aside from what the king had commanded” (8:15).

O sons of Israel. He calls them sons of Israel and names the LORD as the God of “your fathers”. In front of an army he is about to fight, he will not concede that they are not family, or that God is not theirs.

Do not fight against the LORD. To fight God’s anointed king is to fight God, as Psalm 2 warns those who rage “against the LORD and against his Anointed” (Psalm 2:2). The apostles read that psalm of Jesus (Acts 4:25–27), and its invitation, like Abijah’s, comes before the battle: “Kiss the Son, lest he be angry” (Psalm 2:12).

For the first readers. The community back from exile had a rebuilt temple and its daily offerings, but no king and no army worth counting (see the introduction). Abijah’s sermon told them that what they still had was what had always marked out God’s people: priests at the altar, the lamps lit, and a people who had not forsaken the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — The Trumpets, and the Shout
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah wins because God fights for those who cry to him and rely on him, and the chapter keeps the credit with God. Jeroboam answers the sermon with an ambush, so that Judah is caught front and rear (vv. 13–14a). Judah’s response is prayer and obedience at once: they cry to the LORD, the priests blow the trumpets as the law prescribed, and the men raise the battle shout (vv. 14b–15a). Then God defeats Israel, and half a million fall (vv. 15b–17). The verdict is given in one word: Judah prevailed “because they relied on the LORD” (v. 18). Abijah takes Bethel, Jeroboam never recovers, and the LORD strikes him down (vv. 19–20), while Abijah grows mighty and multiplies wives (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Judah does what was written and leaves the outcome to God, and the text credits the victory to God.
verseByVerse.examples: When surrounded, the first move is to cry to God. Prayer is not a last resort but the front line.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeroboam had sent an ambush around to come upon them from behind. Thus his troops were in front of Judah, and the ambush was behind them. And when Judah looked, behold, the battle was in front of and behind them. And they cried to the LORD, and the priests blew the trumpets. Then the men of Judah raised the battle shout. And when the men of Judah shouted, God defeated Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah. The men of Israel fled before Judah, and God gave them into their hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Surrounded, Judah cries to the LORD and the priests sound the trumpets as God had commanded, and God himself defeats the enemy.

Jeroboam had sent an ambush around. The north does not call the battle off. While Abijah has been preaching, Jeroboam has been moving; the sermon is answered with a manoeuvre, and Judah is surrounded on ground that is not theirs.

They cried to the LORD, and the priests blew the trumpets. The order is not the natural one: first the cry and the trumpets, and only then the battle shout. The trumpets are not a military signal. The law had said that when Israel went to war against an oppressor, “you shall sound an alarm with the trumpets, that you may be remembered before the LORD your God, and you shall be saved from your enemies” (Numbers 10:9). Surrounded on a hillside in Ephraim, the priests do exactly what was written for exactly this situation.

God defeated Jeroboam. The next clause does not say the men of Judah broke out. The subject of the verb is God. They cried, they blew, they shouted, and God won it.

A cry that is always heard. Judah was remembered because God had promised to hear the alarm sounded his way. We are heard through a better priest, who “always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). When trouble is in front and behind at once, the order here is still the right one: cry to the LORD first, do what he has said, then go forward.

verseByVerse.quote: Abijah and his people struck them with great force, so there fell slain of Israel 500,000 chosen men. Thus the men of Israel were subdued at that time, and the men of Judah prevailed, because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers. And Abijah pursued Jeroboam and took cities from him, Bethel with its villages and Jeshanah with its villages and Ephron with its villages. Jeroboam did not recover his power in the days of Abijah. And the LORD struck him down, and he died. But Abijah grew mighty. And he took fourteen wives and had twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. The rest of the acts of Abijah, his ways and his sayings, are written in the story of the prophet Iddo.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD; but the man who preached so truly did not live what he preached.

There fell slain of Israel 500,000 chosen men. The slaughter is enormous, more than Judah’s whole army in verse 3, and the numbers should not distract from the point.

How should a Christian read a slaughter like this? As God’s judgment in a war between two kingdoms of the old covenant, in which he defended the throne he had promised to David. It is not a pattern for the church, for “we do not wrestle against flesh and blood” (Ephesians 6:12), and Christ’s kingdom is never advanced by the sword. It is a sober warning that rebellion against God’s anointed King ends in ruin.

Because they relied on the LORD. The reason is one word: they relied on the LORD, leaning their whole weight on him. Outnumbered, outmanoeuvred and surrounded, Judah put its weight on God, and he held. The word ties the next chapters together: Asa will pray “we rely on you” (14:11), and later a seer will charge him, “you relied on the king of Syria, and did not rely on the LORD” (16:7).

Bethel with its villages. Abijah takes Bethel, the town with one of the calves in it, and Jeroboam never recovers his power. “The LORD struck him down, and he died” closes Jeroboam’s story rather than dating his death; he seems to have outlived Abijah by about two years (1 Kings 14:20; 15:9).

He took fourteen wives. The last thing said about Abijah is not the sermon: fourteen wives, twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. His father had eighteen wives and sixty concubines (11:21). The man who told an army that Judah had not forsaken the LORD went home and did what the law of the king forbids (Deuteronomy 17:17).

Chronicles and Kings. Kings is short and severe: “his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God” (1 Kings 15:3). Both books tell the truth. Chronicles is not rehabilitating Abijah; it records that on one day, on one hill, this man said exactly the right thing about God, and God honoured what was said. The sermon was true. It did not describe his own life.

The Preacher whose life matched. Only one Son of David has taught on a mountain and then lived every word of it to the cross (Matthew 5:1–2; 1 Peter 2:22). Our standing before God does not rest on closing the gap between our words and our lives, but on his perfect life counted to those who trust him; and that is the only safe place from which to begin closing it.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “story” (“the story of the prophet Iddo”) is the Hebrew midrash, found in the Old Testament only here and in 24:27. Its later Jewish sense, a commentary on Scripture, is probably too specific; it most likely means a written account, one of the prophetic records the Chronicler names as sources.

13.theology:
Abijah’s proof that Judah is God’s kingdom is a routine: not the army or the king, but the right men doing the right things at the right hours, the offerings morning and evening, the showbread, the lamps. Nobody writes songs about the evening lamp. But when everything impressive about a nation has gone, its daily worship of God is what remains, and that turns out to be what matters.

And when Judah is surrounded, the text does not say Judah broke out. It says God defeated Jeroboam, because they leaned on him (v. 18).

Abijah's two claims, a throne promised by a covenant of salt and a priesthood God appointed rather than one anyone could buy, both meet in Christ. The angel told Mary that God would give her son the throne of his father David and that his kingdom would have no end (Luke 1:32–33). And Hebrews insists that no one takes the honour of priesthood for himself: Christ was appointed by the one who said, You are a priest forever (Hebrews 5:4–6). The north's priests were made with a bull and seven rams; ours was made by an oath (Hebrews 7:20–21).
13.examples: The man who said all this correctly went home and took fourteen wives. Saying the right thing about God, in public, is not the same as living by it; and no one's standing before God rests on how well he lives his own sermon, but on the Son of David who lived his perfectly.

keyVerse.quote: Thus the men of Israel were subdued at that time, and the men of Judah prevailed, because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers.
keyVerse.note: This verse gives the reason for the victory in one word, and it is not numbers, strategy or Abijah’s eloquence: they relied on the LORD. The same verb runs through the reign of Abijah’s son Asa, who will rely on God against a million men and then on Syria against a smaller threat (14:11; 16:7–8), so this verse sets the question the next three chapters ask of every reader: what are you leaning on?

13.reflection:
Abijah’s evidence that Judah belonged to God was not its army but its daily worship: priests serving, lamps lit, offerings morning and evening (vv. 10–11). What would ordinary, unspectacular faithfulness look like in your church and in your home this week?

The north had a priesthood anyone could buy, serving “what are not gods” (v. 9). Where are people today offered religion that costs a fee and leads nowhere, and why is it good news that Christ’s priesthood could not be bought (Hebrews 5:4–6)?

Surrounded, Judah cried to the LORD, the priests did what God had commanded, and only then did the army shout (vv. 14–15). When you feel hemmed in, what do you reach for first, and what would it look like to put prayer first?

Abijah preached the truth on the mountain and then lived against it at home (v. 21; 1 Kings 15:3). Where do you see a gap between what you say about God and how you live, and how does Christ’s perfect life both comfort and challenge you there?

14.title: He Sought the LORD
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Abijah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David. And Asa his son reigned in his place. In his days the land had rest for ten years.<sup>2</sup>And Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God.<sup>3</sup>He took away the foreign altars and the high places and broke down the pillars and cut down the Asherim<sup>4</sup>and commanded Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and to keep the law and the commandment.<sup>5</sup>He also took out of all the cities of Judah the high places and the incense altars. And the kingdom had rest under him.<sup>6</sup>He built fortified cities in Judah, for the land had rest. He had no war in those years, for the LORD gave him peace.<sup>7</sup>And he said to Judah, "Let us build these cities and surround them with walls and towers, gates and bars. The land is still ours, because we have sought the LORD our God. We have sought him, and he has given us peace on every side." So they built and prospered.<sup>8</sup>And Asa had an army of 300,000 from Judah, armed with large shields and spears, and 280,000 men from Benjamin that carried shields and drew bows. All these were mighty men of valor.<sup>9</sup>Zerah the Ethiopian came out against them with an army of a million men and 300 chariots, and came as far as Mareshah.<sup>10</sup>And Asa went out to meet him, and they drew up their lines of battle in the Valley of Zephathah at Mareshah.<sup>11</sup>And Asa cried to the LORD his God, "O LORD, there is none like you to help, between the mighty and the weak. Help us, O LORD our God, for we rely on you, and in your name we have come against this multitude. O LORD, you are our God; let not man prevail against you."<sup>12</sup>So the LORD defeated the Ethiopians before Asa and before Judah, and the Ethiopians fled.<sup>13</sup>Asa and the people who were with him pursued them as far as Gerar, and the Ethiopians fell until none remained alive, for they were broken before the LORD and his army. The men of Judah carried away very much spoil.<sup>14</sup>And they attacked all the cities around Gerar, for the fear of the LORD was upon them. They plundered all the cities, for there was much plunder in them.<sup>15</sup>And they struck down the tents of those who had livestock and carried away sheep in abundance and camels. Then they returned to Jerusalem.
14.overview:
Where we are. Abijah has died after his victory over Jeroboam, won because Judah “relied on the LORD” (13:18). His son Asa now begins a reign the Chronicler tells over three chapters (14–16): the bright beginning here, the reform and covenant of chapter 15, and the sad ending of chapter 16.

The message. Rest is God’s gift to those who seek him, and it is given to be used, not merely enjoyed. And when trouble comes that no preparation could meet, the one who leans on God finds that the gap between the strong and the weak means nothing to him: “there is none like you to help, between the mighty and the weak” (v. 11).

Why it was said. The first readers lived in a quiet but small province under Persian rule, with no army to speak of (see the introduction). The chapter told them what to do with quiet years, seek the LORD and build, and that their weakness was no obstacle to a God who helps the powerless against the mighty.

How the chapter makes its case. Ten years of rest open the reign, and Asa spends them clearing away foreign altars, high places, pillars and Asherim, and commanding Judah to seek the LORD (vv. 1–5). He builds fortified cities because the land is at rest, and gives the reason for the peace: “we have sought the LORD our God” (vv. 6–8). Then Zerah the Ethiopian invades with a million men; Asa prays three sentences (vv. 9–11), and “the LORD defeated the Ethiopians” (vv. 12–15). The word “rest” occurs three times in the first six verses (vv. 1, 5, 6), so that we watch what Asa did with it.

Where it leads. To Christ through the character of God he reveals, and by pattern. The God who helps “between the mighty and the weak” is the God who chose “what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27) and told Paul, “my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9); he did it supremely at the cross, where the Son was “crucified in weakness” and lives “by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4). And Asa’s rest was a lull between wars. The rest it pictures is the one Christ gives: “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9).

For us. Use the quiet seasons God gives to clear out what rivals him and to build what hard times will need. And when you are outnumbered, pray Asa’s prayer: not “make up what we lack” but “there is none like you to help”, and leave the outcome with the God who has already won the greater battle for you in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Ten Years of Rest, and What He Did With Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asa treats rest from war as God’s gift for seeking him, not as a holiday. “In his days the land had rest for ten years” (v. 1), and he uses the quiet first to clear out false worship: foreign altars, high places, pillars, Asherim and incense altars, while commanding Judah to seek the LORD and keep his law (vv. 2–5). Then he builds, because the land is at rest, fortifying cities while there is time to do it (vv. 6–7). In his only recorded speech he will not let the peace be explained by anything but God: “we have sought him, and he has given us peace on every side” (v. 7). Finally he raises a large and well-armed army (v. 8), which the next section will show was not what saved Judah.
verseByVerse.theology: The peace is not luck, and Asa will not let it be called luck: it follows seeking the LORD (v. 7).
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter does not mock Asa's preparations; they were wise. But a fortified country and 580,000 well-equipped men are exactly what tempt a king to trust what he has built, and verses 9-15 are about to show what he has actually been trusting.

verseByVerse.quote: Abijah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David. And Asa his son reigned in his place. In his days the land had rest for ten years. And Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God. He took away the foreign altars and the high places and broke down the pillars and cut down the Asherim and commanded Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and to keep the law and the commandment. He also took out of all the cities of Judah the high places and the incense altars. And the kingdom had rest under him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asa begins with demolition: he removes the shrines of other gods and commands Judah to seek the LORD and keep his law, and God gives the land rest. The verdict comes at the front of the reign, not the end.

He took away the foreign altars. The list is all removal: foreign altars, high places, pillars, Asherim, incense altars taken out of every city. The pillars were standing stones set up at Canaanite shrines, and the Asherim wooden poles or trees for the goddess Asherah; the law had ordered both destroyed when Israel entered the land (Deuteronomy 7:5; 16:21–22). His great-grandfather Solomon had built some of these shrines, his grandmother Maacah had made one of them (15:16), and his father had preached against the northern calves while leaving Judah’s own idols standing.

Reform as removal. Reform is mostly removal, and removal is unpopular in a way building never is. Somebody had paid for each of those altars, and somebody’s family had used it.

Commanded Judah to seek the LORD. Then the positive half, a command rather than a project: Judah is to seek the LORD, the Chronicler’s great word for turning to God in trust and obedience, the word of the promise at the temple’s dedication, “seek my face” (7:14). Asa issues it in his first years. It will be said of him, nearly forty years later, that in his last illness “he did not seek the LORD” (16:12).

Which high places? Asa removed the high places of foreign gods (v. 3), but not all the high places where the LORD was worshipped in ways the law did not allow (15:17; 1 Kings 15:14). The same is true of Jehoshaphat (17:6; 20:33).

verseByVerse.quote: He built fortified cities in Judah, for the land had rest. He had no war in those years, for the LORD gave him peace. And he said to Judah, "Let us build these cities and surround them with walls and towers, gates and bars. The land is still ours, because we have sought the LORD our God. We have sought him, and he has given us peace on every side." So they built and prospered. And Asa had an army of 300,000 from Judah, armed with large shields and spears, and 280,000 men from Benjamin that carried shields and drew bows. All these were mighty men of valor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asa builds and arms because God has given rest, and he gives God alone the credit for it: “we have sought him, and he has given us peace.”

For the land had rest. He built because there was rest, the opposite of the usual logic. Most people treat a quiet season as the reward and work as what trouble forces on them. Asa treats the quiet as the time to work, because walls cannot be raised during a siege.

The land is still ours, because we have sought the LORD. In his only recorded speech he says it twice in one breath, and he will not let the calm be explained by anything else: not his neighbours’ weakness, not his army, not his own competence, all of which were available as explanations. The land “is still ours” because it was God’s gift, kept by seeking the Giver.

All these were mighty men of valor. Then the army is counted: 300,000 from Judah with the heavy shield and spear, and 280,000 Benjaminites with the lighter shield and the bow. Five hundred and eighty thousand men, well equipped, in a fortified country, after ten years of preparation. The next verses will show that this was not what saved Judah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Between the Mighty and the Weak
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The decisive help comes from God, not from Asa’s preparations, and the chapter keeps every verb of victory for him. Zerah the Ethiopian comes with “a million men and 300 chariots”, already inside Judah at Mareshah (v. 9). Asa goes out to meet him and prays: “there is none like you to help, between the mighty and the weak” (vv. 10–11). He rests the battle on God’s honour, “let not man prevail against you”. Then “the LORD defeated the Ethiopians” (v. 12). The pursuit runs to Gerar, for the enemy “were broken before the LORD and his army” (v. 13), and the surrounding towns are plundered because “the fear of the LORD was upon them” (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Asa's prayer rests on who God is (there is none like you) before it asks for anything at all.
verseByVerse.examples: Prayer under pressure can be short. Asa's is three sentences, because he has already settled who God is and whose battle this is.

verseByVerse.quote: Zerah the Ethiopian came out against them with an army of a million men and 300 chariots, and came as far as Mareshah. And Asa went out to meet him, and they drew up their lines of battle in the Valley of Zephathah at Mareshah. And Asa cried to the LORD his God, "O LORD, there is none like you to help, between the mighty and the weak. Help us, O LORD our God, for we rely on you, and in your name we have come against this multitude. O LORD, you are our God; let not man prevail against you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faced with an army far larger than his own, Asa prays that God, for whom the gap between strong and weak is nothing, will help those who rely on him and defend his own name.

Zerah the Ethiopian. An Ethiopian here is a Cushite, from the Nile lands south of Egypt (see the box below). His army made Asa’s 580,000 look thin, and it had come as far as Mareshah, one of the cities Rehoboam had fortified (11:8) in the low hills on the south-west approach to Judah’s heartland. The invader was already past the outer frontier.

None like you to help, between the mighty and the weak. This settles the question of numbers before the battle begins. The gap between a strong army and a weak one is everything to a commander counting shields, and nothing to God. Asa is not asking God to make up a deficit; he is saying that before God there is no deficit to make up.

For we rely on you. This is the word used of his father’s army surrounded on a hillside, when Judah prevailed “because they relied on the LORD” (13:18). Asa has learned his father’s word.

In your name. Not in our strength, but as men sent, carrying someone else’s authority.

Let not man prevail against you. The last clause changes whose fight it is: not against us, but against you. Asa asks God to defend his own honour, since a defeat here would be a defeat of God rather than of a king. It is the argument Moses used after the golden calf (Exodus 32:11–12) and David before Goliath, “for the battle is the LORD’s” (1 Samuel 17:47), and it is open to anyone genuinely on God’s business rather than his own.

Strength in weakness. This is the God the gospel reveals, who won his greatest victory when his Son was “crucified in weakness” (2 Corinthians 13:4). The believer who comes to him with nothing in hand is at no disadvantage: “my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

Uncertain wording. Two things are not certain. Zerah is not called a king and is not known outside the Bible; some suggest an Egyptian pharaoh, but he was more likely a Cushite commander serving Egypt, whose army had included Cushites and Libyans a generation earlier (12:3; 16:8). And “between the mighty and the weak” is compressed in Hebrew, roughly “to help between the many and the powerless”. It most likely means that God helps the powerless against the mighty, or that it is all one to him whether those he helps are strong or weak. The point is the same either way.
verseByVerse.note: “Ethiopian” here means Cushite, from the region south of Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD defeated the Ethiopians before Asa and before Judah, and the Ethiopians fled. Asa and the people who were with him pursued them as far as Gerar, and the Ethiopians fell until none remained alive, for they were broken before the LORD and his army. The men of Judah carried away very much spoil. And they attacked all the cities around Gerar, for the fear of the LORD was upon them. They plundered all the cities, for there was much plunder in them. And they struck down the tents of those who had livestock and carried away sheep in abundance and camels. Then they returned to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD gave the victory: the invaders were broken “before the LORD and his army”, and the fear of the LORD fell on the region.

So the LORD defeated the Ethiopians. The subject of the verb is God, exactly as when Abijah was surrounded (13:15). Judah fought; the sentence does not say that Judah won.

The LORD and his army. The pursuit runs more than twenty miles to Gerar. At the moment of victory the record calls Asa’s men God’s troops. Asa had said “let not man prevail against you”, and God has taken the battle as his own.

For the fear of the LORD was upon them. The towns around Gerar, which had probably given the invaders a base, are plundered, and the fear is on the towns, not on Judah. The spoil from this campaign will supply the sacrifices of the covenant in the next chapter (15:11).

What it does not mean. This was a defensive war fought by Israel under the old covenant against an invader. It gives no warrant for advancing Christ’s kingdom by force; his servants do not fight for it (John 18:36), and the church’s weapons “are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4).

What the record says. A decade of rest, spent building; one prayer, three sentences long, offered by a man outnumbered nearly two to one. The record does not say that he was brave or that his preparations paid off, though both were true. It says “the LORD defeated” them. So the Bible tells every victory of God’s people, above all the last: “thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57).

14.theology:
The verb in we rely on you means to lean your weight onto something. The whole account of Asa is built on that one word: a seer will use it against this same king when he leans on Syria instead.

Asa's first line has its fullest answer in the gospel, where God's help comes through weakness. The weakness of God is stronger than men (1 Corinthians 1:25): at the cross Christ disarmed the powers that held his people (Colossians 2:15), and the risen Lord tells his servants that his power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Christians still pray as Asa did, in your name, and the name is Jesus', whose decisive victory has already been won.
14.examples:
A calm season is the time to prepare what a hard one will need. Asa built his walls in the ten quiet years, because there is no other time to build them.

Clearing out what rivals God in a life is the same kind of work as Asa's demolition, done not to earn his favour but because, like Judah, we already have rest from him; the Spirit who lives in believers gives the strength for it.

keyVerse.quote: And Asa cried to the LORD his God, “O LORD, there is none like you to help, between the mighty and the weak. Help us, O LORD our God, for we rely on you, and in your name we have come against this multitude. O LORD, you are our God; let not man prevail against you.”
keyVerse.note: Asa’s three-sentence prayer is the heart of his reign at its best. It sets the size of the enemy against the greatness of God, rests the battle on reliance and on God’s own name, and becomes the standard by which the seer will judge him when he later leans on Syria instead (16:7–8).

14.reflection:
Asa used ten years of rest to clear out idols and build walls (vv. 2–7). What does a quiet season in your life or church tend to be used for, and what might God want built or cleared away in yours now?

Asa would not let Judah’s peace be credited to anything but God: “we have sought him, and he has given us peace” (v. 7). What do we tend to credit when things go well, and why does it matter whom we thank?

“There is none like you to help, between the mighty and the weak” (v. 11). Where do you feel outnumbered at the moment, and how does this prayer, and Paul’s “my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9), change the way you pray about it?

Asa asked God to defend his own name: “let not man prevail against you.” How can we tell whether we are on God’s business or asking him to bless our own?

15.title: Seek Him and He Will Be Found
15.text: <sup>1</sup>The Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded,<sup>2</sup>and he went out to meet Asa and said to him, "Hear me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin: The LORD is with you while you are with him. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you.<sup>3</sup>For a long time Israel was without the true God, and without a teaching priest and without law,<sup>4</sup>but when in their distress they turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and sought him, he was found by them.<sup>5</sup>In those times there was no peace to him who went out or to him who came in, for great disturbances afflicted all the inhabitants of the lands.<sup>6</sup>They were broken in pieces. Nation was crushed by nation and city by city, for God troubled them with every sort of distress.<sup>7</sup>But you, take courage! Do not let your hands be weak, for your work shall be rewarded."<sup>8</sup>As soon as Asa heard these words, the prophecy of Azariah the son of Oded, he took courage and put away the detestable idols from all the land of Judah and Benjamin and from the cities that he had taken in the hill country of Ephraim, and he repaired the altar of the LORD that was in front of the vestibule of the house of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>And he gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and those from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who were residing with them, for great numbers had deserted to him from Israel when they saw that the LORD his God was with him.<sup>10</sup>They were gathered at Jerusalem in the third month of the fifteenth year of the reign of Asa.<sup>11</sup>They sacrificed to the LORD on that day from the spoil that they had brought 700 oxen and 7,000 sheep.<sup>12</sup>And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, with all their heart and with all their soul,<sup>13</sup>but that whoever would not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, should be put to death, whether young or old, man or woman.<sup>14</sup>They swore an oath to the LORD with a loud voice and with shouting and with trumpets and with horns.<sup>15</sup>And all Judah rejoiced over the oath, for they had sworn with all their heart and had sought him with their whole desire, and he was found by them, and the LORD gave them rest all around.<sup>16</sup>Even Maacah, his mother, King Asa removed from being queen mother because she had made a detestable image for Asherah. Asa cut down her image, crushed it, and burned it at the brook Kidron.<sup>17</sup>But the high places were not taken out of Israel. Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true all his days.<sup>18</sup>And he brought into the house of God the sacred gifts of his father and his own sacred gifts, silver, and gold, and vessels.<sup>19</sup>And there was no more war until the thirty-fifth year of the reign of Asa.
15.overview:
Where we are. Asa’s army is coming home from Gerar loaded with plunder, after the LORD defeated Zerah’s million men in answer to a three-sentence prayer (chapter 14). God sends a prophet to meet him on the road.

The message. “If you seek him, he will be found by you” (v. 2). God gives himself to those who turn to him, and history proves it; so seek him with the whole heart, whatever it costs, even when it reaches your own family. The chapter shows the promise tested and kept within a few verses: they sought him “with their whole desire, and he was found by them” (v. 15).

Why it was said. The first readers knew what verses 3–6 describe: an age of upheaval, nation crushed by nation, a people driven by distress back to God (see the introduction). Azariah’s word told them that the God who had been found in Israel’s darkest days could still be found by a small community that sought him.

How the chapter makes its case. The Spirit comes on Azariah, who states the rule, seek him and he will be found, forsake him and he will forsake you, and proves it from Israel’s past (vv. 1–6), then urges, “But you, take courage!” (v. 7). Asa takes courage at once: he clears away the idols, repairs the neglected altar, and gathers Judah with northerners who had seen that God was with him (vv. 8–11). They covenant to seek the LORD with all their heart, and he is found by them (vv. 12–15). Asa removes his own grandmother from office for her idol; the high places remain, yet his heart is “wholly true all his days” (vv. 16–19).

Where it leads. To Christ first through the character of God. The promise to those who seek rests on a God who seeks first: “I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me” (Isaiah 65:1), and in Christ he came looking, for “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). And it leads by covenant and by the need it exposes. Judah’s wholehearted oath did not last; the high places stayed, and Asa himself would turn. God promised a new covenant in which he would write his law “on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33), and Christ made it in his blood (Luke 22:20).

For us. God is not hiding from those who seek him in Christ. Seek him on purpose: in his word, in prayer, in bringing him your decisions before you make them. Take courage in work for him that seems unrewarded. And let your loyalty to him come first, even above family, while you honour them in every way you can.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — If You Seek Him, He Will Be Found
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Azariah’s message is that God gives himself to those who seek him and withdraws from those who forsake him, and Israel’s history proves it. The Spirit of God comes upon an otherwise unknown prophet (v. 1), who meets the victorious army with the rule: “The LORD is with you while you are with him” (v. 2). His evidence is a dark age when Israel was without the true God, without a teaching priest and without law, yet when they turned to God in distress “he was found by them” (vv. 3–4). That age had no peace; God himself troubled the nations to drive his people back (vv. 5–6). So the application is courage: “Do not let your hands be weak, for your work shall be rewarded” (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The Spirit gives Azariah no new message. He brings back an old promise at the moment a victorious king most needs to hear it.
verseByVerse.examples: Azariah speaks to a man flushed with victory, the moment when advice is least welcome. A word of warning is often most needed when things are going well.

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded, and he went out to meet Asa and said to him, "Hear me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin: The LORD is with you while you are with him. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you. For a long time Israel was without the true God, and without a teaching priest and without law, but when in their distress they turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and sought him, he was found by them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is with those who are with him: he will be found by those who seek him and will forsake those who forsake him, and Israel’s own history proves it.

Azariah the son of Oded. The army is coming home from Gerar, and Azariah, named nowhere else in Scripture, walks out to meet it at the one moment when a victorious king is least inclined to listen to advice.

The Spirit of God came upon Azariah. What he says has been said once before. When the aged David handed Solomon the plans for the temple, he told him, “If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever” (1 Chronicles 28:9). Three generations later a prophet nobody had heard of says it to David’s great-great-grandson almost word for word. What was spoken privately to one son about one building has become the standing rule for every king of David’s line, and the Spirit of God is what brought it back.

What it means to seek the LORD. Seeking can sound as though God were hidden and only the devout could track him down. Verse 4 shows what it means: “they turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and sought him”. To seek the LORD is to turn to him on purpose: to ask him, to listen to his word, to bring him the decision before it is made, and to want him and not only his help. What we run to first in trouble shows what we are really seeking. It is rarely dramatic. Timothy Keller tells in his book Prayer how, in a hard season, his wife Kathy asked him to imagine an illness that would kill him unless he took a pill every night: he would never forget it, she said, and they needed to pray together like that. Seeking God looks like a set time, an open Bible, and a plain request made before you reach for anything else.

He came seeking first. The surprise is that the seeking began on the other side. “I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me; I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me” (Isaiah 65:1), and “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). We look for him because he came looking for us, which is why the promise is sure.

Without a teaching priest. Azariah’s evidence is a time when Israel was “without the true God, and without a teaching priest and without law”. The middle one is easy to skip. Israel still had priests, but none who taught. The office continued and the instruction stopped, and a nation went generations not knowing what it had been told. Yet even then, when they turned to God, “he was found by them”: the promise had been tested by people far worse off than Asa.

Can a believer lose God’s presence? The warning was to Judah as a nation, whose blessing depended on its faithfulness. For the believer in Christ the promise is “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5); those who forsake him for good show that they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). The warning is still real, and it is one of the ways God keeps his people from drifting.

Uncertain wording. Verse 3 has no verb in Hebrew (“Many days for Israel without the true God…”), so its time reference is not certain. Most take it, as the ESV does, as the past, the age of the judges, which fits the description of anarchy and of turning to God in distress (Judges 2:16–18; 21:25). Some read it of the northern kingdom since Jeroboam, or as a warning of what was to come. The lesson Azariah draws is the same in each case.

verseByVerse.quote: In those times there was no peace to him who went out or to him who came in, for great disturbances afflicted all the inhabitants of the lands. They were broken in pieces. Nation was crushed by nation and city by city, for God troubled them with every sort of distress. But you, take courage! Do not let your hands be weak, for your work shall be rewarded."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That dark age was no accident: God himself troubled the nations to drive his people back to him, so Asa can take courage, because work done for God will not be wasted.

No peace to him who went out. No one could leave home and expect to arrive. The breaking apart is told twice over, nation by nation and then city by city, which is worse, because the collapse had reached inside the borders.

For God troubled them with every sort of distress. The prophet is not describing a time when God was absent and things fell apart, but one when he was actively making things difficult. God said the same in his own voice at the dedication, “When I shut up the heavens… or command the locust” (7:13), and for the same reason: the distress was sent to bring his people back. The trouble was not an obstacle to finding God but the road to it.

But you, take courage! Weak hands are the Bible’s picture of a person who has given up, and the encouragement is aimed at a king about to begin a reform that will make him unpopular. Azariah does not say it will be easy or that people will thank him. He says, “your work shall be rewarded”: it will not be wasted.

A Father’s reward. This is not a wage that buys God’s favour. The LORD was already with Asa and had just given him the victory; the reward is a father’s promise to a son already his. The Spirit who came upon Azariah now lives in all believers, and he strengthens weak hands for work that “is not in vain” in the Lord (1 Corinthians 15:58).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — A Covenant Sworn With Shouting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asa answers God’s word at once, and a whole people binds itself to seek the LORD with all its heart. He takes courage, clears the idols out of Judah, Benjamin and the captured towns of Ephraim, and repairs the altar of the LORD (v. 8). He gathers Judah and Benjamin together with many from Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon who had come over “when they saw that the LORD his God was with him” (v. 9). In the third month they offer sacrifices from the spoil (vv. 10–11) and enter a covenant to seek the LORD “with all their heart and with all their soul” (v. 12), with death for any who will not (v. 13). They swear with shouts and trumpets and rejoice, and God “was found by them” and gives them rest (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology: The covenant has one verb at its centre, seek. What God asked of Judah was not first a programme but a person to look for.
verseByVerse.examples: The northerners moved because they could see that the LORD was with Asa (v. 9). A faithful life is noticed, and it draws others to God more than argument does.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Asa heard these words, the prophecy of Azariah the son of Oded, he took courage and put away the detestable idols from all the land of Judah and Benjamin and from the cities that he had taken in the hill country of Ephraim, and he repaired the altar of the LORD that was in front of the vestibule of the house of the LORD. And he gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and those from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who were residing with them, for great numbers had deserted to him from Israel when they saw that the LORD his God was with him. They were gathered at Jerusalem in the third month of the fifteenth year of the reign of Asa. They sacrificed to the LORD on that day from the spoil that they had brought 700 oxen and 7,000 sheep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asa obeys at once: he clears away the idols, repairs the neglected altar, and gathers a people that now includes northerners who had seen that God was with him.

As soon as Asa heard these words. The prophet finished and the king moved, and what he does with the courage is more demolition.

He repaired the altar of the LORD. This was the altar fire came down on when Solomon dedicated the temple and the glory filled the house (7:1). Some sixty years later it needed repair. Nobody had destroyed it or moved it; it was simply left to decay in the courtyard of a working temple, while priests walked past it every day.

Great numbers had deserted to him from Israel. The list of those who gather is unexpected: people from Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon, who had come over “when they saw that the LORD his God was with him”. It is the movement south of Rehoboam’s early years again (11:13–17), but this time no one had been thrown out of office. They watched a king of another country, drew a conclusion about where God was, and moved house on the strength of it. Simeon’s land lay within Judah’s south (Joshua 19:1), but some Simeonites evidently counted themselves among the northern tribes.

A people drawn by God’s presence. Nothing draws people like the evident presence of God among his people. Paul pictures an outsider in a worshipping church falling on his face and declaring “that God is really among you” (1 Corinthians 14:25).

Textual note. In verse 8 the Hebrew reads, literally, “the prophecy, Oded the prophet”, apparently a shortened phrase, since verse 1 names the prophet as Azariah the son of Oded. Some ancient translations read “Azariah the son of Oded”, and most English versions follow them. Either way the words are Azariah’s.

verseByVerse.quote: And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, with all their heart and with all their soul, but that whoever would not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, should be put to death, whether young or old, man or woman. They swore an oath to the LORD with a loud voice and with shouting and with trumpets and with horns. And all Judah rejoiced over the oath, for they had sworn with all their heart and had sought him with their whole desire, and he was found by them, and the LORD gave them rest all around.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah binds itself by covenant to seek the LORD with the whole heart, and rejoices; and God keeps his promise: “he was found by them.”

They entered into a covenant to seek the LORD. The covenant’s content is a single verb: not to keep particular laws or fund particular works, but to seek him “with all their heart and with all their soul”, in the language of the Shema, Israel’s daily confession (Deuteronomy 6:4–5). They seek the God who had just come looking for them through a prophet.

In the third month. The date in verse 10 is probably not chance. The third month was the season of the Feast of Weeks, the grain harvest festival (Leviticus 23:15–21; see Pentecost), and the month in which Israel first came to Sinai to receive the covenant (Exodus 19:1). A nation gathered at harvest to renew its covenant was standing where its fathers had stood. At the same feast, centuries later, the Spirit was poured out and a new covenant people was gathered from many nations (Acts 2:1–11).

Should be put to death. Verse 13 is hard and should not be softened: whoever would not seek the LORD “should be put to death, whether young or old, man or woman”. The warrant is in the law, which set the death penalty for apostasy in Israel: for the prophet who called the nation after other gods, for the family member who whispered it, for anyone found serving other gods within its gates (Deuteronomy 13:1–10; 17:2–7). Asa’s covenant invents no new penalty; the nation binds itself by oath to a law it already had.

What it does not mean. It does not carry over to the church or to any state. That penalty belonged to one nation, under one covenant, in one land held on those terms. The New Testament rules out carrying it forward in the plainest words: “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4), and Christ’s kingdom “is not of this world”, or his servants would fight (John 18:36). A church that reaches for verse 13 has misunderstood which covenant it stands in.

All Judah rejoiced over the oath. The covenant is sworn with shouting, trumpets and horns, and “all Judah rejoiced over the oath”. A nation cheering as it binds itself is not a common sight, and the reason is given: they had sought him “with their whole desire, and he was found by them”. Wholehearted commitment to God is where joy is found.

The promise kept. That is the promise of verse 2 kept within the same chapter. Yet the oath did not hold for long, for the high places remained and Asa himself would turn. No people keeps such a covenant by its own resolve, and God’s answer was a new one: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33), made in the blood of Christ (Luke 22:20).

Where Christians differ. A few Christians, often called theonomists, hold that Israel’s civil laws, including penalties like this one, should be applied by governments today. In earlier centuries Protestants as well as Catholics often used the state to punish heresy.

This commentary’s view. Israel’s civil laws are fulfilled and ended in Christ; the moral law remains the rule of life. Christ’s kingdom is never advanced by the sword or by coercion, and faith cannot be forced.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asa’s reform reaches his own family, and though it is not complete, God judges his heart true. He removes Maacah, his grandmother, from her office as queen mother for making an image for Asherah, and cuts it down, crushes it and burns it at the Kidron (v. 16). “But the high places were not taken out of Israel”: the work was not finished (v. 17a). “Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true all his days” (v. 17b), a verdict on which way his life was turned. He brings his father’s and his own dedicated gifts into the house of God (v. 18), and there is no more war for many years (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The Asherah was burned at the Kidron, where Josiah would later burn the same kind of thing (2 Kings 23:6). Reformers in Judah kept having to do the same work again.
verseByVerse.examples: Asa brought into God's house the gifts he and his father had dedicated (v. 18). Promises made to God in a good moment are worth keeping in a quiet one.

verseByVerse.quote: Even Maacah, his mother, King Asa removed from being queen mother because she had made a detestable image for Asherah. Asa cut down her image, crushed it, and burned it at the brook Kidron. But the high places were not taken out of Israel. Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true all his days. And he brought into the house of God the sacred gifts of his father and his own sacred gifts, silver, and gold, and vessels. And there was no more war until the thirty-fifth year of the reign of Asa.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asa’s loyalty to God reached even his grandmother, and though his reform left the high places standing, God judged his heart wholly true.

Even Maacah, his mother. The word “even” is the Chronicler’s. Maacah is called his mother by the title of her office; she was in fact his grandmother, the wife Rehoboam loved above all the others (11:21), who had seen her son Abijah made chief prince among his brothers. Queen mother in Judah was a real position with real power, and she had held it through two reigns.

Asa cut down her image. He takes the position from her, then cuts down her image, crushes it and burns it at the brook Kidron, in the valley below the city where refuse went, in public. This is the woman who raised his father and probably him.

Loyalty that costs. Jesus said, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37); yet from the cross he provided for his mother (John 19:26–27).

What it does not mean. No licence for harshness toward relatives who do not share our faith. Asa removed Maacah from office and destroyed her idol; he did not harm her. Christians honour and care for parents and grandparents (1 Timothy 5:4), while letting no one, however dear, take Christ’s place.

But the high places were not taken out of Israel. Chapter 14 said he took the high places out of the cities of Judah (14:3, 5). These, “not taken out of Israel”, were most likely in the northern territory he had annexed, or shrines to the LORD himself that survived the purge. He did not finish, and the sentence does not pretend he did.

The heart of Asa was wholly true all his days. Remember that verdict, because chapter 16 is coming, where this same king will buy a foreign army with temple silver, put a prophet in the stocks, oppress his own people, and in his disease not seek the LORD. “All his days” still stands. Scripture is judging which way a life was turned, not adding up its deeds, and it says both things about the same man without withdrawing either. Kings uses the same words (1 Kings 15:14), after saying that his father Abijah’s heart “was not wholly true” (1 Kings 15:3).

There was no more war. “No more war until the thirty-fifth year” most likely counts from the division of the kingdom rather than from Asa’s accession (see the note on 16:1–6); the border fighting with Baasha (1 Kings 15:16) was skirmishing, not open war.

15.theology:
Verse 2 is David's charge to Solomon (1 Chronicles 28:9) in a prophet's mouth, and verse 15 reports the promise kept inside the same chapter. In between, Azariah names God as the author of the distress that drove Israel back to him, as in 7:13: the trouble was not an obstacle to the finding but the road to it. That is said of a nation under discipline; it does not mean every sorrow is a punishment, as the paragraph below makes clear.

The promise has a hard edge: if you forsake him, he will forsake you. The gospel shows where that edge fell. The one Son of David who sought his Father with a whole heart, as no king of Judah did, cried on the cross that God had forsaken him (Matthew 27:46), bearing the forsaking the unfaithful had earned, so that his whole-hearted obedience is counted to all who come to God through him, and they are never forsaken. And the seeking began on God's side: Jesus came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10).

Does seeking God always bring success? Chronicles often shows reward or judgment arriving within a reign, because it was written for a small community back from exile who needed to know that turning to God was never wasted. But it does not teach that the faithful always prosper or that sufferers must have sinned. In the chapters that follow a faithful seer goes into the stocks (16:10), a true prophet is jailed (18:26), and Zechariah is stoned for speaking God's word (24:21). Jesus refused to read suffering as proof of guilt (John 9:2-3). What holds every time is the promise itself: those who seek him find him.
15.examples:
Decline shows in the building first, as with an altar left to crumble in a working temple, and noticing it is already the beginning of the reform.

Reform costs little when it touches strangers and a great deal when it touches family: Asa’s reached his own grandmother.

No believer finishes the work either, any more than Asa did; the verdict on a heart that has turned to God rests on Christ's finished obedience, not on our own record, and failure sends us back to confession, not to despair.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD is with you while you are with him. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you.
keyVerse.note: Azariah’s word repeats David’s charge to Solomon (1 Chronicles 28:9) and states the rule by which the Chronicler measures every king after him. The chapter shows the first half kept within a few verses (v. 15), and the next chapter shows Asa drifting toward the second. Behind it stands a God who seeks before he is sought, and who in Christ came “to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

15.reflection:
Verse 4 describes seeking God as turning to him in trouble. What does seeking the LORD look like in an ordinary week for you, and what do you tend to run to first instead?

The altar had been left to decay in a working temple (v. 8). What signs of quiet neglect can creep into a Christian’s life or a church while everything still looks busy, and how do we notice them?

Judah swore with shouting and “rejoiced over the oath” (vv. 14–15). Why might wholehearted commitment to God bring joy rather than burden, and how does the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33) make such commitment possible for us?

Asa’s loyalty to God reached his own grandmother (v. 16). Where might following Christ cost you something in your family relationships, and how can you put him first while still honouring and caring for them?

16.title: The Eyes of the LORD Run to and Fro
16.text: <sup>1</sup>In the thirty-sixth year of the reign of Asa, Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and built Ramah, that he might permit no one to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah.<sup>2</sup>Then Asa took silver and gold from the treasures of the house of the LORD and the king's house and sent them to Ben-hadad king of Syria, who lived in Damascus, saying,<sup>3</sup>"There is a covenant between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I am sending to you silver and gold. Go, break your covenant with Baasha king of Israel, that he may withdraw from me."<sup>4</sup>And Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel, and they conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the store cities of Naphtali.<sup>5</sup>And when Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah and let his work cease.<sup>6</sup>Then King Asa took all Judah, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and its timber, with which Baasha had been building, and with them he built Geba and Mizpah.<sup>7</sup>At that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah and said to him, "Because you relied on the king of Syria, and did not rely on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Syria has escaped you.<sup>8</sup>Were not the Ethiopians and the Libyans a huge army with very many chariots and horsemen? Yet because you relied on the LORD, he gave them into your hand.<sup>9</sup>For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him. You have done foolishly in this, for from now on you will have wars."<sup>10</sup>Then Asa was angry with the seer and put him in the stocks in prison, for he was in a rage with him because of this. And Asa inflicted cruelties upon some of the people at the same time.<sup>11</sup>The acts of Asa, from first to last, are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.<sup>12</sup>In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa was diseased in his feet, and his disease became severe. Yet even in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but sought help from physicians.<sup>13</sup>And Asa slept with his fathers, dying in the forty-first year of his reign.<sup>14</sup>They buried him in the tomb that he had cut for himself in the city of David. They laid him on a bier that had been filled with various kinds of spices prepared by the perfumer's art, and they made a very great fire in his honor.
16.overview:
Where we are. Asa has had years of rest, a great victory won by prayer, and a covenant renewal sworn with shouting (chapters 14–15), and the Chronicler has called his heart “wholly true all his days” (15:17). Now, late in the reign, the border war with the north flares up, and the last chapter of his story begins.

The message. A faithful life can be undone without any open idolatry, simply by shifting its weight from God to a plan that works. God is not waiting to be asked; his eyes range over the whole earth looking for hearts wholly his, to give them strong support. And how we respond when he corrects us shows where our heart has gone.

Why it was said. The first readers lived as a small province of a great empire, constantly tempted to secure themselves by money, patronage and powerful friends (see the introduction). Asa’s last years warned them, and warn us, that the question is not only whether a plan works but what we are leaning on.

How the chapter makes its case. Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah to blockade Judah; Asa sends temple silver to Ben-hadad of Syria, who breaks his treaty with Baasha, and the plan succeeds completely (vv. 1–6). Hanani the seer charges Asa with relying on the king of Syria and not on the LORD, reminds him of the Ethiopians, declares that God’s eyes search the earth for blameless hearts, and announces wars from now on (vv. 7–9). Asa jails the seer and oppresses some of the people (v. 10). Diseased in his feet, he does not seek the LORD but only the physicians; he dies and is buried with great honour (vv. 11–14).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by the need it exposes. God’s eyes looked for a heart wholly true, and even Asa’s, the best for generations, gave way. They found one at last in Jesus, who was offered every kingdom of the world and would rely on no one but his Father (Matthew 4:8–10), and who died saying, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). Asa put the prophet in the stocks; Jesus was the Prophet whom his own people put to death (Matthew 23:37). For his sake God gives strong support to believers whose hearts are still divided.

For us. Beware the plan that works, because success teaches us that we never needed God. When someone tells you a hard truth, do not silence them, by stocks or by quieter means; listen. And when you are ill, call the doctor and pray, and do not make the doctor your only hope.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Silver Out of the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asa meets a crisis by reaching for money and an alliance instead of for God, and the plan succeeds completely. In his thirty-sixth year Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah, a few miles north of Jerusalem, to stop traffic to and from Judah (v. 1). Asa takes silver and gold from the treasuries of the LORD’s house and his own, and sends them to Ben-hadad of Syria with a request to break his treaty with Baasha (vv. 2–3). Ben-hadad agrees and raids northern Israel, Baasha abandons the work, and Asa carries off the stones and timber of Ramah to fortify Geba and Mizpah (vv. 4–6). Nothing here is incompetent, and that is exactly the difficulty the next section addresses.
verseByVerse.theology: Asa does not ask whether the plan is faithful, only whether it will work. The prophet is about to show that those are different questions.
verseByVerse.examples: Ben-hadad had already broken one treaty for silver. An ally who can be bought by you can be bought by someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: In the thirty-sixth year of the reign of Asa, Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and built Ramah, that he might permit no one to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah. Then Asa took silver and gold from the treasures of the house of the LORD and the king's house and sent them to Ben-hadad king of Syria, who lived in Damascus, saying, "There is a covenant between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I am sending to you silver and gold. Go, break your covenant with Baasha king of Israel, that he may withdraw from me." And Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel, and they conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the store cities of Naphtali. And when Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah and let his work cease. Then King Asa took all Judah, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and its timber, with which Baasha had been building, and with them he built Geba and Mizpah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Baasha blockades the road north, Asa buys an alliance with Syria using silver from God’s house, and the plan works perfectly.

Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah. Baasha fortifies Ramah, about five miles north of Jerusalem on the main road, “that he might permit no one to go out or come in to Asa”. The blockade was aimed at the migration of 15:9: northerners who had been coming south because they saw that the LORD was with Asa.

From the treasures of the house of the LORD. Asa’s answer is efficient, and the source of the money matters. One chapter ago he brought his father’s sacred gifts and his own into that treasury (15:18). Now the temple funds a foreign general.

There is a covenant between me and you. The message is ordinary statecraft: there is a treaty between us, as between our fathers; here is silver; break your treaty with Baasha. Asa is buying a man who has already shown that he will sell. And the king who had led Judah into a covenant with God now reaches for a covenant with Damascus.

A plan that worked. Ben-hadad raids Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim and the store cities of Naphtali, Baasha abandons Ramah, and Asa carries off the stones and timber his enemy had stockpiled to build Geba and Mizpah. He has lifted the blockade, humiliated his rival and gained free building materials in one move. There is nothing incompetent here at all.

In the thirty-sixth year? This does not fit Kings, where Baasha is dead by Asa’s twenty-sixth year (1 Kings 15:33; 16:8). The usual suggestions are that the years are counted from the division of the kingdom rather than from Asa’s accession (which would put this in about his sixteenth year), or that a numeral was miscopied. Nothing in the chapter turns on it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — The Eyes of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s complaint is not that Asa’s plan failed, but that he leaned on the wrong thing, and Asa will not hear it. Hanani the seer charges him: “Because you relied on the king of Syria, and did not rely on the LORD your God”, Syria’s army has escaped him (v. 7). He reminds Asa of the far greater Ethiopian army God gave into his hand when he relied on the LORD (v. 8), and lifts the matter to a truth about God: his eyes “run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him” (v. 9). The sentence is wars from now on. Asa responds in rage, putting the seer in the stocks and treating some of the people cruelly (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: A solution that succeeds can still cost more than it gains. Results are not the measure God uses here; trust is.
verseByVerse.examples: Small troubles can be more dangerous than large ones because they look manageable. Asa prayed against a million men and reached for his money against Baasha.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah and said to him, "Because you relied on the king of Syria, and did not rely on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Syria has escaped you. Were not the Ethiopians and the Libyans a huge army with very many chariots and horsemen? Yet because you relied on the LORD, he gave them into your hand. For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him. You have done foolishly in this, for from now on you will have wars."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hanani tells Asa that by leaning on Syria instead of on God he lost more than he gained, because God searches the whole earth to strengthen those whose hearts are wholly his.

Hanani the seer. Hanani was the father of the prophet Jehu who would rebuke Asa’s son (19:2; 1 Kings 16:1). His word turns on one verb, used three times in two verses: “relied”, to lean your weight on a thing.

A word with a history. That verb has a history in this family. Asa’s father’s army prevailed “because they relied on the LORD” (13:18), and Asa himself, outnumbered by the Ethiopians, prayed, “we rely on you” (14:11). He knows the word. He used it rightly under far worse pressure.

The army of the king of Syria has escaped you. The charge is not what anyone expects. The policy did not fail; it succeeded and cost him something larger. Had Asa leaned on God as at Mareshah, Ben-hadad’s army would have been given into his hand along with Baasha’s. Instead he paid silver to a king who is now stronger, richer and still at large, and whose kingdom will trouble Asa’s descendants for generations (18:30–34; 24:23–24).

Yet because you relied on the LORD. Verse 8 makes the comparison plain. The Ethiopians and Libyans were far worse odds than Baasha ever was, and God handed them over. The bigger crisis was met by leaning on God; the smaller one by opening the treasury.

The danger of a plan that works. Ours is a pragmatic age. Asked whether something is right, we answer whether it works. William James, who did more than anyone to popularise pragmatism as a philosophy, taught people to judge an idea by its practical payoff, and Asa’s treaty would pass that test with honours: quick, cheap in lives, and successful. That is what makes it dangerous. Failure sends us looking for help; success teaches us that we never needed any, and nobody prays to be delivered from a plan that has worked. Hanani asks instead what you leaned on to make it work, and what it cost that never appeared in the accounts.
