The cross did not “work”. By every practical measure the cross failed: the King rejected, his friends scattered, the legions of angels he might have called never sent for (Matthew 26:53). Yet that failure, leaned wholly on the Father, won what no treaty could buy. A Christian may plan, negotiate and build, as Asa did at his best; what he may not do is trust the results.

The eyes of the LORD run to and fro. Then verse 9 looks far beyond this one reign. God is not waiting to be asked; his eyes range “throughout the whole earth”, actively looking for someone to put his strength behind. Solomon had asked that God’s eyes be open toward one house (6:20), and God answered, “My eyes and my heart will be there for all time” (7:16). Here the same eyes range over the whole world.

Whose heart is blameless toward him. What they look for is not competence or success but a heart “blameless toward him”, literally whole: undivided, all pointing one way. Asa had one at Mareshah. At Ramah the eyes that had been ranging the earth found him leaning on Damascus.

The heart God found. Those eyes found a whole heart at last in Jesus, who under far worse pressure than a blockade “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). God’s strong support rested on him without measure, and for his sake it rests on believers whose hearts are still divided.

From now on you will have wars. The sentence is short. The rest that had marked the reign is over, and the reason is a single decision that worked.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Asa was angry with the seer and put him in the stocks in prison, for he was in a rage with him because of this. And Asa inflicted cruelties upon some of the people at the same time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asa, who once obeyed a prophet at once, now jails one in rage and turns cruel to his own people, because he cannot bear to be corrected over a plan that worked.

Then Asa was angry with the seer. This is the man who burned his grandmother’s idol at the Kidron, repaired a neglected altar, and “took courage” the moment a prophet spoke to him (15:8). This time the prophet goes into the stocks, a restraint meant to humiliate as much as to hold.

Asa inflicted cruelties upon some of the people. Not only the seer: in the same period Asa “inflicted cruelties upon some of the people”, perhaps those who sided with Hanani. After thirty-five years of rest, reform and answered prayer, what he could not bear was being corrected.

The Prophet they silenced. Asa’s stocks belong to a long line: Jeremiah was beaten and put in the stocks by a priest (Jeremiah 20:2), and Jesus grieved over “Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets” (Matthew 23:37) before that city put him to death. He bore the rage of those who would not be told, and prayed for them (Luke 23:34).

Receiving correction. “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you” (Proverbs 9:8). We have quieter ways than stocks of silencing someone who tells us a hard truth: the cold shoulder, the changed subject. Asa’s story asks us to listen instead, especially when the rebuke concerns something that has gone well.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asa’s reign ends with a narrowing, not a revolt: in his last illness he seeks help everywhere except from God, yet Judah honours him in death. The Chronicler points to his sources (v. 11). In the thirty-ninth year Asa’s feet become severely diseased, “yet even in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but sought help from physicians” (v. 12). He dies two years later (v. 13), and is buried in the tomb he had cut for himself, laid on a bier filled with spices, with “a very great fire in his honor” (v. 14). The verdict of 15:17 is not withdrawn, and the last years are not hidden: both records stand.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith cannot be stored up from one season for the next. The same man can trust God in one crisis and not in the next one.
verseByVerse.examples: Long illness tests faith as sharply as war does. If you are ill and find prayer hard, the answer is not to try harder alone but to bring that weakness itself to God, who knows it already.

verseByVerse.quote: The acts of Asa, from first to last, are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa was diseased in his feet, and his disease became severe. Yet even in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but sought help from physicians. And Asa slept with his fathers, dying in the forty-first year of his reign. They buried him in the tomb that he had cut for himself in the city of David. They laid him on a bier that had been filled with various kinds of spices prepared by the perfumer's art, and they made a very great fire in his honor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his last illness Asa sought help from everyone except God, and the king who had called Judah to seek the LORD died without seeking him, though Judah buried him with honour.

Yet even in his disease he did not seek the LORD. The verb “seek” has followed him through three chapters. He commanded Judah to seek the LORD in his first years (14:4); a prophet told him that if he sought him he would be found (15:2); a whole nation swore to seek him and he was found by them (15:15). Now, in pain, at the end, the record says he did not seek him. Kings mentions only that “in his old age he was diseased in his feet” (1 Kings 15:23); Chronicles adds the date and what Asa did with it.

But sought help from physicians. The charge lies in the first half of the clause: he did not seek the LORD, and then went looking elsewhere. Had he sought God and called the physicians, no one would have written this sentence. He sought help everywhere except the one place he had spent his reign telling the country to look.

What it does not mean. This verse has been used to wound sick people, so it must be said plainly: it is not a criticism of doctors, and taking medicine is no failure of faith. Scripture never treats medicine as faith’s rival: Isaiah prescribed a cake of figs for a dying king (Isaiah 38:21), Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and Luke was “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14). Some suggest Asa’s physicians used pagan healing rites, but the text does not say so. A Christian who is ill sees the doctor, takes what is prescribed, and prays, and the prayer is not the last resort. God heals in answer to prayer, but not always, and he is just as present when he does not.

The shape of the decline. Not a conversion to idolatry: there is no Asherah at the end of Asa’s life. Just a slow narrowing, from a man who prayed three sentences against a million men, to a man who bought an alliance, to a man who jailed the one who told him so, to a man in agony who would ask anybody but God.

A very great fire in his honor. He is buried in the tomb he had cut for himself, on a bier filled with spices. The fire was a burning of spices, a royal custom (Jeremiah 34:5; see Burial Customs and Tombs), not cremation. Judah gave him everything it could, and was not wrong to think well of him.

Was Asa a true believer? The Chronicler has already given his verdict, that “the heart of Asa was wholly true all his days” (15:17), and he does not withdraw it; nor does he tidy away the last five years. Scripture is judging which way a life was turned, and true believers can fall into grievous sin and stay there for a time, as David did. Whether Asa repented at the end we are not told. Those God has truly saved are kept by his power and will never finally perish (John 10:28–29), and a believer’s standing rests on Christ’s whole heart, not on the steadiness of his own last years. That is a comfort, never a licence: Asa’s story is written so that we will finish better.

The Physician who is sought. Asa looked everywhere but to God in his sickness. Jesus said, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Mark 2:17), and he turns away no one who comes to him (John 6:37). It is never too late, in an illness or a life, to seek the LORD.

Uncertain wording. What Asa’s disease was is not known. Gout and a circulatory disease leading to gangrene are common guesses, given his age and that it began in the feet and “became severe”. Kings and Chronicles say only that it was in his feet.

16.theology:
One verb runs through the whole account of Asa: rely (13:18; 14:11; 16:7-8). Verse 9 shows God not waiting to be asked but looking, his eyes ranging over the world for an undivided heart to support.

Those eyes found a whole heart at last. Jesus was offered every kingdom of the world if he would once rely on another, and refused (Matthew 4:8-10); under far worse pressure than a blockade he continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). God's strong support rested on him without measure, and for his sake it rests on believers whose hearts are still divided. That is the comfort for a believer who, like Asa, ends worse than he began: his standing rests on Christ's whole heart, not on the steadiness of his own last years.
16.examples:
A Christian who is ill calls the doctor and prays, and the prayer is not the last resort, because the Spirit of adoption who lives in believers teaches them to cry to the Father in exactly such hours (Romans 8:15).

What ruined Asa was a decision that worked, and then his refusal to be corrected for it. When someone tells us a hard truth, the stocks are not the only way to silence them; we have quieter ways of our own, and Asa's story asks us to listen instead.

keyVerse.quote: For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him. You have done foolishly in this, for from now on you will have wars.
keyVerse.note: This verse lifts Asa’s story into a truth about God: he is not waiting to be asked but searching the whole world for hearts that lean wholly on him, in order to strengthen them. It explains both Asa’s great victory and his decline, and it finds its answer in Christ, the one whose heart was wholly blameless, for whose sake God strengthens believers whose hearts are still divided.

16.reflection:
Asa’s alliance with Syria worked perfectly, yet God called it foolish (vv. 2–9). Why can success be more spiritually dangerous than failure, and where are you tempted to judge something only by whether it works?

“The eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him” (v. 9). Is this verse more of a comfort or a challenge to you, and how does Christ’s wholehearted trust in the Father change the way you hear it?

Asa put the seer in the stocks for telling him the truth (v. 10). What quieter ways do we have of silencing people who correct us, and what helps us to receive a rebuke well?

In his illness Asa sought the physicians but not the LORD (v. 12). How can we take medical care seriously and still make prayer our first resort, not our last? What would that look like the next time you or someone you love is ill?

17.title: He Sought the God of His Father
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place and strengthened himself against Israel.<sup>2</sup>He placed forces in all the fortified cities of Judah and set garrisons in the land of Judah, and in the cities of Ephraim that Asa his father had captured.<sup>3</sup>The LORD was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the earlier ways of his father David. He did not seek the Baals,<sup>4</sup>but sought the God of his father and walked in his commandments, and not according to the practices of Israel.<sup>5</sup>Therefore the LORD established the kingdom in his hand. And all Judah brought tribute to Jehoshaphat, and he had great riches and honor.<sup>6</sup>His heart was courageous in the ways of the LORD. And furthermore, he took the high places and the Asherim out of Judah.<sup>7</sup>In the third year of his reign he sent his officials, Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah, to teach in the cities of Judah;<sup>8</sup>and with them the Levites, Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tobadonijah; and with these Levites, the priests Elishama and Jehoram.<sup>9</sup>And they taught in Judah, having the Book of the Law of the LORD with them. They went about through all the cities of Judah and taught among the people.<sup>10</sup>And the fear of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands that were around Judah, and they made no war against Jehoshaphat.<sup>11</sup>Some of the Philistines brought Jehoshaphat presents and silver for tribute, and the Arabians also brought him 7,700 rams and 7,700 goats.<sup>12</sup>And Jehoshaphat grew steadily greater. He built in Judah fortresses and store cities,<sup>13</sup>and he had large supplies in the cities of Judah. He had soldiers, mighty men of valor, in Jerusalem.<sup>14</sup>This was the muster of them by fathers' houses: Of Judah, the commanders of thousands: Adnah the commander, with 300,000 mighty men of valor;<sup>15</sup>and next to him Jehohanan the commander, with 280,000;<sup>16</sup>and next to him Amasiah the son of Zichri, a volunteer for the service of the LORD, with 200,000 mighty men of valor.<sup>17</sup>Of Benjamin: Eliada, a mighty man of valor, with 200,000 men armed with bow and shield;<sup>18</sup>and next to him Jehozabad with 180,000 armed for war.<sup>19</sup>These were in the service of the king, besides those whom the king had placed in the fortified cities throughout all Judah.
17.overview:
Where we are. Asa’s long reign ended badly: he leaned on Syria, put the seer in the stocks, and in his illness sought only the physicians (chapter 16). His son Jehoshaphat now receives the fullest account of any king since Solomon, four chapters (17–20), and this chapter is its bright opening.

The message. God establishes the king who seeks him, and the clearest mark of seeking God is putting his word in front of his people. Jehoshaphat’s security, wealth and strength are presented as gifts that follow, not achievements: “Therefore the LORD established the kingdom in his hand” (v. 5).

Why it was said. The first readers had no king, no army worth mustering and little wealth (see the introduction). What they did have was the Book of the Law, read and explained among them by Ezra and the Levites (Nehemiah 8:7–8). The chapter told them this was no small thing: Judah’s blessing in its best days had grown from that same root.

How the chapter makes its case. The verdict comes first: the LORD was with Jehoshaphat because he sought the God of his father and not the Baals, so God established the kingdom in his hand, and his heart was bold in the LORD’s ways (vv. 1–6). Then the act at the centre: officials, Levites and priests take the Book of the Law round every city of Judah (vv. 7–9). Then the fruit: the fear of the LORD falls on the neighbours, tribute comes in and the king grows steadily greater (vv. 10–13), with a vast muster in which one man is remembered as a volunteer (vv. 14–19).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern. Jehoshaphat sent the book round the cities; the Son of David “went throughout all the cities and villages, teaching” (Matthew 9:35), and then sent his disciples to all nations, “teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:20). Jehoshaphat was a king who put God’s word before his people; Jesus is the King who is himself the Word (John 1:14), and by his Spirit the law is written on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33), which no circuit of teachers could do (20:33).

For us. Seeking God is not a mood but a direction, and it shows in what we do with his word. Homes and churches are strengthened less by impressive resources than by patient, ordinary teaching of Scripture. Receive whatever strength God gives as a gift, and offer yourself, like Amasiah, as a volunteer for the service of the Lord who first gave himself for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Book Taken Round the Cities
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A king who seeks God puts God’s word in front of his people. Jehoshaphat secures his borders with garrisons (vv. 1–2), but the Chronicler’s verdict rests elsewhere: the LORD was with him because he walked in David’s earlier ways and sought the God of his father, not the Baals then in fashion in Ahab’s Israel (vv. 3–4). So God establishes the kingdom in his hand; riches and honour follow, and his heart, lifted up in the LORD’s ways, takes the high places out of Judah (vv. 5–6). In his third year he sends officials, Levites and priests through every city with the Book of the Law (vv. 7–9), the act at the centre of his good years.
verseByVerse.theology: Jehoshaphat's first recorded act of faith is to put God's word in front of ordinary people. A reform that does not teach does not last.
verseByVerse.examples: He was given a model to follow, and it was a good man at his best. Young believers are helped by examples, and the wise ones choose them carefully.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place and strengthened himself against Israel. He placed forces in all the fortified cities of Judah and set garrisons in the land of Judah, and in the cities of Ephraim that Asa his father had captured. The LORD was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the earlier ways of his father David. He did not seek the Baals, but sought the God of his father and walked in his commandments, and not according to the practices of Israel. Therefore the LORD established the kingdom in his hand. And all Judah brought tribute to Jehoshaphat, and he had great riches and honor. His heart was courageous in the ways of the LORD. And furthermore, he took the high places and the Asherim out of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD was with Jehoshaphat because he sought the God of his father and not the Baals, so God established his kingdom and gave him a heart bold in God’s ways. The reign opens with garrisons, and then, before it has done anything, the verdict that explains why the kingdom stood.

The earlier ways of his father David. One word matters: earlier. That is David before Bathsheba, the letter that sent Uriah to his death, and the census: the man in the cave and the tent with the ark in it. The model held up to a new king is another man’s best period rather than his whole record.

He did not seek the Baals, but sought the God of his father. The same verb, seek, is used twice, once each way. Everyone seeks something; the question the Chronicler always asks is what (see the introduction), and the sentence is built to force the comparison. It had an edge in Jehoshaphat’s day: in the north Ahab and Jezebel had made Baal worship the religion of the court, with a house of Baal in Samaria (1 Kings 16:31–32), and that is what the practices of Israel meant.

His heart was courageous. Literally high, lifted up. The same phrase turns up twice more in this book, both times as pride: Uzziah “grew proud, to his destruction” (26:16), and of Hezekiah it is said that “his heart was proud” (32:25). What makes the lifted heart a virtue here is the phrase attached to it: in the ways of the LORD. Confidence in yourself is pride; confidence in God’s commandments is the courage to take down the high places your father left standing.

The King who always pleased his Father. Jehoshaphat sought God unevenly, as the next chapter shows. Only Jesus could say, “He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29).

Textual note. The Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation) and some Hebrew manuscripts lack the name David here, which would make the model Asa’s own earlier and better years; either way the young king is pointed to a father at his best.

verseByVerse.quote: In the third year of his reign he sent his officials, Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah, to teach in the cities of Judah; and with them the Levites, Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tobadonijah; and with these Levites, the priests Elishama and Jehoram. And they taught in Judah, having the Book of the Law of the LORD with them. They went about through all the cities of Judah and taught among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his third year Jehoshaphat sends officials, Levites and priests through every city of Judah to teach the people the Book of the Law. No other king in this book is said to do anything like it.

To teach in the cities of Judah. Sixteen men, named one by one, sent out on circuit with a book. It met the need Azariah had diagnosed two chapters earlier: Israel had long been “without a teaching priest and without law” (15:3). The office had survived; the instruction had stopped.

And with them the Levites. The make-up of the party is deliberate: royal officials at its head, then the Levites, whose calling was to teach Israel the law (Deuteronomy 33:10), then two priests (see Priests and Levites). The crown stands behind the teaching, so that no town could treat the visit as an optional religious event put on by the clergy.

They went about through all the cities. Not a festival in Jerusalem that people might come up to, but a circuit of every town, with the book, on the road, for as long as it took.

The least glamorous reform. The Chronicler sets it at the root of Judah’s security (v. 10), and churches still rise or wane with whether ordinary people are patiently taught the Scriptures where they live. The Son of David did it himself, going “throughout all the cities and villages, teaching” (Matthew 9:35), and he is the Word the book speaks of.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–19 — The Fear of the LORD, and the Muster
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Security and strength come to Jehoshaphat as gifts from God, not as conquests. In the verse straight after the teaching mission the fear of the LORD falls on the surrounding kingdoms, and they make no war against him (v. 10). Old enemies, Philistines and Arabians, bring tribute (v. 11), and he grows steadily greater, building fortresses and store cities (vv. 12–13). The muster that follows lists a huge army by its commanders (vv. 14–19), yet among the totals one man is remembered not for his numbers but for his heart: Amasiah, “a volunteer for the service of the LORD” (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Jehoshaphat's growing strength is reported as something that happened to him (v. 12), not something he won. Prosperity is God's gift before it is anyone's achievement.
verseByVerse.examples: Tribute from old enemies is a picture, small but real, of the nations bringing gifts to the true King, which the prophets would later describe at large (Isaiah 60:5-7).

verseByVerse.quote: And the fear of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands that were around Judah, and they made no war against Jehoshaphat. Some of the Philistines brought Jehoshaphat presents and silver for tribute, and the Arabians also brought him 7,700 rams and 7,700 goats. And Jehoshaphat grew steadily greater. He built in Judah fortresses and store cities, and he had large supplies in the cities of Judah. He had soldiers, mighty men of valor, in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the teaching mission, God makes the surrounding nations afraid to attack Judah, and Jehoshaphat’s strength grows without a battle.

The fear of the LORD fell. It falls on the surrounding kingdoms in the verse immediately after the teaching mission, and the order is the Chronicler’s point. A king sends the law round his own villages and the nations stop attacking him; no campaign, treaty or show of force is described in between. He does not say the teaching frightened them, but he places it so that the reader connects the two. So a terror from God once kept Jacob’s family safe (Genesis 35:5).

Some of the Philistines brought Jehoshaphat presents. Philistines who had been raiding the lowlands for centuries send tribute. Arabians bring seven thousand seven hundred rams and the same number of goats, a herdsman’s way of saying a great deal.

Jehoshaphat grew steadily greater. Fortresses, store cities, large supplies, and soldiers in Jerusalem. The growth is reported as something that followed, not something he achieved.

verseByVerse.quote: This was the muster of them by fathers' houses: Of Judah, the commanders of thousands: Adnah the commander, with 300,000 mighty men of valor; and next to him Jehohanan the commander, with 280,000; and next to him Amasiah the son of Zichri, a volunteer for the service of the LORD, with 200,000 mighty men of valor. Of Benjamin: Eliada, a mighty man of valor, with 200,000 men armed with bow and shield; and next to him Jehozabad with 180,000 armed for war. These were in the service of the king, besides those whom the king had placed in the fortified cities throughout all Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The muster shows a kingdom grown too strong to be attacked, and in the middle of the totals one man is remembered for offering himself to the LORD.

This was the muster of them by fathers’ houses. Enormous totals, besides those whom the king had placed in the fortified cities. What the register plainly records is a country that had become, in a few years, too strong to be worth attacking.

A volunteer for the service of the LORD. Everyone else in the list is a commander with a number. Amasiah is described rather than counted: he offered himself. Somebody kept a note that he came forward without being called up, and it is the only thing anybody knows about him.

Willing people. Grace makes volunteers. “Your people will offer themselves freely on the day of your power” (Psalm 110:3), says the psalm of the King the New Testament identifies as Christ, who first “gave himself for us” (Titus 2:14).

Uncertain wording. The totals come to 1,160,000 men. The Hebrew word for thousand can also mean a unit or contingent, which may account for figures on this scale here and elsewhere in these books; which sense is meant cannot now be settled.

17.theology:
The teaching mission supplies what Azariah said Israel had once lacked, a teaching priest (15:3), and the Chronicler puts the surrounding nations' fear of the LORD in the very next verse.

The circuit has a greater sequel. The Son of David went through all the cities and villages himself, teaching and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom (Matthew 9:35), then sent his apostles to every nation to teach all that he had commanded (Matthew 28:19-20). Jehoshaphat sent the book round; Christ is the Word it speaks of, and by his Spirit the law that once went round on a scroll is now written on his people's hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).
17.examples:
The reform was a circuit of every town with a book, the least glamorous thing any king in this book does. Patient teaching in ordinary places rarely looks like strength, but the Chronicler sets it at the root of Judah's security.

Amasiah the volunteer is a reminder that willing service is what grace produces. The Spirit makes God's people offer themselves freely (Psalm 110:3), because their Lord first gave himself for them.

keyVerse.quote: And they taught in Judah, having the Book of the Law of the LORD with them. They went about through all the cities of Judah and taught among the people.
keyVerse.note: This is the act at the centre of Jehoshaphat’s good years and the clearest sign of what it meant that he “sought the God of his father” (v. 4): he put God’s word in front of his people, in every town. The fear of the LORD on the nations follows in the very next verse, and the pattern runs on to the Son of David who taught in all the cities and villages, and who is himself the Word.

17.reflection:
Jehoshaphat was pointed to “the earlier ways of his father David”, a good man at his best (v. 3). Whose example has shaped your faith, and how can we learn from flawed believers without copying their faults?

The Chronicler writes, “Therefore the LORD established the kingdom in his hand” (v. 5). What difference does it make to see your health, work or success as God’s gift rather than your achievement?

Jehoshaphat sent teachers with the Book of the Law to every town (vv. 7–9). How are ordinary people in our church taught the Bible, and what part could you play in it?

Amasiah is remembered only as “a volunteer for the service of the LORD” (v. 16). Where might God be asking you to offer yourself without waiting to be asked?

18.title: Is There Not Here Another Prophet of the LORD?
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Jehoshaphat had great riches and honor, and he made a marriage alliance with Ahab.<sup>2</sup>After some years he went down to Ahab in Samaria. And Ahab killed an abundance of sheep and oxen for him and for the people who were with him, and induced him to go up against Ramoth-gilead.<sup>3</sup>Ahab king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, "Will you go with me to Ramoth-gilead?" He answered him, "I am as you are, my people as your people. We will be with you in the war."<sup>4</sup>And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "Inquire first for the word of the LORD."<sup>5</sup>Then the king of Israel gathered the prophets together, four hundred men, and said to them, "Shall we go to battle against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I refrain?" And they said, "Go up, for God will give it into the hand of the king."<sup>6</sup>But Jehoshaphat said, "Is there not here another prophet of the LORD of whom we may inquire?"<sup>7</sup>And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of the LORD, Micaiah the son of Imlah; but I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but always evil." And Jehoshaphat said, "Let not the king say so."<sup>8</sup>Then the king of Israel summoned an officer and said, "Bring quickly Micaiah the son of Imlah."<sup>9</sup>Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah were sitting on their thrones, arrayed in their robes. And they were sitting at the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying before them.<sup>10</sup>And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made for himself horns of iron and said, "Thus says the LORD, 'With these you shall push the Syrians until they are destroyed.'"<sup>11</sup>And all the prophets prophesied so and said, "Go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph. The LORD will give it into the hand of the king."<sup>12</sup>And the messenger who went to summon Micaiah said to him, "Behold, the words of the prophets with one accord are favorable to the king. Let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak favorably."<sup>13</sup>But Micaiah said, "As the LORD lives, what my God says, that I will speak."<sup>14</sup>And when he had come to the king, the king said to him, "Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall I refrain?" And he answered, "Go up and triumph; they will be given into your hand."<sup>15</sup>But the king said to him, "How many times shall I make you swear that you speak to me nothing but the truth in the name of the LORD?"<sup>16</sup>And he said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. And the LORD said, 'These have no master; let each return to his home in peace.'"<sup>17</sup>And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Did I not tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?"<sup>18</sup>And Micaiah said, "Therefore hear the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing on his right hand and on his left.<sup>19</sup>And the LORD said, 'Who will entice Ahab the king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?' And one said one thing, and another said another.<sup>20</sup>Then a spirit came forward and stood before the LORD, saying, 'I will entice him.' And the LORD said to him, 'By what means?'<sup>21</sup>And he said, 'I will go out, and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' And he said, 'You are to entice him, and you shall succeed; go out and do so.'<sup>22</sup>Now therefore behold, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these your prophets. The LORD has declared disaster concerning you."<sup>23</sup>Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek and said, "Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go from me to speak to you?"<sup>24</sup>And Micaiah said, "Behold, you shall see on that day when you go into an inner chamber to hide yourself."<sup>25</sup>And the king of Israel said, "Seize Micaiah and take him back to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king's son,<sup>26</sup>and say, 'Thus says the king, Put this fellow in prison and feed him with meager rations of bread and water until I return in peace.'"<sup>27</sup>And Micaiah said, "If you return in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me." And he said, "Hear, all you peoples!"<sup>28</sup>So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead.<sup>29</sup>And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your robes." And the king of Israel disguised himself, and they went into battle.<sup>30</sup>Now the king of Syria had commanded the captains of his chariots, "Fight with neither small nor great, but only with the king of Israel."<sup>31</sup>As soon as the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "It is the king of Israel." So they turned to fight against him. And Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him; God drew them away from him.<sup>32</sup>For as soon as the captains of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him.<sup>33</sup>But a certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the scale armor and the breastplate. Therefore he said to the driver of his chariot, "Turn around and carry me out of the battle, for I am wounded."<sup>34</sup>And the battle continued that day, and the king of Israel was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians until evening. Then at sunset he died.
18.overview:
Where we are. Jehoshaphat has sought God, sent the law round his towns and grown rich and secure (chapter 17). Now, for the only time at such length, the Chronicler takes us into the court of the northern kingdom, because a king of Judah has gone there.

The message. A good man can walk into disaster by binding himself to those who hate the LORD and by asking for God’s word only after he has made up his mind. God’s word cannot be managed: one faithful prophet speaks it against four hundred, it judges the king who refuses it, and it is carried out even by an arrow drawn at random. Yet the same God hears the foolish believer who cries out to him.

Why it was said. The first readers lived among neighbours whose friendship was tempting and whose families were marrying into theirs (Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:23–27), and they too had to choose which voices to believe (see the introduction). The chapter warned them what such alliances cost, and taught them that the truth is not decided by a majority.

How the chapter makes its case. Jehoshaphat ties his house to Ahab’s by marriage and promises his army before asking a single question (vv. 1–3). He does ask for the word of the LORD; four hundred prophets say go, and he asks for one more, whom Ahab hates (vv. 4–11). Micaiah swears to speak only what his God says, mocks the chorus, then tells the truth: Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd, and a lying spirit sent from God’s court in heaven (vv. 12–22). For this he is struck and jailed (vv. 23–27). In battle Ahab disguises himself and leaves Jehoshaphat in his robes; Jehoshaphat cries out and God draws the enemy away, while an arrow drawn at random finds Ahab (vv. 28–34).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. Micaiah is the faithful prophet who will say only what God says and is struck in the face for it, as Jesus was struck and mocked, “Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who is it that struck you?” (Matthew 26:68). The sheep scattered without a shepherd are the crowds Jesus looked on with compassion (Mark 6:34), and he is the good shepherd who lays down his life for them (John 10:11). Ahab put another king in the place of danger to save himself; the Son of David put himself in ours.

For us. Ask for God’s guidance before you commit yourself, not after, and be wary of advice whose chief recommendation is that everyone agrees with it. Love the voice that tells you the truth about yourself. And when you have walked foolishly into trouble, cry out anyway: God helped Jehoshaphat, and he does not wait for us to deserve rescue.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — A Marriage, and Four Hundred Prophets
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A good king walks into danger by joining himself to a bad one and then asking God to bless a decision already made. Jehoshaphat’s riches make him worth marrying into, and he ties his house to Ahab’s (v. 1). Feasted in Samaria, he commits his army to Ahab’s war before a single question is asked: “I am as you are” (vv. 2–3). Only then does he ask for the word of the LORD. Four hundred prophets answer as one, but their unanimity troubles him, and he asks for another, Micaiah, whom Ahab hates because he never prophesies good concerning him (vv. 4–7). The stage is set at the gate of Samaria, with thrones, iron horns and a chorus (vv. 8–11).
verseByVerse.theology: God's gifts can become the doorway to temptation. Nothing in verse 1 is called sin, yet the chapter shows how far a good man can be drawn by flattery and family ties.
verseByVerse.examples: It is easy to be bold for God among people who share our faith and pliable among people who flatter us. Jehoshaphat was both within a single chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jehoshaphat had great riches and honor, and he made a marriage alliance with Ahab. After some years he went down to Ahab in Samaria. And Ahab killed an abundance of sheep and oxen for him and for the people who were with him, and induced him to go up against Ramoth-gilead. Ahab king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, "Will you go with me to Ramoth-gilead?" He answered him, "I am as you are, my people as your people. We will be with you in the war."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoshaphat ties his family to Ahab’s by marriage and, after a royal feast, commits himself to Ahab’s war before he has asked a single question.

Jehoshaphat had great riches and honor. This is the one story from Ahab’s court that Chronicles, which otherwise leaves the northern kings out, tells at length, and it tells it because a king of Judah is in it. The riches and honour came a chapter ago to a king who sought God (17:5). Here they make him worth marrying into: a strong, wealthy Judah is a country the house of Omri wants a treaty with, and treaties in that world were sealed by marriages. What God gave him made him attractive to the worst family in Israel.

He made a marriage alliance with Ahab. The marriage is not described, but everything terrible in the next five chapters grows out of it. Jehoshaphat’s son Jehoram married Athaliah, Ahab’s daughter (21:6). She will watch her son die and then destroy the royal family, and the line of David will survive by one infant hidden for six years in the house of God (22:10–12).

Induced him to go up against Ramoth-gilead. Ahab feasts him and induced him, talked him round. Ramoth-gilead was a fortified town east of the Jordan, on the road through Gilead, which Syria held and Israel claimed as its own (1 Kings 22:3).

I am as you are. Jehoshaphat’s answer is total before a single question has been asked. He has committed his army, his nation and himself to a campaign he knows nothing about, for a king whose wife has been killing the LORD’s prophets (1 Kings 18:4). He is a good man, and this is what a good man sounds like when somebody powerful has flattered him.

The pull of the inner ring. C. S. Lewis, in a lecture he called “The Inner Ring”, argued that one of the strongest forces in ordinary life is the longing to be inside: in the circle that matters, on first-name terms with the people who count. It seldom asks for anything dramatic, only for small things, a laugh at the right moment, a silence when we ought to speak, and that, Lewis warned, is how it gets good people to do bad things. Jehoshaphat needed nothing Ahab had. But the court at Samaria, with its feasts and its four hundred prophets, was the most glittering room in his world, and he wanted to be in it. Most of us have a Samaria of our own. The gospel does not cure it by telling us to stop wanting to belong. It gives us the one belonging that cannot be withdrawn: in Christ those who were far off have been brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13). A person sure of that room can afford to be left out of every other.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "Inquire first for the word of the LORD." Then the king of Israel gathered the prophets together, four hundred men, and said to them, "Shall we go to battle against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I refrain?" And they said, "Go up, for God will give it into the hand of the king." But Jehoshaphat said, "Is there not here another prophet of the LORD of whom we may inquire?" And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of the LORD, Micaiah the son of Imlah; but I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but always evil." And Jehoshaphat said, "Let not the king say so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoshaphat rightly asks for God’s word, but only after promising everything, and when four hundred prophets agree he senses that unanimity is not the same as a word from God.

Inquire first for the word of the LORD. The instinct is right, and it arrives one sentence too late. The whole chapter turns on that gap: from here on he is asking God’s leave for what he has already promised.

Two kings inquiring. The verb inquire comes three times in four verses. It is the Chronicler’s word for seeking God, the thing Saul died for not doing (1 Chronicles 10:13–14). Two kings are about to spend the day inquiring, and only one of them wants an answer he has not already chosen.

Four hundred men. Asked a yes-or-no question, they give the answer the king wants. They are not prophets of Baal. They use God’s name, and they are unanimous.

Is there not here another prophet of the LORD of whom we may inquire? It is the best moment of Jehoshaphat’s day. Four hundred men have just agreed with each other, and something in the sound of it is wrong to him. He cannot say what is missing, but he knows that agreement is not the same as a word from God.

I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me. Ahab’s reply gives him away. He does not say Micaiah is a liar; he says the man is always right about him, and hates him for it. He has had a genuine prophet within reach, in Samaria, for years, and has arranged his life so as never to have to listen. Jesus met the same thing: “because I tell the truth, you do not believe me” (John 8:45).

A test for advice. Of any counsel we love, it is worth asking whether we love it because it is true or because it agrees with us. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Proverbs 27:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king of Israel summoned an officer and said, "Bring quickly Micaiah the son of Imlah." Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah were sitting on their thrones, arrayed in their robes. And they were sitting at the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying before them. And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made for himself horns of iron and said, "Thus says the LORD, 'With these you shall push the Syrians until they are destroyed.'" And all the prophets prophesied so and said, "Go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph. The LORD will give it into the hand of the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The court stages a show of certainty, with thrones, robes, props and a chorus of prophets, but God has not spoken in any of it.

Sitting on their thrones, arrayed in their robes. The scene is a stage: two thrones, full royal dress, the threshing floor by the city gate where public business was done, and four hundred men performing.

Horns of iron. Zedekiah has made himself iron horns and uses the true prophets’ formula, Thus says the LORD. He knows his Scriptures (the horns come from Moses’ blessing on Joseph, Deuteronomy 33:17) and he has props. Everything about him is correct except that God has not spoken to him.

Go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph. Their line is given twice, in verse 5 and verse 11, with one accord and in the same words, because it is about to be used again. The decision has already been made; Micaiah is sent for only to agree with it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — What My God Says, That I Will Speak
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One man bound to his God speaks the truth against four hundred, and the truth is that God himself has passed sentence on Ahab. Pressed to agree with the others, Micaiah swears, “what my God says, that I will speak” (vv. 12–13). He first repeats the chorus in mockery, then, put on oath, describes Israel scattered on the mountains like sheep without a shepherd: the king will fall (vv. 14–17). Then he draws back the curtain on God’s court in heaven, where a lying spirit is sent into the mouths of Ahab’s prophets (vv. 18–22). The vision is hard, but it is told to Ahab’s face, a last warning before judgment.
verseByVerse.theology: Micaiah's whole ministry is summed up in verse 13: he is answerable to God and not to the room. That is what makes a prophet true, not the size of his following.
verseByVerse.examples: Faithfulness here costs Micaiah a slap and a prison cell, and the chapter never tells us he was released. Being right before God does not always mean being vindicated before people in this life.

verseByVerse.quote: And the messenger who went to summon Micaiah said to him, "Behold, the words of the prophets with one accord are favorable to the king. Let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak favorably." But Micaiah said, "As the LORD lives, what my God says, that I will speak." And when he had come to the king, the king said to him, "Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall I refrain?" And he answered, "Go up and triumph; they will be given into your hand." But the king said to him, "How many times shall I make you swear that you speak to me nothing but the truth in the name of the LORD?" And he said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. And the LORD said, 'These have no master; let each return to his home in peace.'" And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Did I not tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Micaiah refuses to be coached, mocks the chorus by repeating it, and then, put on oath, tells Ahab he will fall and leave Israel like sheep without a shepherd.

Speak favorably. The officer sent to fetch him gives advice on the road. It is the oldest pressure in the world, offered kindly. He is not asked to lie, exactly, only to say what the others say, and the messenger is probably trying to save his life.

As the LORD lives, what my God says, that I will speak. Micaiah answers an argument with an oath, the only answer there is to that particular argument, because there is no counter-case to make against four hundred men. Where Kings has what the LORD says to me (1 Kings 22:14), this book has what my God says. Micaiah is not citing an office or a rule; he is naming the one he belongs to.

Go up and triumph. Then he arrives and says exactly what he was told to say, in the four hundred’s own words. He is mocking them: a man who repeats your words back to you exactly is not agreeing with you.

Nothing but the truth. Ahab, who has never listened to this man, hears the tone at once. The irony is complete: the king demands the truth from the one man who always tells it, in a room full of people he has gathered to avoid it.

As sheep that have no shepherd. So Micaiah gives it, and the picture is not of an army defeated but of a flock with nobody in front of it: the king will fall, and his men will go home. Moses had used the same phrase when he asked God for a successor, “that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd” (Numbers 27:17).

The Shepherd who came. Centuries later Jesus looked out over a crowd in Galilee and “had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things” (Mark 6:34). Ahab led his flock to scatter and died to save no one. “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11), and gathers them.

Did I not tell you? Ahab turns to his guest: I told you so. A hardened heart hears every warning only as proof that the messenger is against him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Micaiah said, "Therefore hear the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing on his right hand and on his left. And the LORD said, 'Who will entice Ahab the king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?' And one said one thing, and another said another. Then a spirit came forward and stood before the LORD, saying, 'I will entice him.' And the LORD said to him, 'By what means?' And he said, 'I will go out, and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' And he said, 'You are to entice him, and you shall succeed; go out and do so.' Now therefore behold, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these your prophets. The LORD has declared disaster concerning you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Micaiah reveals that God, in judgment on Ahab, has let a lying spirit speak through his prophets, and by telling Ahab so he gives him a last chance to turn.

I saw the LORD sitting on his throne. Micaiah shows what has happened in God’s court in heaven, the host of heaven standing on either side, and it is the hardest thing in the chapter to understand.

A real difficulty. Scripture says without qualification that God is not a man that he should lie, and that he cannot lie (Numbers 23:19; Hebrews 6:18). This vision shows him presiding over a council in which a deceiving spirit is commissioned and sent. Both are in the Bible and neither is going to be withdrawn. Three things can be said, and the third matters most.

A spirit came forward. First, God does not speak the lie. He permits and directs a spirit that is already willing, and every false word is spoken by Zedekiah and his four hundred out of their own mouths, for their own reasons: a court prophet’s living depends on telling a king what he wants. Nobody in that gateway was forced to say anything.

Who will entice Ahab? Second, this is judgment, not a trap set for an innocent man. Ahab has spent a reign refusing the truth. He married Jezebel, let prophets be killed, hunted Elijah, and by his own account keeps Micaiah at arm’s length because the man is always right. The New Testament states the same principle: because people refused to love the truth and so be saved, God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11). The delusion is not the beginning of the story but the judgment at the end of it.

A lying spirit in the mouth of these your prophets. Third, and this eases most of the difficulty, Micaiah tells him. The deception is announced to its intended victim, in public, before a horse has moved. Ahab is told in plain words that the four hundred who have just promised him victory speak under a lying spirit and that God has declared disaster concerning him. He has the truth, from a prophet whose truthfulness he has himself admitted, in front of a witness. A deception you have been warned about, by name, in advance, has stopped being a deception; it has become a last chance to turn back. What Ahab does with it is arrest the messenger and go to war in disguise, the behaviour of someone who believed every word and meant to outmanoeuvre it anyway.

The truth spoken plainly. The God who cannot lie has spoken to us finally “by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2), who is “the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). His warnings, like Micaiah’s, are mercy given in advance.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew says the spirit came forward, and who is meant is not clear. Some think of a particular evil spirit, or of Satan, who appears in God’s heavenly court in Job 1–2; others think of the spirit of prophecy personified, turned to falsehood as judgment. The text does not say, and its point stands either way: the deception is under God’s rule and serves his judgment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–34 — A Bow Drawn at Random
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Neither violence nor cleverness can stop God’s word, and the God who judges Ahab hears Jehoshaphat’s cry. Zedekiah strikes Micaiah, and Ahab jails him on bread and water until he returns in peace; Micaiah stakes his name on the outcome (vv. 23–27). In battle Ahab disguises himself and leaves his ally in royal robes; the Syrian chariots turn on Jehoshaphat, he cries out, and the LORD helps him and draws them away (vv. 28–32). Then an arrow drawn at random finds the gap in Ahab’s armour, and at sunset he dies (vv. 33–34). The word Micaiah spoke has come true in every detail.
verseByVerse.theology: No disguise hides a man from God. Ahab could plan against Micaiah's word, but not escape it.
verseByVerse.examples: When you are caught in a place you should never have gone, the first thing to do is what Jehoshaphat did: cry out. God hears that cry even from the wrong battlefield.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek and said, "Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go from me to speak to you?" And Micaiah said, "Behold, you shall see on that day when you go into an inner chamber to hide yourself." And the king of Israel said, "Seize Micaiah and take him back to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king's son, and say, 'Thus says the king, Put this fellow in prison and feed him with meager rations of bread and water until I return in peace.'" And Micaiah said, "If you return in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me." And he said, "Hear, all you peoples!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Micaiah is slapped and jailed for telling the truth, and he stakes his standing as a prophet on Ahab not returning in peace.

Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go from me to speak to you? Zedekiah’s answer is a slap and a sarcastic question that assumes the very thing in dispute, that the Spirit was in him to begin with.

You shall see on that day. Micaiah does not argue either: you will know which of us spoke for God on the day you are looking for somewhere to hide.

Seize Micaiah. Then the king disposes of him: prison, and meager rations of bread and water until I return in peace. It is not an execution; Ahab is confident enough to plan a conversation afterwards.

If you return in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me. Micaiah applies to himself the test the law lays down for a prophet (Deuteronomy 18:22), in front of the court, and then turns to everyone standing there: Hear, all you peoples!

The Prophet who was struck. Micaiah’s cheek points forward. Jesus too was struck for telling the truth, and answered, “if what I said is right, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23). His tormentors even repeated Zedekiah’s taunt in their own words: “Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who is it that struck you?” (Matthew 26:68). Anyone mocked for faithfulness to God’s word walks a road their Lord walked first.

verseByVerse.quote: So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead. And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your robes." And the king of Israel disguised himself, and they went into battle. Now the king of Syria had commanded the captains of his chariots, "Fight with neither small nor great, but only with the king of Israel." As soon as the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "It is the king of Israel." So they turned to fight against him. And Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him; God drew them away from him. For as soon as the captains of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him. But a certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the scale armor and the breastplate. Therefore he said to the driver of his chariot, "Turn around and carry me out of the battle, for I am wounded." And the battle continued that day, and the king of Israel was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians until evening. Then at sunset he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahab tries to outwit God’s word by disguise, using his ally as a decoy; God rescues Jehoshaphat when he cries out, and an arrow shot at random finds Ahab exactly as Micaiah said.

Going anyway. Both kings go up. The man who asked for another prophet, got one and heard him, goes anyway.

I will disguise myself. Ahab’s plan makes sense only if he believes Micaiah. He makes his ally the most conspicuous man on the field: not asking Jehoshaphat to share a risk, but using him as a decoy, and Jehoshaphat agrees to it.

Only with the king of Israel. The Syrians have orders to fight nobody else, so the chariot captains see a man in royal robes and turn on him.

The LORD helped him; God drew them away from him. In Kings, Jehoshaphat cries out and the captains realise their mistake (1 Kings 22:32–33). Chronicles keeps that and puts these two clauses in front of it. The king who should never have been in that battle, dressed as bait by a man deceiving him, shouts in the middle of a chariot charge, and God gets him out.

Rescue, not reward. Jehoshaphat had promised his army before asking, asked afterwards, heard the true word, and marched. He was wrong at every stage and God rescued him at the last one, and a prophet will be waiting for him when he gets home (19:2). A believer who has walked into trouble by his own folly should still cry out: the God of Jehoshaphat does not wait for us to deserve help.

A certain man drew his bow at random. Nobody aimed at Ahab; nobody could, because nobody could see him. An unnamed soldier let one arrow go in the general direction of the enemy, and it found the one gap in the armour of the one man the whole day was about. Ahab had taken the only precaution available, and it was beaten by what looked like chance, which in this book is another name for God’s hand. He is propped up in his chariot until evening so that the army will not break, and at sunset he dies, and Micaiah’s word about the scattered sheep comes true (v. 16; 1 Kings 22:36).

A king in another’s place. Ahab put another man in the place of danger so that he himself might live, and could not escape. The Son of David did the opposite. He took the place marked out for us, “the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18), and no arrow of judgment is left for those who hide in him.

18.theology:
The vision of verses 18-22 is judgment on a man who had spent a reign refusing the truth, and because Micaiah tells him, it becomes a last chance to turn back. Against that stands verse 31, which only this book has. Jehoshaphat was wrong at every stage, and when the chariots turned on him, the LORD helped him; God drew them away from him. It is not a reward, and there is a prophet waiting for him in the next chapter. It is mercy to a man who had earned none, and his cry in the chariot charge is the way back for every believer who has walked into what he was warned against.

Ahab’s last arrangement is the gospel in reverse. A king who knew death was coming put his robes on another man to draw the arrows, and hid among the soldiers. The true Shepherd of Israel went out in front of the flock, took the blows meant for it, and laid down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). Ahab's army was scattered because its king died for his own sin; Christ's flock is gathered because its King died for theirs. Even Micaiah's slap has its echo: the true Prophet was struck in the high priest's house and mocked with the demand to prophesy (Matthew 26:67-68), and every word he had spoken came true.
18.examples:
The time to ask God is before the commitment, not after it. Jehoshaphat's inquire first came after he had promised his army, his people and himself.

The kind advice to say what everyone else is saying is the oldest pressure there is, and Micaiah answered it with an oath. That courage is not a matter of temperament; the Spirit enabled the first Christians to speak the word with boldness when everyone in the room wanted them silent (Acts 4:31).

keyVerse.quote: But Micaiah said, “As the LORD lives, what my God says, that I will speak.”
keyVerse.note: Against four hundred voices, a king’s hatred and a friendly warning on the road, one man binds himself to God’s word, and the whole chapter proves him right. It shows what Jehoshaphat lacked when he said “I am as you are” before asking anything, and it points to the faithful Prophet who spoke only what his Father gave him and was struck for it.

18.reflection:
Jehoshaphat said “I am as you are” to Ahab before he had asked a single question (v. 3). Where are you most tempted to commit yourself first and ask God afterwards, and why is it so hard to ask first?

Four hundred prophets agreed, and they were wrong (vv. 5, 11). How can we tell the difference between advice that is true and advice we like because it agrees with us? Who in your life tells you the truth?

Ahab hated Micaiah because he “never prophesies good concerning me” (v. 7). Are there parts of Scripture you avoid for the same reason? What would it look like to welcome them?

Jehoshaphat was wrong at every stage, yet when he cried out, “the LORD helped him” (v. 31). How does God’s rescue of the undeserving point to Christ, and how should it shape the way you pray when trouble is your own fault?

19.title: Fear the LORD and Act Faithfully
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Jehoshaphat the king of Judah returned in safety to his house in Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>But Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him and said to King Jehoshaphat, "Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you from the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Nevertheless, some good is found in you, for you destroyed the Asheroth out of the land, and have set your heart to seek God."<sup>4</sup>Jehoshaphat lived at Jerusalem. And he went out again among the people, from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim, and brought them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers.<sup>5</sup>He appointed judges in the land in all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city,<sup>6</sup>and said to the judges, "Consider what you do, for you judge not for man but for the LORD. He is with you in giving judgment.<sup>7</sup>Now then, let the fear of the LORD be upon you. Be careful what you do, for there is no injustice with the LORD our God, or partiality or taking bribes."<sup>8</sup>Moreover, in Jerusalem Jehoshaphat appointed certain Levites and priests and heads of families of Israel, to give judgment for the LORD and to decide disputed cases. They had their seat at Jerusalem.<sup>9</sup>And he charged them: "Thus you shall do in the fear of the LORD, in faithfulness, and with your whole heart:<sup>10</sup>whenever a case comes to you from your brothers who live in their cities, concerning bloodshed, law or commandment, statutes or rules, then you shall warn them, that they may not incur guilt before the LORD and wrath may not come upon you and your brothers. Thus you shall do, and you will not incur guilt.<sup>11</sup>And behold, Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of the LORD; and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the governor of the house of Judah, in all the king's matters, and the Levites will serve you as officers. Deal courageously, and may the LORD be with the upright!"
19.overview:
Where we are. Jehoshaphat has come home alive from Ramoth-gilead, where Ahab died and he himself was saved only because he cried out to God (chapter 18). Before the next crisis, the Chronicler shows how a good king answers a rebuke.

The message. God tells his servants the truth about themselves, the wrong and the good together, and a heart that receives it turns that truth into service. Jehoshaphat, rebuked and commended in one breath, answers by bringing his people back to God and by setting up courts that copy God’s own justice: “there is no injustice with the LORD our God, or partiality or taking bribes” (v. 7).

Why it was said. The first readers ran their own affairs under Persian rule, with magistrates and judges appointed from among themselves (Ezra 7:25), and lived among powerful families who could buy a verdict (see the introduction). The chapter set before them the standard for their courts, and the pattern of repentance that turns a rebuke into reform.

How the chapter makes its case. Jehoshaphat returns safely, and Jehu the seer meets him with wrath and commendation in the same breath (vv. 1–3). The king answers with action. He goes out himself from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim to bring the people back to the LORD (v. 4). He appoints judges in every fortified city and charges them to judge for the LORD, whose character is their standard (vv. 5–7). And he seats a court in Jerusalem of Levites, priests and heads of families, with the chief priest over the LORD’s matters and a governor over the king’s (vv. 8–11).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God the chapter reveals. The God with whom there is no injustice, partiality or bribery is the God of the cross, where he neither overlooked sin nor took a bribe to drop the case, but bore the penalty himself in his Son, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). And the Father “has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), the one Judge whose verdicts are perfectly true and perfectly merciful, as Jehu’s word was in miniature.

For us. When God’s word rebukes you, do not sulk or hide; repent, and get back to work as Jehoshaphat did. Hear the good he names as well as the wrong, because in Christ you can bear both. And wherever you hold any power to decide, in an office, a classroom, a church or a home, judge “not for man but for the LORD”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Jehoshaphat the whole truth about himself, the wrong and the good together. The king comes home safe from a battle he should never have joined (v. 1). Jehu the son of Hanani, whose father Asa had jailed for a similar rebuke, goes out to meet him with a sharp question: should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? Wrath has gone out against him for it (v. 2). Yet in the same breath God names the good in him: the Asherah poles destroyed and a heart set to seek God (v. 3). The verdict has two columns, and neither cancels the other.
verseByVerse.theology: Jehoshaphat's sin was not only what he did but whom he loved (v. 2). God cares about the attachments of our hearts as well as our actions.
verseByVerse.examples: A believer who has been rebuked, by Scripture, a friend or a conscience, can take heart from this verse: God's correction comes to his own people with his kindness still in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoshaphat the king of Judah returned in safety to his house in Jerusalem. But Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him and said to King Jehoshaphat, "Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you from the LORD. Nevertheless, some good is found in you, for you destroyed the Asheroth out of the land, and have set your heart to seek God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends a prophet to tell Jehoshaphat that his alliance with Ahab has brought wrath on him, and in the same breath that God has seen and valued the good in him.

Returned in safety to his house. He comes home in safety, which looks back to 18:31: dressed as bait, he shouted, and God drew the chariots off. He is alive because of a rescue he did nothing to earn.

Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him. A man is waiting for him: the son of the seer Hanani, whom Asa put in the stocks in a rage for a rebuke three chapters ago (16:7–10). So Hanani’s son walks out to meet Asa’s son, knowing exactly what rebuking this royal family cost his father, and goes anyway.

Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? Two verbs, and the second is the sharper. Helping the wicked is what the alliance did; love those who hate the LORD is what it revealed. Jehoshaphat had not merely made a calculation about Ramoth-gilead. He liked Ahab, had married into the family, and had said I am as you are to a man whose wife was killing prophets.

Nevertheless, some good is found in you. Then the word turns, and this is the heart of the chapter. God’s assessment of a man on the worst day of his reign includes the good in him, named item by item: the Asheroth, the poles of the goddess Asherah, pulled down, and a heart set to seek God. That is the phrase used of the northerners who came south under Rehoboam (11:16), and the very thing Rehoboam himself never did (12:14). Both are true of the same man in the same breath, and neither cancels the other.

A verdict with two columns. Our culture has two ways of judging people, opposite and equally harsh. One finds the worst thing a person has done and lets it define him: one failure, one sentence dug up from years ago, and the whole life is written off. The other refuses to judge at all and calls any verdict intolerance. The first has no mercy and the second no truth. Jehu’s word has both. God sees more clearly than any critic and more kindly than any flatterer, and he names both columns without adding them up into a label. Only someone who will not be destroyed by the truth can bear to hear it said like that, and that is what the gospel makes of a believer. Because the condemnation has fallen on Christ (Romans 8:1–3), a Christian can be told the worst about himself without being crushed and the best without being puffed up, and then go back to work, as Jehoshaphat did in the very next verse.

Where did the wrath fall? The Chronicler does not say. Many see it in the invasion that comes “after this” (20:1), others in the misery his son’s marriage to Ahab’s daughter brought on Judah (chapters 21–22). Either way, the commendation did not cancel the consequences, and the consequences did not cancel the commendation.

Does this forbid Christians any cooperation with unbelievers? It condemns a king of God’s people joining an idolatrous king in his war. Christians work, trade and serve among unbelievers (1 Corinthians 5:10), but must not be yoked with them in what compromises faith (2 Corinthians 6:14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–11 — You Judge Not for Man but for the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehoshaphat answers rebuke with reform, and his reform rests on God’s own character. He goes out in person through the whole land, from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim, bringing the people back to the LORD (v. 4). He appoints judges in every fortified city and reminds them that they judge not for man but for the LORD, who is with them and with whom there is no injustice, partiality or bribery (vv. 5–7). In Jerusalem he seats a court of appeal of Levites, priests and heads of families, to judge in the fear of the LORD and to warn people before they incur guilt, with a chief priest presiding in the LORD’s matters and a governor in the king’s (vv. 8–11).
verseByVerse.theology: Justice is not a secular matter that sits outside faith. God cares how disputes are settled, how the weak are treated in court, and whether anyone can buy a verdict.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone with authority over others, a parent, a manager, an elder, is answerable for how it is used. Verse 10 applies that to judges in so many words.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoshaphat lived at Jerusalem. And he went out again among the people, from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim, and brought them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers. He appointed judges in the land in all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city, and said to the judges, "Consider what you do, for you judge not for man but for the LORD. He is with you in giving judgment. Now then, let the fear of the LORD be upon you. Be careful what you do, for there is no injustice with the LORD our God, or partiality or taking bribes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoshaphat answers the rebuke by going out himself to bring the people back to God, then appoints judges in every city and charges them to judge as God judges, without injustice, partiality or bribes.

He went out again among the people. What he does with the rebuke is the measure of him. Again, because in his third year he had sent officials and Levites round the towns with the Book of the Law (17:7–9). This time he goes himself, the length of the country, from Beersheba in the southern desert to the hill country of Ephraim in the north, and brings them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers.

He appointed judges in the land. Then the courts, the most detailed arrangement for government in these two books: not one central court people must travel to, but judges in every walled town. He was not inventing a system. The law had commanded judges in all the towns (Deuteronomy 16:18) and sent cases too hard for them to the priests and the judge at the place the LORD would choose (Deuteronomy 17:8–9), which is the court verses 8–11 set up in Jerusalem.

You judge not for man but for the LORD. The charge speaks of God before it speaks of procedure. The judge’s seat is not his own; he is not administering the king’s law on the king’s behalf but doing God’s work in God’s place, and he is with you in giving judgment. That is a terrifying thing to be told before a day’s hearings and a great comfort in the middle of one.

There is no injustice with the LORD our God, or partiality or taking bribes. The standard is not a set of rules but God’s own character. Three things are named because they are the three ways a court actually fails: a wrong verdict, a verdict bent toward the important party, and a verdict bought. The law had named the same three (Deuteronomy 16:19). Judges are not told to be fair in the abstract; they are told what God is like and instructed to be like him.

Is justice only the interest of the strong? In Plato’s Republic a sophist named Thrasymachus argues that justice is nothing but the advantage of the stronger: whoever holds power writes the rules and calls them just. Many people today suspect he was right, and not without reason. Laws often protect those who wrote them, and courts have been bought in every age. But the suspicion assumes something. To call a court corrupt you must believe in a justice it has betrayed, one that is not simply whatever the powerful decide. Thrasymachus cannot explain our outrage; he can only explain it away. Jehoshaphat’s charge gives that justice a home. It does not rest in the king or the majority but in the character of a God with whom there is no injustice, partiality or bribery, and judges are to copy him. That is why the Bible can be fiercer about crooked courts than any revolutionary. It is also why the gospel is not a loophole. When God justifies the ungodly he takes no bribe and does not drop the case; he bears the penalty himself in his Son, so that he is both just and the one who justifies (Romans 3:26).
verseByVerse.note: Jehoshaphat means “the LORD judges”, and he reformed Judah’s courts.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, in Jerusalem Jehoshaphat appointed certain Levites and priests and heads of families of Israel, to give judgment for the LORD and to decide disputed cases. They had their seat at Jerusalem. And he charged them: "Thus you shall do in the fear of the LORD, in faithfulness, and with your whole heart: whenever a case comes to you from your brothers who live in their cities, concerning bloodshed, law or commandment, statutes or rules, then you shall warn them, that they may not incur guilt before the LORD and wrath may not come upon you and your brothers. Thus you shall do, and you will not incur guilt. And behold, Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of the LORD; and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the governor of the house of Judah, in all the king's matters, and the Levites will serve you as officers. Deal courageously, and may the LORD be with the upright!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Jerusalem a court of appeal of Levites, priests and family heads is charged to judge faithfully, to warn people before they sin, and to keep the LORD’s matters and the king’s distinct, with courage.

Certain Levites and priests and heads of families. They sit in Jerusalem to give judgment for the LORD and to decide disputed cases, an appeal court for what the town courts cannot settle (see Priests and Levites and Elders). The charge names three ways to judge: in the fear of the LORD, in faithfulness, and with your whole heart.

You shall warn them. Verse 10 says something no modern court would say out loud: the judges are to warn them, so that wrath does not come on the judges and their brothers. The judge’s work includes warning, not only ruling on what has been done but telling people where the edge is before they walk off it. And the judge himself is at risk: the guilt of a bad verdict does not stop with the parties in the case.

Amariah the chief priest … Zebadiah the son of Ishmael. Authority is divided with remarkable clarity for the ninth century before Christ: the chief priest over all matters of the LORD, the governor over all the king’s matters. The same bench hears both kinds of case and knows which authority it answers to in each, and the king who set it up has deliberately put half of it beyond his own reach.

A priest on his throne. In Israel the two offices were kept apart, and a later king who grasped at the priest’s work was struck with leprosy (26:16–21). Zechariah foresaw one in whom they would meet: he “shall sit and rule on his throne. And there shall be a priest on his throne” (Zechariah 6:13). Jesus is both, the King who rules his people and the Priest who offered himself for them (Hebrews 7:1–3, 26–27).

Deal courageously. Literally, be strong and act, as David charged Solomon, “be strong and do it” (1 Chronicles 28:10). Courage is what a judge needs, because the hard cases are hard for one reason: somebody powerful will be unhappy with the answer. And the charge closes with a promise, not a threat: may the LORD be with the upright!

19.theology:
Verses 6 and 7 tell a court in two sentences whom it serves and by what standard: the judge works for the LORD, and the standard is God's own character. Verse 3 shows how God assesses his own people, wrath and good named together, and the man who heard both spent the rest of the chapter working.

Jehoshaphat's charge describes a judge no human bench has fully supplied, with no injustice, no partiality and no bribes. Isaiah promised a shoot from Jesse who would judge with righteousness and not by appearances (Isaiah 11:3-4), and Jesus said the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). That Judge cannot be bribed, which is sobering. He is also the one who bore the wrath that had gone out against his people, so his verdict over them is no condemnation (Romans 8:1).
19.examples:
