Corrected about one thing, Jehoshaphat responded by doing more of the thing he had been right about: after sending others round the towns in his third year, he now went himself.

The charge ends by telling the bench it will need courage. Anyone who must give a hard answer to somebody powerful, at work or in a church, stands in the same place, and the courage is not self-made: the Lord who is with you in giving judgment gives his Spirit to his people for exactly such hours.

keyVerse.quote: Now then, let the fear of the LORD be upon you. Be careful what you do, for there is no injustice with the LORD our God, or partiality or taking bribes.
keyVerse.note: This verse grounds all human justice in the character of God. Judges are not handed a rulebook but shown what God is like and told to be like him, and the king who gives the charge has just received such a verdict himself, truthful about his sin and generous about his good. The same God, without injustice or bribe, justifies sinners at the cross by bearing their penalty in his Son.

19.reflection:
Jehu asked Jehoshaphat, “Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD?” (v. 2). Where is the line between serving unbelievers and being bound to them in ways that compromise faith? Where might you have crossed it?

God named both Jehoshaphat’s sin and the “good” found in him (vv. 2–3). Which do you find harder to hear about yourself, and how does the gospel make it possible to hear both?

Jehoshaphat answered rebuke by going out to bring the people back to the LORD (v. 4). What does it look like for repentance to turn into fresh service rather than lasting gloom?

Judges were to act “not for man but for the LORD”, with no partiality or bribes (vv. 6–7). Where do you have power to decide things for other people, and what would it mean to exercise it as God does?

20.title: The Battle Is Not Yours but God's
20.text: <sup>1</sup>After this the Moabites and Ammonites, and with them some of the Meunites, came against Jehoshaphat for battle.<sup>2</sup>Some men came and told Jehoshaphat, "A great multitude is coming against you from Edom, from beyond the sea; and, behold, they are in Hazazon-tamar" (that is, Engedi).<sup>3</sup>Then Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek the LORD, and proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah.<sup>4</sup>And Judah assembled to seek help from the LORD; from all the cities of Judah they came to seek the LORD.<sup>5</sup>And Jehoshaphat stood in the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem, in the house of the LORD, before the new court,<sup>6</sup>and said, "O LORD, God of our fathers, are you not God in heaven? You rule over all the kingdoms of the nations. In your hand are power and might, so that none is able to withstand you.<sup>7</sup>Did you not, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel, and give it forever to the descendants of Abraham your friend?<sup>8</sup>And they have lived in it and have built for you in it a sanctuary for your name, saying,<sup>9</sup>'If disaster comes upon us, the sword, judgment, or pestilence, or famine, we will stand before this house and before you— for your name is in this house—and cry out to you in our affliction, and you will hear and save.'<sup>10</sup>And now behold, the men of Ammon and Moab and Mount Seir, whom you would not let Israel invade when they came from the land of Egypt, and whom they avoided and did not destroy—<sup>11</sup>behold, they reward us by coming to drive us out of your possession, which you have given us to inherit.<sup>12</sup>O our God, will you not execute judgment on them? For we are powerless against this great horde that is coming against us. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you."<sup>13</sup>Meanwhile all Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children.<sup>14</sup>And the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jahaziel the son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jeiel, son of Mattaniah, a Levite of the sons of Asaph, in the midst of the assembly.<sup>15</sup>And he said, "Listen, all Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem and King Jehoshaphat: Thus says the LORD to you, 'Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed at this great horde, for the battle is not yours but God's.<sup>16</sup>Tomorrow go down against them. Behold, they will come up by the ascent of Ziz. You will find them at the end of the valley, east of the wilderness of Jeruel.<sup>17</sup>You will not need to fight in this battle. Stand firm, hold your position, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf, O Judah and Jerusalem.' Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed. Tomorrow go out against them, and the LORD will be with you."<sup>18</sup>Then Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground, and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fell down before the LORD, worshiping the LORD.<sup>19</sup>And the Levites, of the Kohathites and the Korahites, stood up to praise the LORD, the God of Israel, with a very loud voice.<sup>20</sup>And they rose early in the morning and went out into the wilderness of Tekoa. And when they went out, Jehoshaphat stood and said, "Hear me, Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem! Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be established; believe his prophets, and you will succeed."<sup>21</sup>And when he had taken counsel with the people, he appointed those who were to sing to the LORD and praise him in holy attire, as they went before the army, and say, "Give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever."<sup>22</sup>And when they began to sing and praise, the LORD set an ambush against the men of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir, who had come against Judah, so that they were routed.<sup>23</sup>For the men of Ammon and Moab rose against the inhabitants of Mount Seir, devoting them to destruction, and when they had made an end of the inhabitants of Seir, they all helped to destroy one another.<sup>24</sup>When Judah came to the watchtower of the wilderness, they looked toward the horde, and behold, there were dead bodies lying on the ground; none had escaped.<sup>25</sup>When Jehoshaphat and his people came to take their spoil, they found among them, in great numbers, goods, clothing, and precious things, which they took for themselves until they could carry no more. They were three days in taking the spoil, it was so much.<sup>26</sup>On the fourth day they assembled in the Valley of Beracah, for there they blessed the LORD. Therefore the name of that place has been called the Valley of Beracah to this day.<sup>27</sup>Then they returned, every man of Judah and Jerusalem, and Jehoshaphat at their head, returning to Jerusalem with joy, for the LORD had made them rejoice over their enemies.<sup>28</sup>They came to Jerusalem with harps and lyres and trumpets, to the house of the LORD.<sup>29</sup>And the fear of God came on all the kingdoms of the countries when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel.<sup>30</sup>So the realm of Jehoshaphat was quiet, for his God gave him rest all around.<sup>31</sup>Thus Jehoshaphat reigned over Judah. He was thirty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi.<sup>32</sup>He walked in the way of Asa his father and did not turn aside from it, doing what was right in the sight of the LORD.<sup>33</sup>The high places, however, were not taken away; the people had not yet set their hearts upon the God of their fathers.<sup>34</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, from first to last, are written in the chronicles of Jehu the son of Hanani, which are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel.<sup>35</sup>After this Jehoshaphat king of Judah joined with Ahaziah king of Israel, who acted wickedly.<sup>36</sup>He joined him in building ships to go to Tarshish, and they built the ships in Ezion-geber.<sup>37</sup>Then Eliezer the son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying, "Because you have joined with Ahaziah, the LORD will destroy what you have made." And the ships were wrecked and were not able to go to Tarshish.
20.overview:
Where we are. Jehoshaphat has been rebuked for his alliance with Ahab and has answered by bringing the people back to God and reforming the courts (chapter 19). Now comes the crisis of his reign, one of the high points of the whole book.

The message. When God’s people admit they are helpless and turn their eyes to him, he fights for them: “the battle is not yours but God’s” (v. 15). Prayer that rests on his character and promises, faith that believes his word, and praise sung before the victory are how a weak people lay hold of his strength. Yet after such a day the king drifts back into the old alliance, for only God is faithful to the end.

Why it was said. The first readers were a small, unarmed province with hostile neighbours, among them an Ammonite and an Arab who jeered at the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s wall (Nehemiah 2:19; see the introduction). This chapter showed them that a people with no strength could still stand in God’s house, pray, and find that the battle was his.

How the chapter makes its case. A vast coalition is already at Engedi; Jehoshaphat is afraid, seeks the LORD and calls a fast, and all Judah gathers (vv. 1–4). His prayer rehearses God’s rule over the nations, his gift of the land to Abraham’s descendants and Solomon’s prayer for this very trouble, and ends, “We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you” (vv. 5–13). The Spirit comes on Jahaziel, a temple singer: do not fear; stand firm and see the LORD’s salvation (vv. 14–17). They worship, and at dawn the king calls them to believe and sends singers ahead of the army (vv. 18–21). As they sing, the enemies destroy one another; Judah gathers spoil for three days, blesses God in the Valley of Beracah, and comes home with joy to rest (vv. 22–30). The reign is summed up, and it closes with one more alliance with Ahab’s house and a fleet wrecked (vv. 31–37).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the need it exposes. Judah won a battle it never fought; the gospel tells of a greater battle won by one man alone. At the cross Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15), and his people, who lifted no hand, gather the spoils and bless God. And the chapter’s ending shows why we need him: even Jehoshaphat, after the Valley of Blessing, fell back. The King we need is the one who never turned aside.

For us. When you do not know what to do, say so to God and fix your eyes on him; that is not the end of faith but often its beginning. Believe his word in Scripture, and praise him before you see the outcome. And take the last verses as a warning: a great day of grace does not make us safe from old weaknesses, so keep watch.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — We Do Not Know What to Do
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When danger comes, Judah’s king answers fear with prayer, and his prayer rests on who God is and what he has promised. The news arrives late: a great multitude from Moab, Ammon and the Meunites is already at Engedi (vv. 1–2). Jehoshaphat is afraid, sets his face to seek the LORD and proclaims a fast, and people come from every town to seek him (vv. 3–4). Standing in the temple court, the king appeals to God’s rule over all nations, his gift of the land to Abraham’s offspring, and Solomon’s prayer for this very trouble (vv. 5–9). He names the enemy’s ingratitude and confesses Judah’s helplessness, “our eyes are on you” (vv. 10–12), while all Judah stands there with their little ones (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer spends most of its length on God, his rule, his gifts and his promises, before it names the danger. Praying that way does not make the danger smaller; it sets it in its true size.
verseByVerse.examples: Jehoshaphat was not ashamed to pray in public that he did not know what to do. Leaders who admit their limits before God free others to do the same.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the Moabites and Ammonites, and with them some of the Meunites, came against Jehoshaphat for battle. Some men came and told Jehoshaphat, "A great multitude is coming against you from Edom, from beyond the sea; and, behold, they are in Hazazon-tamar" (that is, Engedi). Then Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek the LORD, and proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah. And Judah assembled to seek help from the LORD; from all the cities of Judah they came to seek the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With an enemy army already inside his borders, Jehoshaphat is afraid, and his fear drives him and all Judah to seek the LORD.

A great multitude is coming against you. The news arrives late. The coalition has come round the Dead Sea and is already at Engedi, some twenty-five miles from Jerusalem across the wilderness.

Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek the LORD. Afraid, and set his face to seek, in a single breath. The Chronicler writes the fear down without embarrassment, of a man he approves of, in a chapter that will end in total victory. The fear did not disqualify the seeking; it produced it. Set his face is a phrase of deliberate turning: a man frightened out of his routine, pointing himself somewhere on purpose. Fear is not the opposite of faith; where it drives us to God, it becomes the occasion of it.

Proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah. Then verse 4 uses this book’s favourite verb twice more: Judah came to seek the LORD, from all the cities of Judah. These are the towns Jehoshaphat had sent teachers round with the Book of the Law (17:7–9). This is what the years of teaching produced: when a coalition crosses the border, the villages empty toward Jerusalem instead of toward the armoury.

Textual note. In verse 2 most Hebrew manuscripts read Aram (Syria); the ESV follows one Hebrew manuscript in reading Edom, which fits the route round the south of the Dead Sea, and in Hebrew the two names differ by one easily confused letter. In verse 1 the Hebrew repeats “Ammonites”, which makes little sense after “Moabites and Ammonites”; the ESV reads Meunites, a desert people named again in 26:7, and they are probably the “Mount Seir” of verses 10 and 22.
verseByVerse.note: En-gedi lay on the western shore of the Dead Sea.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jehoshaphat stood in the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem, in the house of the LORD, before the new court, and said, "O LORD, God of our fathers, are you not God in heaven? You rule over all the kingdoms of the nations. In your hand are power and might, so that none is able to withstand you. Did you not, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel, and give it forever to the descendants of Abraham your friend? And they have lived in it and have built for you in it a sanctuary for your name, saying, 'If disaster comes upon us, the sword, judgment, or pestilence, or famine, we will stand before this house and before you— for your name is in this house—and cry out to you in our affliction, and you will hear and save.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoshaphat’s prayer begins not with the danger but with God: his rule over every nation, his gift of the land to Abraham’s family, and his promise to hear prayer made at his house. The prayer is built in the order a good prayer is built, and it takes a long time to reach the request.

Before the new court. He stands in an extension to the temple precinct whose origin the text does not give. The building has been kept up and enlarged, and the nation is now packed into it.

Are you not God in heaven? Every clause is about how far God’s rule reaches: God in heaven, ruling over all the kingdoms of the nations, including the three now marching. Before he mentions the invasion, Jehoshaphat establishes that it is happening inside God’s territory, and he does it in words from David’s prayer at the end of his life: “In your hand are power and might” (1 Chronicles 29:12).

Abraham your friend. The land was given forever to the descendants of Abraham your friend. Only one other place in the Old Testament calls Abraham that (Isaiah 41:8), and the New Testament picks it up: “he was called a friend of God” (James 2:23). Jehoshaphat is reminding God of someone they both knew.

If disaster comes upon us. Verses 8 and 9 quote, almost clause for clause, Solomon’s dedication prayer, which asked God to hear prayers made in famine, pestilence, siege and war (6:28–35). God had answered then: “my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer that is made in this place” (7:15). About a century later a descendant of Solomon stands in the same courtyard, in exactly that trouble, and reads the clause back. The building is being used for the case it was dedicated for.

Praying on God’s promises. The best prayers are built from what God has already said. We no longer pray toward a building in Jerusalem but through the one who called his body the temple (John 2:19–21), and we have his own promise: “whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you” (John 16:23).

verseByVerse.quote: And now behold, the men of Ammon and Moab and Mount Seir, whom you would not let Israel invade when they came from the land of Egypt, and whom they avoided and did not destroy— behold, they reward us by coming to drive us out of your possession, which you have given us to inherit. O our God, will you not execute judgment on them? For we are powerless against this great horde that is coming against us. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you." Meanwhile all Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoshaphat lays the danger before God, appeals to his justice, and confesses that Judah has neither strength nor plan, only eyes turned to him.

Whom you would not let Israel invade. There is a bitterness in the way he puts it. All three nations, Ammon, Moab and Mount Seir, were peoples Israel had been forbidden to attack on the way from Egypt, because God had given their lands to Esau and to the sons of Lot (Deuteronomy 2:4–19). Israel had gone the long way round them, at some cost.

They reward us. Now they are on the road to Jerusalem. Jehoshaphat is not accusing God; he is reminding him that Israel obeyed, and asking him to see how these nations have repaid it: will you not execute judgment on them?

We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you. Two admissions and one direction. We have no strength. We have no plan: a king saying that in public, in front of his own commanders, about an army already inside the border. And then, instead of a strategy, a posture. It is the shortest honest prayer for anyone in real trouble, and anyone can pray it, because it requires nothing except telling the truth about your position and looking to God. And eyes turned to God meet eyes already turned toward them: “the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth” (16:9).

The sentence our age finds hardest to say. We do not know what to do is close to unsayable for a modern leader, and for most of us in private. Ours is a culture of the plan: the strategy, the five steps, the expert who can make any problem manageable. Much of our anxiety comes from an unspoken belief that life ought to be under control, and that if it is not, somebody, probably me, has failed. So we hide our helplessness and wear ourselves out keeping up appearances. Jehoshaphat says it aloud, and Scripture records it as faith, not failure. That is the reversal the gospel lives by. The door into God’s help is not competence but admitted need. Jesus said it is the sick, not the well, who need a physician (Mark 2:17), and he gave his first blessing to the poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3). Eyes turned to God are not staring at nothing; they are looking at a Father who knows exactly what to do, and who in his Son has already done the decisive thing.

With their little ones. Verse 13 shows who was standing there: the toddlers are at the prayer meeting. Somebody carried them up from the villages and stood holding them in the temple court through the whole prayer. A nation that believed the danger was real, and believed the answer was here, brought its babies to it. For the Chronicler’s first readers, with no army and hostile neighbours on every side, it was a picture of what they too could do (see the introduction).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — The Battle Is Not Yours but God's
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the prayer through his Spirit, and his answer turns helplessness into trust and praise. The Spirit of the LORD comes on Jahaziel, a Levite singer, in the middle of the assembly: do not be afraid, for the battle is not yours but God’s. They are to go out, take their stand, and see the LORD’s salvation (vv. 14–17). King and people fall down in worship, and the Levites stand to praise with a loud voice (vv. 18–19). At dawn in the wilderness of Tekoa the king calls them to believe the LORD and his prophets, and sends singers in holy attire ahead of the army, singing of God’s steadfast love (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology: God answers a prayer that ended we do not know what to do by telling them exactly what to do, and the instruction is mostly to trust. Guidance often comes that way: enough for tomorrow morning, not the whole campaign.
verseByVerse.examples: Thanksgiving offered before the answer is one of the clearest forms faith takes. Judah sang on the strength of God's word alone, a day before anything had happened.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jahaziel the son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jeiel, son of Mattaniah, a Levite of the sons of Asaph, in the midst of the assembly. And he said, "Listen, all Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem and King Jehoshaphat: Thus says the LORD to you, 'Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed at this great horde, for the battle is not yours but God's. Tomorrow go down against them. Behold, they will come up by the ascent of Ziz. You will find them at the end of the valley, east of the wilderness of Jeruel. You will not need to fight in this battle. Stand firm, hold your position, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf, O Judah and Jerusalem.' Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed. Tomorrow go out against them, and the LORD will be with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers through his Spirit, by the mouth of a temple singer: Judah must not fear, because the battle is God’s; they are to go out, stand still and watch him save.

The Spirit of the LORD came upon Jahaziel. Jahaziel was a chorister. Four generations of his family are given, and the last identification is the one that matters: of the sons of Asaph, the guild of temple singers David appointed. The previous book described that guild in a word most readers pass over: they “prophesied with lyres, with harps, and with cymbals” (1 Chronicles 25:1). There it sounded like a figure of speech. Here a man from that choir stands up in a national emergency, and what he says decides the war.

The Spirit who came and the Spirit who remains. Many think of the Holy Spirit as a force, or a feeling in a meeting. In the Old Testament he is the LORD himself, present and at work, and when he “came upon” someone it was to do something through them for a time: strength for a judge, skill for a craftsman, words for a singer. Here he gives a frightened nation the one thing its king had admitted it lacked, a word from God. Isaiah promised a King on whom the Spirit would not come and go: “the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him” (Isaiah 11:2). At the Jordan it happened: “I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him” (John 1:32). And when Jesus had won the battle nobody else could fight, he poured that Spirit out on all his people. The Spirit who spoke through Jahaziel now lives in every believer, and still speaks through the Scriptures with the same message. The next time you have no idea what to do, open the Bible before you open the plans. See God the Holy Spirit in the Theological Dictionary.

For the battle is not yours but God’s. The king had said we are powerless, and God’s answer is that their weakness does not matter, because the fight was never theirs to win. The ownership of the battle changes hands in one clause, as Asa had asked when he prayed, “let not man prevail against you” (14:11).

Tomorrow go down against them. The orders are specific: tomorrow, the ascent of Ziz, the end of the valley east of the wilderness of Jeruel. God gives a map, and then the strangest military instruction in Scripture.

Stand firm, hold your position, and see the salvation of the LORD. These words have been said once before, on the shore of a sea, by a man with Pharaoh’s chariots behind him: “Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD” (Exodus 14:13). Judah is being put back at the Red Sea, and told to turn up, form a line, and watch.

Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed. The word is framed, beginning and end, by the formula of commissioning: Moses’ words to Joshua (Deuteronomy 31:8) and David’s to Solomon, “Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed” (1 Chronicles 28:20), given to a man at the start of a task too big for him. Here they are given to an army told it will not need to fight. Yet they are still ordered out: “stand firm” does not mean “stay at home”. They must walk into a wilderness and stand in front of an army that outnumbers them, and do nothing, so standing still in the right place takes the same nerve as crossing the Jordan.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground, and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fell down before the LORD, worshiping the LORD. And the Levites, of the Kohathites and the Korahites, stood up to praise the LORD, the God of Israel, with a very loud voice. And they rose early in the morning and went out into the wilderness of Tekoa. And when they went out, Jehoshaphat stood and said, "Hear me, Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem! Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be established; believe his prophets, and you will succeed." And when he had taken counsel with the people, he appointed those who were to sing to the LORD and praise him in holy attire, as they went before the army, and say, "Give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah answers God’s word with worship before anything has happened, and marches out believing, with singers in front of the army praising God’s steadfast love.

Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground. The king and the whole assembly go face-down, and the Levites, Kohathites and Korahites (see Korah), stood up to praise the LORD with a very loud voice. Everyone else is on the floor and the choir is on its feet, shouting. The battle is tomorrow and nothing has happened yet.

Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be established. At dawn, in the wilderness of Tekoa, Jehoshaphat stops the column to say one sentence. In Hebrew it is a play on a single root, the root of amen: trust the God who is firm, and you will be made firm. Isaiah would say the same to a later king of Judah who did not take it: “If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all” (Isaiah 7:9). The command rests on the LORD your God, who has already promised the victory: faith is not the price of his help but the hand that receives it.

Believe his prophets, and you will succeed. Remarkable from this king. Two chapters ago he heard four hundred men tell a king what he wanted to hear and one man tell him the truth, and he marched with the four hundred. He has learned something, and he says it out loud to an army.

In holy attire. The singers go first, in front of the whole column, dressed for worship rather than war, unarmed, walking toward a coalition army.

Give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever. The words this book cannot stop quoting. David appointed singers to give thanks with them when the ark came to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:41); the choir sang them when the glory filled the house (5:13); the nation said them face-down on the pavement when fire came down (7:3). Now they are a marching song, sung by men with nothing in their hands, going down a wadi toward an army they have been told they will not need to fight.

Who are “his prophets” for us? The prophets and apostles whose words God gave in Scripture (Ephesians 2:20). Believe them, and you will stand; there is no new word from modern prophets to add.

Is praise a weapon? God won the battle, and Judah praised him; the singing expressed trust, it did not work a formula. It is no technique for breakthroughs.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated in holy attire is the one rendered “in the splendor of holiness” in Psalm 29:2 and 96:9. It may describe the singers’ sacred robes, or the holy majesty in which they worshipped, or the holiness of the God they praised. Either way, they went out dressed and ready for worship, not war.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his word exactly: Judah does not fight, and the LORD gives the victory, the spoil and the rest. As the singing begins, the LORD sets an ambush, and the coalition turns on itself until none escapes (vv. 22–24). Judah spends three days gathering spoil and on the fourth assembles to bless the LORD in a valley ever after called Beracah, blessing (vv. 25–26). They return to Jerusalem with joy, with harps, lyres and trumpets, to the house where they had prayed (vv. 27–28). The fear of God falls on the nations, because they hear that the LORD has fought, and the realm is quiet, for God gives rest all around (vv. 29–30).
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD set the ambush (v. 22). The text does not explain how, and it does not need to: what matters is who acted.
verseByVerse.examples: It is easy to pray hard in a crisis and forget to give thanks after it. Judah stopped on the fourth day, with the carts loaded, to bless God before going home.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they began to sing and praise, the LORD set an ambush against the men of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir, who had come against Judah, so that they were routed. For the men of Ammon and Moab rose against the inhabitants of Mount Seir, devoting them to destruction, and when they had made an end of the inhabitants of Seir, they all helped to destroy one another. When Judah came to the watchtower of the wilderness, they looked toward the horde, and behold, there were dead bodies lying on the ground; none had escaped. When Jehoshaphat and his people came to take their spoil, they found among them, in great numbers, goods, clothing, and precious things, which they took for themselves until they could carry no more. They were three days in taking the spoil, it was so much. On the fourth day they assembled in the Valley of Beracah, for there they blessed the LORD. Therefore the name of that place has been called the Valley of Beracah to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as Judah begins to praise, God turns the enemy armies on one another, and Judah, who never fought, spends three days gathering spoil and a fourth blessing God.

When they began to sing and praise. Not when the singing was finished, nor when the two armies met. The first verse was still going up out of the wadi when it started.

The LORD set an ambush. What happened is described without any attempt to explain it. Ammon and Moab turned on the men of Seir, and then on each other, and they all helped to destroy one another. Three allies in a narrow valley, and the only cause the text gives is the LORD. By the time Judah reaches the watchtower over the wilderness there is nothing to fight: none had escaped.

Until they could carry no more. Then the spoil, and the detail is domestic: goods, clothing, precious things, more than they could carry. An army told it would not need to fight spent three days carrying property home.

The Valley of Beracah. On the fourth day they did not go home. They stopped in the field, with everything loaded, and blessed the LORD, and the name Beracah, blessing, stuck to the ground so firmly that people still called it that when the Chronicler wrote. Three days collecting, one day thanking, and the day of thanks is the one the map remembered.

Spoil from a battle we did not fight. This is the shape of the gospel. Christ fought alone, “triumphing over them” at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and as the risen conqueror “he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men” (Ephesians 4:8). His people did not lift a hand, and they spend their lives gathering what he won, and blessing God for it.

Uncertain wording. Who the LORD’s ambushers were is not said. Some think of unseen heavenly forces; others of men within the coalition whom God set against their allies, perhaps in a quarrel that ran out of control. The text keeps its attention on the one who set them.
verseByVerse.note: “Beracah” means “blessing” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then they returned, every man of Judah and Jerusalem, and Jehoshaphat at their head, returning to Jerusalem with joy, for the LORD had made them rejoice over their enemies. They came to Jerusalem with harps and lyres and trumpets, to the house of the LORD. And the fear of God came on all the kingdoms of the countries when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel. So the realm of Jehoshaphat was quiet, for his God gave him rest all around.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah comes home rejoicing to the house where it prayed, the nations fear the God who fought for it, and Jehoshaphat’s realm has rest.

Returning to Jerusalem with joy. They went out singing and came back singing, with harps, lyres and trumpets, into the same building they had prayed in days before. The march out and the march home are one procession, and the only thing that changed in between is that God did something.

The fear of God came on all the kingdoms. What frightened the neighbours was not Judah’s army. The report that travelled was about who had done the fighting, that the LORD had fought, as Jahaziel had said. The same fear fell after the teaching mission of his third year (17:10): the same result from two very different causes, once because a king taught his own villages, and once because God destroyed an army nobody in Judah had touched.

His God gave him rest all around. The phrase was last used of Asa’s best years, after Judah sought the LORD with their whole desire (15:15). Rest from enemies was a gift God gave his people when they sought him, and it points to the deeper rest Christ offers: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–37 — And He Did It Again
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The summary of a good reign ends with a reminder that no son of David but one is faithful to the end. Jehoshaphat walked in Asa’s way and did what was right, yet the high places remained, because the people had not yet set their hearts on God (vv. 31–34): a king can teach, judge and pray, but he cannot change hearts. Then, after all he had seen, he joined Ahab’s son Ahaziah in a shipbuilding venture, and a prophet’s word wrecked the fleet before it sailed (vv. 35–37). The good and the failure stand side by side, and the Chronicler leaves both on the record.
verseByVerse.theology: Parents, pastors and teachers who have taught faithfully and seen little change can take some comfort from verse 33. The Chronicler does not blame Jehoshaphat for hearts he could not set.
verseByVerse.examples: Great deliverances do not cure every weakness. A believer can know God's help wonderfully and still fall back into an old attachment, and needs his grace for that too.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Jehoshaphat reigned over Judah. He was thirty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi. He walked in the way of Asa his father and did not turn aside from it, doing what was right in the sight of the LORD. The high places, however, were not taken away; the people had not yet set their hearts upon the God of their fathers. Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, from first to last, are written in the chronicles of Jehu the son of Hanani, which are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoshaphat’s reign is summed up as faithful, but the high places remained because the people’s hearts were not yet set on God, something no king could do for them.

He walked in the way of Asa his father. The summary is generous: twenty-five years, and he did not turn aside, doing what was right in the sight of the LORD.

The high places, however, were not taken away. Chapter 17 said he took the high places and the Asherim out of Judah (17:6). The two statements are usually reconciled by supposing the shrines came back, or that some were never reached. What matters more is the reason this verse gives, because it does not blame the king at all.

The people had not yet set their hearts upon the God of their fathers. Set their hearts is the phrase this book has used since Rehoboam: of the northerners who set their hearts to seek the LORD (11:16), of the king who did not (12:14), and of Jehoshaphat himself (19:3). Here it is said of a whole nation that they had not, after a king had sent the law round every town in the country.

What a king cannot do. He taught them, judged them justly, prayed for them publicly, and led them out with singers in front. He could not set their hearts, and the Chronicler does not suggest he should have been able to. Only God can do that, and he promised to: “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26), a promise kept by the Spirit Christ gives.

The chronicles of Jehu the son of Hanani. The record of the reign was kept by the prophet who rebuked him (19:2). The man who told Jehoshaphat the truth to his face also wrote his history, and the Chronicler trusted it.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jehoshaphat king of Judah joined with Ahaziah king of Israel, who acted wickedly. He joined him in building ships to go to Tarshish, and they built the ships in Ezion-geber. Then Eliezer the son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying, "Because you have joined with Ahaziah, the LORD will destroy what you have made." And the ships were wrecked and were not able to go to Tarshish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even after the Valley of Blessing, Jehoshaphat allies himself again with Ahab’s house, and God wrecks the venture as his prophet said.

After this. After the fast and the toddlers in the temple court, after Jahaziel and the ambush and the Valley of Blessing, and after a prophet had asked him whether he should help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD.

Joined with Ahaziah king of Israel, who acted wickedly. He joins the house of Ahab again, the son this time, and the venture is commercial rather than military: a merchant fleet built at Ezion-geber, on the Red Sea, ships to go to Tarshish. Kings calls them ships of Tarshish bound for Ophir (1 Kings 22:48); the phrase probably named a class of large sea-going trader, and both books describe the same fleet.

The LORD will destroy what you have made. Eliezer of Mareshah pronounces the sentence, and the ships were wrecked and never sailed. The Chronicler puts this at the end of the chapter that holds the best day of Jehoshaphat’s life, and offers no comment. He does not withdraw verse 32, which says the man did what was right and did not turn aside. Both sentences stand about the same person.

A repeated fault. Some faults are not cured by their consequences. This one had already cost him a battle he should never have been in, a rebuke, and a marriage that would shortly put Ahab’s daughter on the throne of Judah with murder in her hands. He knew all of it. He liked them anyway, and God broke the ships up.

The King who did not turn back. The last word on the best king for generations is a wrecked fleet. Chronicles keeps showing that the sons of David cannot finish well, and keeps the reader looking for the one who did: “looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2). Our hope rests on his faithfulness, not on our last chapter.

Joined or refused? Kings says Jehoshaphat refused Ahaziah’s offer (1 Kings 22:49); Chronicles says he joined him. Most likely he first joined him, the ships were wrecked as God warned, and then he refused a second venture.

20.theology:
Verses 8-9 show a promise being used as it was meant to be: Solomon asked God to hear prayer toward that house in trouble, and his descendant claims it. Verse 12 is the whole chapter in one line. God’s answer does not give them the strength they lack. It tells them the fight was never theirs to win, the battle is not yours but God’s, and orders them out to stand still and watch, in the words Moses used at the Red Sea.

The shape of this day is the shape of the gospel. God's people were powerless and said so; the enemy fell without a blow from them; and they spent three days carrying home spoil they had not fought for, and a fourth blessing the God who had won it. The New Testament describes the cross the same way: Christ fought the decisive battle alone, disarmed the powers ranged against his people and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15), and those who trust him share the spoils of a victory in which their part was to stand, believe and sing.

Verse 33 then declines to blame the king for the high places (hilltop shrines). A ruler can pull down an altar, but he cannot set a nation's heart; only the Spirit God promised can do that (Ezekiel 36:26-27).
20.examples:
He was afraid, and the text says so in the same breath as the seeking. Fear did not disqualify him; it turned him round.

Children belong at the prayer meeting. Judah brought even the toddlers, because the danger was real and the answer was there.

The singers walked in front of the army in vestments rather than armour, singing the line that had been sung when the ark came home and when the fire fell, and the ambush was set while the first verse was still going up.

keyVerse.quote: Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed at this great horde, for the battle is not yours but God’s.
keyVerse.note: This is God’s answer to the king’s confession, “We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you” (v. 12), and the hinge of the chapter: the ownership of the battle passes from a powerless people to God. It is the shape of the gospel, in which Christ fought the decisive battle alone and his people receive the victory, and it is the word for every believer who has come to the end of their own strength.

20.reflection:
Jehoshaphat “was afraid and set his face to seek the LORD” (v. 3). When fear comes to you, where does it usually drive you? What would it look like for it to drive you to God?

The king’s prayer begins with who God is and what he has promised before it asks for anything (vv. 5–9). How might building your prayers on God’s character and promises change the way you pray?

“We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you” (v. 12). Why is it so hard to admit helplessness, to God and to others? Is there a situation in your life where you need to pray this prayer now?

After the Valley of Blessing, Jehoshaphat went back to the alliance God had rebuked (vv. 35–37). What old weaknesses tend to return after a season of blessing, and how does Christ’s faithfulness to the end give us hope?

21.title: He Departed with No One's Regret
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Jehoram his son reigned in his place.<sup>2</sup>He had brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah; all these were the sons of Jehoshaphat king of Israel.<sup>3</sup>Their father gave them great gifts of silver, gold, and valuable possessions, together with fortified cities in Judah, but he gave the kingdom to Jehoram, because he was the firstborn.<sup>4</sup>When Jehoram had ascended the throne of his father and was established, he killed all his brothers with the sword, and also some of the princes of Israel.<sup>5</sup>Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.<sup>6</sup>And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, for the daughter of Ahab was his wife. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD.<sup>7</sup>Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy the house of David, because of the covenant that he had made with David, and since he had promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever.<sup>8</sup>In his days Edom revolted from the rule of Judah and set up a king of their own.<sup>9</sup>Then Jehoram passed over with his commanders and all his chariots, and he rose by night and struck the Edomites who had surrounded him and his chariot commanders.<sup>10</sup>So Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day. At that time Libnah also revolted from his rule, because he had forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers.<sup>11</sup>Moreover, he made high places in the hill country of Judah and led the inhabitants of Jerusalem into whoredom and made Judah go astray.<sup>12</sup>And a letter came to him from Elijah the prophet, saying, "Thus says the LORD, the God of David your father, 'Because you have not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat your father, or in the ways of Asa king of Judah,<sup>13</sup>but have walked in the way of the kings of Israel and have enticed Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem into whoredom, as the house of Ahab led Israel into whoredom, and also you have killed your brothers, of your father's house, who were better than you,<sup>14</sup>behold, the LORD will bring a great plague on your people, your children, your wives, and all your possessions,<sup>15</sup>and you yourself will have a severe sickness with a disease of your bowels, until your bowels come out because of the disease, day by day.'"<sup>16</sup>And the LORD stirred up against Jehoram the anger of the Philistines and of the Arabians who are near the Ethiopians.<sup>17</sup>And they came up against Judah and invaded it and carried away all the possessions they found that belonged to the king's house, and also his sons and his wives, so that no son was left to him except Jehoahaz, his youngest son.<sup>18</sup>And after all this the LORD struck him in his bowels with an incurable disease.<sup>19</sup>In the course of time, at the end of two years, his bowels came out because of the disease, and he died in great agony. His people made no fire in his honor, like the fires made for his fathers.<sup>20</sup>He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. And he departed with no one's regret. They buried him in the city of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.
21.overview:
Where we are. Jehoshaphat, one of the better kings in this book, has died. His reign ended with prayer answered and enemies routed, but also with a marriage alliance with Ahab’s house that he never undid (18:1), and his son Jehoram now inherits both the throne and the marriage.

The message. God keeps his promise even when the man carrying it deserves nothing. Jehoram murders, builds idol shrines and leads Judah astray, and God judges him exactly as he warned; yet God will not let David’s lamp go out, “because of the covenant that he had made with David” (v. 7). The judgment shows that God means his word, and the lamp shows that he keeps it.

Why it was said. The first readers had no king, and could wonder whether David’s line had been lost through its own sins (see the introduction). This chapter shows them the line close to its worst, and the promise holding all the same, kept by God and not by the kings.

How the chapter makes its case. Jehoram makes his throne safe by killing his six brothers, and walks in Ahab’s ways because Ahab’s daughter is his wife (vv. 1–6); yet the LORD keeps the lamp burning for David’s sake (v. 7). The reign comes apart: Edom and Libnah break away “because he had forsaken the LORD”, and he builds high places (vv. 8–11). A letter from Elijah names the charges and the sentence, and gives him time to turn (vv. 12–15). The sentence falls to the letter: raiders carry off his sons and wives, a slow disease takes him, and he dies “with no one’s regret”, buried outside the tombs of the kings (vv. 16–20).

Where it leads. To Christ first by promise. The lamp God kept alight over this king was not kept for his sake but for the Son of David, whom Matthew traces through this very king, “Jehoshaphat the father of Joram” (Matthew 1:8), and who said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). And by the need it exposes: Jehoram killed brothers better than himself, and our sins put to death the Brother better than us all, whose blood speaks not vengeance but pardon (Hebrews 12:24).

For us. A compromise we tolerate does not stay private; bring it to God now, before it outlives us. Every warning God gives is time to humble ourselves, and the door Jehoram never used is open to anyone who confesses. And when the faithfulness of God’s people looks thin, our hope is the one Judah had: not the strength of those who carry the promise, but the God who swore it and kept it in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Six Brothers, and a Lamp
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A throne made safe by murder is still kept for David’s sake. Jehoshaphat had provided generously for his younger sons, but once Jehoram was established he killed all six, and some of Judah’s leaders besides (vv. 1–4). He reigned eight years and walked in the way of Ahab’s house, and the Chronicler gives the reason in one clause: “the daughter of Ahab was his wife” (vv. 5–6). Then verse 7 sets God against everything the king has done. The LORD would not destroy the house of David, because of his covenant, and because he had promised a lamp to David and his sons forever. The rest of the chapter is lived under that verse.
verseByVerse.theology: God's faithfulness does not depend on the faithfulness of the people he has bound himself to. That is a solemn comfort in this chapter, and the only reason the house of David survives it.
verseByVerse.examples: A father's careful provision for his sons could not protect them from the brother he had put on the throne. Parents can provide and plan, but in the end they must entrust their children to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Jehoram his son reigned in his place. He had brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah; all these were the sons of Jehoshaphat king of Israel. Their father gave them great gifts of silver, gold, and valuable possessions, together with fortified cities in Judah, but he gave the kingdom to Jehoram, because he was the firstborn. When Jehoram had ascended the throne of his father and was established, he killed all his brothers with the sword, and also some of the princes of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once his throne was secure, Jehoram murdered the six brothers his father had generously provided for, and some of Judah’s leaders with them. The chapter opens with a king “buried with his fathers” and ends with one who is not, and the distance between the two graves is the story.

He had brothers. The Chronicler names all six, so that the murders of verse 4 cannot be read as a mere number. (He calls Jehoshaphat “king of Israel”, though he ruled Judah. That is his usual way of speaking: for him the true Israel is wherever the temple stands and David’s son sits.)

Their father gave them great gifts. Silver, gold and fortified cities, as Rehoboam had done for his own sons (11:23). It is what a wise king does: the throne to the firstborn, a living and a place for the rest, so that no brother is left with nothing and nothing to do. Verse 4 turns that provision into a list of places where the brothers could be found.

When Jehoram had ascended the throne … and was established. The sword went past the family and into Judah’s own nobility, “some of the princes of Israel”. And the word established has been used before in this book: “When the rule of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he abandoned the law of the LORD” (12:1). Twice now a king has turned to evil at the moment he felt secure.

What made him a murderer. Not insecurity, but safety. He waited until the succession was past challenging and then removed everyone who could have challenged it. Hard times keep a man on his knees whether he likes it or not. The settled years, money in the account and nobody asking questions, are the ones that show what he wanted all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, for the daughter of Ahab was his wife. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy the house of David, because of the covenant that he had made with David, and since he had promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoram followed Ahab’s ways because he had married Ahab’s daughter, yet God would not destroy David’s house, because he had bound himself by covenant to keep David’s lamp burning.

For the daughter of Ahab was his wife. The cause is mentioned in passing, like a detail of the family record. Trace it back three chapters. The marriage alliance with Ahab (18:1) nearly killed Jehoshaphat at Ramoth-gilead. A prophet met him on his return and told him that wrath had gone out against him for it (19:2). He went into partnership with Ahab’s son anyway and watched his fleet break up (20:35–37). Every warning landed. The one thing he never reversed was the wedding.

One unreversed policy. Jehoshaphat is one of the better men in this book. He sent teachers round the towns, set judges in the fortified cities, and prayed in the temple court while all Judah stood before the LORD with their little ones (20:13). And his one unreversed policy put Ahab’s daughter in the palace, where she will stand in the next chapter over the bodies of her own grandchildren.

Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy the house of David. Verse 7 lifts our eyes from the king to God. Kings tells this in nearly the same words, but says God was not willing to destroy Judah, “for the sake of David his servant” (2 Kings 8:19). The Chronicler writes “the house of David”, and adds a word Kings does not use here: covenant. Not a preference, nor a policy to be reviewed in the light of the king’s conduct, but a sworn bond (1 Chronicles 17:11–14).

A lamp to him and to his sons forever. The image is chosen with care. Not a throne, a fire or a dynasty, but a lamp: one flame, small enough to carry in the hand and to pinch out between two fingers, kept alight over a man who had just murdered his brothers, because of a promise made six generations back to a shepherd. The house of David comes through this chapter for one reason, and the reason is not in the house of David. It is in God’s promise.

In everyday life. A pet compromise does not stay private, and it does not stay yours. It outlives you and goes on working in people you will never meet. The way out is not resolve but the humbling this chapter never records: confession, and the Spirit who gives strength to undo what we have long tolerated.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A king who forsakes God loses ground, and God warns him in writing before the blow falls. Edom throws off Judah’s rule; Jehoram cuts his way out of an encirclement by night but cannot win the country back, and Libnah revolts as well, “because he had forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers” (vv. 8–10). He builds high places and leads Jerusalem into spiritual adultery (v. 11). Then a letter arrives from Elijah: Jehoram has left the ways of Jehoshaphat and Asa for the ways of Ahab’s house and has killed brothers better than himself, so a plague will strike his household and a slow disease his body (vv. 12–15). Because the warning comes first, it is also an open door.
verseByVerse.theology: Forsaking God rarely looks like a decision at the time. It looks like a series of small departures, and one day the map is smaller (v. 10).
verseByVerse.examples: Jehoram had good examples in his own family and chose a bad one from outside it. Godly parents and grandparents are a gift, but no one inherits faith; each must choose whom to follow.

verseByVerse.quote: In his days Edom revolted from the rule of Judah and set up a king of their own. Then Jehoram passed over with his commanders and all his chariots, and he rose by night and struck the Edomites who had surrounded him and his chariot commanders. So Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day. At that time Libnah also revolted from his rule, because he had forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers. Moreover, he made high places in the hill country of Judah and led the inhabitants of Jerusalem into whoredom and made Judah go astray.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Jehoram forsook the LORD, his kingdom shrank: Edom and Libnah broke away, while he filled Judah with hilltop shrines and led Jerusalem into spiritual adultery.

In his days Edom revolted. The reign comes apart at the edges, and the Chronicler shows it as territory lost. Verse 9 repays a slow reading. Jehoram rode out with his chariots to put down the revolt, found himself surrounded, and cut his way clear in the dark; yet Edom stayed free “to this day”. He survived the battle and lost the country. It ended a rule over Edom that went back to David (2 Samuel 8:14), and fulfilled what Isaac had told Esau: “you shall break his yoke from your neck” (Genesis 27:40).

Set beside his father. One chapter back, his father prayed in the temple courtyard, sent the singers out in front of the army, and spent three days carrying the plunder home (20:25). The son takes out the chariots and brings back nothing but himself.

Because he had forsaken the LORD. Libnah goes as well, a priests’ town near the Philistine border, and here the narrator stops narrating and states the cause. Forsaking God is this book’s great charge (12:1; 15:2; 24:20), and it ends in the exile. A man does not usually announce that he is leaving God. He simply stops going where God is, and one day the map is smaller.

He made high places in the hill country of Judah. Verse 11 says what moved into the space. Asa had removed high places (hilltop shrines) (14:3), and Jehoshaphat removed more (17:6); Jehoram builds them. And the word for what he leads Jerusalem into is the marriage word, “whoredom”. Judah is charged not with a policy error but with adultery, which is how God has always spoken of idolatry (Jeremiah 3:1; Hosea 2:2), because that is what it is from his side.

verseByVerse.quote: And a letter came to him from Elijah the prophet, saying, "Thus says the LORD, the God of David your father, 'Because you have not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat your father, or in the ways of Asa king of Judah, but have walked in the way of the kings of Israel and have enticed Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem into whoredom, as the house of Ahab led Israel into whoredom, and also you have killed your brothers, of your father's house, who were better than you, behold, the LORD will bring a great plague on your people, your children, your wives, and all your possessions, and you yourself will have a severe sickness with a disease of your bowels, until your bowels come out because of the disease, day by day.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A letter from Elijah charges Jehoram with abandoning his godly fathers for Ahab’s ways and with murdering brothers better than himself, and announces a plague on his house and a slow disease for the king. Because it comes before the blow, it is also an offer of mercy.

A letter came to him from Elijah the prophet. Elijah appears once in this book, and this is it: not on Carmel with the fire falling, nor at Horeb in the silence, but in a letter delivered to a king in Jerusalem. The prophet who spent his ministry in Ahab’s face writes to Ahab’s son-in-law in the south.

The LORD, the God of David your father. The charge sheet is built out of fathers: Jehoshaphat and Asa, two working models within living memory, both in his own house, and he went to Samaria for a pattern instead.

Who were better than you. The second charge should stop the reader dead. God has read the list in verse 2, and states his verdict on those six men out loud. Jehoram did not merely break a commandment; he removed from Judah six men heaven rated above him.

The LORD will bring a great plague. The sentence has two parts, and both are exact: a blow on his people, his children, his wives and his possessions, and for the king himself a disease of the bowels, “day by day”. Not one sudden stroke, but a slow decline, announced in advance.

A warning is time to repent. In this book the time between God’s warning and the blow is his mercy. Rehoboam heard a prophet, humbled himself, and the sentence was cut down (12:6–7). Manasseh will be dragged to Babylon with hooks, humble himself there, and be brought home (33:11–13). Humbled is the verb 2 Chronicles turns on, and it does not occur once in this chapter. Jehoram had the letter in his hand for two years, and there is no record that he tore his clothes, or asked one person to pray.

The word it speaks is pardon. The charge God brings against Jehoram, that he killed brothers better than himself, lies against us all. Jesus is a brother better than every one of us, who shared our flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14), and our sins put him to death. The difference is what the blood says afterwards. Abel’s blood cried out from the ground against the man who spilled it (Genesis 4:10); this brother’s blood “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24), and the word it speaks is pardon.

How could Elijah send a letter after he was taken up? Most likely he wrote it before his departure, foreseeing Jehoram’s sin, and it was delivered later; or he was still on earth when Jehoram’s reign began, since the account in 2 Kings 2 is not dated. Kings places Elijah’s last recorded oracle, against Ahaziah of Israel, in the second year of Jehoram of Judah (2 Kings 1:17), so the second explanation is quite possible.
verseByVerse.note: The only writing of Elijah recorded in Scripture.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sentence falls exactly as written, and the man who would not humble himself dies unmourned. God stirs up the Philistines and the Arabians, who once brought tribute to his father; they plunder the palace and carry off his sons and wives, leaving only the youngest (vv. 16–17). After all this the disease comes, and after two years he dies in great agony, with no funeral fire in his honour (vv. 18–19). The record of his reign is repeated so that one line can be added: “he departed with no one’s regret”, and he is buried in the city of David but not in the tombs of the kings (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The disease came last, after all this (v. 18). God's patience ran through two years of warning before the end. That is not a reason to read every illness as judgment; it is a reason to heed God's word while there is time.
verseByVerse.examples: How a person is remembered is not the most important thing about them, but it is often an honest summary. The question the chapter leaves is not how to be missed but how to live for God now, by his grace.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD stirred up against Jehoram the anger of the Philistines and of the Arabians who are near the Ethiopians. And they came up against Judah and invaded it and carried away all the possessions they found that belonged to the king's house, and also his sons and his wives, so that no son was left to him except Jehoahaz, his youngest son. And after all this the LORD struck him in his bowels with an incurable disease. In the course of time, at the end of two years, his bowels came out because of the disease, and he died in great agony. His people made no fire in his honor, like the fires made for his fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God turns against Jehoram the nations that once paid his father tribute, and the sentence falls to the letter: his household is carried off, and after two years of disease he dies in agony, unhonoured.

The LORD stirred up against Jehoram. The Philistines and the Arabians have stood together in this book once before, bringing Jehoshaphat tribute: silver from the Philistines, and 7,700 rams and 7,700 goats from the Arabians (17:11). The same two peoples, one generation apart. Under the father they came up with gifts; under the son they come up and empty the palace.

His sons and his wives. The loss is itemised in the letter’s own terms: possessions, sons, wives. The plague on his household did not arrive as an illness. It arrived on horses. He had put six brothers to the sword to make his throne safe, and he ends with one boy left, “his youngest son”, the last one anybody would have counted. Before the next chapter is out, the dynasty he tried to secure by murder will be down to a single baby in a nurse’s arms.

And after all this. The disease comes last. It is not the opening move of a short-tempered God but the closing one, after a massacre, two revolts, a letter and a raid have all gone by without a word of repentance from him.

He died in great agony. Two years of it, day by day as the letter said. Then a line the Chronicler could have left out and did not: his people made no fire in his honour. They had made “a very great fire” for Asa (16:14), a man who jailed the prophet who told him the truth. Jehoram got a cold hearth, and everybody in Jerusalem knew what it meant.

verseByVerse.quote: He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. And he departed with no one's regret. They buried him in the city of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoram died unwanted and was buried apart from the kings, yet the lamp God kept burning through him was being kept for Christ.

He was thirty-two years old. The formula of verse 5 is repeated on purpose, so that the second time through we listen for what is added.

He departed with no one’s regret. The Hebrew is blunt: he went without being wanted. Not cursed from the gate, simply not missed. Eight years on the throne of David, and when the throne emptied, what the city felt was relief.

Not in the tombs of the kings. He got the address and not the room: buried in the city of David, near the man whose covenant is the only reason his family still exists, but outside the chamber where the kings were laid (see Burial Customs and Tombs). His father, in the chapter’s first line, was “buried with his fathers”.

Kept for the light of the world. Set one more grave beside his: the Servant who “had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him” (Isaiah 53:2). Jehoram had nothing anyone wanted, and he had earned every inch of it. The Son of David had nothing anyone wanted, and had earned none of it: despised, condemned outside the city, and buried in a grave that was not his own. The lamp that verse 7 refused to let go out was being kept for him. Not one of the men who carried it deserved it, and this one least of all. It was kept because God had sworn, and because the small flame at the end of that long, dark corridor was the light of the world (John 8:12).

A question for every reader. If the news of your death went round your street tomorrow, who would be relieved? It is not asked to crush anyone. Jehoram was given a letter and two years to turn, and the door he never used stands open to everyone who confesses (1 John 1:9).

21.theology:
Verse 7 holds the chapter together. God keeps his promise under one of the worst kings Judah ever had, not because the king deserves it but because God swore it. Both sides of the covenant come true in these twenty verses: the judgment is announced before it falls and carried out to the letter, and the promise holds, though all that comes out of this reign is a lamp, not a blaze: one surviving son.

The verb this book turns on, humbled, is missing here, and that is the verdict on him. Rehoboam, Manasseh and Josiah all humbled themselves and were answered. Jehoram received the clearest warning any of them got, in writing, with two years to act on it, and never bent.
21.examples:
The Chronicler names six murdered brothers rather than counting them. God knows the names of those the powerful treat as obstacles, and he rated these men above the king who killed them (v. 13).

A good man's one unreversed compromise can outlive him. Jehoshaphat's marriage alliance with Ahab's house was still at work two reigns later. If there is something we have long tolerated, the time to bring it to God is now.

The same roads that brought Jehoshaphat tribute brought his son raiders. The difference between the two reigns was not the neighbours but the king's relation to God.

keyVerse.quote: Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy the house of David, because of the covenant that he had made with David, and since he had promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever.
keyVerse.note: Set in the middle of one of the darkest reigns in Judah’s history, this verse explains why the story goes on at all. The house of David survives not because of anything in Jehoram but because God bound himself by covenant, and the lamp he kept burning through such men was kept for Christ, the light of the world.

21.reflection:
Jehoram’s evil is traced in one clause to his father’s marriage alliance with Ahab’s house (v. 6), a compromise Jehoshaphat never reversed. Are there compromises in your life that you have learned to live with? Who else might they affect, now or later?

Verse 7 says the LORD would not destroy David’s house “because of the covenant”. How does it help to know that God’s promise rests on his faithfulness rather than on the faithfulness of those who carry it? Where do you see that promise kept in Christ?

Elijah’s letter came two years before the disease, yet Jehoram never humbled himself (vv. 12–19). Why do people so often ignore warnings? How should we treat the warnings God gives us in his word and through other people?

“He departed with no one’s regret” (v. 20). What makes a life one that others are glad to have had among them? How does the gospel free us from living for our own reputation, while making us people who bless others?

22.title: Hidden in the House of God
22.text: <sup>1</sup>And the inhabitants of Jerusalem made Ahaziah, his youngest son, king in his place, for the band of men that came with the Arabians to the camp had killed all the older sons. So Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah reigned.<sup>2</sup>Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri.<sup>3</sup>He also walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother was his counselor in doing wickedly.<sup>4</sup>He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as the house of Ahab had done. For after the death of his father they were his counselors, to his undoing.<sup>5</sup>He even followed their counsel and went with Jehoram the son of Ahab king of Israel to make war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead. And the Syrians wounded Joram,<sup>6</sup>and he returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that he had received at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. And Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was wounded.<sup>7</sup>But it was ordained by God that the downfall of Ahaziah should come about through his going to visit Joram. For when he came there, he went out with Jehoram to meet Jehu the son of Nimshi, whom the LORD had anointed to destroy the house of Ahab.<sup>8</sup>And when Jehu was executing judgment on the house of Ahab, he met the princes of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah's brothers, who attended Ahaziah, and he killed them.<sup>9</sup>He searched for Ahaziah, and he was captured while hiding in Samaria, and he was brought to Jehu and put to death. They buried him, for they said, "He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart." And the house of Ahaziah had no one able to rule the kingdom.<sup>10</sup>Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family of the house of Judah.<sup>11</sup>But Jehoshabeath, the daughter of the king, took Joash the son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king's sons who were about to be put to death, and she put him and his nurse in a bedroom. Thus Jehoshabeath, the daughter of King Jehoram and wife of Jehoiada the priest, because she was a sister of Ahaziah, hid him from Athaliah, so that she did not put him to death.<sup>12</sup>And he remained with them six years, hidden in the house of God, while Athaliah reigned over the land.
22.overview:
Where we are. Jehoram has died unmourned, and raiders have carried off every son but the youngest (21:17). The lamp God promised David (21:7) is burning low, and Ahab’s daughter Athaliah is now queen mother in Jerusalem.

The message. The voices we listen to decide where we go, and God rules even the road they send us down. Ahaziah took his counsel from Ahab’s house and shared its judgment, through a visit God had ordained. And when Athaliah set out to wipe out David’s line, God kept his promise alive in one hidden baby: his word looks weakest exactly where it is safest.

Why it was said. The first readers had no king of David’s line and could wonder whether the line had simply ended (see the introduction). Here it came down to a single infant hidden in the temple while a usurper reigned, and it survived, because God was keeping it.

How the chapter makes its case. Jerusalem crowns the one surviving son, and his mother and Ahab’s house counsel him “to his undoing” (vv. 1–4). Their counsel takes him to war at Ramoth-gilead and then to Jezreel, to visit the wounded king of Israel (vv. 5–6). God had ordained that this visit would be his downfall: Jehu, executing judgment on Ahab’s house, kills him with Judah’s princes, and he is buried only for his grandfather’s sake (vv. 7–9). Athaliah then destroys the royal family, but the king’s sister steals away the baby Joash, and he is hidden in the house of God for six years (vv. 10–12).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. God’s promise to David came through this chapter in one child hidden from a ruler who killed children to keep the throne. When the true King was born, another ruler killed the children of Bethlehem to destroy him, and he too was carried away by night and kept (Matthew 2:13–16). Like Joash, he was the rightful King unrecognised in his own land (John 1:11). The promise could not be killed, because God was keeping it, and it was kept for him.

For us. Ask who your real counsellors are, the people whose advice you actually take, and seek those who will point you to Christ. When God’s cause looks almost finished, remember the bedroom in the temple: he has not lost his grip on his promises. And do not despise hidden faithfulness; an unnamed nurse kept God’s promise alive in her arms for six years.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — His Mother Was His Counselor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bad counsel leads a king to ruin. With all his older brothers killed by raiders, the people of Jerusalem crown Ahaziah, Jehoram’s youngest son (v. 1). He reigns one year, and the Chronicler names the cause of his failure twice: his mother Athaliah, of Omri’s house, “was his counselor in doing wickedly”, and after his father’s death Ahab’s house were “his counselors, to his undoing” (vv. 2–4). Following their advice, he joins Joram of Israel against Syria at Ramoth-gilead, the battlefield that nearly killed his grandfather, and then goes down to Jezreel to visit the wounded Joram (vv. 5–6). The scene is set for God’s judgment on Ahab’s house.
verseByVerse.theology: Influence is a moral force. Scripture holds Ahaziah responsible for his sins, and also names the voices that shaped them.
verseByVerse.examples: Families can repeat a mistake for generations without remembering why it was a mistake. Telling our children honestly where we went wrong, and how God met us there, is part of passing on the faith.

verseByVerse.quote: And the inhabitants of Jerusalem made Ahaziah, his youngest son, king in his place, for the band of men that came with the Arabians to the camp had killed all the older sons. So Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah reigned. Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri. He also walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother was his counselor in doing wickedly. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as the house of Ahab had done. For after the death of his father they were his counselors, to his undoing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s one surviving prince became king, and from the start his counsellors were his mother and Ahab’s family, who steered him into evil and to his ruin.

Ahaziah, his youngest son. The people of Jerusalem have to crown him themselves. No orderly succession is left, because the raiders of the last chapter killed the older sons, and the only one left alive is the youngest, called Jehoahaz at 21:17 (the same name with its halves reversed). He has twelve months to live.

Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri. At 21:6 she was the daughter of Ahab; here she is “the granddaughter of Omri”, which reaches back to the founder of the northern dynasty. What came into Judah through one wedding was not only a wife. It was a whole dynasty and its ways.

His counselors, to his undoing. The diagnosis is given twice, so that nobody can blame it only on his character: his mother “was his counselor in doing wickedly”, and Ahab’s house were “his counselors, to his undoing”. Counsellor is a job title, and every chair at that table was filled by Ahab’s family. Rehoboam at least had two sets of advisers to choose between, and chose the flatterers (10:6–8). Jehoshaphat had taken real trouble over who sat on which bench (19:8–11). Ahaziah has one set of advisers, and all of them come from Samaria.

In everyday life. That puts a plain question to every reader. Not whose books are on your shelf, but whom do you actually ring at eleven at night when the decision has to be made by morning? Those people are your council, whatever you would have said if asked. God does not leave his people to find wiser voices by effort alone: he gives his word, his Spirit, and brothers and sisters who will tell them the truth.

Textual note. The Hebrew text of verse 2 gives Ahaziah’s age as forty-two, as the KJV does, which would make him older than his father, who died at forty (21:20). Most translations follow 2 Kings 8:26 and some Greek manuscripts in reading twenty-two; a miscopied numeral is the likeliest explanation.
