verseByVerse.quote: He even followed their counsel and went with Jehoram the son of Ahab king of Israel to make war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead. And the Syrians wounded Joram, and he returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that he had received at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. And Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was wounded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On their advice Ahaziah went to war beside Ahab’s son at Ramoth-gilead, and then went down to Jezreel to visit him when he was wounded.

He even followed their counsel. Four chapters ago, at Ramoth-gilead, his grandfather heard a prophet foretell disaster there, watched him slapped and jailed, and rode out anyway, coming home alive only because he cried out and “God drew them away from him” (18:31). Now the grandson rides to the same town, with the same family, against the same enemy. That warning was given in public, in front of two kings, and proved right within a day. Two reigns later nobody in the palace can remember why the name of that town ought to make them hesitate.

Went down to see Joram. The Syrians wound Joram, who goes back to Jezreel to recover, and Ahaziah goes down to see him. That is the visit that kills him, and there is nothing wicked in it. A man goes to sit with a wounded relative, which would be commended anywhere else in Scripture. The trouble is not the visit. The trouble is that he had made Ahab’s house his family, and spent his one year in office binding himself to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–9 — It Was Ordained by God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rules over the most ordinary choices, and he joined Ahaziah to the judgment of the house he had joined himself to. The narrator says plainly that the visit to Joram was ordained by God for Ahaziah’s downfall (v. 7). Jehu, anointed by the LORD to destroy the house of Ahab, kills the princes of Judah travelling with the king, then has Ahaziah hunted down in Samaria and put to death (vv. 8–9). He is buried only because he was “the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart”, and his house is left with no one able to rule (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Nothing in this chapter happens by accident, not even a sick-visit. That is sobering for the wicked and a deep comfort to anyone who trusts God with the things they cannot control.
verseByVerse.examples: A godly grandparent's life can bless a family long after it ends, even a grandson who did not share his faith.

verseByVerse.quote: But it was ordained by God that the downfall of Ahaziah should come about through his going to visit Joram. For when he came there, he went out with Jehoram to meet Jehu the son of Nimshi, whom the LORD had anointed to destroy the house of Ahab. And when Jehu was executing judgment on the house of Ahab, he met the princes of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah's brothers, who attended Ahaziah, and he killed them. He searched for Ahaziah, and he was captured while hiding in Samaria, and he was brought to Jehu and put to death. They buried him, for they said, "He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart." And the house of Ahaziah had no one able to rule the kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God ordained that Ahaziah’s visit would bring his downfall: Jehu, sent to judge Ahab’s house, killed him along with it, and he was buried only for his grandfather’s sake.

It was ordained by God. The narrator steps forward at the very point where a reader would reach for the word coincidence. The sick-visit that looks like the most incidental thing in the chapter is the turning point, and God put it there.

God’s purpose and man’s guilt. He says this without taking any of the blame off Ahaziah. Three verses earlier the same narrator said the man followed wicked counsel and did evil in the LORD’s sight. Both sentences stand together, and the text feels no strain between them. Scripture does not protect God’s sovereignty by shrinking human guilt, and it does not protect human responsibility by making God a spectator. The man chose his advisers, kept them, obeyed them, and went where they sent him. And God had appointed the road.

Jehu the son of Nimshi. The Chronicler assumes his readers know the story told in Kings: Elisha sent a young prophet to anoint Jehu, an army commander, with orders to strike down the house of Ahab for the blood of the prophets Jezebel had shed (2 Kings 9:1–10). Carrying out that judgment, Jehu finds the princes of Judah and Ahaziah’s nephews travelling in Ahaziah’s party, and kills them (v. 8). A king of David’s line had merged his household so completely with the house of Omri that when judgment came for the one, it swept up the other. Ahaziah is caught hiding in Samaria, of all cities, and put to death.

He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat. Then comes the strangest kindness in the chapter: they bury him because he is “the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart”. Nobody says he was a good king, or a brave one. They describe his grandfather in the language this book keeps for its best men, and the single decent thing that happens to Ahaziah after death happens because of somebody else’s record.

Buried on another man’s record. That is a small picture of the only hope any of us has. Nothing in Ahaziah’s life earned that grave; it was granted because of another man’s wholehearted seeking. Christ sought God with his whole heart from Nazareth to the cross, and the burial of every believer, and the rising after it, is granted on the strength of his record and not our own.

Where did Ahaziah die? Second Kings says Ahaziah was wounded near Ibleam and died at Megiddo (2 Kings 9:27). The two accounts are best put together this way: he hid in Samaria, was caught and wounded, and escaped to Megiddo, where he died.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — A Baby in a Bedroom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Athaliah sets out to destroy David’s line, God keeps it alive in one hidden child. Seeing her son dead, she kills the royal family, her own grandsons, to take the throne for herself (v. 10). But Jehoshabeath, the king’s daughter and the wife of Jehoiada the priest, steals the baby Joash away from among the children about to die and hides him with his nurse in a bedroom (v. 11). For six years, while Athaliah reigns over the land, the heir of David lives hidden in the house of God (v. 12). The promise of 21:7 has never looked so fragile, nor been so safe.
verseByVerse.theology: From Pharaoh’s order to kill the Hebrew boys onward, attacks on the people of promise have a common shape, and so does God’s answer: he keeps his word through the weak and the hidden.
verseByVerse.examples: Courage is not only for kings and prophets. A princess and a nurse, neither of them with any power, risked their lives to keep a child alive, and God's promise passed through their hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family of the house of Judah. But Jehoshabeath, the daughter of the king, took Joash the son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king's sons who were about to be put to death, and she put him and his nurse in a bedroom. Thus Jehoshabeath, the daughter of King Jehoram and wife of Jehoiada the priest, because she was a sister of Ahaziah, hid him from Athaliah, so that she did not put him to death. And he remained with them six years, hidden in the house of God, while Athaliah reigned over the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Athaliah murdered the royal family to seize the throne, but the king’s sister rescued the baby Joash and hid him in the temple for six years, so that God’s promise to David survived in a single child.

She arose and destroyed all the royal family. They are her grandsons. She had married into David’s line, buried her husband and her son, and now she goes through the nursery so that nobody with David’s blood can take back the throne she means to sit on.

An attack on the promise. It is the one moment in this book when somebody sets out deliberately to end the line of David. Jehoram thinned it by murder and the raiders thinned it further, but no one before her had aimed at the promise itself. A chapter ago God said he would not destroy the house of David because of the covenant (21:7); Ahab’s daughter now sets out with soldiers to do exactly that.

Jehoshabeath, the daughter of the king. One woman, the dead king’s sister, goes the wrong way through a palace where children are being killed, and comes out carrying a baby. And the Chronicler tells us something Kings does not (2 Kings 11:2 names her without it): she is the “wife of Jehoiada the priest”. A king’s daughter married to the high priest was the one person in Jerusalem with a reason to be in the palace and a key to the temple, and she used both at once.

Him and his nurse. There is a second woman in the verse, and she is never named. The nurse went into hiding with the child and stayed: six years of keeping an infant fed, quiet and out of sight, in a building where crowds came and went. Whatever else the covenant needed that week, it needed somebody willing to be shut away for six years with a boy who could not be allowed to cry at the wrong moment.

Hidden in the house of God. The rightful king is in the temple and the usurper is on the throne, and for six years anyone in Jerusalem looking for the king of Judah was looking at the wrong building. It would not be the last time. The true King, Jesus, was carried into Egypt by night while Herod killed the children of Bethlehem to be rid of him (Matthew 2:13–16), grew up in a village nobody rated, and stood among people who did not know who was in the room: “among you stands one you do not know” (John 1:26).

Never closer to going out. The lamp of 21:7 is down to a wick in a back room behind a locked door, in the arms of a woman whose name we are never told. It has never been closer to going out, and it was never in any danger at all. God had sworn, and the whole armed strength of Ahab’s house, with the throne in its hand and no opposition left alive, could not put out one small flame that God had promised to keep.

22.theology:
Verse 7 puts God's ordaining and Ahaziah's guilt in the same paragraph and softens neither. The king chose his counsellors; God appointed the road they sent him down.

Verse 9 holds the chapter’s one mercy, and it comes indirectly: Ahaziah is given a burial because of his grandfather’s record, not his own.

And verse 12 is the covenant of 21:7 at its narrowest point. The promise to David comes through this chapter reduced to one hidden child, kept alive by two women in a locked room while the woman on the throne hunts the family. God’s sworn word is safe even when it looks finished, because what keeps it is God, not the strength of the people carrying it.
22.examples:
Who we listen to shapes who we become. Ahaziah's ruin is traced not to his appetites but to his advisers, and the question for us is not whom we admire but whom we actually consult when a decision is due.

Faithful people are often unnamed. The nurse who kept a baby quiet in a back room of the temple for six years has no name in Scripture, but God's promise was in her arms.

keyVerse.quote: And he remained with them six years, hidden in the house of God, while Athaliah reigned over the land.
keyVerse.note: This is God’s promise to David at its narrowest point: one hidden child, while a usurper who has murdered the royal family sits on the throne. The verse shows that God’s word is kept by God, not by the strength of those who carry it, and it foreshadows the true King, hidden and unrecognised, whom no ruler could destroy.

22.reflection:
Ahaziah’s ruin is traced to his counsellors, his mother and Ahab’s family (vv. 3–5). Who are the people whose advice you actually take when decisions are due? How can we make sure that the voices shaping us are pointing us to Christ?

Verse 7 says Ahaziah’s downfall “was ordained by God”, yet verses 3–4 hold him fully responsible. How do God’s sovereign rule and our real responsibility stand together here? Why does it matter to hold on to both?

Ahaziah was buried only because of his grandfather’s faithfulness (v. 9). How is this a picture, however small, of being accepted on the strength of Christ’s record rather than our own?

God’s promise survived through an unnamed nurse and a hidden child (vv. 11–12). When have God’s purposes seemed almost finished to you? What does this chapter, and the story of Jesus’ birth, teach about how God keeps his word?

23.title: The King's Son Shall Reign
23.text: <sup>1</sup>But in the seventh year Jehoiada took courage and entered into a covenant with the commanders of hundreds, Azariah the son of Jeroham, Ishmael the son of Jehohanan, Azariah the son of Obed, Maaseiah the son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat the son of Zichri.<sup>2</sup>And they went about through Judah and gathered the Levites from all the cities of Judah, and the heads of fathers' houses of Israel, and they came to Jerusalem.<sup>3</sup>And all the assembly made a covenant with the king in the house of God. And Jehoiada said to them, "Behold, the king's son! Let him reign, as the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David.<sup>4</sup>This is the thing that you shall do: of you priests and Levites who come off duty on the Sabbath, one third shall be gatekeepers,<sup>5</sup>and one third shall be at the king's house and one third at the Gate of the Foundation. And all the people shall be in the courts of the house of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>Let no one enter the house of the LORD except the priests and ministering Levites. They may enter, for they are holy, but all the people shall keep the charge of the LORD.<sup>7</sup>The Levites shall surround the king, each with his weapons in his hand. And whoever enters the house shall be put to death. Be with the king when he comes in and when he goes out."<sup>8</sup>The Levites and all Judah did according to all that Jehoiada the priest commanded, and they each brought his men, who were to go off duty on the Sabbath, with those who were to come on duty on the Sabbath, for Jehoiada the priest did not dismiss the divisions.<sup>9</sup>And Jehoiada the priest gave to the captains the spears and the large and small shields that had been King David's, which were in the house of God.<sup>10</sup>And he set all the people as a guard for the king, every man with his weapon in his hand, from the south side of the house to the north side of the house, around the altar and the house.<sup>11</sup>Then they brought out the king's son and put the crown on him and gave him the testimony. And they proclaimed him king, and Jehoiada and his sons anointed him, and they said, "Long live the king."<sup>12</sup>When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and praising the king, she went into the house of the LORD to the people.<sup>13</sup>And when she looked, there was the king standing by his pillar at the entrance, and the captains and the trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets, and the singers with their musical instruments leading in the celebration. And Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, "Treason! Treason!"<sup>14</sup>Then Jehoiada the priest brought out the captains who were set over the army, saying to them, "Bring her out between the ranks, and anyone who follows her is to be put to death with the sword." For the priest said, "Do not put her to death in the house of the LORD."<sup>15</sup>So they laid hands on her, and she went into the entrance of the horse gate of the king's house, and they put her to death there.<sup>16</sup>And Jehoiada made a covenant between himself and all the people and the king that they should be the LORD's people.<sup>17</sup>Then all the people went to the house of Baal and tore it down; his altars and his images they broke in pieces, and they killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars.<sup>18</sup>And Jehoiada posted watchmen for the house of the LORD under the direction of the Levitical priests and the Levites whom David had organized to be in charge of the house of the LORD, to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, as it is written in the Law of Moses, with rejoicing and with singing, according to the order of David.<sup>19</sup>He stationed the gatekeepers at the gates of the house of the LORD so that no one should enter who was in any way unclean.<sup>20</sup>And he took the captains, the nobles, the governors of the people, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the LORD, marching through the upper gate to the king's house. And they set the king on the royal throne.<sup>21</sup>So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet after Athaliah had been put to death with the sword.
23.overview:
Where we are. For six years Athaliah has reigned over Judah, having murdered the royal family, while David’s one surviving heir, the boy Joash, lay hidden in the house of God (22:10–12). Now, in the seventh year, Jehoiada the priest acts.

The message. God’s promise to David is the solid ground on which his people act, and God restores his king and his worship together. Jehoiada’s whole case is “as the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David” (v. 3). The boy is crowned with God’s law in his hand, the usurper falls, and the people bind themselves to be the LORD’s. When the rightful king is on the throne and God is honoured in his house, “the city was quiet” (v. 21).

Why it was said. The first readers had no king, but they had a temple served by priests and Levites (see the introduction). This chapter showed them priests and Levites guarding God’s promise in its darkest hour, and assured them that a line which seemed finished was still in God’s hand.

How the chapter makes its case. Jehoiada binds five commanders by covenant, gathers the Levites and family heads, and presents the king’s son on the strength of God’s promise (vv. 1–3). His plan guards the holiness of the house and rings the boy with armed Levites (vv. 4–7). Both Sabbath shifts are kept on duty, David’s own weapons are issued, and Joash is crowned, given the testimony and anointed (vv. 8–11). Athaliah cries treason and is executed outside the temple (vv. 12–15). Then come a covenant to be the LORD’s people, Baal’s house torn down, worship restored as Moses wrote and David ordered, and the king set on his throne (vv. 16–21).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. The promise to David’s sons is the warrant for crowning Joash, and it reaches its goal in Jesus, to whom “the Lord God will give … the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32). Joash was brought out of the temple to be crowned to shouts of “Long live the king”; Jesus was brought out crowned with thorns, and the crowd shouted for his death. By dying he won a throne no usurper can take, and a peace that does not end with one reign (Isaiah 9:7).

For us. God’s promises are firm ground to act on, even when acting on them takes years of patient waiting. Anyone given authority must hold it under God’s word, as Joash received the crown and the testimony together. And real repentance, then and now, both pulls something down and builds up the daily worship of the God who has kept his word to us in Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehoiada acts on God’s promise, with courage and with reverence. In the seventh year he binds five named commanders by covenant, and they bring the Levites and family heads from all Judah to Jerusalem (vv. 1–2). There the assembly makes a covenant with the king, and Jehoiada presents the boy: “Behold, the king’s son! Let him reign, as the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David” (v. 3). His orders divide the Sabbath shifts between the gates and the palace, keep everyone except the priests and ministering Levites out of the house, because they are holy, and ring the young king with armed Levites wherever he goes (vv. 4–7).
verseByVerse.theology: God's promises are meant to be acted on. Jehoiada did not merely believe the word about David's sons; he staked his life on it.
verseByVerse.examples: Waiting is not the opposite of courage; sometimes it is most of it. Anyone in a long season of holding on without visible progress can find a friend in Jehoiada.

verseByVerse.quote: But in the seventh year Jehoiada took courage and entered into a covenant with the commanders of hundreds, Azariah the son of Jeroham, Ishmael the son of Jehohanan, Azariah the son of Obed, Maaseiah the son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat the son of Zichri. And they went about through Judah and gathered the Levites from all the cities of Judah, and the heads of fathers' houses of Israel, and they came to Jerusalem. And all the assembly made a covenant with the king in the house of God. And Jehoiada said to them, "Behold, the king's son! Let him reign, as the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After six patient years Jehoiada gathered Judah’s leaders, made a covenant with them and presented the hidden boy as king, resting everything on God’s promise to David’s sons.

In the seventh year Jehoiada took courage. Read the date before the courage. For six years Jehoiada had the rightful king of Judah living in the house of God, while he served under Athaliah’s rule in a city with a working Baal temple down the road. Whatever we mean by courage has to be big enough to include those years. He was not waiting because he was frightened. He was waiting because a child who can be crowned at seven cannot be crowned at one, and because a coup that fails kills the boy.

The commanders of hundreds. Then five names, with their fathers’ names as well. Kings tells this story and names none of them. The Chronicler writes down the five men who agreed to risk execution for a child they had never met, because somebody should know.

They gathered the Levites from all the cities of Judah. They go quietly round Judah and bring in the Levites from every town and the heads of the families. Kings tells of the coup with the Carites, foreign guards on the palace payroll (2 Kings 11:4). Chronicles tells it from inside the temple, and the men in the corridors are priests and Levites and clan elders. The two accounts stand together; this one is interested in the house of God and who serves in it.

Behold, the king’s son! The boy is brought out before an assembly that had spent six years believing the family was finished. And the priest’s ground for what they are about to do is not a claim about blood but a promise: “as the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David”. Not a treaty, a precedent or the will of the people, though they have that too. God had said something about David’s sons more than a century and a half before (1 Chronicles 17:11–14), and these men treat that sentence as still binding, on a Sabbath with soldiers in the courtyard.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the thing that you shall do: of you priests and Levites who come off duty on the Sabbath, one third shall be gatekeepers, and one third shall be at the king's house and one third at the Gate of the Foundation. And all the people shall be in the courts of the house of the LORD. Let no one enter the house of the LORD except the priests and ministering Levites. They may enter, for they are holy, but all the people shall keep the charge of the LORD. The Levites shall surround the king, each with his weapons in his hand. And whoever enters the house shall be put to death. Be with the king when he comes in and when he goes out."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoiada’s orders guard the holiness of God’s house even in an armed emergency, and surround the young king with armed Levites wherever he goes.

This is the thing that you shall do. What follows is a set of orders, and what they are made of is the surprise. The guard posts are ordinary military arrangements, but the instruction that follows is about doors: no one may enter the house “except the priests and ministering Levites”.

They may enter, for they are holy. The priest is running an armed operation against a reigning monarch, in the temple, with the life of David’s last heir at stake, and he spends his instructions on who may go through which door. A man in that position has every excuse to say that the rules can wait until tomorrow. He does not. The holiness of the house is not suspended because the stakes are high. It is one of the most impressive things in the chapter, and exactly what a later king will fail to do: Uzziah, with far less pressure on him, will walk into that same house with a censer in his hand because he is strong (26:16).

The Levites shall surround the king. The last order shows what Jehoiada was really thinking about: the Levites are to surround the king, weapons in hand, and “be with the king when he comes in and when he goes out”. Not hold the gate, not take the palace, but stay with the boy. Every other objective is negotiable, and this one is not. God had promised a lamp to David’s sons, and on this day the lamp was seven years old and could be picked up in two hands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — The Crown and the Testimony
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The true king is crowned under God’s law, and the usurper falls. The Levites and all Judah do as Jehoiada commands, keeping both Sabbath shifts on duty, and he arms the captains with King David’s own spears and shields (vv. 8–10). Joash is brought out, crowned, given the testimony, anointed and acclaimed: “Long live the king” (v. 11). Hearing the noise, Athaliah comes into the temple, sees the boy standing by the king’s pillar amid trumpets and singers, and cries, “Treason! Treason!” (vv. 12–13). Jehoiada has her taken out between the ranks, so that she is not killed in the house of the LORD, and she is put to death at the horse gate (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Joy and justice arrive together in this section: the people shout and sing, and the woman who murdered children is brought to account. God's kingdom brings both.
verseByVerse.examples: God's great deliverances often run through ordinary arrangements, a rota, a storeroom, a door. Faithfulness in routine duties is never wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: The Levites and all Judah did according to all that Jehoiada the priest commanded, and they each brought his men, who were to go off duty on the Sabbath, with those who were to come on duty on the Sabbath, for Jehoiada the priest did not dismiss the divisions. And Jehoiada the priest gave to the captains the spears and the large and small shields that had been King David's, which were in the house of God. And he set all the people as a guard for the king, every man with his weapon in his hand, from the south side of the house to the north side of the house, around the altar and the house. Then they brought out the king's son and put the crown on him and gave him the testimony. And they proclaimed him king, and Jehoiada and his sons anointed him, and they said, "Long live the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Using the Sabbath change of shifts and King David’s own weapons, Jehoiada had Joash crowned, given the book of God’s law, anointed and acclaimed as king.

Jehoiada the priest did not dismiss the divisions. The plan turns on the rota. Every Sabbath one division of priests and Levites came off duty and another came on, and for a while both were in the building: the one time in the week when twice the usual number of men could be inside the temple courts and nobody at the palace thought anything of it. Jehoiada simply did not send the outgoing shift home, and the most dangerous day of Athaliah’s reign was staged inside the duty roster.

The spears and the large and small shields that had been King David’s. Then he opens the store: David’s own weapons, laid up in the house of God, put into the hands of men guarding David’s last descendant. The founder’s armoury is issued to defend the founder’s promise, and the scene says what this book keeps saying: what God gave in the past is there to be used.

Put the crown on him and gave him the testimony. Crown and testimony, two objects in one gesture. The crown is the power. The testimony is the law, the covenant document that Deuteronomy required a king to keep beside him and read all the days of his life, so that his heart would not be lifted up above his brothers (Deuteronomy 17:18–20). Judah hands its king his authority and the limits of that authority in the same minute, before he has given a single order.

Jehoiada and his sons anointed him. The anointing marked the boy as the king God had chosen, and in Hebrew the LORD’s anointed is his messiah. Every anointed son of David pointed beyond himself to the one God would anoint with the Spirit, Jesus the Christ: the King who needed no scroll beside him to keep him humble, because God’s law was within his heart (Psalm 40:8), and who did not lift himself above his brothers but came to serve them and give his life for them (Mark 10:45).

No crown without the book. Every ruler wants the crown, and this ceremony says you may not have it without the book. The same holds wherever anyone is given charge of anything: a department, a household, a class, a congregation. Authority handed over without a standard above it is not a gift. It is a trap with a ribbon on.

verseByVerse.quote: When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and praising the king, she went into the house of the LORD to the people. And when she looked, there was the king standing by his pillar at the entrance, and the captains and the trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets, and the singers with their musical instruments leading in the celebration. And Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, "Treason! Treason!" Then Jehoiada the priest brought out the captains who were set over the army, saying to them, "Bring her out between the ranks, and anyone who follows her is to be put to death with the sword." For the priest said, "Do not put her to death in the house of the LORD." So they laid hands on her, and she went into the entrance of the horse gate of the king's house, and they put her to death there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Athaliah came into the temple, saw the crowned boy and cried treason, and Jehoiada had her taken out and executed at the palace gate rather than in the house of the LORD.

When Athaliah heard the noise. What brought her out was “the noise of the people running and praising the king”. She had ruled six years without ever needing to enter that building, and the one thing that finally drew her through its gate was a noise she could not account for.

There was the king standing by his pillar. Then the scene through her eyes. There was a fixed station in the temple where the king of Judah stood, empty for six years, and she knew it was empty. Now a child is standing in it, with the captains and trumpeters beside him and the singers leading the celebration. Judah’s worship and Judah’s throne have found each other again in the space of one day.

Treason! Treason! These are the last words of a woman who took the throne by killing the children who were heirs to it. She is not wrong that a conspiracy has taken place. She is simply the last person in Judah entitled to be shocked by one.

Do not put her to death in the house of the LORD. The crowd has her, the captains are armed, and everybody in that courtyard has a personal reason to want her dead. Jehoiada says two things: bring her out between the ranks, and do not kill her in the house of the LORD. At the moment of victory, his one instruction is about God’s honour, not his own satisfaction. She is taken to the entrance of the horse gate of the palace and executed there, at the seat of the power she seized, and not in the house she despised, which she does not get to defile even by dying in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — And the City Was Quiet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The restored king leads a restored people back to God. Jehoiada makes a covenant between himself, all the people and the king that they should be the LORD’s people (v. 16). They go straight to the house of Baal, tear it down and kill its priest Mattan before the altars (v. 17). Jehoiada restores the worship of the house as it is written in the Law of Moses and as David ordered it, with rejoicing and singing, and posts gatekeepers to keep out anyone unclean (vv. 18–19). Then the people bring the king down to the palace and set him on the royal throne, the land rejoices, and “the city was quiet” (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Political deliverance is not the goal in itself. The chapter's real end is a people bound to the LORD and worshipping him with joy.
verseByVerse.examples: Repentance has a negative and a positive side. Tearing down what dishonours God is necessary, but the daily work of worship that follows is where faith lives.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jehoiada made a covenant between himself and all the people and the king that they should be the LORD's people. Then all the people went to the house of Baal and tore it down; his altars and his images they broke in pieces, and they killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. And Jehoiada posted watchmen for the house of the LORD under the direction of the Levitical priests and the Levites whom David had organized to be in charge of the house of the LORD, to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, as it is written in the Law of Moses, with rejoicing and with singing, according to the order of David. He stationed the gatekeepers at the gates of the house of the LORD so that no one should enter who was in any way unclean. And he took the captains, the nobles, the governors of the people, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the LORD, marching through the upper gate to the king's house. And they set the king on the royal throne. So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet after Athaliah had been put to death with the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people bound themselves by covenant to be the LORD’s, tore down Baal’s temple, restored the worship of God’s house and set the king on his throne, and the city was at peace.

That they should be the LORD’s people. Count the covenants in this chapter and watch them climb. A priest binds five officers to himself (v. 1); the assembly binds itself to the king (v. 3); and now priest, people and king together bind themselves to God. The politics were finished at verse 15, and this is what they were for.

All the people went to the house of Baal and tore it down. A covenant that is meant leads to action. There had been a house of Baal in Jerusalem: not a shrine on a hill outside town but a working temple, with altars in use and a priest, Mattan, whose name everybody knew. It was Athaliah’s import from her father’s court. Ahab had built a house of Baal in Samaria (1 Kings 16:32), and Jehu had already torn that one down (2 Kings 10:27). The people who pulled this one down had been walking past it for six years. That is what real national repentance looks like: it happens on a known day, in public, and it pulls something down.

As it is written in the Law of Moses. Then the positive half, which matters as much. The order of priests and Levites is restored, burnt offerings resume “with rejoicing and with singing, according to the order of David”, and gatekeepers are posted so that nothing unclean comes in, with Moses and David named in one breath, as at Solomon’s dedication. Tearing down Baal’s house was one day’s work. Restarting the daily offerings and the singing is the work of every morning after, and it rests on what God had just done in keeping his promise and giving them back their king. For Christians that daily work is carried by the Spirit, who keeps renewing what one day of repentance began.

They set the king on the royal throne. The last two verses are a procession: the boy brought down from the house of the LORD to the house of the king, through the upper gate, escorted by the whole nation, along a route the city could watch.

The city was quiet. Not triumphant, not loud. After six years of a woman who came to power over her grandchildren’s bodies, what the Chronicler chooses to record is that Jerusalem could breathe out.

Brought out to reign, brought out to die. Set one more coronation beside this one. A priest stood before a crowd, pointed to the rightful king and said, “Behold, the king’s son!”, and the people shouted, “Long live the king.” Nearly nine centuries later a governor stood before another crowd, pointed to another son of David, beaten and crowned with thorns, and said, “Behold your King!”, and that crowd shouted for his blood (John 19:14–15). The first king was hidden in the temple and brought out to reign. The second was brought out to die, and by dying he took a throne no coup will ever touch, and the peace he won for his city is not for one reign but forever (Isaiah 9:7).

23.theology:
The legal ground for the whole chapter is a promise: as the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David. Jehoiada does not argue from the boy's blood or from Athaliah's crimes, though both would have served.

Verse 11 gives the king the crown and the testimony (the written law) together: Israel’s king is under God’s law and does not make it. And the holiness of the house governs the day from beginning (v. 6) to end (v. 14); reverence does not bend for the emergency.

Was it right to kill Athaliah and Mattan? Athaliah had murdered the royal children and seized the throne, and under Israel's law murder was a capital crime (Numbers 35:31); so was enticing the nation after other gods (Deuteronomy 13:6-10), which was Mattan's office. The chapter records judgment carried out on behalf of the rightful king, not a licence for private vengeance. Those laws belonged to Israel as a nation under God's direct rule. The church does not wield the sword against unbelievers or false teachers; its weapons are the word and prayer (2 Corinthians 10:4).
23.examples:
Five officers agreed to risk execution for a child they had never met, and the Chronicler writes down their names and their fathers' names. God remembers those who take risks for his promises, even when history forgets them.

Jehoiada's one instruction at the moment of victory was about God's honour, not his own satisfaction. In the hour when we finally have the upper hand over someone who has wronged us, his example is worth remembering.

A Baal temple everybody had walked past for six years was rubble by the end of one day. Long-tolerated sin does not have to stay standing.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, the king’s son! Let him reign, as the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David.
keyVerse.note: Jehoiada’s whole warrant for the coronation is not the boy’s blood or Athaliah’s crimes but God’s word to David. The verse shows God’s people acting on his promise as still binding after six dark years, and it points to the Son of David in whom that promise is finally fulfilled.

23.reflection:
Jehoiada waited six years before he acted (v. 1). What helps us tell the difference between faithful patience and fearful delay? Where might God be calling you to wait, or to act?

Jehoiada based everything on what “the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David” (v. 3). Which of God’s promises in Christ do you most need to treat as firm ground to stand and act on this week?

Joash received the crown and the testimony, God’s law, together (v. 11). Where have you been given authority, at home, at work or in church? What would it look like to hold it under God’s word, following the King who came to serve?

The covenant of verse 16 led straight to tearing down Baal’s house and restoring daily worship (vv. 17–19). What does repentance that both pulls down and builds up look like in a Christian life today?

24.title: As Long as Jehoiada Lived
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Joash was seven years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Zibiah of Beersheba.<sup>2</sup>And Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.<sup>3</sup>Jehoiada got for him two wives, and he had sons and daughters.<sup>4</sup>After this Joash decided to restore the house of the LORD.<sup>5</sup>And he gathered the priests and the Levites and said to them, "Go out to the cities of Judah and gather from all Israel money to repair the house of your God from year to year, and see that you act quickly." But the Levites did not act quickly.<sup>6</sup>So the king summoned Jehoiada the chief and said to him, "Why have you not required the Levites to bring in from Judah and Jerusalem the tax levied by Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the congregation of Israel for the tent of testimony?"<sup>7</sup>For the sons of Athaliah, that wicked woman, had broken into the house of God, and had also used all the dedicated things of the house of the LORD for the Baals.<sup>8</sup>So the king commanded, and they made a chest and set it outside the gate of the house of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>And proclamation was made throughout Judah and Jerusalem to bring in for the LORD the tax that Moses the servant of God laid on Israel in the wilderness.<sup>10</sup>And all the princes and all the people rejoiced and brought their tax and dropped it into the chest until they had finished.<sup>11</sup>And whenever the chest was brought to the king's officers by the Levites, when they saw that there was much money in it, the king's secretary and the officer of the chief priest would come and empty the chest and take it and return it to its place. Thus they did day after day, and collected money in abundance.<sup>12</sup>And the king and Jehoiada gave it to those who had charge of the work of the house of the LORD, and they hired masons and carpenters to restore the house of the LORD, and also workers in iron and bronze to repair the house of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>So those who were engaged in the work labored, and the repairing went forward in their hands, and they restored the house of God to its proper condition and strengthened it.<sup>14</sup>And when they had finished, they brought the rest of the money before the king and Jehoiada, and with it were made utensils for the house of the LORD, both for the service and for the burnt offerings, and dishes for incense and vessels of gold and silver. And they offered burnt offerings in the house of the LORD regularly all the days of Jehoiada.<sup>15</sup>But Jehoiada grew old and full of days, and died. He was 130 years old at his death.<sup>16</sup>And they buried him in the city of David among the kings, because he had done good in Israel, and toward God and his house.<sup>17</sup>Now after the death of Jehoiada the princes of Judah came and paid homage to the king. Then the king listened to them.<sup>18</sup>And they abandoned the house of the LORD, the God of their fathers, and served the Asherim and the idols. And wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this guilt of theirs.<sup>19</sup>Yet he sent prophets among them to bring them back to the LORD. These testified against them, but they would not pay attention.<sup>20</sup>Then the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, and he stood above the people, and said to them, "Thus says God, 'Why do you break the commandments of the LORD, so that you cannot prosper? Because you have forsaken the LORD, he has forsaken you.'"<sup>21</sup>But they conspired against him, and by command of the king they stoned him with stones in the court of the house of the LORD.<sup>22</sup>Thus Joash the king did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada, Zechariah's father, had shown him, but killed his son. And when he was dying, he said, "May the LORD see and avenge!"<sup>23</sup>At the end of the year the army of the Syrians came up against Joash. They came to Judah and Jerusalem and destroyed all the princes of the people from among the people and sent all their spoil to the king of Damascus.<sup>24</sup>Though the army of the Syrians had come with few men, the LORD delivered into their hand a very great army, because Judah had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers. Thus they executed judgment on Joash.<sup>25</sup>When they had departed from him, leaving him severely wounded, his servants conspired against him because of the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest, and killed him on his bed. So he died, and they buried him in the city of David, but they did not bury him in the tombs of the kings.<sup>26</sup>Those who conspired against him were Zabad the son of Shimeath the Ammonite, and Jehozabad the son of Shimrith the Moabite.<sup>27</sup>Accounts of his sons and of the many oracles against him and of the rebuilding of the house of God are written in the Story of the Book of the Kings. And Amaziah his son reigned in his place.
24.overview:
Where we are. Athaliah is dead, the boy Joash sits on David’s throne, and Jehoiada the priest has renewed the covenant and restored the temple worship (23:16–21). Joash is seven, and the old priest who hid and crowned him now stands beside him.

The message. A faith that leans entirely on someone else is tested the day that person dies. Joash did right “all the days of Jehoiada the priest” (v. 2), and when Jehoiada was buried, the king listened to flatterers, abandoned the house he had repaired and killed the prophet God sent to call him back. God is patient, sending prophet after prophet, but he is not mocked: those who forsake him are forsaken, and the honour that office cannot buy goes to faithfulness.

Why it was said. The first readers had a rebuilt temple and its priests, and they knew what it was to depend on a few faithful leaders (see the introduction). The chapter warned them that a good start, a repaired house and a godly mentor do not by themselves keep a people faithful; each generation must seek the LORD for itself.

How the chapter makes its case. Joash begins well under Jehoiada’s care, and decides to restore the house of the LORD; when the Levites drag their feet, he calls the high priest back to the law of Moses (vv. 1–7). A chest at the gate fills with joyful gifts, the work is done honestly, and the offerings go up “all the days of Jehoiada” (vv. 8–14). Then Jehoiada dies and is buried among the kings, the princes bow, and the king listens (vv. 15–17). Judah turns to idols; God sends prophets, and last of all Jehoiada’s own son, whom the king has stoned in the temple court (vv. 18–22). Within a year a small Syrian force routs Judah, Joash is murdered in his bed, and he is buried outside the tombs of the kings (vv. 23–27).

Where it leads. To Christ above all by the need it exposes. Joash’s goodness lasted only as long as his priest, and Jehoiada, for all his 130 years, died. Jesus is the priest who “holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:24), and the King whose faithfulness never leaned on anyone else. The chapter also gives a pattern Jesus himself drew on: God sending messenger after messenger to a people who would not listen, until the murdered Zechariah became his example of Jerusalem’s guilt (Matthew 23:35), and the Son himself was sent last and killed.

For us. Thank God for the people who have held you up, and then ask whether your faith is your own. Watch for the voices that flatter, because they decide more than we think. And remember that the God who answered Zechariah’s cry also heard the better prayer of the Son who died for those who killed him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — All the Days of Jehoiada
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joash begins well, and the chapter tells us at once why: he did right “all the days of Jehoiada the priest”. The opening verses set out the reign (forty years, a mother from Beersheba) and the time limit written into its verdict, and show Jehoiada rebuilding the royal household around a boy whose family had been massacred (vv. 1–3). Then Joash takes up a project of his own, the repair of the house that had sheltered him. When the Levites are slow to collect, he does not invent a tax but calls the high priest back to the law of Moses, because Athaliah’s sons had plundered the house for the Baals (vv. 4–7).
verseByVerse.theology: A good beginning is a gift, not a guarantee. The chapter opens with every advantage a young king could have and asks what he will do when the man beside him is gone.
verseByVerse.examples: Correcting someone we owe a great deal is hard. Joash did it by appealing to God's word rather than to his own position, which is the right way to do it.

verseByVerse.quote: Joash was seven years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Zibiah of Beersheba. And Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest. Jehoiada got for him two wives, and he had sons and daughters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joash reigned forty years, but his doing right is tied from the start to the lifetime of Jehoiada the priest, who also rebuilt the royal household around him.

Zibiah of Beersheba. After Athaliah, a daughter of Ahab’s house from Samaria, the Chronicler names a queen mother from Beersheba in the far south of Judah. The detail makes a quiet point: the northern house is out of the palace.

He reigned forty years. A long reign, the length of David’s and Solomon’s, and yet the verdict has a time limit built in.

All the days of Jehoiada the priest. Kings tells it more warmly: he did right “all his days, because Jehoiada the priest instructed him” (2 Kings 12:2). The Chronicler cuts the sentence to the length of one old man’s life, not unkindly but precisely, and the rest of the chapter is the proof.

Jehoiada got for him two wives. A domestic note that is easy to read past. Two chapters ago this dynasty was one baby hidden in a bedroom (22:11), and the man who hid him is now deliberately rebuilding a household around him. Somebody had to think about grandchildren before there were any, and here it was not the king. Scripture records the two marriages as a way of securing the royal line after Athaliah’s massacre (22:10), without approving polygamy (Genesis 2:24).

verseByVerse.quote: After this Joash decided to restore the house of the LORD. And he gathered the priests and the Levites and said to them, "Go out to the cities of Judah and gather from all Israel money to repair the house of your God from year to year, and see that you act quickly." But the Levites did not act quickly. So the king summoned Jehoiada the chief and said to him, "Why have you not required the Levites to bring in from Judah and Jerusalem the tax levied by Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the congregation of Israel for the tent of testimony?" For the sons of Athaliah, that wicked woman, had broken into the house of God, and had also used all the dedicated things of the house of the LORD for the Baals.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joash resolved to repair the temple, and when the Levites were slow, he held the high priest to the tax Moses had commanded, because Athaliah’s sons had plundered God’s house for the Baals.

Joash decided to restore the house of the LORD. It is his own idea, and the right one for this particular man. For six years the temple was his nursery and his hiding place, and the first great project of his reign is to put it back in order.

But the Levites did not act quickly. The order is to collect “quickly”, and the Levites “did not act quickly”. The religious staff of Judah, freshly restored to their duties by Jehoiada himself, were slow about the very work they existed for, and the Chronicler neither explains nor excuses it.

The tax levied by Moses. The king summons the high priest (see Chief priests and the high priest), and what he does and does not do matters. He does not invent a levy or appeal to his own authority. He asks why an existing statute is not being enforced: the half shekel each Israelite gave for the tent of meeting (Exodus 30:12–16). A young king rebukes the old priest who saved his life by opening the law of Moses on the table between them. That is a hard thing to do well, and it was done well here.

The sons of Athaliah, that wicked woman. Verse 7 says why the house needed the money at all: Athaliah’s sons had broken into it and spent its dedicated things on the Baals. The repair fund is not decorating. It is undoing a robbery.

Uncertain wording. Who “the sons of Athaliah” were is not clear. Her son Ahaziah is the only one named, and his brothers were carried off and killed (21:17; 22:1). The phrase may mean sons of hers not otherwise recorded, or more likely her followers and partisans, as “sons of” can mean in Hebrew. Either way the point stands: under her rule the temple was looted for Baal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — The Chest at the Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God’s work is set before his people plainly and handled honestly, they give gladly. Instead of sending collectors out, Joash sets a chest at the temple gate; the people rejoice and give until the work is paid for (vv. 8–10). The chest is emptied daily by officials of the king and the chief priest together, and the money goes straight to the craftsmen, who restore the house to its proper condition (vv. 11–13). The surplus becomes vessels for the service, and the burnt offerings go up regularly “all the days of Jehoiada” (v. 14), the second time the phrase has sounded, and a warning that those days will end.
verseByVerse.theology: Generous giving followed a simple, visible arrangement and a clear purpose. People give gladly when they can see what the gift is for.
verseByVerse.examples: Joy is the note of this giving: they rejoiced (v. 10). Giving to God's work is meant to be glad, not grudging (2 Corinthians 9:7).

verseByVerse.quote: So the king commanded, and they made a chest and set it outside the gate of the house of the LORD. And proclamation was made throughout Judah and Jerusalem to bring in for the LORD the tax that Moses the servant of God laid on Israel in the wilderness. And all the princes and all the people rejoiced and brought their tax and dropped it into the chest until they had finished. And whenever the chest was brought to the king's officers by the Levites, when they saw that there was much money in it, the king's secretary and the officer of the chief priest would come and empty the chest and take it and return it to its place. Thus they did day after day, and collected money in abundance. And the king and Jehoiada gave it to those who had charge of the work of the house of the LORD, and they hired masons and carpenters to restore the house of the LORD, and also workers in iron and bronze to repair the house of the LORD. So those who were engaged in the work labored, and the repairing went forward in their hands, and they restored the house of God to its proper condition and strengthened it. And when they had finished, they brought the rest of the money before the king and Jehoiada, and with it were made utensils for the house of the LORD, both for the service and for the burnt offerings, and dishes for incense and vessels of gold and silver. And they offered burnt offerings in the house of the LORD regularly all the days of Jehoiada.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Given a plain, public and honest way to give, the people gave gladly until the work was done, the house was restored, and the daily offerings went up again.

They made a chest. It stands “outside the gate”, where the people are. The Levites had been asked to go and fetch the money and had not gone; so instead of chasing the collectors, Joash puts a box where every worshipper in Jerusalem walks past it.

All the princes and all the people rejoiced. They gave until the giving was done, not until they were tired of it. The chest filled so fast it had to be emptied every day, and by two officials together, one from the palace and one from the temple, so that neither institution could be accused and neither man ever handled the money alone.

Wisdom that has not aged. Money given in public, into a container people can see, counted by more than one pair of hands from more than one office. It protects the giver, it protects the work, and it protects the man who does the counting, who is usually the person most in need of protecting.

They restored the house of God to its proper condition. The work is done properly, the house restored and strengthened, and the surplus is turned into vessels for the service. Nobody pockets it.

They offered burnt offerings. The last line says what all the scaffolding was for: burnt offerings “regularly all the days of Jehoiada”. The plaster and ironwork existed so that a nation could come morning and evening and meet its God at an altar still standing. And “all the days of Jehoiada” has now been said twice, a warning that those days will end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — Then the King Listened to Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With Jehoiada gone, Joash shows where his heart has been leaning. The old priest dies at 130 and is buried among the kings for the good he did (vv. 15–16). The princes come, bow to the king, and he listens to them (v. 17). Judah abandons the house so lately repaired for Asherim and idols, and wrath comes; yet God sends prophets to bring them back, and they will not listen (vv. 18–19). Last, the Spirit clothes Jehoiada’s own son Zechariah, who tells them that those who forsake the LORD are forsaken. At the king’s command they stone him in the temple court, and he dies crying, “May the LORD see and avenge!” (vv. 20–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Ingratitude is a doorway to worse sins (v. 22). Remembering God's kindness, and the people through whom it came, is a guard for the heart.
verseByVerse.examples: Grief is a vulnerable time. Joash was turned in the season after a death, and those who mourn need friends who will keep them near God's word.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jehoiada grew old and full of days, and died. He was 130 years old at his death. And they buried him in the city of David among the kings, because he had done good in Israel, and toward God and his house. Now after the death of Jehoiada the princes of Judah came and paid homage to the king. Then the king listened to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoiada died full of years and was buried among the kings for the good he had done, and as soon as he was gone the princes bowed to Joash and won his ear.

He was 130 years old at his death. Moses died at a hundred and twenty and Aaron at a hundred and twenty-three. The Chronicler gives this priest a longer life than either, in a book that counts years carefully. This is a patriarch’s death notice.

They buried him in the city of David among the kings. A priest buried among the kings. No law required it; the nation decided that the man who hid the king, crowned him, tore down Baal’s house and restarted the offerings belonged there, and gave its reasons: good done in Israel, toward God, and toward his house. Hold that sentence, because the chapter’s last verses will say the opposite of the actual king.

Then the king listened to them. The hinge of the chapter turns on a bow: the princes “paid homage”, and “the king listened to them”. Nobody argued Joash out of decades of temple religion; the text records no crisis and no seduction. Men of rank did obeisance to a king who had spent his life as a priest’s ward, he found that he liked it, and the men who flattered him got their way.

A priest who does not die. Joash’s faithfulness lasted exactly as long as his priest, and even 130 years run out. The letter to the Hebrews makes this the great weakness of every earthly priesthood, that its priests were “prevented by death from continuing in office”, and the great strength of Christ’s: “he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:23–24). He will never be buried and leave us to the flatterers.

In everyday life. The people whose respect we want end up deciding what we do, and they arrive politely, at a funeral, with excellent manners, not looking like a turning point. The defence is not suspicion of everyone, but a heart that already has the approval that matters, the Father’s, given in Christ, to which no bow can add.

verseByVerse.quote: And they abandoned the house of the LORD, the God of their fathers, and served the Asherim and the idols. And wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this guilt of theirs. Yet he sent prophets among them to bring them back to the LORD. These testified against them, but they would not pay attention. Then the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, and he stood above the people, and said to them, "Thus says God, 'Why do you break the commandments of the LORD, so that you cannot prosper? Because you have forsaken the LORD, he has forsaken you.'" But they conspired against him, and by command of the king they stoned him with stones in the court of the house of the LORD. Thus Joash the king did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada, Zechariah's father, had shown him, but killed his son. And when he was dying, he said, "May the LORD see and avenge!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah abandoned the house Joash had repaired for idols; God sent prophets and at last Jehoiada’s own son, and the king had him stoned in the temple court, forgetting all the kindness he owed his father.

They abandoned the house of the LORD. The very building Joash had repaired. Every beam had been paid for by people dropping coins in a box at the gate, and the vessels on its tables were made from the surplus of his own appeal.

Yet he sent prophets among them. God does not go straight from their idolatry to the sword. He sends men to talk, repeatedly (v. 27 mentions “the many oracles against him”), to people who have stopped listening. Jesus told the same story in his parable of the vineyard: servant after servant sent and beaten, and then, “Finally he sent his son to them” (Matthew 21:37).

The Spirit of God clothed Zechariah. The verb used of Gideon (Judges 6:34): the Spirit putting the man on like a garment. This is Jehoiada’s own son, standing above the crowd in the courtyard his father saved.

Because you have forsaken the LORD, he has forsaken you. Zechariah is not innovating. It is Azariah’s word to Asa in this same book, “If you forsake him, he will forsake you” (15:2), and the message his family has always preached, in the place it has always preached it.

In the court of the house of the LORD. Here a baby was hidden and a boy crowned. In this courtyard, at the height of his triumph, Jehoiada gave one order: Athaliah, who had butchered the royal children, must not be put to death inside these walls (23:14). Now Joash has his old guardian’s son killed on those very stones. Out of reverence for the place, the murderess was led out to the horse gate. The prophet was stoned where he stood.

Joash the king did not remember the kindness. His whole life was a kindness he had not earned: the arms that carried him out of the nursery, the room that hid him, the covenant that crowned him, the marriages that gave him children. Ingratitude is not a small sin with a mild name. It is the soil this murder grew in.

Why is gratitude so hard? The story we tell about ourselves pushes against it: we are self-made, our achievements earned, our life our own project. The more a person believes that, the less he owes anyone, and the more irritating it is to be reminded of those who carried him. Joash had more reason than any king in this book to know his life was a gift, and that may be exactly why the reminder became unbearable: Zechariah’s face was a debt he did not want to look at. Paul punctures the self-made story: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). The gospel answers by giving us something too large to resent. When we see that our standing with God was bought at the cost of the Son, gratitude stops being a debt to be settled and avoided, and becomes the ordinary air of a rescued life.

Two dying prayers. Zechariah dies praying, “May the LORD see and avenge!” Centuries later Stephen was stoned for saying the same kind of thing, and as he went down he prayed the opposite: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:60). Both prayers are righteous, and what stands between them is the cross. Zechariah asked God to see, and God saw. Stephen could ask God not to charge the sin to the men throwing the stones, because he knew that a better blood than his own had been poured out for such men, in a city with a long habit of killing those God sent to it.

Which Zechariah did Jesus mean? Jesus speaks of “the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar” (Matthew 23:35). Some think he means the prophet Zechariah, son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1); others that Barachiah was a grandfather or another name of Jehoiada, or that the name was miscopied. The likeliest reading is this Zechariah, killed in the temple court: the last murder of a righteous man in the traditional Hebrew order of books, where Chronicles stands last, as Abel’s is the first. Luke gives no father’s name (Luke 11:51). Two verses later Jesus grieves over Jerusalem, “the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it” (Matthew 23:37), and within days it did the same to him.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus places the murder “between the sanctuary and the altar” (Matthew 23:35), which fits this killing in the temple court.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–27 — At the End of the Year
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sees, and he answers within the year. A small Syrian army defeats Judah’s great one, kills the princes who led the king astray, and leaves Joash badly wounded, “because Judah had forsaken the LORD” (vv. 23–24). His own servants then kill him in his bed “because of the blood of the son of Jehoiada”, and he is buried in the city of David but not in the tombs of the kings, where the priest lies (v. 25). The assassins are named, both the sons of foreign mothers, and the reign is closed with a note of its many prophetic warnings and its rebuilt temple (vv. 26–27).
verseByVerse.theology: Zechariah's cry was heard. God does not forget the blood of his servants, even when the courts of the powerful do.
verseByVerse.examples: No one is too privileged to fall. Joash had been rescued, raised and crowned by grace, and he still turned.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of the year the army of the Syrians came up against Joash. They came to Judah and Jerusalem and destroyed all the princes of the people from among the people and sent all their spoil to the king of Damascus. Though the army of the Syrians had come with few men, the LORD delivered into their hand a very great army, because Judah had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers. Thus they executed judgment on Joash. When they had departed from him, leaving him severely wounded, his servants conspired against him because of the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest, and killed him on his bed. So he died, and they buried him in the city of David, but they did not bury him in the tombs of the kings. Those who conspired against him were Zabad the son of Shimeath the Ammonite, and Jehozabad the son of Shimrith the Moabite. Accounts of his sons and of the many oracles against him and of the rebuilding of the house of God are written in the Story of the Book of the Kings. And Amaziah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Within the year God answered Zechariah’s cry: a small Syrian force crushed Judah and killed the princes, Joash was murdered in his bed by his servants, and he was buried apart from the kings.

At the end of the year. Inside twelve months. The Chronicler dates the answer to that dying prayer and puts it in the first clause.

All the princes of the people. Look who dies: the men who paid homage in verse 17, whose flattery turned a king. The counsel room that ruined him is emptied in one campaign.

Though the army of the Syrians had come with few men. This book has told us what God does with numbers. Abijah’s men were outnumbered two to one and won “because they relied on the LORD” (13:18); Asa prayed to the God who helps “between the mighty and the weak” (14:11). The rule has not changed: God gives victory to those who rely on him, whatever the numbers. But Judah is now on the wrong side of it, “because Judah had forsaken the LORD”, and a small Syrian force walks through a very great army.

Because of the blood of the son of Jehoiada. The narrator states the motive, so the prayer of verse 22 is answered exactly. And the man smuggled as an infant into a bedroom to keep him alive is killed in his bed by his own servants.

They did not bury him in the tombs of the kings. Set beside verse 16, this sums up the chapter (see Burial Customs and Tombs). The priest lies among the kings because he did good in Israel and toward God and his house; the king lies in the same city, outside that room. Kings records the burial without the sting, “they buried him with his fathers in the city of David” (2 Kings 12:21), and the Chronicler leaves out “with his fathers”. Office does not settle the honour. Faithfulness does.

Zabad the son of Shimeath the Ammonite. Verse 26 names the two assassins by their mothers, and both mothers are foreign, an Ammonite and a Moabite; Kings gives the men’s names without the nationalities (2 Kings 12:21). A king who forsook the God of his fathers is put down in his own house by sons of the very nations the law kept out of the LORD’s assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3).

Another man’s faith. Forty years, and all the good in them depended on another man’s faith. That is the warning this chapter exists to give, and it should be taken personally by anyone whose faith has always had a Jehoiada in it: a parent, a pastor, a friend, a church. Those gifts are real. But the day comes when the person who held us up is buried, and what is left standing is whatever faith was really our own. The Lord Jesus is not a scaffold but the foundation. He does not grow old and die as Jehoiada did; he is risen and lives for ever, and the house that rests on him still stands when every prop around it has gone into the ground. By his Spirit he makes a borrowed faith a person’s own.

Uncertain wording. Where the ESV has “Story” in verse 27, the Hebrew word is midrash, from a verb meaning to seek or study. Here it probably means a written account or commentary on the kings’ history (compare 13:22). What exactly this source was is not known; it is not the later Jewish genre called midrash.

24.theology:
The chapter is built on one clause used twice, all the days of Jehoiada (vv. 2, 14). A faith held up entirely by another person's faith is not thereby false, but it is not yet the man's own, and it is tested on the day that person dies.

God's patience is written in before the judgment, as it was with Jehoram: prophets sent repeatedly (vv. 19, 27), and only after the word has been refused does the sword come, dated at the end of the year.

Kings tells the reign differently. It omits Jehoiada's death, the apostasy and Zechariah, and says Joash bought off Hazael of Syria with the temple's gifts (2 Kings 12:17-18), where Chronicles reports a Syrian raid that killed the princes. These are different selections, not rival histories: the payment may well have followed the defeat. Kings shows how Judah was stripped; Chronicles shows why.

Zechariah also answers a question this book's swift judgments can raise. He was faithful, filled with the Spirit and right, and he was stoned for it. Chronicles does not promise that the righteous always prosper in this life. It leaves his cry with God, who answered within the year and will answer fully on the last day.
24.examples:
Religious people can be slow about the very work they exist for, as the Levites were (v. 5). The Chronicler records it without softening it, and it is a fair question for churches and their staff today.

Buildings and budgets serve worship, not the other way round. The roof was mended so that the offerings could go up morning and evening.

A whole reign turned on the bows of flatterers after a funeral. Flattery rarely looks like danger when it arrives.

keyVerse.quote: And Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter hangs on its final phrase, which is repeated in verse 14 and then fulfilled when Jehoiada dies and Joash falls. It warns that a faith resting on another person’s faith is tested when that person is gone, and it sends us to Christ, the priest who does not die and who makes our faith our own.

24.reflection:
Joash did right “all the days of Jehoiada the priest” (v. 2). Who have been the Jehoiadas in your life? How can you tell whether your faith is truly your own, and what helps it become so?

The chest at the gate made giving public, joyful and honestly handled (vv. 8–14). What does this passage teach about how churches should ask for and look after money?

After Jehoiada’s death the princes bowed and “the king listened to them” (v. 17). Whose approval most shapes your decisions? How does the Father’s approval, given in Christ, free us from flattery?

Zechariah died praying “May the LORD see and avenge!”, and Stephen prayed “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:60). What has changed between the two prayers, and how does the cross shape the way we respond to those who wrong us?

25.title: Not with His Whole Heart
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jehoaddan of Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not with a whole heart.<sup>3</sup>And as soon as the royal power was firmly his, he killed his servants who had struck down the king his father.<sup>4</sup>But he did not put their children to death, according to what is written in the Law, in the Book of Moses, where the LORD commanded, "Fathers shall not die because of their children, nor children die because of their fathers, but each one shall die for his own sin."<sup>5</sup>Then Amaziah assembled the men of Judah and set them by fathers' houses under commanders of thousands and of hundreds for all Judah and Benjamin. He mustered those twenty years old and upward, and found that they were 300,000 choice men, fit for war, able to handle spear and shield.<sup>6</sup>He hired also 100,000 mighty men of valor from Israel for 100 talents of silver.<sup>7</sup>But a man of God came to him and said, "O king, do not let the army of Israel go with you, for the LORD is not with Israel, with all these Ephraimites.<sup>8</sup>But go, act, be strong for the battle. Why should you suppose that God will cast you down before the enemy? For God has power to help or to cast down."<sup>9</sup>And Amaziah said to the man of God, "But what shall we do about the hundred talents that I have given to the army of Israel?" The man of God answered, "The LORD is able to give you much more than this."<sup>10</sup>Then Amaziah discharged the army that had come to him from Ephraim to go home again. And they became very angry with Judah and returned home in fierce anger.<sup>11</sup>But Amaziah took courage and led out his people and went to the Valley of Salt and struck down 10,000 men of Seir.<sup>12</sup>The men of Judah captured another 10,000 alive and took them to the top of a rock and threw them down from the top of the rock, and they were all dashed to pieces.<sup>13</sup>But the men of the army whom Amaziah sent back, not letting them go with him to battle, raided the cities of Judah, from Samaria to Beth-horon, and struck down 3,000 people in them and took much spoil.<sup>14</sup>After Amaziah came from striking down the Edomites, he brought the gods of the men of Seir and set them up as his gods and worshiped them, making offerings to them.<sup>15</sup>Therefore the LORD was angry with Amaziah and sent to him a prophet, who said to him, "Why have you sought the gods of a people who did not deliver their own people from your hand?"<sup>16</sup>But as he was speaking, the king said to him, "Have we made you a royal counselor? Stop! Why should you be struck down?" So the prophet stopped, but said, "I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel."<sup>17</sup>Then Amaziah king of Judah took counsel and sent to Joash the son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, "Come, let us look one another in the face."<sup>18</sup>And Joash the king of Israel sent word to Amaziah king of Judah, "A thistle on Lebanon sent to a cedar on Lebanon, saying, 'Give your daughter to my son for a wife,' and a wild beast of Lebanon passed by and trampled down the thistle.<sup>19</sup>You say, 'See, I have struck down Edom,' and your heart has lifted you up in boastfulness. But now stay at home. Why should you provoke trouble so that you fall, you and Judah with you?"<sup>20</sup>But Amaziah would not listen, for it was of God, in order that he might give them into the hand of their enemies, because they had sought the gods of Edom.<sup>21</sup>So Joash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced one another in battle at Beth-shemesh, which belongs to Judah.<sup>22</sup>And Judah was defeated by Israel, and every man fled to his home.<sup>23</sup>And Joash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Joash, son of Ahaziah, at Beth-shemesh, and brought him to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem for 400 cubits, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate.<sup>24</sup>And he seized all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of God, in the care of Obed-edom. He seized also the treasuries of the king's house, also hostages, and he returned to Samaria.<sup>25</sup>Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, lived fifteen years after the death of Joash the son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel.<sup>26</sup>Now the rest of the deeds of Amaziah, from first to last, are they not written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel?<sup>27</sup>From the time when he turned away from the LORD they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But they sent after him to Lachish and put him to death there.<sup>28</sup>And they brought him upon horses, and he was buried with his fathers in the city of David.
25.overview:
Where we are. Joash, who began well and ended by stoning Jehoiada’s son, has been murdered in his bed (24:25). His son Amaziah is the second of three kings in a row who begin well and end badly (chapters 24 to 26).

The message. A heart that obeys God only in part will not stay obedient. Amaziah does right “yet not with a whole heart” (v. 2): he keeps the law and obeys a prophet at real cost, then bows to the gods of the people he has just beaten and silences the prophet who asks why. God, who is able to give “much more than this” (v. 9), will not share a divided heart, and the man who will not listen is finally given the deafness he chose.

Why it was said. The first readers were a small, poor community tempted to keep the LORD as one loyalty among several, and to measure faithfulness by what it cost them (see the introduction). Amaziah shows them both the price of obedience honestly counted and the far greater price of a heart kept half for something else.

How the chapter makes its case.
