First, the good beginning (vv. 1–10): Amaziah spares his father’s murderers’ children because the Book of Moses says so, and at a prophet’s word sends home an army he has already paid for. Then the turn (vv. 11–16): he wins in Edom by God’s help, behaves with savage cruelty, and comes home with Edom’s gods, silencing the prophet who protests. Then the fall (vv. 17–24): proud of his victory, he provokes Israel, ignores a stinging fable and is routed, and Jerusalem’s wall and temple treasury are lost. Last, the end (vv. 25–28): the Chronicler dates the conspiracy that killed him from the day “he turned away from the LORD”.

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes. Amaziah is Judah’s own verdict on most of us: right in public, divided within. The only whole heart ever offered to God in this world belonged to the Son of David, who could say, “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8). God promised to give his people “one heart” (Ezekiel 11:19), and he does it by joining them to that Son, whose undivided obedience is counted to those who trust him.

For us. Obedience is not proved by one costly decision in a crisis, but by what we do afterwards, when the prophet has gone home. Ask what you have quietly kept room for beside the Lord, and bring that divided heart to the Saviour who gave his whole heart for you and can make yours one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Right, Yet Not with a Whole Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amaziah begins with real obedience, though not wholehearted. Once secure, he executes his father’s assassins but spares their children because the Book of Moses forbids punishing children for their fathers’ sins (vv. 1–4). He musters a smaller army than his predecessors and hires a hundred thousand soldiers from Israel for a hundred talents of silver (vv. 5–6). A man of God tells him to send them home, because the LORD is not with Israel and God alone has power to help or to cast down (vv. 7–8). Amaziah asks about the money, is told that the LORD can give much more than this, and obeys, at the cost of angering the men he dismisses (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: A divided heart can still do many right things. What it cannot do is keep doing them when no one is watching, which is what the rest of the chapter shows.
verseByVerse.examples: Scripture is meant to stand on the table when our feelings run highest. Amaziah's best moment is a king letting a sentence of God's law overrule his grief.

verseByVerse.quote: Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jehoaddan of Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not with a whole heart. And as soon as the royal power was firmly his, he killed his servants who had struck down the king his father. But he did not put their children to death, according to what is written in the Law, in the Book of Moses, where the LORD commanded, "Fathers shall not die because of their children, nor children die because of their fathers, but each one shall die for his own sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amaziah did right, but not with a whole heart, and his first act as a secure king was to do justice by the book of God rather than by the custom of revenge.

Yet not with a whole heart. This is the verdict on the whole chapter. Kings puts it as a comparison: he did right, “yet not like David his father” (2 Kings 14:3). The Chronicler goes past the comparison to the heart itself. A whole heart has been this book’s measure of a king for ten chapters: Asa’s heart “was wholly true all his days” (15:17); “the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him” (16:9); Jehoshaphat “sought the LORD with all his heart” (22:9). Amaziah is weighed on Judah’s own scales and found wanting.

The divided heart. Søren Kierkegaard gave one of his books a title that is a sermon in itself, Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing. Most of us do not choose evil outright; we want too many things at once, and offer God a share of a heart already promised elsewhere. We live in compartments, work, family, leisure, faith, each with its own rules, and call it balance. Amaziah would have recognised the arrangement. Such a heart can never rest, because every master it serves wants more. The gospel’s answer is not first a demand to try harder but a heart made whole by grace: “I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them” (Ezekiel 11:19).

As soon as the royal power was firmly his. This book keeps noticing what a man does the moment he is safe. Rehoboam abandoned the law when his rule was established (12:1); Jehoram murdered his brothers (21:4). Amaziah executes the men who murdered his father in his bed (24:25), which is justice and not revenge.

But he did not put their children to death. Power, motive and the custom of the age all pointed the other way: three chapters back a queen went through the royal nursery (22:10), and four chapters back a king put six brothers to the sword (21:4). Amaziah has the assassins’ sons in front of him and spares them, “according to what is written in the Law, in the Book of Moses” (Deuteronomy 24:16).

In everyday life. A man held back by God’s written word is safer than a man held back only by his temperament, because temperament gives way when he is angry. Whatever else was wrong with Amaziah’s heart, on this day the book on the table was stronger than the grief in his chest.

Does this contradict God “visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children” (Exodus 20:5)? No. Deuteronomy 24:16 governs human courts: only the guilty may be put to death by a judge or a king. Exodus 20:5 speaks of God’s own providence over families that go on hating him, generation after generation. Before God, too, “The soul who sins shall die” (Ezekiel 18:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amaziah assembled the men of Judah and set them by fathers' houses under commanders of thousands and of hundreds for all Judah and Benjamin. He mustered those twenty years old and upward, and found that they were 300,000 choice men, fit for war, able to handle spear and shield. He hired also 100,000 mighty men of valor from Israel for 100 talents of silver. But a man of God came to him and said, "O king, do not let the army of Israel go with you, for the LORD is not with Israel, with all these Ephraimites. But go, act, be strong for the battle. Why should you suppose that God will cast you down before the enemy? For God has power to help or to cast down." And Amaziah said to the man of God, "But what shall we do about the hundred talents that I have given to the army of Israel?" The man of God answered, "The LORD is able to give you much more than this." Then Amaziah discharged the army that had come to him from Ephraim to go home again. And they became very angry with Judah and returned home in fierce anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At a prophet’s word Amaziah sent home an army he had already paid for, because God, not numbers, decides battles, and God is richer than any loss obedience costs.

300,000 choice men. Judah and Benjamin together muster fewer than under Abijah (13:3), Asa (14:8) or Jehoshaphat (17:14–18). Judah has not recovered from the Syrian raid in his father’s last year, which destroyed all the princes of the people (24:23–24).

He hired also 100,000 mighty men of valor from Israel. The price is a hundred talents, something over three tonnes of silver, paid up front.

But a man of God came to him. His word is going to cost a fortune: send the northerners home, “for the LORD is not with Israel, with all these Ephraimites.” The northern kingdom had worshipped Jeroboam’s calves for two centuries, and an army hired from it was an alliance with apostasy (compare 19:2). Then the heart of the matter: “God has power to help or to cast down.” Numbers will not decide this battle.

But what shall we do about the hundred talents? Amaziah asks the question anybody would ask, and the Chronicler records it without mockery. It is an accountant’s problem, and a real one: the money is gone and the contract signed. Obedience here does not mean giving up something he might have had; it means writing off something he has already bought.

The LORD is able to give you much more than this. This is the sentence to take out of the chapter and keep. It does not say the hundred talents were nothing, or that Amaziah was wrong to count them. It lets the cost stand at full value and then sets God beside it: God is richer than the mistake. That is the shape of most hard obedience. It is rarely a choice between loss and no loss, but between a loss you can see on the ledger and a God whose resources are not on the ledger at all, and the deposit already paid is the hardest money in the world to walk away from.

Much more than this, in Christ. What makes such obedience possible is not nerve but the God the prophet names. For Christians he has already shown how much more he is able to give: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). The one who gave the Son will not be outbid by a hundred talents.

What it does not mean. Not that every sum given up for God comes back in kind, or quickly; the dismissed troops went home in fierce anger, and worse followed (v. 13). It is a statement about God’s riches, not a formula for recovering losses.
verseByVerse.note: 100 talents of silver is about 3¾ tons (a talent was about 75 pounds, ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — The Gods of the Losers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Victory given by God becomes the occasion of Amaziah’s fall. He goes out with a reduced army and defeats Edom in the Valley of Salt, but his men throw ten thousand prisoners off a cliff (vv. 11–12), while the dismissed troops raid Judah’s towns (v. 13). Then, astonishingly, he brings home the gods of the people he has just defeated and worships them (v. 14). The LORD sends a prophet with an unanswerable question: why seek gods that could not save their own people? Amaziah silences him with a threat, and the prophet leaves him with a sentence of judgment (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Victory is a dangerous moment. Amaziah's slide into idolatry began not in defeat but the day after a triumph.
verseByVerse.examples: The cruelty of verse 12 is recorded, not approved. A reader troubled by it is reading rightly; Scripture tells the truth about what God's people did, including what shamed them.

verseByVerse.quote: But Amaziah took courage and led out his people and went to the Valley of Salt and struck down 10,000 men of Seir. The men of Judah captured another 10,000 alive and took them to the top of a rock and threw them down from the top of the rock, and they were all dashed to pieces. But the men of the army whom Amaziah sent back, not letting them go with him to battle, raided the cities of Judah, from Samaria to Beth-horon, and struck down 3,000 people in them and took much spoil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave Amaziah victory over Edom with a reduced army, but the victory did not excuse his cruelty, and his obedience was followed at once by painful loss.

Amaziah took courage. It is the verb used of Jehoiada in the seventh year (23:1). He goes out short-handed, having just sent away a quarter of his force at the word of a prophet, and he wins. God has power to help, and he helped.

Why Edom. Edom had broken free of Judah in the days of his great-grandfather Jehoram (21:8–10), and this campaign was an attempt to win it back. The Valley of Salt, probably near the south end of the Dead Sea, was where David’s army had once struck down eighteen thousand Edomites (1 Chronicles 18:12), so the battlefield itself announced what Amaziah meant to restore.

Threw them down from the top of the rock. Then verse 12, which no honest reader can hurry past: ten thousand prisoners marched to a cliff edge and pushed off it. The Chronicler reports it and says not one word in its favour: no divine command, no prophet approving it. He lets it stand against the man who did it. A victory won in God’s strength does not make right what the winner does with his prisoners, and a man can be carried by God’s help one day and act as a butcher the next.

Raided the cities of Judah. Then the bill for obedience arrives, and the Chronicler puts it here on purpose. The men he had obediently sent away have killed three thousand of his people, and nothing in the text tidies this up. The word of God was right, the obedience was right, and the short-term account is a disaster.

Obedience and results. Scripture is more honest here than much preaching. Obedience is not a way of getting comfortable results in the short term; it is trust placed in the character of a God who has promised to give much more than this, on a timetable he has not shown us, and who is not obliged to make the first consequence of doing right feel like a reward. The Son of God obeyed perfectly, and the first consequence was a cross; the reward came on the third day.

Uncertain wording. “From Samaria to Beth-horon” is puzzling, since Samaria was Israel’s capital, not a town of Judah. Most take it to mean that the troops, setting out from Samaria, raided Judah’s border towns as far as Beth-horon, north-west of Jerusalem; some suggest an otherwise unknown place of the same name. Either way, the towns along Judah’s northern edge paid for the king’s obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: After Amaziah came from striking down the Edomites, he brought the gods of the men of Seir and set them up as his gods and worshiped them, making offerings to them. Therefore the LORD was angry with Amaziah and sent to him a prophet, who said to him, "Why have you sought the gods of a people who did not deliver their own people from your hand?" But as he was speaking, the king said to him, "Have we made you a royal counselor? Stop! Why should you be struck down?" So the prophet stopped, but said, "I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having beaten Edom, Amaziah worshipped Edom’s gods, and when God’s prophet asked the obvious question he silenced him, sealing his own judgment.

He brought the gods of the men of Seir. Here is the absurdity. He has seen what these gods did for their own people: nothing. Their worshippers lie dead in the Valley of Salt and broken at the foot of a cliff. He carries the images home to Jerusalem, sets them up “as his gods”, and makes offerings to them. Conquerors often carried off a defeated enemy’s images as trophies; Amaziah bowed to them.

Why have you sought the gods of a people who did not deliver their own people from your hand? The prophet puts his finger exactly on it. No idol has ever been chosen because the evidence was good. The evidence is almost always in plain view and almost always against it. The heart decides first, out of what it wants, and finds its reasons afterwards. Ask it of anything that has our confidence: what has it actually delivered, for anybody, under pressure?

Have we made you a royal counselor? Stop! The king’s answer shows the whole state of him. For the third reign running this book locates the trouble in whose advice a king will take (22:3–4; 24:17). Amaziah tells a man carrying God’s word that he has no seat at the table, threatens him with death, and in the very next verse “took counsel” and declared war. He had a room full of advisers; he simply would not have the one who contradicted him.

So the prophet stopped. That is its own kind of courage. He did not stay to argue. He said one more sentence, that God had determined to destroy the king who would not listen, and walked out, leaving a verdict the king could not unhear. There comes a point at which the kindest thing God’s servant can do is stop talking and let the silence be the sermon.

The prophet who was not silenced. Joash had stoned one prophet (24:21); Amaziah threatens another. God’s final Prophet, his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), spoke his Father’s word to the end, and when they killed him the word was not stopped but sealed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — A Thistle Wrote to a Cedar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pride goes before a fall, and the whole nation pays for it. Flushed with his Edomite victory, Amaziah challenges Joash king of Israel (v. 17). Joash replies with a mocking fable of a thistle and a cedar, names Amaziah’s pride, and tells him to stay at home (vv. 18–19). Amaziah will not listen, and the Chronicler gives the deeper reason: God was handing Judah over for seeking the gods of Edom (v. 20). Judah is routed at Beth-shemesh, the king is captured, Jerusalem’s wall is broken down, and the temple and palace are stripped (vv. 21–24).
verseByVerse.theology: Pride picks fights it cannot win. Amaziah had no quarrel with Israel except his own need for a bigger stage.
verseByVerse.examples: Truth sometimes comes to us from unlikely and unfriendly mouths. It is worth asking whether a critic's words, however unkindly meant, are true.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amaziah king of Judah took counsel and sent to Joash the son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, "Come, let us look one another in the face." And Joash the king of Israel sent word to Amaziah king of Judah, "A thistle on Lebanon sent to a cedar on Lebanon, saying, 'Give your daughter to my son for a wife,' and a wild beast of Lebanon passed by and trampled down the thistle. You say, 'See, I have struck down Edom,' and your heart has lifted you up in boastfulness. But now stay at home. Why should you provoke trouble so that you fall, you and Judah with you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Proud of one victory, Amaziah picked a fight he could not win, and the right diagnosis of his pride came, by God’s irony, from an idolatrous rival.

Amaziah king of Judah took counsel. He did take advice, only not the advice he had just been given. The prophet’s last words were that the king had “not listened to my counsel” (v. 16), and the same word now describes the counsellors he does listen to. Taking counsel is no virtue when we choose counsellors who will tell us what we have already decided.

Come, let us look one another in the face. This is a challenge to fight. A man who has just silenced a prophet provokes the stronger army on his border, Israel under Joash, grandson of Jehu. He is not defending anything. He has been to Edom and won, and he wants a bigger stage.

A thistle on Lebanon sent to a cedar on Lebanon. The reply is one of the coldest pieces of writing in the Old Testament, and it is a fable. A weed on the mountain writes to the great tree of the mountain (see Cedars of Lebanon) proposing a marriage alliance, and while the letter is being read a wild beast comes through the scrub and flattens the weed without noticing it was there. The insult is about size, Amaziah the thistle and Israel the cedar.

Your heart has lifted you up in boastfulness. Joash makes the point plain. A lifted-up heart is a thing to keep watching for, because this book is about to show it twice more: Uzziah “grew proud, to his destruction” (26:16), and Hezekiah’s heart “was proud” after God healed him (32:25). Jehoshaphat’s heart, by contrast, “was courageous in the ways of the LORD” (17:6). A confident heart is not the problem; a confident heart that bows to no one above it is. “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18).

The diagnosis from Samaria. The man who diagnoses Amaziah correctly is an idolatrous king of Israel writing to humiliate him. Judah had a prophet for this work a few verses earlier and shouted him down, so the accurate word about Judah’s king arrives from Samaria, wrapped in a joke, from a man with no interest at all in whether he repents. God is never short of people to speak his truth.

But now stay at home. Whatever the motive, the advice is sound: nothing Judah needed lay across that border. Joash also names the cost Amaziah has not counted: “you and Judah with you.” A proud ruler never falls alone. His people pay for his ambition, as verses 21–24 show.

verseByVerse.quote: But Amaziah would not listen, for it was of God, in order that he might give them into the hand of their enemies, because they had sought the gods of Edom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amaziah’s refusal to listen was his own sin and at the same time God’s judgment on him for seeking Edom’s gods.

But Amaziah would not listen, for it was of God. Both truths stand in one sentence, with no attempt to reconcile them for us. His deafness is his own guilt; it is also God’s judgment, giving a man the deafness he had already chosen. The Chronicler said the same of Ahaziah’s fatal visit to Joram (22:7). The judgment on a man who will not hear is sometimes simply that he gets his wish (compare Romans 1:24).

Because they had sought the gods of Edom. The Chronicler names the reason. Amaziah brought home the gods of the people he had defeated and worshipped them (v. 14), and when a prophet asked why, he silenced him (vv. 15–16). The defeat that follows is the judgment that prophet announced. The plural “they” suggests that king and people had sought these gods together, and Judah shares the cost.

What it does not mean. Not that God pushes an unwilling man into sin. Amaziah wanted this war, and God gave him what he wanted. Scripture holds God’s rule over all things and man’s full responsibility together, and never uses the first to excuse the second.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced one another in battle at Beth-shemesh, which belongs to Judah. And Judah was defeated by Israel, and every man fled to his home. And Joash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Joash, son of Ahaziah, at Beth-shemesh, and brought him to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem for 400 cubits, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate. And he seized all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of God, in the care of Obed-edom. He seized also the treasuries of the king's house, also hostages, and he returned to Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The war Amaziah provoked to prove his greatness cost Judah its army, Jerusalem its wall and the temple its treasure.

At Beth-shemesh, which belongs to Judah. Amaziah had meant to march out and meet Israel; instead Joash came to him. Beth-shemesh lay in the low hills some fifteen miles west of Jerusalem, so the king who issued the challenge ended up defending his own ground. It was a rout, and every man ran home.

Broke down the wall of Jerusalem for 400 cubits. The king is taken prisoner and brought to his own capital to watch some six hundred feet of its wall pulled down between the Ephraim Gate and the Corner Gate, on the north side, the side facing Israel. The city is left standing but defenceless.

In the care of Obed-edom. One name in the stripping deserves a pause. Obed-edom is the man whose house kept the ark in David’s day and was blessed for it (1 Chronicles 13:14), and to whose sons the temple storehouse was later allotted (1 Chronicles 26:4–8, 15). Two centuries on, his family, it seems, is still minding the temple treasury, and they have to watch it carried north because the king wanted a fight.

Also hostages, and he returned to Samaria. Joash took the palace treasuries as well, and hostages, probably to keep Judah quiet, and went home. Amaziah was left on his throne (he outlived Joash by fifteen years, v. 25), but as a beaten king in a breached and emptied city. The fight he picked to prove his greatness cost the temple its treasure, the city its wall and some of its people their freedom.
verseByVerse.note: Four hundred cubits is about 600 feet (a cubit was about 18 inches, ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–28 — From the Time When He Turned Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Chronicler’s last word on Amaziah dates his ruin from his idolatry, not from his defeat. He outlives the king who humiliated him by fifteen years, but the record of those years is left to the court annals (vv. 25–26). “From the time when he turned away from the LORD” a conspiracy grew against him; he fled to Lachish and was killed there, then carried back on horses and buried with his fathers in the city of David (vv. 27–28). A reign that began with the Book of Moses open ends as the slow consequence of an altar to Edom’s gods.
verseByVerse.theology: The consequences of turning from God can take years to arrive, and their slowness is not proof that they will not come.
verseByVerse.examples: Fifteen silent years followed Amaziah's defeat. Time given after failure is time for repentance, and God's patience in such years is an invitation, not an oversight.

verseByVerse.quote: Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, lived fifteen years after the death of Joash the son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel. Now the rest of the deeds of Amaziah, from first to last, are they not written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel? From the time when he turned away from the LORD they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But they sent after him to Lachish and put him to death there. And they brought him upon horses, and he was buried with his fathers in the city of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Chronicler dates Amaziah’s ruin from the day he turned from the LORD, and leaves us facing the verdict of verse 2 in our own hearts.

Lived fifteen years after the death of Joash. He outlives the man who humiliated him and reigns on over a capital with a gap in its wall and an empty treasury, and the Chronicler tells us nothing of those years. There is no story of recovery. He simply continues.

From the time when he turned away from the LORD. Look where the clock is started. Not from the lost battle or the broken wall, which is what a political historian would have written, but from the Edomite altars. The Chronicler names them as the real event of the reign, and everything afterwards, the challenge, the rout, the breached wall, the silent years and the death at Lachish, as their slow consequences.

He was buried with his fathers. Jehoram was kept out of the royal tombs (21:20), and so was Amaziah’s own father (24:25), but this king is buried with his fathers, as Kings also records (2 Kings 14:20). This book weighs its kings honestly at both ends: the Book of Moses open in verse 4, the Edomite altars in verse 14, and a grave in David’s city at the last.

The uncomfortable verdict. That leaves the reader with verse 2, uncomfortable precisely because most of us recognise it. Right, yet not with a whole heart. Obedient in the public crisis, with a prophet in the room and three tonnes of silver at stake; quietly fascinated afterwards by something that never saved anybody.

The one whole heart. The only whole heart ever offered to God in this world belonged to the Son of David, who could say, “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8), and mean every syllable of it, at the Jordan, in the wilderness, in Gethsemane and on the cross. He was never half anything. And the astonishing arrangement of the gospel is that his whole-hearted obedience is counted to people like Amaziah, and like us, when we trust him: people who have never once managed it, saved not by the wholeness of our love for him but by the wholeness of his love for his Father and for us.

25.theology: Half a heart will carry a man through a public crisis with a prophet in the room; it will not carry him through the quiet stretch afterwards. The prophet's reply in verse 9 is the clearest word on the cost of obedience in these two books, and the chapter then refuses to make obedience look safe (v. 13). Verse 20 puts God's purpose and the king's guilt in a single sentence: a man who shouts down God’s word may find that God stops speaking to him, as he asked.
25.examples:
When obeying God means walking away from money already spent, verse 9 is the word to hold: The LORD is able to give you much more than this. It does not pretend the loss is small.

Doing right does not always make the next day easier. Amaziah obeyed and three thousand of his people died in the raids that followed. If obedience has cost you dearly, the chapter does not tell you that you were wrong to obey.

Faithful families pay for unfaithful leaders. Obed-edom's descendants, who had kept the temple stores since David's day, watched the vessels carried away because a king wanted a fight.

keyVerse.quote: And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not with a whole heart.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the verdict on Amaziah’s whole reign, and the rest of the chapter shows what it means: real obedience in a crisis, followed by idols kept on the side. It measures him by the book’s standard of the whole heart, and so exposes our need of the Son of David, whose heart was wholly given to his Father and who gives his people one heart.

25.reflection:
Amaziah “did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not with a whole heart” (v. 2). What does a divided heart look like in an ordinary Christian life today, and why is it so easy to call it balance?

The man of God told Amaziah, “The LORD is able to give you much more than this” (v. 9), but the first result of obeying was loss (v. 13). Have you ever obeyed God at a cost that was not quickly repaid? How does Romans 8:32 help you trust him?

Amaziah worshipped the gods of the people he had just defeated (v. 14). What things do people around you trust that have plainly failed others? Why does the heart choose them anyway?

Amaziah silenced the prophet and then “took counsel” from others (vv. 16–17). How can we make sure we are listening to people who will tell us the truth, and not only to those who agree with us?

26.title: When He Was Strong, He Grew Proud
26.text: <sup>1</sup>And all the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king instead of his father Amaziah.<sup>2</sup>He built Eloth and restored it to Judah, after the king slept with his fathers.<sup>3</sup>Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem.<sup>4</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that his father Amaziah had done.<sup>5</sup>He set himself to seek God in the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God, and as long as he sought the LORD, God made him prosper.<sup>6</sup>He went out and made war against the Philistines and broke through the wall of Gath and the wall of Jabneh and the wall of Ashdod, and he built cities in the territory of Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines.<sup>7</sup>God helped him against the Philistines and against the Arabians who lived in Gurbaal and against the Meunites.<sup>8</sup>The Ammonites paid tribute to Uzziah, and his fame spread even to the border of Egypt, for he became very strong.<sup>9</sup>Moreover, Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate and at the Valley Gate and at the Angle, and fortified them.<sup>10</sup>And he built towers in the wilderness and cut out many cisterns, for he had large herds, both in the Shephelah and in the plain, and he had farmers and vinedressers in the hills and in the fertile lands, for he loved the soil.<sup>11</sup>Moreover, Uzziah had an army of soldiers, fit for war, in divisions according to the numbers in the muster made by Jeiel the secretary and Maaseiah the officer, under the direction of Hananiah, one of the king's commanders.<sup>12</sup>The whole number of the heads of fathers' houses of mighty men of valor was 2,600.<sup>13</sup>Under their command was an army of 307,500, who could make war with mighty power, to help the king against the enemy.<sup>14</sup>And Uzziah prepared for all the army shields, spears, helmets, coats of mail, bows, and stones for slinging.<sup>15</sup>In Jerusalem he made machines, invented by skillful men, to be on the towers and the corners, to shoot arrows and great stones. And his fame spread far, for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong.<sup>16</sup>But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction. For he was unfaithful to the LORD his God and entered the temple of the LORD to burn incense on the altar of incense.<sup>17</sup>But Azariah the priest went in after him, with eighty priests of the LORD who were men of valor,<sup>18</sup>and they withstood King Uzziah and said to him, "It is not for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the LORD, but for the priests, the sons of Aaron, who are consecrated to burn incense. Go out of the sanctuary, for you have done wrong, and it will bring you no honor from the LORD God."<sup>19</sup>Then Uzziah was angry. Now he had a censer in his hand to burn incense, and when he became angry with the priests, leprosy broke out on his forehead in the presence of the priests in the house of the LORD, by the altar of incense.<sup>20</sup>And Azariah the chief priest and all the priests looked at him, and behold, he was leprous in his forehead! And they rushed him out quickly, and he himself hurried to go out, because the LORD had struck him.<sup>21</sup>And King Uzziah was a leper to the day of his death, and being a leper lived in a separate house, for he was excluded from the house of the LORD. And Jotham his son was over the king's household, governing the people of the land.<sup>22</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Uzziah, from first to last, Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz wrote.<sup>23</sup>And Uzziah slept with his fathers, and they buried him with his fathers in the burial field that belonged to the kings, for they said, "He is a leper." And Jotham his son reigned in his place.
26.overview:
Where we are. Amaziah has been murdered at Lachish after turning from the LORD (25:27–28). His sixteen-year-old son Uzziah, called Azariah in Kings, now begins the longest reign so far in this book, the last of three kings who begin well and end badly (chapters 24 to 26).

The message. Everything Uzziah had, he had because “God helped him”, and the moment he forgot it his strength became his ruin. Pride turns God’s gifts into grounds for grasping at what God has not given. Uzziah, made strong by grace, pushed into the holy place to burn incense as though success had earned him a priest’s access to God, and left it a leper, shut out of God’s house for life.

Why it was said. The first readers had no king, but they had a temple and a priesthood (see the introduction). This chapter taught them that God’s house is approached on his terms, through the priests he appointed, and that the gifts of a prosperous season are held from God’s hand, never as a claim upon him.

How the chapter makes its case. First the rise (vv. 1–8): Uzziah seeks God “in the days of Zechariah”, and “as long as he sought the LORD, God made him prosper”, with victories on every side. Then the wealth (vv. 9–15): towers, cisterns, herds and vineyards, a great army and ingenious engines of war, “for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong.” Then the fall (vv. 16–21): “when he was strong, he grew proud”; he enters the temple with a censer, eighty priests withstand him, and leprosy breaks out on his forehead as he rages. Last, the epitaph (vv. 22–23): Isaiah writes his story, and even in death he is buried beside the kings rather than among them, “for they said, ‘He is a leper.’”

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. Uzziah grasped at a priesthood God had not given him; Christ “did not exalt himself to be made a high priest” (Hebrews 5:5), yet was appointed by God to be both priest and king (Psalm 110:4; Zechariah 6:13). Uzziah went out of God’s house unclean and alone; Jesus touched the unclean and “suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12), so that the unclean might be brought in. In the year Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the true King on his throne (Isaiah 6:1).

For us. Every blessing we enjoy is God’s help, and the danger season for a Christian is often success rather than trouble. We may draw near to God with great boldness, but only through the one Mediator he has given, never on the strength of our record.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — As Long as He Sought the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Uzziah’s early years show what God does for a king who seeks him. The people crown the sixteen-year-old after his father’s murder, and his first recorded act restores the Red Sea port of Eloth to Judah (vv. 1–2). He reigns fifty-two years, doing right as his father had (vv. 3–4), and verse 5 gives the key: he sought God in the days of Zechariah, his teacher, and “as long as he sought the LORD, God made him prosper.” Victories follow over the Philistines, Arabians and Meunites, the Ammonites pay tribute, and his fame reaches Egypt, because “God helped him” (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 4 measures him by his father, and this book has just measured his father: right, yet not with a whole heart (25:2). The commendation is real, and it has a limit. Verse 5 describes God's dealings with this king, not a guarantee that the faithful always prosper; this same book shows faithful prophets jailed and stoned (16:10; 24:21).
verseByVerse.examples: For the second time in three reigns the Chronicler dates a king's seeking to the lifetime of the man who taught him. Joash did right all the days of Jehoiada the priest (24:2); Uzziah sought God in the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God. Good teachers are a gift, but they are not a substitute for a faith of one's own.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king instead of his father Amaziah. He built Eloth and restored it to Judah, after the king slept with his fathers. Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that his father Amaziah had done. He set himself to seek God in the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God, and as long as he sought the LORD, God made him prosper.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Uzziah began as a young king who sought God under a godly teacher, and God prospered him for as long as he kept seeking.

All the people of Judah took Uzziah. The people act again, as they did for Ahaziah (22:1); Judah has learned how to survive its own kings. Kings usually calls him Azariah, “the LORD has helped” (2 Kings 15:1–7); Uzziah means “the LORD is my strength”. Help and strength are the two ideas this chapter will put to the test.

He built Eloth. Eloth (Elath) is the port at the head of the Red Sea, lost when Edom revolted under Jehoram (21:8–10), and the young king rebuilds it after his father’s death.

Fifty-two years in Jerusalem. The second longest reign in this book after Manasseh’s fifty-five, and the verdict measures him by Amaziah, a man who did right but not with a whole heart.

He set himself to seek God in the days of Zechariah. Note the two time clauses: “in the days of Zechariah” and “as long as he sought the LORD”. Both warn in advance where the story will break. This Zechariah is otherwise unknown.

Who instructed him in the fear of God. A teacher of the fear of God is one of God’s better gifts, and a dangerous one, because it is possible to be carried a long way by someone else’s convictions and think the faith is one’s own. The test is what a man still believes at his teacher’s funeral, and in the years after. Parents and teachers can do what Zechariah did; only God can give a heart that goes on seeking when the teacher has gone (Ezekiel 36:26).

Textual note. The Hebrew manuscripts differ here, by a single letter. Many, with the ancient Greek translation, read “fear”, which the ESV follows; others read “vision”, that is, understanding the visions God gave. Either way, Zechariah taught the young king to know and revere God.
verseByVerse.note: Uzziah is also called Azariah.

verseByVerse.quote: He went out and made war against the Philistines and broke through the wall of Gath and the wall of Jabneh and the wall of Ashdod, and he built cities in the territory of Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines. God helped him against the Philistines and against the Arabians who lived in Gurbaal and against the Meunites. The Ammonites paid tribute to Uzziah, and his fame spread even to the border of Egypt, for he became very strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Uzziah’s victories on every side were God’s doing, and the Chronicler says so in the middle of the list.

Broke through the wall of Gath. Gath was Goliath’s town. Uzziah does not merely raid that coast; he takes the walls down and puts his own towns up inside Philistine territory. Then south and east: Arabians, Meunites, tribute from Ammon, and a name that carries to the Egyptian frontier.

God helped him. In the middle of the list, so that we cannot admire the good years without knowing their source, stand three words echoing the king’s other name: “God helped him.”

For he became very strong. Keep an eye on the last clause of verse 8. Nothing is wrong with it yet; in this book strength is a gift. But since Rehoboam was strong and abandoned the law (12:1), the reader has learned to feel a chill whenever a king of Judah becomes strong.

Uncertain wording. Gurbaal appears nowhere else and its location is unknown. The Meunites were probably a desert people of the far south, near Edom (compare 20:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Marvelously Helped, till He Was Strong
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Uzziah’s prosperity is real, many-sided and entirely the gift of God. He fortifies Jerusalem’s gates, builds towers and cuts cisterns in the wilderness, and keeps herds, farmers and vinedressers, “for he loved the soil” (vv. 9–10). He organises a large, well-equipped army under named officers (vv. 11–14) and sets ingenious machines on the walls to shoot arrows and great stones (v. 15). The section ends with the hinge of the chapter: his fame spread far, “for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong.” The help was God’s; the danger lay in the moment he could feel the strength as his own.
verseByVerse.theology: Helped is the word that holds these good years together: God helped him in verse 7, marvelously helped in verse 15. Everything in the inventory came in through that word.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 10 is the line that makes him likeable. Among the towers and the artillery, the one motive the Chronicler records for anything Uzziah built is that he loved the soil. Faithful work in a ruler can look like cisterns dug for the herds as much as walls built for war.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate and at the Valley Gate and at the Angle, and fortified them. And he built towers in the wilderness and cut out many cisterns, for he had large herds, both in the Shephelah and in the plain, and he had farmers and vinedressers in the hills and in the fertile lands, for he loved the soil. Moreover, Uzziah had an army of soldiers, fit for war, in divisions according to the numbers in the muster made by Jeiel the secretary and Maaseiah the officer, under the direction of Hananiah, one of the king's commanders. The whole number of the heads of fathers' houses of mighty men of valor was 2,600. Under their command was an army of 307,500, who could make war with mighty power, to help the king against the enemy. And Uzziah prepared for all the army shields, spears, helmets, coats of mail, bows, and stones for slinging. In Jerusalem he made machines, invented by skillful men, to be on the towers and the corners, to shoot arrows and great stones. And his fame spread far, for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Uzziah’s building, farming and army were God’s generous gifts, and the danger came only when the strength began to feel like his own.

Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem. Towers at the Corner Gate, where Joash of Israel had broken the wall down in his father’s reign (25:23), now rebuilt; towers in the open country, cisterns cut in the rock, farmers in the lowlands, vinedressers in the hills.

For he loved the soil. The Chronicler gives a reason for none of the other building work, but he gives one here. What the record says of his farming is that he loved it. That is a good thing in a king and in a man.

An army of soldiers, fit for war. Mustered by name, 2,600 heads of families over 307,500 men. His father had mustered only 300,000 (25:5). The recovery is complete.

Machines, invented by skillful men. The Hebrew plays on a single root, something like devices devised by a deviser; the writer is enjoying it.

He was marvelously helped, till he was strong. Then the last clause, after which everything is downhill. Not because he was strong, but until. He was carried all the way up by help that was not his own, and the moment he could feel the strength in his own hands he stopped noticing whose it was. Moses had warned of exactly this: “Beware lest you say in your heart, ‘My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth’” (Deuteronomy 8:17). The dangerous season for a believer is often not the year of trouble, when he prays, but the year when everything grows.

Can the numbers be trusted? Kings gives no figures here to compare. Where the two books differ elsewhere, numbers were easily miscopied or different things are counted; this commentary holds that the text as God first gave it was without error, which a miscopied numeral does not disturb.

Uncertain wording. What the “machines” were is not certain. Catapults are not otherwise known for some centuries, so many think of protective structures on the towers from which defenders could shoot and hurl stones in safety; others think of early throwing devices.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — It Is Not for You, Uzziah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pride makes Uzziah grasp at the one thing God had not given a king. Strong at last, he enters the temple to burn incense on the altar reserved for Aaron’s sons (v. 16). Azariah the priest and eighty brave priests follow him in and tell him to leave: this is not his to do, and it will bring him no honour (vv. 17–18). Uzziah rages with the censer in his hand, and leprosy breaks out on his forehead before the altar; the priests hurry him out, and he hurries too, because the LORD has struck him (vv. 19–20). He lives the rest of his life in a separate house, cut off from the house of the LORD, while his son Jotham governs (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The charge in verse 16 is unfaithfulness, the charge laid against Saul's breach of faith (1 Chronicles 10:13) and against the generation that lost the temple, who were exceedingly unfaithful (36:14). The boundary he crossed is not a ceremony about rank. It is the difference between a holy God and a creature, and it is guarded for the creature's sake.
verseByVerse.examples: Courage here is not loudness. The priests' only weapon was a plain word from God's law, said respectfully to the king's face, and said before the judgment fell rather than after. Faithful warning still sounds like that: it is given for the other person's good, while there is still time to turn.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction. For he was unfaithful to the LORD his God and entered the temple of the LORD to burn incense on the altar of incense. But Azariah the priest went in after him, with eighty priests of the LORD who were men of valor, and they withstood King Uzziah and said to him, "It is not for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the LORD, but for the priests, the sons of Aaron, who are consecrated to burn incense. Go out of the sanctuary, for you have done wrong, and it will bring you no honor from the LORD God." Then Uzziah was angry. Now he had a censer in his hand to burn incense, and when he became angry with the priests, leprosy broke out on his forehead in the presence of the priests in the house of the LORD, by the altar of incense. And Azariah the chief priest and all the priests looked at him, and behold, he was leprous in his forehead! And they rushed him out quickly, and he himself hurried to go out, because the LORD had struck him. And King Uzziah was a leper to the day of his death, and being a leper lived in a separate house, for he was excluded from the house of the LORD. And Jotham his son was over the king's household, governing the people of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Made strong by God, Uzziah grew proud and grasped at the priest’s place before God, and God struck him with leprosy and shut him out of the house he had forced his way into.

But when he was strong, he grew proud. This book keeps watching kings reach the moment when nothing can touch them (12:1; 21:4). Now Uzziah, strong at last, walks into the sanctuary with a censer. The Chronicler calls it being “unfaithful”, the sin that will finally send Judah into exile (36:14).

To burn incense on the altar of incense. The law is not obscure. Exodus 30 sets that altar before the veil, gives its incense to Aaron’s line, and says, “You shall not offer unauthorized incense on it” (30:9; compare Numbers 16:40).

Why it mattered. The incense altar stood just before the Most Holy Place, and the priesthood existed to say that a sinner does not approach the Holy One on his own account and on his own terms. Uzziah is claiming that his years of success have made him fit to walk in with no priest between him and God.

Did not David and Solomon offer sacrifices? They led the nation in offering them (2 Samuel 6:17; 1 Kings 8:62–64), but no faithful king entered the holy place to burn incense, the priest’s own ministry. Saul lost his dynasty for taking a priest’s part (1 Samuel 13:8–14).

Eighty priests of the LORD who were men of valor. The bravest scene in the chapter. “Men of valor” is a title this book uses for soldiers, yet these men carried no weapons. They followed the most powerful man in the country into the holy place with nothing in their hands, and told him to his face.

It will bring you no honor from the LORD God. They put their finger on what he came in for. He did not want the incense; he wanted the honour. And they tell him, in the one room where it matters, that this is the way to lose it.

Leprosy broke out on his forehead. On his forehead the high priest wore a gold plate engraved “Holy to the LORD” (Exodus 28:36–38). Uzziah came in wanting a priest’s place and was marked unclean on the very spot where the priest carried the word holy. The Hebrew word covers a range of serious skin diseases; what mattered was that it made a person unclean, to live alone, outside the camp (Leviticus 13:46).

They rushed him out quickly. Both parties hurry: “he himself hurried to go out.” The man who forced his way in cannot get out fast enough.

A leper to the day of his death. Verse 21 is an exact reversal. He wanted more access to God than God had given him, and he got none at all. For the rest of his life the king of Judah lived apart, shut out of every festival in the house he had forced his way into.

Why can’t I come to God my own way? Many today think a sincere person can approach God directly, without priests, churches or one particular Saviour in the way. But that assumes that the distance between us and God is a matter of protocol rather than guilt, and that the Holy One is approachable on our terms because we are, on the whole, decent and successful people. That is what Uzziah believed, and it is the oldest form of pride. Yet God does want us to come right in, more boldly than Uzziah imagined, into the holy places through the curtain (Hebrews 10:19–22). It simply insists that the way in is a person: “there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). He does not stand there to keep us out, but to bring us in.

The true Priest-King. Uzziah tried to make himself priest as well as king. God had promised one who would rightly be both, “a priest on his throne” (Zechariah 6:13), and “Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest, but was appointed by him” (Hebrews 5:5). Uzziah was carried out of the temple unclean; Jesus touched a leper and said, “I will; be clean” (Mark 1:41), and himself “suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12), so that the unclean could be brought in.

What it does not mean. Not that illness or disability is God’s punishment for a particular sin. Here the text says plainly that “the LORD had struck him”; without such a word we have no right to read sickness that way (John 9:2–3).

Uncertain wording. The “separate house” (also 2 Kings 15:5) translates a rare Hebrew phrase that may mean “house of freedom”, perhaps release from royal duties, or simply a house set apart. Clearly the king lived in isolation, as the law required, while Jotham governed.
verseByVerse.note: Only priests could burn incense in the temple. The Hebrew word translated leprosy covered a range of serious skin diseases, not only the disease that bears the name today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–23 — In the Year That King Uzziah Died
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Uzziah’s story ends with a prophet’s pen and a leper’s grave. The Chronicler names Isaiah the son of Amoz as the writer of the rest of his acts (v. 22), the prophet who would date his great vision of the Lord on his throne to the year of this king’s death (Isaiah 6:1). Uzziah is buried near his fathers, in the burial field that belonged to the kings, but not in the royal tombs, because the people said, “He is a leper” (v. 23). His son Jotham reigns in his place, and the long, brilliant reign closes under the shadow of its last years.
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler names Isaiah as his source, and Isaiah's own book dates its great vision In the year that King Uzziah died (Isaiah 6:1). The two men are set side by side in the note below.
verseByVerse.examples: Count the graves. Jehoram was buried in the city of David but kept out of the royal tombs (21:20). Joash was kept out too (24:25). Amaziah was laid with his fathers (25:28). Uzziah is buried in the field beside the tombs, and the reason is given in seven words: for they said, He is a leper. Fifty-two years, and the last sentence about him is a diagnosis.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Uzziah, from first to last, Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz wrote. And Uzziah slept with his fathers, and they buried him with his fathers in the burial field that belonged to the kings, for they said, "He is a leper." And Jotham his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah recorded Uzziah’s reign, and the king who forced his way into the holy place is set beside the prophet who confessed he had no right to be there and was cleansed.

Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz wrote. The name stops the reader. This is a record of the reign by Isaiah, now lost, not our book of Isaiah, which says little about Uzziah. But Isaiah dated the great vision of his book by this king’s death: “In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne” (Isaiah 6:1).

Two scenes in one building. A proud king walks up to the altar to take a place that was not his, and is carried out marked. A prophet stands in the same house, sees who is really on the throne, and cries, “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isaiah 6:5). One man claimed the holy place; the other confessed he had no business in it. And the second was cleansed, by “a burning coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar” (Isaiah 6:6), in the house where the king had grabbed at the altar.

Pride and worship. Holiness is not less dangerous to the humble man; Isaiah thought he was a dead man. But the humble man is met by a God who sends fire from his own altar to touch the mouth that confessed.

In the burial field that belonged to the kings. Uzziah gets the family field but not the family tombs, because of what his own subjects said over the coffin. A stone plaque in Aramaic from around the time of Christ, now in the Israel Museum, records that his bones were later moved and must not be disturbed.

A door opened from the inside. Only one man ever entered God’s presence in his own right, and he carried no censer, because he was the offering. Jesus went in as our priest, and the invitation that follows is not “stay out” but “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16), by a door opened from the inside, for people who would never have survived forcing it.

26.theology:
The chapter turns on one word in verse 15: marvelously helped, till he was strong. Uzziah is the fourth king in this book to reach the point where nothing could touch him (12:1; 21:4; 25:3; 26:16), and each time the story turns there.

What he does is called unfaithfulness. The priesthood he pushed past was not a privilege kept from him. It was a mercy God provided, the only way a sinner could approach the Holy One at all, so stepping over it was no mere breach of a rule. He wanted more access than God had granted and ended with none.

Kings, which calls him Azariah, says only that the LORD struck the king and he was a leper to the day of his death (2 Kings 15:5); Chronicles gives the reason, and the reason carries a promise. In Israel a king could not be a priest, and Uzziah died proving it. Yet David's psalm spoke of a king at God's right hand who would be a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 110:4), and Hebrews says Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest but was appointed by the one who said it (Hebrews 5:5-6). What Uzziah tried to seize, the Son of David was given.
26.examples:
Uzziah left a great deal worth admiring: the harbour his great-great-grandfather lost was rebuilt, the broken wall repaired, cisterns cut in the desert, engineers set to work on the towers, and Judah's name carried as far as Egypt. Yet the record remembers him most for one afternoon, when he was rushed out of the sanctuary with leprosy on his forehead, where the high priest wore the gold plate engraved Holy to the LORD.

A lifetime of good work does not make anyone safe from pride; it is often what makes pride possible. The way back is not to stop working but to keep remembering whose help it was.

keyVerse.quote: But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction. For he was unfaithful to the LORD his God and entered the temple of the LORD to burn incense on the altar of incense.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the hinge of Uzziah’s reign. Strength that was entirely God’s help (vv. 7, 15) became the ground of a pride that grasped at the priest’s place before God. It warns every believer that success is a more dangerous season than trouble, and it points to the true Priest-King, who did not exalt himself but was appointed by God to bring us near.

26.reflection:
Uzziah prospered “as long as he sought the LORD” (v. 5), and his early faith owed much to his teacher Zechariah. How can we help the young people in our lives to own their faith rather than borrow it? What does seeking the Lord look like for you when no one is watching?

“He was marvelously helped, till he was strong” (v. 15). Why is success often more spiritually dangerous than trouble? Where in your life are you most tempted to forget that what you have was given?

Uzziah wanted to approach God on his own terms. Why do so many people today feel that coming to God “my own way” is reasonable? How would you explain Christ as the one Mediator to a friend who thinks so?

Eighty priests risked their lives to tell the king the truth (vv. 17–18). When have you needed someone to tell you a hard truth? How can we become people who say such things with courage and humility, and receive them too?

27.title: He Became Mighty Because He Ordered His Ways
27.text: <sup>1</sup>Jotham was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jerushah the daughter of Zadok.<sup>2</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD according to all that his father Uzziah had done, except he did not enter the temple of the LORD. But the people still followed corrupt practices.<sup>3</sup>He built the upper gate of the house of the LORD and did much building on the wall of Ophel.<sup>4</sup>Moreover, he built cities in the hill country of Judah, and forts and towers on the wooded hills.<sup>5</sup>He fought with the king of the Ammonites and prevailed against them. And the Ammonites gave him that year 100 talents of silver, and 10,000 cors of wheat and 10,000 of barley. The Ammonites paid him the same amount in the second and the third years.<sup>6</sup>So Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God.<sup>7</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jotham, and all his wars and his ways, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.<sup>8</sup>He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem.<sup>9</sup>And Jotham slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David, and Ahaz his son reigned in his place.
27.overview:
Where we are. Uzziah, made strong by God, grew proud, forced his way into the temple and died a leper, while his son Jotham governed for him (26:21). Now Jotham reigns in his own right, in the shortest chapter of the book, between a father who fell and a son, Ahaz, who will be among the worst of all.

The message. A quiet life ordered before God is blessed by him, even when it makes no stir. Jotham “became mighty, because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God” (v. 6). He learned from his father’s sin as well as from his strengths. Yet his faithfulness could not make his people faithful, nor his son. A good king can order his own ways; only God can change a heart.

Why it was said. The first readers lived ordinary, unspectacular lives in a small province (see the introduction). Jotham showed them that steady faithfulness, with no miracles and no crises, is seen and honoured by God. The note on the people’s corruption warned them that the faith of a leader cannot stand in for the faith of the people.

How the chapter makes its case. First the verdict (vv. 1–2): Jotham does right like his father, “except he did not enter the temple of the LORD”, while “the people still followed corrupt practices.” Then his works (vv. 3–5): he builds the temple’s upper gate and the wall of Ophel, fortifies the hill country, and subdues Ammon, who pays tribute three years running. Then the reason (v. 6): he ordered his ways before the LORD. Last, a plain burial in the city of David, and Ahaz his son reigns in his place (vv. 7–9).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need exposed. Jotham ordered his ways before God; the Son of David could say, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), not for sixteen years but for a whole life, and to the death of the cross. And where Jotham could not change the hearts of his people or his son, Christ the King gives his people “a new heart” (Ezekiel 36:26), so that his reign is not undone by the next generation.

For us. Most faithful lives look like chapter 27, not chapter 20: no great deliverance, just steady obedience before God where no one else is watching. That life is not dull to him; he writes it down. And when we cannot make our children or our churches follow, we can entrust them to the King who can change hearts.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Except He Did Not Enter the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jotham does what is right, learning from his father’s sin as well as his strengths. He reigns sixteen years (v. 1). The verdict is Uzziah’s, with one exception: he did not enter the temple of the LORD, where his father had sinned so disastrously. In the same verse comes a sober note: the people still followed corrupt practices (v. 2). A good king does not automatically make a good people. Jotham builds the upper gate of the house of the LORD and strengthens the wall of Ophel near the temple (v. 3), and builds cities, forts and towers in the hill country and the wooded hills of Judah (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The exception in verse 2 sums the man up. He took everything his father did in the good years and left out the one act that ruined him.
verseByVerse.examples: The same verse that commends the king condemns the country. A parent, a pastor or a king can set a direction and cannot set a heart. A leader whose people do not follow has not necessarily failed, and the Chronicler says so in the same breath as the commendation rather than saving it for a footnote.

verseByVerse.quote: Jotham was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jerushah the daughter of Zadok. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD according to all that his father Uzziah had done, except he did not enter the temple of the LORD. But the people still followed corrupt practices. He built the upper gate of the house of the LORD and did much building on the wall of Ophel. Moreover, he built cities in the hill country of Judah, and forts and towers on the wooded hills.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jotham followed his father’s good example and avoided his father’s great sin, yet his own faithfulness could not cure the corruption of his people.

What Jotham had seen. Jotham had run the country while his father lived apart, unclean, shut out of the building he had forced his way into (26:21). He knew exactly which day had changed his family’s life, and which door his father had walked through.

Except he did not enter the temple of the LORD. He copied the good years, and when he came to the one act that had finished his father, he stopped. No one alive could have prevented a king of Judah walking into that room. He did not go in.

In everyday life. Learning from what damaged our families is harder than copying what they did well, because the thing that damaged them usually looked, at the time, like the natural next step for someone who had earned it.

But the people still followed corrupt practices. The second half of the verse stops the chapter from being sentimental. A good king for sixteen years, and the country did not follow him. Kings names one form it took: “The people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places” (2 Kings 15:35). Jotham was not a failure because Judah stayed corrupt, and Judah was not excused because Jotham was good. Isaiah and Micah were already preaching in Jotham’s days (Isaiah 1:1; Micah 1:1), and their books show what the corruption looked like: bribed courts, fields seized from the poor, and worship kept up by people whose hands were full of blood (Isaiah 1:15, 23; Micah 2:2; 3:11).

The King who changes hearts. Here is a limit no good leader can pass. Jotham could order his own ways, but not his people’s hearts. Israel needed a king who could do that, and God promised one: “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26). Christ rules his people from the inside.

He built the upper gate of the house of the LORD. Perhaps the gate through which the boy king Joash was brought down to the palace (23:20). He also strengthened the wall of Ophel, the hill running south from the temple towards the old city of David. Somebody has to keep the hinges working on the places where God once did something, and much of what faithful people do is just that.

Uncertain wording. “Except he did not enter the temple of the LORD” is compressed. Nearly all readers take it as praise: unlike his father, he did not intrude on the priests’ work (26:16). A few have read it as a fault, that he neglected the temple, but verse 3 shows him building its gate, and verse 6 commends him without reserve.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — Because He Ordered His Ways
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jotham’s strength has one explanation: he ordered his ways before the LORD his God. He defeats the Ammonites, who pay a hundred talents of silver and twenty thousand cors of grain each year for three years (v. 5). The Chronicler gives the reason plainly: “Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God” (v. 6). The rest of his wars and ways are in the royal records (v. 7). His age and the length of his reign are repeated (v. 8), and he is buried in the city of David without any shadow over his grave, but Ahaz his son reigns in his place (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 6 puts cause and effect in one sentence. He became mighty because he ordered his ways, and the ordering was done before the LORD his God, his own covenant God, in the one place where nobody else could see it.
verseByVerse.examples: This book does not promise that obedience which costs money will be repaid in money. But it lets the reader notice, in the note below, that a hundred talents written off at a prophet's word in one reign come back as a hundred talents of tribute two reigns later.

verseByVerse.quote: He fought with the king of the Ammonites and prevailed against them. And the Ammonites gave him that year 100 talents of silver, and 10,000 cors of wheat and 10,000 of barley. The Ammonites paid him the same amount in the second and the third years. So Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God. Now the rest of the acts of Jotham, and all his wars and his ways, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And Jotham slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David, and Ahaz his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jotham grew strong because he ordered his life before God, and his quiet faithfulness, though it could not secure his son, was seen and recorded by the God he served.

He fought with the king of the Ammonites. The numbers matter. Two reigns earlier Amaziah paid a hundred talents for northern soldiers, a man of God told him to send them home, and to his question about the money came the answer, “The LORD is able to give you much more than this” (25:9). Now Ammon pays a hundred talents into Judah’s treasury, three years running. Nobody connects the two sums; they are left for whoever is counting.

10,000 cors of wheat and 10,000 of barley. There is grain with the silver, twenty thousand cors of it a year. A man whose father loved the soil is paid in harvests.

Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways. Not because he was clever or lucky in his enemies. “Ordered” is the language of arrangement, a life set in order on purpose and in a direction. It is the same Hebrew verb used of Rehoboam, who “did not set his heart to seek the LORD” (12:14): one man fixed his heart, the other never did.

Before the LORD his God. It was done before God, where nobody could check it: what he refused when it was offered quietly, which room he would not enter when the door was open. For the Christian reader that private ordering is not a ladder up to God. It is the life of someone God has already made his own, and it is the Spirit who keeps us in step (Galatians 5:25), with mercy for the days we fall out of it.

The Son who always pleased the Father. Jotham ordered his ways for sixteen years. Jesus could say, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), every day of his life and to the end of it. His ordered life is the one our salvation rests on, and ours is the fruit of it, not the price.

A short, clean record. Nine verses: no prophet, because none was needed; no crisis, no dramatic rescue of the kind that fills chapter 20. This book gives one of its cleanest verdicts to a man whose story will not fill a page. Most faithful lives are chapter 27, not chapter 20, and God is not disappointed by that. He wrote it down.

They buried him in the city of David. His age and reign are repeated in verse 8, as they were for Jehoram, where the repetition led to “he departed with no one’s regret” (21:20). Here it leads to nothing worse than a plain burial: no exclusion, no burial field, no verdict muttered over the coffin.

And Ahaz his son reigned in his place. Then the clause the reader learns to dread: the steadiest king in generations hands the throne to one of the worst. Jotham could not order his son’s ways any more than his people’s, and God does not promise that a quiet, well-ordered life will be copied by those we love most. He promises something better and slower: that the ordering itself was seen, in the place where it was done, by the One it was done before.

For parents. Faithful parents whose children wander are not thereby proved unfaithful. Jotham’s record stands, and Ahaz answered for himself (Ezekiel 18:20). Keep praying: Ahaz’s own son would be Hezekiah.

27.theology:
Verse 6 gives one cause and no other: Jotham grew strong because he ordered his ways, living deliberately before the LORD his God.

Kings adds that in Jotham's days the LORD began to send Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel against Judah (2 Kings 15:37). The Chronicler keeps that war for the next reign, where it falls on Ahaz; he is selecting, not denying.

Verse 2 keeps two truths in one sentence: a king can be genuinely faithful and his nation still corrupt.

Jotham's restraint points beyond him. His father grasped at a priest's place and he declined to. The Son of God did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself and became obedient to death (Philippians 2:6-8), and he always did what pleased his Father (John 8:29). The faithfulness God recorded in part in Jotham he found whole in his Son, and that whole obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19), whose own ordering of their ways is never more than partial.
27.examples:
Jotham had watched his father carried leprous out of the sanctuary, and when he held the same power, with the censer within reach, he did not go in. He kept the upper gate of God's house in repair, and Judah was paid in silver and harvests, twenty thousand cors of grain in the reign after a king who loved the soil.

Yet the best king in five generations fathered one of the worst. Many faithful parents know that grief. The ordering of our own ways does not guarantee our children's, and God does not ask us to carry what only he can do.

keyVerse.quote: So Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God.
keyVerse.note: This is the Chronicler’s only explanation of Jotham’s reign, and it is the heart of the chapter. Strength came not from cleverness or circumstance but from a life deliberately set in order before God, in private as well as in public. It points to the Son who always did what pleased his Father, whose obedience is the ground of ours.

27.reflection:
Jotham copied his father’s strengths but refused to repeat his father’s great sin (v. 2). What good things have you received from your family, and what patterns do you need, by God’s grace, to refuse?

“The people still followed corrupt practices” under a good king (v. 2). Why can’t a good leader, or a good pastor, make people faithful? What does that teach us about our need of Christ?

Jotham “ordered his ways before the LORD his God” (v. 6). What would it look like for you to order your week, your money or your private life before God, and not merely in front of other people?

This short chapter records a quiet, faithful life with no dramatic rescue. How does it encourage those whose faithfulness seems ordinary and unnoticed, including parents whose children have not followed them?

28.title: He Was Unfaithful to the LORD
28.text: <sup>1</sup>Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done,<sup>2</sup>but he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel. He even made metal images for the Baals,<sup>3</sup>and he made offerings in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom and burned his sons as an offering, according to the abominations of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.<sup>4</sup>And he sacrificed and made offerings on the high places and on the hills and under every green tree.<sup>5</sup>Therefore the LORD his God gave him into the hand of the king of Syria, who defeated him and took captive a great number of his people and brought them to Damascus. He was also given into the hand of the king of Israel, who struck him with great force.<sup>6</sup>For Pekah the son of Remaliah killed 120,000 from Judah in one day, all of them men of valor, because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers.<sup>7</sup>And Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, killed Maaseiah the king's son and Azrikam the commander of the palace and Elkanah the next in authority to the king.<sup>8</sup>The men of Israel took captive 200,000 of their relatives, women, sons, and daughters. They also took much spoil from them and brought the spoil to Samaria.<sup>9</sup>But a prophet of the LORD was there, whose name was Oded, and he went out to meet the army that came to Samaria and said to them, "Behold, because the LORD, the God of your fathers, was angry with Judah, he gave them into your hand, but you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven.<sup>10</sup>And now you intend to subjugate the people of Judah and Jerusalem, male and female, as your slaves. Have you not sins of your own against the LORD your God?<sup>11</sup>Now hear me, and send back the captives from your relatives whom you have taken, for the fierce wrath of the LORD is upon you."<sup>12</sup>Certain chiefs also of the men of Ephraim, Azariah the son of Johanan, Berechiah the son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah the son of Shallum, and Amasa the son of Hadlai, stood up against those who were coming from the war<sup>13</sup>and said to them, "You shall not bring the captives in here, for you propose to bring upon us guilt against the LORD in addition to our present sins and guilt. For our guilt is already great, and there is fierce wrath against Israel."<sup>14</sup>So the armed men left the captives and the spoil before the princes and all the assembly.<sup>15</sup>And the men who have been mentioned by name rose and took the captives, and with the spoil they clothed all who were naked among them. They clothed them, gave them sandals, provided them with food and drink, and anointed them, and carrying all the feeble among them on donkeys, they brought them to their kinsfolk at Jericho, the city of palm trees. Then they returned to Samaria.<sup>16</sup>At that time King Ahaz sent to the king of Assyria for help.<sup>17</sup>For the Edomites had again invaded and defeated Judah and carried away captives.<sup>18</sup>And the Philistines had made raids on the cities in the Shephelah and the Negeb of Judah, and had taken Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soco with its villages, Timnah with its villages, and Gimzo with its villages.
