And they settled there.<sup>19</sup>For the LORD humbled Judah because of Ahaz king of Israel, for he had made Judah act sinfully and had been very unfaithful to the LORD.<sup>20</sup>So Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came against him and afflicted him instead of strengthening him.<sup>21</sup>For Ahaz took a portion from the house of the LORD and the house of the king and of the princes, and gave tribute to the king of Assyria, but it did not help him.<sup>22</sup>In the time of his distress he became yet more faithless to the LORD—this same King Ahaz.<sup>23</sup>For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him and said, "Because the gods of the kings of Syria helped them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me." But they were the ruin of him and of all Israel.<sup>24</sup>And Ahaz gathered together the vessels of the house of God and cut in pieces the vessels of the house of God, and he shut up the doors of the house of the LORD, and he made himself altars in every corner of Jerusalem.<sup>25</sup>In every city of Judah he made high places to make offerings to other gods, provoking to anger the LORD, the God of his fathers.<sup>26</sup>Now the rest of his acts and all his ways, from first to last, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.<sup>27</sup>And Ahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city, in Jerusalem, for they did not bring him into the tombs of the kings of Israel. And Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.
28.overview:
Where we are. Jotham, who “ordered his ways before the LORD” (27:6), has died, and his son Ahaz takes the throne. Three kings have begun well and ended badly; this one begins badly and gets worse. It is the lowest point of the book so far, the reign in which, as the introduction puts it, Ahaz shuts the temple doors.

The message. Unfaithfulness to God does not stop at one sin; it goes on until it shuts the door to God himself, and every substitute it turns to ruins it. Ahaz trusts every power except the LORD: Baal, Molech, Assyria, the gods of Damascus. Each takes his payment and fails him, and in distress he becomes “yet more faithless” (v. 22). Yet God shows mercy through a prophet and four men of Ephraim, and the lamp of David still burns in Hezekiah.

Why it was said. The first readers’ fathers had gone into exile for unfaithfulness (see the introduction), and they too were tempted to lean on the powers of their day. Ahaz shows where that road ends, and Oded reminds them that north and south were still one family, under a God who judges cruelty even in those he uses.

How the chapter makes its case. First the sin (vv. 1–4): Ahaz casts images for the Baals and burns his sons in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom. Then the judgment (vv. 5–8): Syria and Israel defeat him, and 200,000 of Judah are marched to Samaria. Then the surprise (vv. 9–15): the prophet Oded rebukes the victors, and four chiefs of Ephraim send the captives home clothed and fed. Then the deepening (vv. 16–22): Ahaz buys Assyria’s help and is afflicted by it, and in distress turns further from God. Last, the doors (vv. 23–27): he worships the gods of Damascus, shuts the house of the LORD, and is denied the tombs of the kings, but Hezekiah reigns in his place.

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by contrast. In this very war Isaiah gave Ahaz the sign he refused: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel” (Isaiah 7:14). A king who gave his sons to the fire to buy help was promised God’s own Son, given and not taken. The kindness on the Jericho road foreshadows the Good Samaritan, and the One who told that parable came to rescue his enemies.

For us. Every rival trust demands more than it gives and fails in the day of trouble. Distress is meant to turn us back to God, not further away. And no one is beyond the reach of the God who spoke Immanuel over Ahaz’s head.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Metal Images, and the Valley of Hinnom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahaz falls lower than any king of Judah before him, and God hands him over to his enemies. Measured against David, he fails (v. 1). He walks in the ways of Israel’s kings, casts metal images for the Baals, burns his sons in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom as the nations did, and sacrifices on every hill and under every green tree (vv. 2–4). “Therefore the LORD his God” gives him into the hands of Syria, who carries off many captives to Damascus, and of Israel, whose king Pekah kills 120,000 of Judah in a day (vv. 5–6). A son of the king and two high officials die (v. 7), and 200,000 women and children are taken captive to Samaria (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 1 measures him against David, twelve generations back, and not against Jotham, who was a good man and only just dead. The standard for a son of David is never the man immediately in front of him. It is the covenant the family was given.
verseByVerse.examples: The descent in these verses is gradual: a foundry first, then the fire, then the hills. Few people set out to do the worst thing; they take the next step, and then the next. The way back is open at every step, but it is easiest to take before the furnace is lit.

verseByVerse.quote: Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done, but he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel. He even made metal images for the Baals, and he made offerings in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom and burned his sons as an offering, according to the abominations of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel. And he sacrificed and made offerings on the high places and on the hills and under every green tree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahaz abandoned the way of David for the worst practices of the nations, even burning his own sons as offerings.

As his father David had done. His father Jotham was one of the best men in this book, and the Chronicler walks straight past him to David, the measure of every king. The descent that follows is taken in four steps, each further than the last: the ways of Israel’s kings, metal images, child sacrifice, and worship on every hill.

He even made metal images for the Baals. Not tolerated shrines on a hillside but a foundry, with a furnace and a royal commission.

Burned his sons as an offering. His sons, plural, were burned in a ravine on the south side of the city. And the Chronicler says why it is unbearable: this is the practice for which God drove out the nations who lived in the land before Israel. Israel was put into Canaan because Canaan did this. Now the son of David does it within sight of the temple. God said of it, through Jeremiah, that it was a thing “which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind” (Jeremiah 7:31).

One son or several? Kings mentions one son burned (2 Kings 16:3); the plural here probably means more than one, or speaks of the practice as a whole.

The Valley of the Son of Hinnom. The name of that ravine did not die with him. Where the ESV prints “hell” on the lips of Jesus, its footnote gives the Greek, Gehenna (Matthew 5:22), the name of this valley. Judah’s burning-ground gave its name to final judgment, and it was a king of David’s line who lit the fires.

The Father who gave his own Son. Ahaz gave his sons to gods who wanted something from him. The living God never asked it: when he tested Abraham he stopped the knife and provided a ram in Isaac’s place (Genesis 22:12–13). The only Son ever offered to God was offered by God, “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). Every false god takes our children; the true God gave his.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the LORD his God gave him into the hand of the king of Syria, who defeated him and took captive a great number of his people and brought them to Damascus. He was also given into the hand of the king of Israel, who struck him with great force. For Pekah the son of Remaliah killed 120,000 from Judah in one day, all of them men of valor, because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers. And Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, killed Maaseiah the king's son and Azrikam the commander of the palace and Elkanah the next in authority to the king. The men of Israel took captive 200,000 of their relatives, women, sons, and daughters. They also took much spoil from them and brought the spoil to Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Ahaz and Judah had forsaken the LORD, God gave them into the hands of Syria and Israel, with terrible losses in battle and a vast number taken captive.

The LORD his God. The Chronicler will not drop the word “his” even here, with the foundry running and the valley smoking. The God sinned against is still this man’s God, which makes his sin treachery rather than ignorance.

He was also given into the hand of the king of Israel. The war comes from two directions at once. Isaiah dates his seventh chapter to exactly this crisis, when “Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah the king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to wage war against it”, and “the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind” (Isaiah 7:1–2).

Because they had forsaken the LORD. A hundred and twenty thousand in a day, and the cause is given in the same sentence as the number. Not a failure of tactics: they had forsaken the LORD. This book has laid that charge against Rehoboam’s generation (12:1, 5), against Judah after Jehoiada (24:18, 20), and it will lay it against the last generation before the exile.

Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim. Verse 7 names three of the dead, together the top of the government: a son of the king, the head of the palace, and the second man in the kingdom. If Maaseiah was Ahaz’s own son, there is a quiet horror here. Ahaz gave some of his children to the fire to buy safety, and one he kept was killed anyway. Idols never take what you offer and leave the rest alone; they take the payment and come back for the thing it was meant to protect.

200,000 of their relatives. Now the numbers are no longer soldiers. Two hundred thousand women and children walked north to Samaria, and the word for what they were to their captors is “relatives”. The kingdom had been divided for two hundred years, and they were still one family.

Uncertain wording. Two things are uncertain. The Hebrew word for thousand, eleph, can also name a clan or military unit, so some faithful scholars think units rather than individuals are counted; others take the figures as they stand. Either way Judah lost a generation of fighting men in a day. And “the king’s son” (v. 7) is sometimes the title of a royal official, so Maaseiah may have been an officer or a prince of an earlier generation rather than Ahaz’s own son.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God shows mercy to Judah through the people of the north. The prophet Oded meets the victorious army at Samaria: God gave Judah into their hand, but their rage has reached up to heaven; they mean to enslave their own relatives, and have they not sins of their own? Let the captives go, for God’s fierce wrath is on them too (vv. 9–11). Four named chiefs of Ephraim back him, confessing Israel’s guilt (vv. 12–13). The soldiers give up captives and spoil (v. 14), and the chiefs clothe, shoe, feed and anoint the prisoners, set the weak on donkeys, and bring them all to their kinsfolk at Jericho (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Oded grants that God handed Judah over, and still holds the northern army guilty for the rage with which it did the work. Being used by God is not the same as being approved by him.
verseByVerse.examples: Four men stood in the road and said no to a victorious army, and an army listened. Most of us will never face a crowd like that, but the same courage is asked in smaller rooms: the one voice that says, "This is wrong, and we should put it right," while there is still time.

verseByVerse.quote: But a prophet of the LORD was there, whose name was Oded, and he went out to meet the army that came to Samaria and said to them, "Behold, because the LORD, the God of your fathers, was angry with Judah, he gave them into your hand, but you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven. And now you intend to subjugate the people of Judah and Jerusalem, male and female, as your slaves. Have you not sins of your own against the LORD your God? Now hear me, and send back the captives from your relatives whom you have taken, for the fierce wrath of the LORD is upon you." Certain chiefs also of the men of Ephraim, Azariah the son of Johanan, Berechiah the son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah the son of Shallum, and Amasa the son of Hadlai, stood up against those who were coming from the war and said to them, "You shall not bring the captives in here, for you propose to bring upon us guilt against the LORD in addition to our present sins and guilt. For our guilt is already great, and there is fierce wrath against Israel." So the armed men left the captives and the spoil before the princes and all the assembly. And the men who have been mentioned by name rose and took the captives, and with the spoil they clothed all who were naked among them. They clothed them, gave them sandals, provided them with food and drink, and anointed them, and carrying all the feeble among them on donkeys, they brought them to their kinsfolk at Jericho, the city of palm trees. Then they returned to Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Samaria, of all places, God raised up a prophet and four unknown men who rebuked the victors’ cruelty and showed the captives astonishing kindness.

But a prophet of the LORD was there. This scene, found nowhere else in the Bible, is the moral centre of the chapter. A prophet stands not in Jerusalem, where the king is burning children, but in the capital of the northern kingdom, in the road in front of an army that has just won the largest victory in its history, with two hundred thousand prisoners behind it.

In a rage that has reached up to heaven. His argument holds two things at once. God was angry with Judah and gave them into Israel’s hand; he grants it. But the rage was theirs. God used them, and he will hold them responsible for how they behaved while he used them. Being an instrument in God’s hand is no certificate of good conduct.

Have you not sins of your own against the LORD your God? The question lands on every victor in every age. Nothing licenses cruelty like the conviction that our enemies deserve it, and the northern army was not wrong that Judah had sinned. That is exactly what made them merciless. Crowds sure they are on the right side of history can march their own relatives off in chains and feel righteous doing it. Oded’s question does not deny the other side’s guilt; it puts the accuser in the dock beside them. And it is not a door slammed: he asks it so that they will turn back while they can, to the LORD who is “your God” as well.

The gospel and outrage. This is the gospel’s strange gift to a divided world. At the cross the religious and the irreligious, the winners and the losers, stand equally guilty, and everyone who is forgiven is forgiven freely. People who know that cannot keep their outrage pure for long. They begin, like four men of Ephraim nobody had heard of, to look for sandals and bread for the people they were taught to hate.

Certain chiefs also of the men of Ephraim. Four northerners, named with their fathers, in a book that gives the northern kingdom almost nothing. “Our guilt is already great,” they say. They do not argue that the prisoners deserve better; they argue that Israel cannot afford another sin, an honest thing for a nation to say about itself.

The armed men left the captives. An army marching home with the plunder of a kingdom put it down in the street because four men and a prophet told them to. No threat, no miracle. Somebody spoke God’s word, and they obeyed.

They clothed all who were naked among them. Clothes, sandals, food and drink, oil on the skin, and those who could not walk set on donkeys, all the way to Jericho, out of the very goods taken from them.

The Good Samaritan. Any reader of the Gospels will recognise the scene: a man stripped and left half dead on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho, and a Samaritan who pours on oil, sets him on his own animal and cares for him (Luke 10:30–34). Whether or not Jesus had this chapter in mind, the road is the same road, and the rescuers again come from the people Judah despised (see Samaritans). The one who told that parable did more than any of them: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10).

North and south. In the south the anointed son of David is putting his sons in a fire. In the north four men nobody has heard of are putting sandals on the feet of prisoners of war. God’s grace is at work where the titles are not.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho, the “city of palm trees,” lay near the border between the two kingdoms.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahaz turns to Assyria instead of God, and gets worse, not better, under God’s discipline. He sends to the king of Assyria for help (v. 16) while Edom invades and the Philistines seize and settle the towns of the lowlands and the Negeb (vv. 17–18). The Chronicler explains: “the LORD humbled Judah because of Ahaz”, who had been very unfaithful (v. 19). Tiglath-pileser comes, but afflicts him instead of strengthening him; the tribute stripped from temple, palace and princes does not help (vv. 20–21). And in his distress Ahaz becomes yet more faithless, “this same King Ahaz” (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 19 turns the book’s key verb round. Since 7:14 the promise has run: if my people ... humble themselves. Here God does the humbling, to a nation, from the outside, and nothing comes of it.
verseByVerse.examples: Hard times do not make anyone better by themselves. If you are in distress now, the question is not whether the trouble will change you but which way you will turn in it, and the God who heard Manasseh in a Babylonian prison (33:12) is still listening.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time King Ahaz sent to the king of Assyria for help. For the Edomites had again invaded and defeated Judah and carried away captives. And the Philistines had made raids on the cities in the Shephelah and the Negeb of Judah, and had taken Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soco with its villages, Timnah with its villages, and Gimzo with its villages. And they settled there. For the LORD humbled Judah because of Ahaz king of Israel, for he had made Judah act sinfully and had been very unfaithful to the LORD. So Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came against him and afflicted him instead of strengthening him. For Ahaz took a portion from the house of the LORD and the house of the king and of the princes, and gave tribute to the king of Assyria, but it did not help him. In the time of his distress he became yet more faithless to the LORD—this same King Ahaz.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahaz trusted Assyria instead of God, and the help he bought turned against him; brought low by God, he did not humble himself but grew more faithless still.

King Ahaz sent to the king of Assyria for help. This is the decision the reign turns on, and Isaiah stood in front of him as he made it. The prophet had urged him, “If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all” (Isaiah 7:9), and offered him any sign, “deep as Sheol or high as heaven” (Isaiah 7:11). Ahaz answered with the most pious sentence in the story: “I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test” (Isaiah 7:12). Then he sent for Assyria. Refusing God’s help is rarely announced as unbelief; it is dressed as modesty, with another plan already drafted.

The Edomites had again invaded. Meanwhile the map comes apart. Edom raids from the south; the Philistines take Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soco, Timnah and Gimzo, “and they settled there”. Not a raid but an occupation, town by named town, undoing Uzziah’s victories (26:6–7).

For the LORD humbled Judah. “Humble” is the word this book is built on: “if my people who are called by my name humble themselves” (7:14). But being brought low is not the same as humbling oneself. A man can be flattened by God and get up angrier than he went down, and that is what happens next. Why “Ahaz king of Israel”? Chronicles sometimes uses “Israel” of Judah as the true heir of the covenant people.

Afflicted him instead of strengthening him. The help he bought turned on him. He stripped the temple, the palace and his own princes to pay for it, “but it did not help him”. Two chapters ago God helped Uzziah for nothing; Ahaz paid a fortune and got an overlord. Tiglath-pileser III had made Assyria the great power of the age. He did crush Damascus and take Galilee and Gilead from Israel (2 Kings 15:29; 16:9), but Ahaz had called himself “your servant and your son” (2 Kings 16:7), and from then on Judah was a tribute-paying vassal of Assyria.

In the time of his distress. Here the historian, who hardly ever raises his voice, raises it: “this same King Ahaz”. Distress is where the kings of this book turn back to God. Rehoboam humbled himself when Shishak was at the gate (12:6); Ahaz is given the same kind of trouble and walks the other way. What turns a person in distress is the mercy he turns toward, and that door stood open to Ahaz as it would to Manasseh, the worst of them, who “humbled himself greatly” and was heard (33:12–13).

In everyday life. Trouble does not make anyone better by itself; the same hardship softens one heart and hardens another. The question is whom it is turning us toward.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahaz reaches the bottom: he shuts God’s house and fills the land with other altars. He sacrifices to the gods of Damascus because they seemed to help Syria, and they ruin him and all Israel (v. 23). He cuts up the vessels of the house of God, shuts the doors of the house of the LORD, and builds altars in every corner of Jerusalem and high places in every city of Judah, provoking the LORD to anger (vv. 24–25). His acts are recorded in the royal annals (v. 26). He is buried in Jerusalem but not in the tombs of the kings, and his son Hezekiah reigns in his place (v. 27), the king who will open the doors again.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 24 is where the descent ends: not in idolatry alongside the temple but in the temple closed. Everything the book has said about seeking and forsaking arrives at a locked door.
verseByVerse.examples: The next sentence of the story is the first verse of the next reign: In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of the house of the LORD and repaired them (29:3). No door shut by one generation is beyond God's reopening in the next.

verseByVerse.quote: For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him and said, "Because the gods of the kings of Syria helped them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me." But they were the ruin of him and of all Israel. And Ahaz gathered together the vessels of the house of God and cut in pieces the vessels of the house of God, and he shut up the doors of the house of the LORD, and he made himself altars in every corner of Jerusalem. In every city of Judah he made high places to make offerings to other gods, provoking to anger the LORD, the God of his fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahaz worshipped the gods of the enemy who had beaten him and shut the doors of God’s house, filling the land instead with altars to other gods.

He sacrificed to the gods of Damascus. His great-grandfather Amaziah carried home the gods of Edom in silence (25:14). Ahaz explains himself, and the reasoning makes it worse. He has watched Syria win and concluded that Syria’s gods have the power, when verse 5 has told us exactly who handed him over. He is worshipping the weapon used on him and ignoring the hand that swung it. “But they were the ruin of him and of all Israel.”

He shut up the doors of the house of the LORD. The vessels Solomon made are cut up for the metal, and the doors are barred: not shared with another god, but shut. The lamps go out, and the incense and burnt offerings in the holy place stop (29:7). For the first time since Solomon built it, the house of the LORD stands locked.

Does this fit 2 Kings 16? Kings tells how Ahaz copied an altar he saw at Damascus, set it in the temple court and had the priest offer the daily sacrifices on it (2 Kings 16:10–16). The accounts fit together: the courtyard was given over to the king’s new altar, while the house itself, where the lamps, incense and true worship belonged, was shut up, as Hezekiah’s reopening confirms (29:3, 7).

Altars in every corner of Jerusalem. He replaces the one house with altars everywhere, in every corner of the capital and high places in every city. A man who shuts one door has to open a hundred others. Nobody in Judah worshipped less under Ahaz; they worshipped everything else.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of his acts and all his ways, from first to last, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. And Ahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city, in Jerusalem, for they did not bring him into the tombs of the kings of Israel. And Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahaz was denied the tombs of the kings, yet God’s promise to David survived even this reign, and Hezekiah took the throne.

One more grave. Count the graves one more time. Jehoram was buried in the city of David but not in the tombs (21:20); Joash likewise (24:25). Amaziah was laid with his fathers (25:28). Uzziah went into the burial field beside the tombs (26:23). Jotham was buried without qualification (27:9). And Ahaz is buried “in the city, in Jerusalem”; the Chronicler will not even write “the city of David” over him, and notes that they did not bring him where the kings go.

Where was Ahaz buried? Kings says he “was buried with his fathers in the city of David” (2 Kings 16:20). The two do not clash: he was laid inside the city, but not in the royal tombs themselves.

Judah at its darkest. This is the lowest point of the book so far: the temple dark and locked, the borders gone, a hundred and twenty thousand dead, two hundred thousand marched away and home again only because four strangers had a conscience, and the king who did it in a grave nobody wanted to name.

Hezekiah his son reigned in his place. A son of Ahaz, one of the boys not taken down into the valley. The lamp God promised to David (21:7) is still burning, through a foundry, a fire, two invasions and a locked temple, and now it is in the hands of a young man who will open the doors in the first month of his first year (29:3).

A sign for the king who refused one. The king who refused a sign was given one anyway. In the middle of this war Isaiah said to him: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel” (Isaiah 7:14). A father was putting his own sons into the fire to buy help from gods who were not there, and over his head God promised a Son of his own, not taken but given, and given for people exactly like Ahaz: “God with us” (Matthew 1:23), spoken over one of the worst kings in the book.

Where Christians differ: young woman or virgin? The Hebrew word Isaiah used, almah, means a young woman of marriageable age, and some read the prophecy only of a child born in Ahaz’s day. Others see it as a direct prediction of Christ alone. The Greek translation of the Old Testament made before Christ rendered it parthenos, virgin, and Matthew reads it of Mary’s virgin conception (Matthew 1:22–23).

This commentary’s view. The sign spoke to Ahaz’s own day, since before the child was grown the two kings he feared would be gone (Isaiah 7:16), and its full meaning reached beyond that to Immanuel himself, born of the virgin in Bethlehem, as Matthew says (see the note on Isaiah 7).

28.theology:
Oded's speech is the chapter's clearest theology. God handed Judah over, and the army he used is guilty for what it did while being used. Isaiah says the same of Assyria: the rod of God's anger is judged for the pride with which it swung (Isa 10:5-7). Being used by God does not excuse what a person does.

Verse 19 turns round the promise the whole book rests on (7:14): there the people humble themselves, here God humbles Judah and no repentance follows. Being brought low is not repentance; trouble makes a man more of what he already is, which is why the narrator interrupts himself in verse 22.

And the descent ends not in rival worship but in no worship: the vessels cut up, the doors shut, the lamps out, and nowhere in Judah to bring a sacrifice. Yet God keeps David's line alive through it, and the first act of the next reign is to open the doors again.
28.examples:
This chapter sets two pictures side by side. In Jerusalem a foundry casts idols to royal order and a king puts his sons in the fire to buy safety. In Samaria four northerners nobody has heard of block the road, and their army dresses the naked out of the plunder, puts sandals on their feet and carries the ones who cannot walk to Jericho on donkeys.

The anointed king had every privilege and used none of it; the strangers had none and showed mercy. Mercy often comes from the people we least expect, and God is not limited to the ones we would have chosen.

keyVerse.quote: In the time of his distress he became yet more faithless to the LORD
keyVerse.note: This is the Chronicler’s own outburst over Ahaz, and it sums up the reign. Distress is meant to drive us to humble ourselves before God (7:14), but Ahaz turned it into a reason to trust every other power. Over this same king God spoke the promise of Immanuel, the Son given for people who have run every other way.

28.reflection:
Ahaz gave his own sons to false gods to buy safety (v. 3), and lost a son anyway (v. 7). What do people today sacrifice, even their families, to the things they trust for security? How does Romans 8:32 show us a different kind of God?

Oded asked the victorious army, “Have you not sins of your own against the LORD your God?” (v. 10). Where are we most tempted to be cruel because we are sure the other side deserves it? How does the gospel change that?

The men of Ephraim clothed, fed and carried home the prisoners of war (v. 15). Who are the people we are taught to despise, and what would it look like to show them practical kindness this week?

In his distress Ahaz became “yet more faithless” (v. 22), while Manasseh in distress humbled himself (33:12). When hard times come, what helps us turn toward God rather than away from him?

29.title: He Opened the Doors of the House of the LORD
29.text: <sup>1</sup>Hezekiah began to reign when he was twenty-five years old, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Abijah the daughter of Zechariah.<sup>2</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that David his father had done.<sup>3</sup>In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of the house of the LORD and repaired them.<sup>4</sup>He brought in the priests and the Levites and assembled them in the square on the east<sup>5</sup>and said to them, "Hear me, Levites! Now consecrate yourselves, and consecrate the house of the LORD, the God of your fathers, and carry out the filth from the Holy Place.<sup>6</sup>For our fathers have been unfaithful and have done what was evil in the sight of the LORD our God. They have forsaken him and have turned away their faces from the habitation of the LORD and turned their backs.<sup>7</sup>They also shut the doors of the vestibule and put out the lamps and have not burned incense or offered burnt offerings in the Holy Place to the God of Israel.<sup>8</sup>Therefore the wrath of the LORD came on Judah and Jerusalem, and he has made them an object of horror, of astonishment, and of hissing, as you see with your own eyes.<sup>9</sup>For behold, our fathers have fallen by the sword, and our sons and our daughters and our wives are in captivity for this.<sup>10</sup>Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel, in order that his fierce anger may turn away from us.<sup>11</sup>My sons, do not now be negligent, for the LORD has chosen you to stand in his presence, to minister to him and to be his ministers and make offerings to him."<sup>12</sup>Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai, and Joel the son of Azariah, of the sons of the Kohathites; and of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi, and Azariah the son of Jehallelel; and of the Gershonites, Joah the son of Zimmah, and Eden the son of Joah;<sup>13</sup>and of the sons of Elizaphan, Shimri and Jeuel; and of the sons of Asaph, Zechariah and Mattaniah;<sup>14</sup>and of the sons of Heman, Jehuel and Shimei; and of the sons of Jeduthun, Shemaiah and Uzziel.<sup>15</sup>They gathered their brothers and consecrated themselves and went in as the king had commanded, by the words of the LORD, to cleanse the house of the LORD.<sup>16</sup>The priests went into the inner part of the house of the LORD to cleanse it, and they brought out all the uncleanness that they found in the temple of the LORD into the court of the house of the LORD. And the Levites took it and carried it out to the brook Kidron.<sup>17</sup>They began to consecrate on the first day of the first month, and on the eighth day of the month they came to the vestibule of the LORD. Then for eight days they consecrated the house of the LORD, and on the sixteenth day of the first month they finished.<sup>18</sup>Then they went in to Hezekiah the king and said, "We have cleansed all the house of the LORD, the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils, and the table for the showbread and all its utensils.<sup>19</sup>All the utensils that King Ahaz discarded in his reign when he was faithless, we have made ready and consecrated, and behold, they are before the altar of the LORD."<sup>20</sup>Then Hezekiah the king rose early and gathered the officials of the city and went up to the house of the LORD.<sup>21</sup>And they brought seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats for a sin offering for the kingdom and for the sanctuary and for Judah. And he commanded the priests, the sons of Aaron, to offer them on the altar of the LORD.<sup>22</sup>So they slaughtered the bulls, and the priests received the blood and threw it against the altar. And they slaughtered the rams, and their blood was thrown against the altar. And they slaughtered the lambs, and their blood was thrown against the altar.<sup>23</sup>Then the goats for the sin offering were brought to the king and the assembly, and they laid their hands on them,<sup>24</sup>and the priests slaughtered them and made a sin offering with their blood on the altar, to make atonement for all Israel. For the king commanded that the burnt offering and the sin offering should be made for all Israel.<sup>25</sup>And he stationed the Levites in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres, according to the commandment of David and of Gad the king's seer and of Nathan the prophet, for the commandment was from the LORD through his prophets.<sup>26</sup>The Levites stood with the instruments of David, and the priests with the trumpets.<sup>27</sup>Then Hezekiah commanded that the burnt offering be offered on the altar. And when the burnt offering began, the song to the LORD began also, and the trumpets, accompanied by the instruments of David king of Israel.<sup>28</sup>The whole assembly worshiped, and the singers sang, and the trumpeters sounded. All this continued until the burnt offering was finished.<sup>29</sup>When the offering was finished, the king and all who were present with him bowed themselves and worshiped.<sup>30</sup>And Hezekiah the king and the officials commanded the Levites to sing praises to the LORD with the words of David and of Asaph the seer. And they sang praises with gladness, and they bowed down and worshiped.<sup>31</sup>Then Hezekiah said, "You have now consecrated yourselves to the LORD. Come near; bring sacrifices and thank offerings to the house of the LORD." And the assembly brought sacrifices and thank offerings, and all who were of a willing heart brought burnt offerings.<sup>32</sup>The number of the burnt offerings that the assembly brought was 70 bulls, 100 rams, and 200 lambs; all these were for a burnt offering to the LORD.<sup>33</sup>And the consecrated offerings were 600 bulls and 3,000 sheep.<sup>34</sup>But the priests were too few and could not flay all the burnt offerings, so until other priests had consecrated themselves, their brothers the Levites helped them, until the work was finished— for the Levites were more upright in heart than the priests in consecrating themselves.<sup>35</sup>Besides the great number of burnt offerings, there was the fat of the peace offerings, and there were the drink offerings for the burnt offerings. Thus the service of the house of the LORD was restored.<sup>36</sup>And Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced because God had provided for the people, for the thing came about suddenly.
29.overview:
Where we are. Ahaz has died after the darkest reign yet in this book: he burned his sons, shut the doors of the LORD’s house and set up altars on every corner of Jerusalem (28:3, 24–25), leaving Judah beaten and paying tribute to Assyria. His son Hezekiah now takes the throne, and the Chronicler gives him four chapters, more than any king since Solomon.

The message. The way back to God begins where God has always put it: at confession and at the altar where sin is atoned for. Hezekiah opens the house and owns the nation’s sin as his own, and before anyone sings, a sin offering is made for all Israel. Then the song begins with the offering, and the people discover that what looked impossible “came about suddenly”, because God had prepared it.

Why it was said. The first readers had a rebuilt temple and a long record of their fathers’ unfaithfulness behind them (see the introduction). This chapter showed them that ruined worship can be restored within a month when God’s people humble themselves, and that restoration starts not with music or buildings but with confession and atonement.

How the chapter makes its case. In his first month Hezekiah opens the doors, names “our fathers’” sin and its cost, and resolves to make a covenant with the LORD (vv. 1–11). In sixteen days the Levites carry the filth to the Kidron and bring Ahaz’s discarded vessels back to the altar (vv. 12–19). A sin offering is made for kingdom, sanctuary and Judah, with atonement for all Israel; when the burnt offering begins the song begins, and everyone bows (vv. 20–31). The gifts outrun the priests, the service of the house is restored, and all rejoice that God has provided (vv. 32–36).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by pattern, and by the need the pattern exposes. The order of the chapter, blood first and then song, is the order of the gospel. Every goat on which the king laid his hands pointed to the one on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all, and whose blood, unlike theirs, actually takes sin away (Hebrews 10:4, 12). Hezekiah, a son of David who reopens the way to God and orders atonement for all Israel, foreshadows the greater Son of David, who by his own blood opened “the new and living way” into God’s presence (Hebrews 10:20). Because his offering is finished (John 19:30), the church’s song never has to stop.

For us. Renewal does not start with the music but with honest confession, even of sins we inherited, and with the sacrifice God has provided in his Son. Then come the quiet days of carrying out the rubbish, and the joy of finding that God had it ready all along.
29.theology:
Verse 6 is a model of confessing sins we inherited: a young king, personally guiltless of what he describes, says our fathers. Owning a family's or a church's sin as one's own, out loud, is the hardest and most fruitful sentence a reformer ever speaks.

Verses 27-28 make the praise begin and end with the sacrifice, and verse 31 gives the order plainly: offering, blood, song, and only then come near. We come near to God only after sin has been atoned for, never before.

Verse 24 stretches the atonement past the border, to the northern kingdom that had so lately killed and captured Judah's people. The next chapter posts the invitations.

And verse 36 gives the credit away. They rejoiced because God had provided, and the speed of it was the evidence. What looked like a young king's project had been prepared behind a locked door.
29.examples:
Much of this chapter is unglamorous work: sixteen days of men whose hereditary work was music carrying rubbish down to the Kidron, and the vessels Ahaz threw out found, cleaned and set back before the altar. Revival is often remembered for its singing; this chapter remembers the cleaning that came first.

And the people gave more than there were consecrated priests to handle, while the juniors had got ready first. Readiness is not a matter of rank, and the quiet, early preparation of people nobody notices is often what lets the rest of the church rejoice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — In the First Month, He Opened the Doors
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A new king’s first act is to reopen the way to God, and his first words are a confession. Hezekiah is given the verdict his father was denied, doing right as David had done, and in the first month of his first year he opens the temple doors and repairs them (vv. 1–3). He gathers the priests and Levites outside the defiled building and tells them to consecrate themselves and then the house (vv. 4–5). He names the sin of the last generation as “our” sin and traces Judah’s defeats and captives to it (vv. 6–9). Then he says what is in his heart, a covenant with the LORD, and urges the Levites not to be negligent, because the LORD has chosen them (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 6 is honest confession by a man who inherited the mess. He names the sin without softening it, states what it cost, and moves in the same speech to what he intends to do.
verseByVerse.examples: If you have inherited a mess, in a family, a church or a workplace, you do not have to fix all of it in the first month. But Hezekiah shows where to begin: with the door to God, before the walls, the budget or the reputation.

verseByVerse.quote: Hezekiah began to reign when he was twenty-five years old, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Abijah the daughter of Zechariah. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that David his father had done. In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of the house of the LORD and repaired them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah is given back the verdict his father was denied, and he proves it in his first month by opening the doors Ahaz had shut.

He reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. Amaziah too was twenty-five at his crowning and reigned twenty-nine years (25:1). Same age, same span, and one carried home the gods of the people he had defeated, while the other opened the house of God in his first month. The figures on a man’s file tell you nothing about him.

Abijah the daughter of Zechariah. His mother lived in Ahaz’s palace in the years when sons of that household were burned in the Hinnom valley (28:3), and this son of hers was not one of them. The record keeps her name and not a word of her story, which is how it usually goes with the people God uses most.

According to all that David his father had done. The verdict is the one refused to his father at the head of the last chapter (28:1), with the negative taken out. Ahaz is the only king in this book given that sentence in the negative, and his son is handed it back whole, measured against David himself.

In the first year of his reign, in the first month. Verse 17 adds that the work began on the first day. A new king’s first weeks are usually spent making the throne safe, and this book has shown how. Jehoram put his six brothers to the sword (21:4). Amaziah waited until the royal power was firmly his and then executed his father’s assassins (25:3). Athaliah used hers on the nursery (22:10). Hezekiah spent his on God’s house.

He opened the doors of the house of the LORD and repaired them. With a father dead in disgrace, tribute owed to Assyria, six lowland towns in Philistine hands (28:18) and altars on every corner of the city, he went to a locked building and got the doors open, and then repaired them, because his father had shut them and let them rot (28:24). The first public act of the reign was carpentry, and it announced everything that followed: whatever else this king would be short of, it would not be access to God.

The door that stays open. The greater Son of David did not merely unlock a building. He called himself the door (John 10:9), and by his own blood opened “the new and living way” into God’s presence (Hebrews 10:19–20), a door no later king can shut.

A question of dates. Hezekiah was twenty-five at his accession, yet Ahaz began to reign at twenty and reigned sixteen years (28:1), which on the bare figures makes him a father at about eleven. The likeliest answer is overlapping reigns: kings of Judah often shared the throne with their fathers, and if Ahaz’s age is counted from a shared reign and his sixteen years from his reign alone, he was older than the sum suggests (see Regnal years). Others think a number has been miscopied. Nothing here depends on the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: He brought in the priests and the Levites and assembled them in the square on the east and said to them, "Hear me, Levites! Now consecrate yourselves, and consecrate the house of the LORD, the God of your fathers, and carry out the filth from the Holy Place. For our fathers have been unfaithful and have done what was evil in the sight of the LORD our God. They have forsaken him and have turned away their faces from the habitation of the LORD and turned their backs. They also shut the doors of the vestibule and put out the lamps and have not burned incense or offered burnt offerings in the Holy Place to the God of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah calls the priests and Levites to make themselves and the house holy again, and begins with an honest confession: the nation turned its back on God, and his worship went dark.

He brought in the priests and the Levites. He assembles the priests and Levites in the square on the east, outside the building, because the building is not yet fit to stand in, and there gives the speech that starts the reformation.

Now consecrate yourselves. The order is Scripture’s order throughout: consecrate yourselves first, then the house. Men who have not dealt with themselves cannot cleanse anything holy. And filth is a brutal word to use of the Holy Place, but that is what was lying in the temple of God after the years of Ahaz.

For our fathers have been unfaithful. The first word of the diagnosis shows what kind of man is speaking. He is twenty-five. He personally shut nothing, melted nothing and burned no child in the Hinnom valley, and the man who did all of it was his own father, only just buried. He could have said your fathers and been correct, or “my father Ahaz” and been popular. He says our, and stands inside the guilt with the men he is about to ask for sixteen days of filthy work. Unfaithful is the sin that will end in exile (36:14; see the introduction).

They have forsaken him. The three verbs of verse 6 picture one movement: they forsook the LORD, turned away their faces from the habitation of the LORD, and turned their backs. First the heart leaves, then the eyes, last the body, and each step looks like nothing much on the day it is taken.

They also shut the doors of the vestibule and put out the lamps. Verse 7 lists what stopped: the doors shut, the lamps out, no incense, no burnt offerings. Each was a daily thing. The temple did not blow up. It went quiet.

Can I repent of what I did not do? Few questions are more charged than what to do with the sins of the past, a nation’s, a church’s or a family’s. Two answers come easily. One says: I was not there; it has nothing to do with me. The other turns the past into a weapon, always someone else’s guilt. Hezekiah takes neither road. He does not pretend he burned children in the valley, nor stand apart from those who did. He says our, because he belongs to this people, has inherited what they did and is living in its consequences. That is not taking personal guilt for his father’s crimes, which Ezekiel 18:20 rules out; it is the solidarity of confession, and Nehemiah and Daniel prayed the same way (Nehemiah 1:6; Daniel 9:5–8). Behind it stands someone greater. Jesus, who had no sin of his own, joined sinners in the Jordan and went to the cross under sins he had never committed (2 Corinthians 5:21). Those he has forgiven need neither deny the past nor use it as a club. They can say our, and then pick up a broom.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the wrath of the LORD came on Judah and Jerusalem, and he has made them an object of horror, of astonishment, and of hissing, as you see with your own eyes. For behold, our fathers have fallen by the sword, and our sons and our daughters and our wives are in captivity for this. Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel, in order that his fierce anger may turn away from us. My sons, do not now be negligent, for the LORD has chosen you to stand in his presence, to minister to him and to be his ministers and make offerings to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ruin Judah could see was God’s wrath on its unfaithfulness, so Hezekiah resolves to make a covenant with the LORD that his anger may turn away, and calls the Levites to their work as men God has chosen.

As you see with your own eyes. He does not ask them to accept a doctrine but to look out of the window: Philistine garrisons in Judah’s towns, tribute to pay to Assyria, households in that square with no father in them.

In captivity for this. He draws the line himself, in public, from the locked doors to the graves. A hundred and twenty thousand fell in a single day under Ahaz (28:6); two hundred thousand women and children were marched north, sent home only because a prophet in Samaria spoke up (28:8–15); and the Edomites had carried off captives of their own (28:17). The young king tells them what that was, and he does not blame Pekah for it.

It is in my heart to make a covenant. Nobody made him do this. There is no prophet in this chapter and no crisis forcing his hand; Sennacherib’s invasion is still years away. He wants this, says so in the first person, and the whole reformation of chapters 29 to 31 grows out of one man’s settled desire.

My sons, do not now be negligent. From a man of twenty-five to the priesthood of Judah, it is a father’s word, not a commander’s. What he gives them is not a threat but their own job description: do not be slack, because of who chose you and what he chose you for.

For the LORD has chosen you. The only motive he offers, and the right one. Not that the nation needs them or history is watching, but that the LORD picked them out to stand in his presence and minister to him. The grace of being chosen comes first, and diligence grows out of it, as it still does for a people chosen in Christ to be a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — Out to the Brook Kidron
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Reform needs people willing to do slow, dirty, unseen work, and the Levites rise to it. Fourteen named men from seven families, singers among them, gather their brothers and consecrate themselves, acting on the king’s command, which rested on the words of the LORD (vv. 12–15). The priests bring the uncleanness out of the inner house, the Levites carry it down to the Kidron, and in sixteen days the whole house is clean (vv. 16–17). Their report to the king ends with the vessels Ahaz threw away, cleaned, consecrated and set before the altar (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 15 gives the chain of authority in one clause: they went in as the king had commanded, by the words of the LORD. The king's order is obeyed because of what stands behind it, and a command that rests on Scripture can move men to sixteen days of filthy work.
verseByVerse.examples: People who would not move for a scolding will often move for a calling. The difference between these Levites and their slow predecessors was a king who spoke to them as sons and reminded them that God had chosen them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai, and Joel the son of Azariah, of the sons of the Kohathites; and of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi, and Azariah the son of Jehallelel; and of the Gershonites, Joah the son of Zimmah, and Eden the son of Joah; and of the sons of Elizaphan, Shimri and Jeuel; and of the sons of Asaph, Zechariah and Mattaniah; and of the sons of Heman, Jehuel and Shimei; and of the sons of Jeduthun, Shemaiah and Uzziel. They gathered their brothers and consecrated themselves and went in as the king had commanded, by the words of the LORD, to cleanse the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites answered the king’s call at once, a team drawn from every branch of Levi’s house, singers included, and they began by making themselves holy.

Then the Levites arose. Four words that answer the days of Joash, when the Levites were told to be quick and were not (24:5). This time they get up.

Seven pairs from seven families. Then fourteen names, the sort of list a modern reader skims and the Chronicler never wastes. They come in seven pairs from seven families: two each from Kohath, Merari and Gershon, the three ancient clans of Levi; two from Elizaphan, a leading Kohathite house (Numbers 3:30); and two each from Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, the three guilds of singers David set apart for the service (1 Chronicles 25:1). The whole house of Levi is represented.

Of the sons of Asaph. The musicians are in the cleaning party. Men whose hereditary work was harps and cymbals spent the next sixteen days carrying rubbish out of a building, and nobody said the job was beneath him.

verseByVerse.quote: The priests went into the inner part of the house of the LORD to cleanse it, and they brought out all the uncleanness that they found in the temple of the LORD into the court of the house of the LORD. And the Levites took it and carried it out to the brook Kidron. They began to consecrate on the first day of the first month, and on the eighth day of the month they came to the vestibule of the LORD. Then for eight days they consecrated the house of the LORD, and on the sixteenth day of the first month they finished. Then they went in to Hezekiah the king and said, "We have cleansed all the house of the LORD, the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils, and the table for the showbread and all its utensils. All the utensils that King Ahaz discarded in his reign when he was faithless, we have made ready and consecrated, and behold, they are before the altar of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In sixteen days of hard, unseen work the priests and Levites cleansed the whole house, keeping God’s boundaries as they did it, and restored even the vessels Ahaz had thrown away.

The priests went into the inner part of the house. The work is done in two stages. Only priests may enter the inner house, so they bring out what they find to the court, and the Levites carry it down the hill. Even in this emergency the boundary Uzziah was struck for crossing (26:16–21) is kept. Reform does not mean the rules stop applying; it means somebody has finally started keeping them.

To the brook Kidron. The right address. There Asa burned his grandmother’s Asherah image (15:16), and there Jerusalem’s altars will go in the next chapter (30:14). It was where Judah dumped its dead gods.

On the first day of the first month. The calendar of verse 17 repays a slow walk. They start on the first day. It takes a week simply to work through the courts, and on the eighth day they reach the vestibule, the porch of the house itself. Then eight more days inside, and they finish on the sixteenth. No fire falls and no prophet speaks, and a modern account of a revival would leave the sixteen days out. But the singing later in this chapter stands on them.

All the utensils that King Ahaz discarded. The itemised report ends with the sentence that made the sixteen days worth it. Whatever Ahaz had thrown out rather than cut up (28:24) had been lying somewhere for years, and the Levites found it, cleaned it, consecrated it and set it before the altar where the king would see it as he came in: a son standing in a courtyard looking at the vessels his father threw away, back in their places, ready for use.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–31 — When the Burnt Offering Began, the Song Began
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Worship begins with atonement, and only then with song. On the morning the house is ready, Hezekiah takes the city’s officials up, and a sin offering of seven of each kind is made for the kingdom, the sanctuary and Judah. King and assembly lay their hands on the goats, and atonement is made for all Israel, north as well as south (vv. 20–24). The Levites take their places with David’s instruments and the priests with the trumpets, and the song begins when the burnt offering begins and lasts until it ends (vv. 25–28). Everyone bows, the psalms of David and Asaph are sung with gladness, and the people are invited to come near with offerings of their own (vv. 29–31).
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 27-28 set the singing and the sacrifice to the same clock, as the note on those verses explains. Praise here is not a warm-up or an afterthought, and it has no existence apart from the altar.
verseByVerse.examples: Nobody in that courtyard left the confession to the professionals, and nobody needs to now. Owning your own sin before God is not a task for the specially devout; it is where every one of us comes in.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Hezekiah the king rose early and gathered the officials of the city and went up to the house of the LORD. And they brought seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats for a sin offering for the kingdom and for the sanctuary and for Judah. And he commanded the priests, the sons of Aaron, to offer them on the altar of the LORD. So they slaughtered the bulls, and the priests received the blood and threw it against the altar. And they slaughtered the rams, and their blood was thrown against the altar. And they slaughtered the lambs, and their blood was thrown against the altar. Then the goats for the sin offering were brought to the king and the assembly, and they laid their hands on them, and the priests slaughtered them and made a sin offering with their blood on the altar, to make atonement for all Israel. For the king commanded that the burnt offering and the sin offering should be made for all Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before any celebration, a sin offering was made for the kingdom, the sanctuary and the people, and atonement for all Israel, because cleaning a building does not remove guilt.

Hezekiah the king rose early. Sixteen days of waiting while other men worked, and on the morning the house was ready he was up before he needed to be.

Seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats. What comes first is a sin offering. Seven of each kind, the number of completeness four times over, for three spheres: the kingdom, the sanctuary and the people. Everything the last generation had touched needed cleansing, and the government was named first.

So they slaughtered the bulls. Verse 22 reports the killing three times and will not abbreviate it, because it happened three times and each time a creature died. A sacrificial system was never meant to be efficient. It was slow, physical and repetitive, so that nobody in that courtyard could mistake forgiveness for a formality.

They laid their hands on them. King and assembly lay their hands on the goats. By that act every man said: what is done to this creature should be done to me, and I am putting my guilt where it can be carried away.

What no goat could carry. That is the question every sacrifice raised and none could answer: how can an animal carry a man’s guilt? Hebrews says plainly that the blood of bulls and goats could never take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). Those goats pointed to the one on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:6), who was made sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21) and offered himself once for all (Hebrews 10:10–12).

Made for all Israel. Verse 24 goes further than anyone would expect from a king of Judah in that decade: the offerings are made for all Israel. Within living memory the northern kingdom had killed a hundred and twenty thousand Judeans in one day. Hezekiah pays for their sin offering anyway. He is not their king, they have not asked, and Assyria has broken their kingdom or is about to (the exact dates of his reign are debated). The next chapter shows him writing to them to invite them to the Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: And he stationed the Levites in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres, according to the commandment of David and of Gad the king's seer and of Nathan the prophet, for the commandment was from the LORD through his prophets. The Levites stood with the instruments of David, and the priests with the trumpets. Then Hezekiah commanded that the burnt offering be offered on the altar. And when the burnt offering began, the song to the LORD began also, and the trumpets, accompanied by the instruments of David king of Israel. The whole assembly worshiped, and the singers sang, and the trumpeters sounded. All this continued until the burnt offering was finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The worship followed what God had commanded through David and the prophets, and the song began when the burnt offering began and lasted until it was finished.

According to the commandment of David. The music is not a matter of taste. The Chronicler traces it through David, Gad the king’s seer and Nathan the prophet, and behind all three: the commandment was from the LORD through his prophets. Israel sang because God told them to.

And the priests with the trumpets. Two groups, two authorities. The strings and cymbals are David’s; the trumpets are older, two of silver given to the sons of Aaron with a statute for when to sound them: “you shall blow the trumpets over your burnt offerings” (Numbers 10:2, 8, 10). Moses and David in one orchestra, and neither part invented by Hezekiah.

When the burnt offering began, the song to the LORD began also. The chapter turns on one word of timing in verse 27: when. Not before, while the crowd gathered, and not after, once the hard part was over. And verse 28 gives the other end: it continued until the burnt offering was finished.

What praise is. The singing and the sacrifice run on the same clock. That is not a stage direction but a statement about what praise is: the sound a rescued people make while the price of their rescue is paid in front of them. It is why the church has never stopped singing. Our offering was made once and is finished, and finished is the word Jesus himself spoke on the cross (John 19:30). Since that offering is never repeated and never loses its power, the song never has to stop.

Does this mean instruments are commanded today? God commanded them for the temple. The New Testament neither commands nor forbids them; some Reformed churches sing unaccompanied, others use instruments to serve the singing. What God requires is singing from the heart, with his word at the centre (Colossians 3:16).

verseByVerse.quote: When the offering was finished, the king and all who were present with him bowed themselves and worshiped. And Hezekiah the king and the officials commanded the Levites to sing praises to the LORD with the words of David and of Asaph the seer. And they sang praises with gladness, and they bowed down and worshiped. Then Hezekiah said, "You have now consecrated yourselves to the LORD. Come near; bring sacrifices and thank offerings to the house of the LORD." And the assembly brought sacrifices and thank offerings, and all who were of a willing heart brought burnt offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the offering was finished, everyone bowed, the Levites sang the psalms with gladness, and the king invited the people, now cleansed, to come near with offerings of their own.

Bowed themselves and worshiped. The music stops and the whole company goes down on its face. The music was never the point; the God they bow to is.

With the words of David and of Asaph the seer. They sang the Psalms. The hymnbook had been written for centuries, and it went on existing all through Ahaz’s reign in a building nobody could get into. Then somebody opened the doors, and the words were still there. Hold on to that in a dark decade: the songs of the church outlive the people who stop singing them. They wait.

They sang praises with gladness, and they bowed down. Gladness and prostration in the same sentence, with no sense that the two pull against each other. A people can be flat on the floor and delighted at the same time; that is what worship is.

Come near. The invitation comes in an exact order: sin offering, blood, song, and only now, come near. What comes in response is not a levy but a flood from all who were of a willing heart. They had been shut out of that courtyard for years, and they arrived carrying what they had. The same order runs through Hebrews: because Jesus’ blood has opened the way, “let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith” (Hebrews 10:19–22).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–36 — The Thing Came About Suddenly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What God prepares can happen faster than anyone dared to hope. The people bring burnt offerings and consecrated gifts in such numbers that the priests are too few to flay them, and the Levites, readier in heart than the priests, step in to help (vv. 32–34). With the fat of the peace offerings and the drink offerings, the whole service of the house is restored, and king and people rejoice, giving the credit to God, “for the thing came about suddenly” (vv. 35–36).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 36 hands the credit for the whole chapter back to God. The man who did the most in the chapter is not the subject of its last verb; God is.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 34 is an awkward line that the Chronicler prints anyway: the senior order was outpaced by its juniors. He does not protect the priests' reputation, and churches are not served by protecting theirs either. Owning slowness honestly is the first step to getting ready, and the juniors' quickness was a gift to their seniors, not a rebuke to be resented.

verseByVerse.quote: The number of the burnt offerings that the assembly brought was 70 bulls, 100 rams, and 200 lambs; all these were for a burnt offering to the LORD. And the consecrated offerings were 600 bulls and 3,000 sheep. But the priests were too few and could not flay all the burnt offerings, so until other priests had consecrated themselves, their brothers the Levites helped them, until the work was finished— for the Levites were more upright in heart than the priests in consecrating themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people gave so much that the priests could not keep up, and the Levites, readier in heart than the priests, stepped in until the work was done.

70 bulls, 100 rams, and 200 lambs. The numbers tell you the mood. A country paying tribute to Assyria out of a stripped treasury brought all this to Jerusalem within days.

But the priests were too few. Then a problem, the best kind a reformer can have: the generosity outran the staffing, and the Levites took up the knives until enough priests had got themselves ready.

The Levites were more upright in heart. The Chronicler adds an uncomfortable line he did not have to add. The priests, the senior order, were the slower; the men with the higher office dragged their feet about getting ready, and their juniors were quicker. It is stated flatly, by a writer who plainly loves the temple and its ministry.

Rank is not readiness. A man can hold the office, know the liturgy and have the right training, and be the last person in the building to deal with himself. No office makes us ready. Christ is the only priest who was ever wholly consecrated, and he consecrated himself for us (John 17:19), so that our readiness is his gift, worked by his Spirit, before it is our effort.

A shortage that lasted. The shortage outlasts the chapter: 30:3 gives it as the reason the Passover had to be moved to the second month.

verseByVerse.quote: Besides the great number of burnt offerings, there was the fat of the peace offerings, and there were the drink offerings for the burnt offerings. Thus the service of the house of the LORD was restored. And Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced because God had provided for the people, for the thing came about suddenly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Within a month the whole service of God’s house was restored, and king and people rejoiced because they knew God had prepared it.

Thus the service of the house of the LORD was restored. What verse 7 listed as stopped is going again: the doors open, the vessels back before the altar, the offerings going up and the choir in its place singing David’s words.

Because God had provided for the people. Neither clause of the last verse is what a court chronicler would have written. The first gives the credit away; the verb means to prepare or make ready. Hezekiah opened the doors, made the speech, supplied the bulls and stood there from dawn, and the sentence that closes the account does not have him as its subject.

For the thing came about suddenly. The second clause is stranger and better. After years of a locked temple, Baals cast in a foundry and children burned in the Hinnom valley, it took under a month: the doors on day one, the house clean by the sixteenth, the altar smoking and the choir singing before the month was out. Reformations of that size are supposed to take a generation, and these men had no funds, an empire on the border and a priesthood that could not get itself ready.

Why it went fast. It went fast because God had prepared it. What looked like Hezekiah’s project turned out to be something God had been arranging while nobody could see it, waiting on the far side of a locked door for a young man to come with a key. That is how it usually is. The long dark stretch is not God waiting for us to become worth helping, and the sudden turn, when it comes, is not the reward for the sixteen days of cleaning. It is the uncovering of what he had ready all along.

keyVerse.quote: Then Hezekiah commanded that the burnt offering be offered on the altar. And when the burnt offering began, the song to the LORD began also, and the trumpets, accompanied by the instruments of David king of Israel.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on the word “when”. The song does not begin before the sacrifice or after it, but with it, because praise is the sound a rescued people make as the price of their rescue is paid. The church sings for the same reason, over an offering that is finished and never loses its power.

29.reflection:
Hezekiah said “our fathers have been unfaithful” (v. 6) about sins he had not committed. What inherited sins, in a family, a church or a nation, might we need to own in confession without either denying them or using them as a weapon?

The cleansing took sixteen unglamorous days before any singing began (vv. 15–17). What “rubbish” might need carrying out of your life or your church before worship can be renewed, and why are we tempted to skip that stage?

The song began when the burnt offering began (v. 27). How does remembering what Christ’s sacrifice cost change the way you sing on a Sunday?

The chapter ends by giving God the credit: “God had provided for the people, for the thing came about suddenly” (v. 36). Where have you seen God do quickly what had seemed impossible for years? How does that encourage you to keep praying for situations that look locked?

30.title: The LORD Heard Hezekiah and Healed the People
30.text: <sup>1</sup>Hezekiah sent to all Israel and Judah, and wrote letters also to Ephraim and Manasseh, that they should come to the house of the LORD at Jerusalem to keep the Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>2</sup>For the king and his princes and all the assembly in Jerusalem had taken counsel to keep the Passover in the second month—<sup>3</sup>for they could not keep it at that time because the priests had not consecrated themselves in sufficient number, nor had the people assembled in Jerusalem—<sup>4</sup>and the plan seemed right to the king and all the assembly.<sup>5</sup>So they decreed to make a proclamation throughout all Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, that the people should come and keep the Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel, at Jerusalem, for they had not kept it as often as prescribed.<sup>6</sup>So couriers went throughout all Israel and Judah with letters from the king and his princes, as the king had commanded, saying, "O people of Israel, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, that he may turn again to the remnant of you who have escaped from the hand of the kings of Assyria.<sup>7</sup>Do not be like your fathers and your brothers, who were faithless to the LORD God of their fathers, so that he made them a desolation, as you see.<sup>8</sup>Do not now be stiff-necked as your fathers were, but yield yourselves to the LORD and come to his sanctuary, which he has consecrated forever, and serve the LORD your God, that his fierce anger may turn away from you.<sup>9</sup>For if you return to the LORD, your brothers and your children will find compassion with their captors and return to this land. For the LORD your God is gracious and merciful and will not turn away his face from you, if you return to him."<sup>10</sup>So the couriers went from city to city through the country of Ephraim and Manasseh, and as far as Zebulun, but they laughed them to scorn and mocked them.<sup>11</sup>However, some men of Asher, of Manasseh, and of Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.<sup>12</sup>The hand of God was also on Judah to give them one heart to do what the king and the princes commanded by the word of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>And many people came together in Jerusalem to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the second month, a very great assembly.<sup>14</sup>They set to work and removed the altars that were in Jerusalem, and all the altars for burning incense they took away and threw into the brook Kidron.<sup>15</sup>And they slaughtered the Passover lamb on the fourteenth day of the second month. And the priests and the Levites were ashamed, so that they consecrated themselves and brought burnt offerings into the house of the LORD.<sup>16</sup>They took their accustomed posts according to the Law of Moses the man of God. The priests threw the blood that they received from the hand of the Levites.<sup>17</sup>For there were many in the assembly who had not consecrated themselves. Therefore the Levites had to slaughter the Passover lamb for everyone who was not clean, to consecrate it to the LORD.<sup>18</sup>For a majority of the people, many of them from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, had not cleansed themselves, yet they ate the Passover otherwise than as prescribed. For Hezekiah had prayed for them, saying, "May the good LORD pardon everyone<sup>19</sup>who sets his heart to seek God, the LORD, the God of his fathers, even though not according to the sanctuary's rules of cleanness."<sup>20</sup>And the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.<sup>21</sup>And the people of Israel who were present at Jerusalem kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days with great gladness, and the Levites and the priests praised the LORD day by day, singing with all their might to the LORD.<sup>22</sup>And Hezekiah spoke encouragingly to all the Levites who showed good skill in the service of the LORD. So they ate the food of the festival for seven days, sacrificing peace offerings and giving thanks to the LORD, the God of their fathers.<sup>23</sup>Then the whole assembly agreed together to keep the feast for another seven days. So they kept it for another seven days with gladness.<sup>24</sup>For Hezekiah king of Judah gave the assembly 1,000 bulls and 7,000 sheep for offerings, and the princes gave the assembly 1,000 bulls and 10,000 sheep. And the priests consecrated themselves in great numbers.<sup>25</sup>The whole assembly of Judah, and the priests and the Levites, and the whole assembly that came out of Israel, and the sojourners who came out of the land of Israel, and the sojourners who lived in Judah, rejoiced.<sup>26</sup>So there was great joy in Jerusalem, for since the time of Solomon the son of David king of Israel there had been nothing like this in Jerusalem.<sup>27</sup>Then the priests and the Levites arose and blessed the people, and their voice was heard, and their prayer came to his holy habitation in heaven.
30.overview:
Where we are. The temple is open, cleansed and back in service within a month of Hezekiah’s accession (chapter 29). But the Passover, the feast that told Israel who it was, fell due while the cleaning was still going on, and the northern tribes, broken by Assyria, have had no part in Jerusalem’s worship for two centuries.

The message. God’s door is open to everyone who will come home, because “the LORD your God is gracious and merciful” (v. 9). Hezekiah invites the whole of Israel; most of the north laughs, but some humble themselves and come. When many of them eat the feast unprepared, the king prays, and “the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people” (v. 20). The God who keeps his worship holy also pardons those who set their hearts to seek him, and where he pardons, joy overflows.

Why it was said. The first readers were a small community home from exile, unsure who truly belonged to Israel (see the introduction; compare Ezra 6:21). This chapter showed them that the door had always stood open to every Israelite and every foreigner who came to seek the LORD, and that God hears prayer for the humble who come imperfectly.

How the chapter makes its case. King and assembly agree to keep the Passover in the second month and proclaim it from Beersheba to Dan (vv. 1–5). The letter calls the survivors of the north to return to a God who will turn to them; most mock, some come, and God gives Judah one heart (vv. 6–12). The crowd clears the city of its altars, the clergy are shamed into readiness, and when many eat unclean, Hezekiah prays and God heals (vv. 13–20). The feast is doubled, and joy unknown since Solomon ends with a blessing heard in heaven (vv. 21–27).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by promise. The Passover itself pointed forward, for “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Hezekiah’s prayer for the unclean is a faint picture of a greater intercessor, who does not ask God to overlook our uncleanness but has borne it, and whom the Father always hears.
