And the mixed table of Judah, the north and the sojourners looks ahead to the gospel feast, where those who were far off are brought near and Jew and Gentile sit together (Ephesians 2:13–19), and the invitation still goes out: “Come, for everything is now ready” (Luke 14:17).

For us. Keep inviting people home, even when they laugh. Come to the Lord’s Table not because you feel fit but because your heart is set on seeking him and your intercessor is always heard. And expect joy where God gathers his scattered people.
30.theology:
Verses 18-20 are the chapter’s centre, where this book’s great promise (7:14) is kept. The people are in the wrong and the narrator says so. Hezekiah asks not for permission but for pardon, pleading that these people have set their hearts to seek God, and God answers with the two verbs of 7:14: he heard, and he healed. The standard was not lowered; the people were forgiven.

The letter of verses 6-9 shows what a summons to repentance sounds like when the one issuing it has no power to compel. Hezekiah cannot command a foreign kingdom. He describes God and asks them to come. Most of them mock, and nothing in the invitation is altered on that account.

And verse 27 answers Solomon's prayer at the dedication (6:21): the temple did what Solomon had prayed it would do.
30.examples:
This chapter is full of ordinary faithfulness. A courier read the king's letter in one market square after another, was jeered at, and went on to the next town. Men from Asher and Zebulun made the longest journey in the country from towns where the messenger had just been laughed at. Tens of thousands of pilgrims spent their first day in Jerusalem pulling down street altars.

And the leaders behaved well. The king went round the musicians and told the skilled ones they were doing well, and when his princes outgave him, the record prints both figures without embarrassment.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love for the whole people of God moves Hezekiah to invite everyone, and wisdom lets him move the date rather than lose the feast. He sends to all Israel and Judah, and writes to Ephraim and Manasseh, the heart of the broken northern kingdom, to come to Jerusalem for the Passover (v. 1). Because too few priests were ready and the people had not gathered, king and assembly agree to keep it in the second month, as the law allowed for people kept away by uncleanness or distance (vv. 2–4). A proclamation goes out from Beersheba to Dan, for the feast had long been neglected (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Hezekiah takes a provision of the law written for an individual and applies it to a nation, and verse 4 does not hide that this was a judgment call: the plan seemed right. The note below sets out why.
verseByVerse.examples: A reformation that is one month old has to work around its own unreadiness, and this one did. Churches and families starting again after a long neglect will rarely get everything right at once; better a Passover a month late than none at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Hezekiah sent to all Israel and Judah, and wrote letters also to Ephraim and Manasseh, that they should come to the house of the LORD at Jerusalem to keep the Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel. For the king and his princes and all the assembly in Jerusalem had taken counsel to keep the Passover in the second month— for they could not keep it at that time because the priests had not consecrated themselves in sufficient number, nor had the people assembled in Jerusalem— and the plan seemed right to the king and all the assembly. So they decreed to make a proclamation throughout all Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, that the people should come and keep the Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel, at Jerusalem, for they had not kept it as often as prescribed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah invited the whole of Israel, including the northern tribes who had lately made war on Judah, to keep the Passover, and moved it a month rather than lose the feast.

Wrote letters also to Ephraim and Manasseh. Take in who is being invited. Ephraim and Manasseh stand for the northern kingdom, and within living memory it had killed a hundred and twenty thousand men of Judah in a single day and marched two hundred thousand women and children up the road to Samaria, until a prophet sent them home (28:6–15). Hezekiah’s own generation buried those men, and he writes to the people who did it and invites them to the Passover meal. He had already provided their sin offering, commanding atonement for all Israel (29:24). Note the order: provision before invitation.

To keep the Passover in the second month. Passover falls on the fourteenth of the first month (see The Jewish calendar and months), and the cleansing of the temple ran from the first to the sixteenth (29:17), straight through the date. The two reasons in verse 3, too few priests ready and the people not gathered, are the very problem the last chapter ended with (29:34).

The plan seemed right. So they move it a month. The law allowed a second-month Passover for a man made unclean by a dead body or away on a long journey (Numbers 9:10–11). Hezekiah applies a provision made for one man in awkward circumstances to a nation in awkward circumstances, and the text does not pretend this was obvious: it seemed right. The alternative was to keep the calendar exactly and hold no Passover at all, letting a nation go another year without the meal that told it who it was. The date existed to serve the feast, and to keep the date while losing the feast would have missed the point of both.

From Beersheba to Dan. The usual phrase names Dan first, running north to south; the Chronicler reverses it, here and when David counts the people (1 Chronicles 21:2), measuring outward from Judah. Then a quiet admission: they had not kept it as often as prescribed.

Why does Kings not mention this Passover? Kings gives Hezekiah’s reform only a few verses (2 Kings 18:3–6) and spends its space on Assyria. The Chronicler, writing for a community rebuilding its worship, draws on other records and lingers where his readers needed to look. Leaving something out is not contradicting it.
verseByVerse.note: Ephraim and Manasseh, the two tribes descended from Joseph, often stand for the whole northern kingdom.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s call to return stays the same whether people welcome it or laugh at it. Couriers carry the king’s letter through the land: return to the LORD, and he will turn to you; do not be stiff-necked like your fathers; come to his sanctuary, for he is gracious and merciful and will not turn his face away (vv. 6–9). Most of the north laughs the messengers to scorn (v. 10), but some men of Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun humble themselves and come (v. 11), and in Judah the hand of God gives the people one heart to obey (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The letter is the promise of 7:14 put in an envelope and posted. Return, and he will turn again to you; the word runs three times in four verses. And the ground offered is not Judah's hospitality or Hezekiah's goodwill but God's own character.
verseByVerse.examples: Faithful invitations are often mocked, and the temptation is to rewrite them until nobody can laugh. Hezekiah did not. If you have spoken of Christ and been laughed at, you are in good company, and you do not know yet who in that town is quietly packing for the journey.

verseByVerse.quote: So couriers went throughout all Israel and Judah with letters from the king and his princes, as the king had commanded, saying, "O people of Israel, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, that he may turn again to the remnant of you who have escaped from the hand of the kings of Assyria. Do not be like your fathers and your brothers, who were faithless to the LORD God of their fathers, so that he made them a desolation, as you see. Do not now be stiff-necked as your fathers were, but yield yourselves to the LORD and come to his sanctuary, which he has consecrated forever, and serve the LORD your God, that his fierce anger may turn away from you. For if you return to the LORD, your brothers and your children will find compassion with their captors and return to this land. For the LORD your God is gracious and merciful and will not turn away his face from you, if you return to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter calls the survivors of the north to come back to the LORD, warns them not to repeat their fathers’ stubbornness, and promises that a gracious and merciful God will turn to those who return.

Return to the LORD, … that he may turn again. A king of Judah writes to a people who had lately made war on him, asking them to come home to God. The shape of the sentence is the shape of the gospel: return, that he may turn again, the same verb both ways. God does not have to be talked round; his turning toward them is his settled response to their turning toward him.

The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel. He calls the third patriarch Israel, not Jacob, the name these people still carry: it is their God he is speaking of, not a god who belongs only to Judah.

The remnant of you who have escaped. The word tells us where in history we stand. Assyria has already begun its deportations, and whole districts of the north are gone. The people reading this letter are survivors, and Hezekiah says so to their faces, without cruelty and without pretending it happened by accident.

Your fathers and your brothers. Not only fathers: some who caused this are still alive. As you see is the appeal Hezekiah made to his own priests (29:8); the evidence is standing in their own countryside.

Do not now be stiff-necked. The picture is an ox that will not turn when the rein is pulled. Yield yourselves is literally “give the hand”: the man who stops pulling against the rein.

Compassion with their captors. Then a promise almost unbearable to read for families with sons in Assyria: your brothers and your children will find compassion with their captors.

The LORD your God is gracious and merciful. The last verse of the letter does not argue. It describes God, in the words he used of himself to Moses on the mountain (Exodus 34:6). Hezekiah sends God’s own self-description to a hostile audience days’ walk away as the whole reason for making the journey. The call to return rests entirely on who God already is.

verseByVerse.quote: So the couriers went from city to city through the country of Ephraim and Manasseh, and as far as Zebulun, but they laughed them to scorn and mocked them. However, some men of Asher, of Manasseh, and of Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem. The hand of God was also on Judah to give them one heart to do what the king and the princes commanded by the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Most of the north mocked the invitation, but some humbled themselves and came, and God himself gave Judah one heart to obey.

From city to city. Picture the job. A man with a letter walks into a market square, reads out an invitation from the king of Judah to come and worship at Jerusalem, and is jeered at. Then he walks to the next town and does it again, all the way to Zebulun in the northern hills.

They laughed them to scorn and mocked them. The best invitation in the book, from a king who had already provided their sin offering, carrying God’s own description of his kindness, was received in most of the north as a joke, and the Chronicler does not tidy that away. Nor does anything change in response. Hezekiah does not recall the couriers, soften the terms or drop the bit about being stiff-necked. Those who carry the gospel’s invitation today should expect the same, and keep walking to the next town.

However, some men of Asher, of Manasseh, and of Zebulun. One word, and the chapter turns. Two of the three tribes named, Asher and Zebulun, lay in the far north. Those men had the longest walk and the loudest neighbours. They set out from towns where the messenger had just been laughed out of the square, so every one of them was known to be going, and known to be a fool for going.

Humbled themselves. The verb is the one this whole book is built on, the word of 7:14, used here of a handful of northerners with no temple, no priesthood and no record of obedience, who read a letter and did what it said.

The hand of God was also on Judah to give them one heart. Even the good response is credited elsewhere: the hand of God gave them one heart. It is the gift the prophets later promised, a new heart and God’s own Spirit within his people (Ezekiel 36:26–27). Where unity in worship appears, somebody should thank God for it rather than the committee.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — May the Good LORD Pardon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God pardons those who set their hearts to seek him, even when they come imperfectly. A very great assembly gathers and first clears Ahaz’s altars out of the city into the Kidron (vv. 13–14). The Passover lamb is killed, and the priests and Levites, ashamed at the people’s readiness, consecrate themselves and take their posts (vv. 15–16). Many, especially from the north, have not been cleansed and eat the Passover against the written rule; Hezekiah prays for them, and the LORD hears him and heals the people (vv. 17–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 19 puts this book's two great verbs in one clause: a man who sets his heart to seek God. Verse 20 answers with the two verbs of 7:14, heard and healed. The note on verses 17-20 follows both through.
verseByVerse.examples: Some readers will recognise themselves in the crowd who arrived late, unclean and half-taught. The way in was not to pretend they were ready but to come anyway, with someone praying for them. That is still the way in.

verseByVerse.quote: And many people came together in Jerusalem to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the second month, a very great assembly. They set to work and removed the altars that were in Jerusalem, and all the altars for burning incense they took away and threw into the brook Kidron. And they slaughtered the Passover lamb on the fourteenth day of the second month. And the priests and the Levites were ashamed, so that they consecrated themselves and brought burnt offerings into the house of the LORD. They took their accustomed posts according to the Law of Moses the man of God. The priests threw the blood that they received from the hand of the Levites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the lamb was killed, the crowd cleared the city of its idol altars, and the people’s eagerness shamed the priests and Levites into getting ready.

A very great assembly. The phrase was used of the crowd at Solomon’s dedication (7:8), and Solomon will be named before the chapter is out (v. 26). They come to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the week that followed the Passover meal. And the first thing this enormous, joyful crowd does is not sing.

They set to work and removed the altars. Ahaz’s altars in every corner of Jerusalem (28:24) were still standing; the temple had been scrubbed, the streets had not. So before the lamb is killed, the pilgrims pull down the altars of the last reign and carry them to the Kidron valley, where the temple’s filth had gone. Worship and demolition in the same week, in that order. It is no use holding a feast to God in a city that keeps the alternatives standing on every corner in case the feast does not work out.

The priests and the Levites were ashamed. Then a sentence about the clergy that must have stung to write. What shamed them was ordinary people, northerners who had walked for days, arriving ready when the men whose whole life was this building were not. In chapter 29 the Levites outpaced the priests (29:34); here the congregation outpaces them both. No rebuke, no royal order: shame did it. A man in ministry who has never felt that shame while watching someone else’s devotion is probably not paying attention.

They took their accustomed posts according to the Law of Moses. Everyone is at his post, with one irregularity: the Levites, not the heads of households, hand the blood to the priests, and verse 17 explains why.

verseByVerse.quote: For there were many in the assembly who had not consecrated themselves. Therefore the Levites had to slaughter the Passover lamb for everyone who was not clean, to consecrate it to the LORD. For a majority of the people, many of them from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, had not cleansed themselves, yet they ate the Passover otherwise than as prescribed. For Hezekiah had prayed for them, saying, "May the good LORD pardon everyone who sets his heart to seek God, the LORD, the God of his fathers, even though not according to the sanctuary's rules of cleanness." And the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many ate the Passover without being ceremonially clean, against the written rule, and when Hezekiah prayed for those whose hearts were set on seeking God, the LORD heard him and healed them.

Many in the assembly who had not consecrated themselves. Here is the problem the chapter has been walking toward: much of the crowd is not in a fit state to be there. Some almost certainly did not know how to be; they had grown up in a kingdom that had not kept this feast properly for two hundred years. So the Levites kill the lambs for them, which is not how Passover works.

Otherwise than as prescribed. This is the narrator’s own verdict. It was against the written rule, and nobody in the text pretends the rules had been suspended.

May the good LORD pardon. Into that situation comes a prayer, and it asks for pardon. Not permission, not an exemption, not a ruling that it was fine after all: he asks God to forgive people who are doing this wrongly, and what he pleads is the direction of their hearts.

Who sets his heart to seek God. The clause carries both of this book’s great verbs. Setting the heart to seek is what Rehoboam never did (12:14) and what ordinary northerners did in his day (11:16). Hezekiah asks God to look at the direction a man is facing.

The LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people. The two verbs of the promise this book was built on, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land (7:14), come back over a crowd of half-instructed northerners eating the wrong way.

He always hears his Son. There is a greater intercessor than Hezekiah, and he does not stand beside the table asking God to overlook the state of the people at it. He is the Lamb on it, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). His prayer for the unready, the half-taught and the ceremonially hopeless is not a request that the standard be waived, because he has met the standard himself and offers it on their behalf (Hebrews 7:25). The LORD heard Hezekiah. He always hears his Son.

A word against two errors. This can be misused both ways. It is no licence to be careless with what God commanded; the text calls the irregularity irregular. But neither is God’s house a place where the badly prepared are turned away at the door.

Coming to the Table unfit. Anyone who has come to the Lord’s Table feeling unfit should keep verse 20 close. These people were unfit, knew it, and came anyway, because they wanted God more than they wanted to be safe from criticism. A man prayed for them, and God pardoned them.

Why was this irregularity pardoned when Uzzah and Uzziah were struck down? Hezekiah prayed, and God saw hearts set on seeking him (v. 19); Uzzah and Uzziah acted in presumption, Uzziah in open pride (26:16). God judges defiance, and pardons the humble who come to him even imperfectly.

Uncertain wording. The text does not say what the people needed healing from. Some think of sickness that broke out, or was feared, among those who ate unclean, since the law warned that uncleanness brought into God’s presence could bring death (Leviticus 15:31). Others take it as the healing of 7:14, God restoring a people he has forgiven. The echo of 7:14 makes that at least part of the meaning.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Where God has pardoned, joy overflows. For seven days the people keep the feast with great gladness, while the Levites and priests sing with all their might and the king encourages them (vv. 21–22). Then by common consent they keep it seven days more, with king and princes giving thousands of animals, and the priests are at last ready in great numbers (vv. 23–24). Judah, the northerners and the resident foreigners rejoice together as no one had since Solomon, and the priests’ blessing reaches God’s holy dwelling in heaven (vv. 25–27).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 27 answers a prayer made at the dedication. Solomon had asked God to listen from heaven your dwelling place (6:21), and here the blessing of the priests reaches exactly that address.
verseByVerse.examples: Joy that people choose to extend is a good sign. Nobody had to be kept at this feast; they asked for more. Worship that leaves people wanting to stay longer is worth more than worship that is merely correct.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel who were present at Jerusalem kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days with great gladness, and the Levites and the priests praised the LORD day by day, singing with all their might to the LORD. And Hezekiah spoke encouragingly to all the Levites who showed good skill in the service of the LORD. So they ate the food of the festival for seven days, sacrificing peace offerings and giving thanks to the LORD, the God of their fathers. Then the whole assembly agreed together to keep the feast for another seven days. So they kept it for another seven days with gladness. For Hezekiah king of Judah gave the assembly 1,000 bulls and 7,000 sheep for offerings, and the princes gave the assembly 1,000 bulls and 10,000 sheep. And the priests consecrated themselves in great numbers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The feast ran for seven days of glad singing and then, by common consent and with generous gifts from king and princes, for seven days more, until even the priests were ready in great numbers.

Singing with all their might to the LORD. Not tastefully or professionally, but with everything they had, every day for a week, from men who days earlier had been too embarrassed to consecrate themselves.

Hezekiah spoke encouragingly to all the Levites who showed good skill. The Hebrew is warmer than the English: he spoke to their heart. In the middle of the largest gathering Jerusalem had seen in two and a half centuries, with a nation to govern and an Assyrian empire on his border, the king went round the musicians and told them they were doing it well. He did not merely thank them for turning up; he commended the ones who showed good skill. Somebody had practised, and the king noticed and said so. Anyone who leads anything should read that verse and then go and thank three people.

The whole assembly agreed together. Nobody ordered this. A crowd that had been mocked on the way, had arrived unclean and been prayed over, decided at the end of a week that they were not finished, and stayed. Solomon’s dedication ran seven days and seven days (7:8–9), and this is the first time since then that anybody has wanted two weeks.

The princes gave. Do the arithmetic and something quietly good appears. The king gave a thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep; the princes gave a thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep. His own officials outgave him, publicly, and the Chronicler writes down both figures without comment. A leader who has taught his people to give will one day be outgiven by them, and the healthiest response is Hezekiah’s: no jealousy, and no comment at all.

The priests consecrated themselves in great numbers. The last clause closes a wound. The shortage that pushed the Passover back a month is over, and it took two weeks of other people’s worship to fix it.

verseByVerse.quote: The whole assembly of Judah, and the priests and the Levites, and the whole assembly that came out of Israel, and the sojourners who came out of the land of Israel, and the sojourners who lived in Judah, rejoiced. So there was great joy in Jerusalem, for since the time of Solomon the son of David king of Israel there had been nothing like this in Jerusalem. Then the priests and the Levites arose and blessed the people, and their voice was heard, and their prayer came to his holy habitation in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah, the northerners and resident foreigners rejoiced together as Jerusalem had not since Solomon, and the priests’ blessing was heard in God’s holy dwelling in heaven.

And the sojourners. Read verse 25 as a guest list. Five groups: Judah; the clergy; the northerners who made the journey; and then, twice over, the sojourners, resident foreigners from the north and from Judah who had attached themselves to Israel’s God and were welcomed at that table by a provision as old as the first Passover (Exodus 12:48).

A mixed table. The meal that remembered a nation’s rescue from Egypt is eaten by Judeans, by Ephraimites who had been at war with them, and by foreigners. That is what the God of Israel does with a table when he is allowed to set it. The Chronicler’s first readers, a small community home from exile and arguing over who truly belonged to Israel (compare Ezra 6:21), needed this guest list: under Hezekiah the door had stood open to every northerner and every foreigner who came to seek the LORD.

Since the time of Solomon. The comparison with Solomon measures the joy. Josiah’s Passover will be measured differently: “No Passover like it had been kept in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet” (35:18). The two do not compete; one is about the gladness, the other about the keeping of the feast. Between them lies the reign of Manasseh, and the Chronicler knows it as he writes. The great joy of chapter 30 did not protect Judah from falling away later. It was still worth having.

Their prayer came to his holy habitation in heaven. Verse 27 answers a prayer made in the same courtyard some two and a half centuries earlier, when Solomon asked God to “listen from heaven your dwelling place, and when you hear, forgive” (6:21). He had no guarantee; he was asking God to hear prayer made at a building. Now, after the division, the Baals, the locked doors and the burning children, the priests lift their hands over a mixed and irregular crowd, and the sound goes to the place Solomon named.

The greater Son of David. The temple is gone now, and the arrangement it stood for was never the final one. But the prayers it carried have not stopped. A greater Son of David, Jesus, has gone into the holy dwelling itself, not with the blood of a thousand bulls but with his own (Hebrews 9:12, 24), and the prayers of people who come to him unclean, half-taught and late in the month still arrive, heard, pardoned and healed, in the heaven Solomon could only pray toward.

keyVerse.quote: For the LORD your God is gracious and merciful and will not turn away his face from you, if you return to him.
keyVerse.note: The whole invitation rests on this description of God, the words he used of himself to Moses (Exodus 34:6). Hezekiah does not argue the north into coming; he tells them who God is. The chapter then shows it true, as God hears prayer for the unready and heals them, the same welcome the gospel holds out to all who return.

30.reflection:
Hezekiah invited people who had recently made war on Judah, and provided their sin offering before he asked anything of them (29:24; 30:1). What does this show about God’s way with sinners? Who might you be slow to invite?

Most of the north laughed at the couriers, but some humbled themselves and came (vv. 10–11). How do you respond when the gospel invitation is mocked? What would it have cost those few to make the journey, and what might it cost people today?

Hezekiah prayed, “May the good LORD pardon everyone who sets his heart to seek God” (vv. 18–19). How does this passage help someone who feels unfit to come to the Lord’s Table, without making us careless about what God has commanded?

The people were so glad that they kept the feast another seven days, and Judeans, northerners and foreigners rejoiced together (vv. 23–26). What signs of that kind of joy and that kind of mixed table do you see in your church, and what gets in the way?

31.title: He Did What Was Good and Right and Faithful
31.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when all this was finished, all Israel who were present went out to the cities of Judah and broke in pieces the pillars and cut down the Asherim and broke down the high places and the altars throughout all Judah and Benjamin, and in Ephraim and Manasseh, until they had destroyed them all. Then all the people of Israel returned to their cities, every man to his possession.<sup>2</sup>And Hezekiah appointed the divisions of the priests and of the Levites, division by division, each according to his service, the priests and the Levites, for burnt offerings and peace offerings, to minister in the gates of the camp of the LORD and to give thanks and praise.<sup>3</sup>The contribution of the king from his own possessions was for the burnt offerings: the burnt offerings of morning and evening, and the burnt offerings for the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the appointed feasts, as it is written in the Law of the LORD.<sup>4</sup>And he commanded the people who lived in Jerusalem to give the portion due to the priests and the Levites, that they might give themselves to the Law of the LORD.<sup>5</sup>As soon as the command was spread abroad, the people of Israel gave in abundance the firstfruits of grain, wine, oil, honey, and of all the produce of the field. And they brought in abundantly the tithe of everything.<sup>6</sup>And the people of Israel and Judah who lived in the cities of Judah also brought in the tithe of cattle and sheep, and the tithe of the dedicated things that had been dedicated to the LORD their God, and laid them in heaps.<sup>7</sup>In the third month they began to pile up the heaps, and finished them in the seventh month.<sup>8</sup>When Hezekiah and the princes came and saw the heaps, they blessed the LORD and his people Israel.<sup>9</sup>And Hezekiah questioned the priests and the Levites about the heaps.<sup>10</sup>Azariah the chief priest, who was of the house of Zadok, answered him, "Since they began to bring the contributions into the house of the LORD, we have eaten and had enough and have plenty left, for the LORD has blessed his people, so that we have this large amount left."<sup>11</sup>Then Hezekiah commanded them to prepare chambers in the house of the LORD, and they prepared them.<sup>12</sup>And they faithfully brought in the contributions, the tithes, and the dedicated things. The chief officer in charge of them was Conaniah the Levite, with Shimei his brother as second,<sup>13</sup>while Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismachiah, Mahath, and Benaiah were overseers assisting Conaniah and Shimei his brother, by the appointment of Hezekiah the king and Azariah the chief officer of the house of God.<sup>14</sup>And Kore the son of Imnah the Levite, keeper of the east gate, was over the freewill offerings to God, to apportion the contribution reserved for the LORD and the most holy offerings.<sup>15</sup>Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah were faithfully assisting him in the cities of the priests, to distribute the portions to their brothers, old and young alike, by divisions,<sup>16</sup>except those enrolled by genealogy, males from three years old and upward—all who entered the house of the LORD as the duty of each day required—for their service according to their offices, by their divisions.<sup>17</sup>The enrollment of the priests was according to their fathers' houses; that of the Levites from twenty years old and upward was according to their offices, by their divisions.<sup>18</sup>They were enrolled with all their little children, their wives, their sons, and their daughters, the whole assembly, for they were faithful in keeping themselves holy.<sup>19</sup>And for the sons of Aaron, the priests, who were in the fields of common land belonging to their cities, there were men in the several cities who were designated by name to distribute portions to every male among the priests and to everyone among the Levites who was enrolled.<sup>20</sup>Thus Hezekiah did throughout all Judah, and he did what was good and right and faithful before the LORD his God.<sup>21</sup>And every work that he undertook in the service of the house of God and in accordance with the law and the commandments, seeking his God, he did with all his heart, and prospered.
31.overview:
Where we are. The great Passover is over (chapter 30), and the joy of the last two chapters now has to become ordinary life. The pilgrims go home, and the question is whether the revival will last beyond the feast.

The message. Grace received changes what people do when they go home. Joy at God’s table pulls down the idols in the villages and fills God’s storehouses, and the reformation is completed not by singing but by faithful people keeping careful accounts, so that every servant of God is fed. The surplus is the LORD’s blessing on his people, their generosity is the overflow, and the king who led it all did it “with all his heart” (v. 21).

Why it was said. The first readers had to keep a temple going on their own gifts, and they knew what happened when the tithes failed: the Levites drifted back to their fields (Nehemiah 13:10–12; see the introduction). This chapter showed them what faithful giving and faithful administration look like, and that both flow from gladness in God.

How the chapter makes its case. The pilgrims destroy the shrines on the way home, north as well as south (v. 1). Hezekiah restores the priestly divisions, funds the regular offerings from his own estate and asks Jerusalem to support the clergy so that they can give themselves to the law (vv. 2–4). The people bring firstfruits and tithes in heaps for five months; king and princes bless the LORD and his people, Azariah reports plenty left over, and storerooms are prepared (vv. 5–11). Named men faithfully receive and distribute the gifts, down to the smallest child of every enrolled priest and Levite (vv. 12–19). Then the verdict: good, right and faithful, done with all his heart (vv. 20–21).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by the need it exposes. “With all his heart” is high praise, yet the next chapter shows that even Hezekiah could not keep a whole heart to the end (32:25). Only one Son of David loved God with all his heart all his life, and he gives that obedience to the half-hearted who trust him. The chapter’s generosity points the same way. Christian giving grows from the grace of the one who, “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

For us. Measure renewal by what happens after the meeting: idols taken down at home, giving that lasts through the long months, and someone counting sacks faithfully so that the smallest are fed. And rest your worth not on being remarkable but on Christ’s wholehearted obedience for you.
31.theology:
Verse 1 records the first complete clearance in the book of the high places (the local hilltop shrines), done not by a stronger decree but by the congregation itself on the way home from worship.

Verses 3-4 set the order of leadership: the king gives first, and the stated purpose of the clergy's portion is that they may give themselves to the law of God. Provision exists for the sake of teaching.

And the word this chapter keeps using of men handling other people's goods is faithful. Where the subject is money and food given to God, Scripture asks for reliability rather than brilliance, and it puts the king and the storekeepers under the same adjective.

Verse 21 gives Hezekiah the whole heart that Amaziah was denied (25:2), and 32:25 will report that same heart grown proud. Whole-hearted love for God is not a target a good king can reach and hold; it waited for a better Son of David.
31.examples:
Most of this chapter is about what happens after a great day of worship: farmers going home and bringing in the first of each crop for half a year, storerooms built because nobody had expected so much, and nineteen men named for receiving sacks and handing out portions.

It is a picture of ordinary church life done well. The feast is remembered, but the faithfulness that follows it, month after month, is what feeds people. Even a Levite's small child in an outlying town was on the roll, with men named to see that his portion reached him. Nobody in God's household is too small or too far away to be remembered.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Every Man to His Possession
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joy at God’s table goes home with the worshippers and becomes faithfulness in ordinary life. Fresh from the Passover, the people break down pillars, Asherim, high places and altars through Judah and Benjamin and on into Ephraim and Manasseh, and then go back to their own land (v. 1). Hezekiah restores the divisions of priests and Levites for sacrifice, thanks and praise (v. 2), pays for the regular burnt offerings of the whole calendar from his own possessions (v. 3), and commands the people of Jerusalem to give the clergy their portion, so that they can devote themselves to the Law of the LORD (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The high places have stood through every reform in this book; Asa and Jehoshaphat both pulled some down and the record still says they remained (15:17; 20:33). Here at last they are destroyed, all of them. It took the joy of the Passover in chapter 30 to do what earlier reforms could not.
verseByVerse.examples: Leaders who ask others to give should give first, as Hezekiah did, out of their own pocket and before the appeal goes out. And churches that support their ministers do it for a purpose: so that those who teach have the time to study and pray, not so that they may live comfortably.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when all this was finished, all Israel who were present went out to the cities of Judah and broke in pieces the pillars and cut down the Asherim and broke down the high places and the altars throughout all Judah and Benjamin, and in Ephraim and Manasseh, until they had destroyed them all. Then all the people of Israel returned to their cities, every man to his possession. And Hezekiah appointed the divisions of the priests and of the Levites, division by division, each according to his service, the priests and the Levites, for burnt offerings and peace offerings, to minister in the gates of the camp of the LORD and to give thanks and praise. The contribution of the king from his own possessions was for the burnt offerings: the burnt offerings of morning and evening, and the burnt offerings for the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the appointed feasts, as it is written in the Law of the LORD. And he commanded the people who lived in Jerusalem to give the portion due to the priests and the Levites, that they might give themselves to the Law of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The joy of the Passover went home with the people and swept away the shrines in their own villages, while Hezekiah put the temple’s worship on a lasting footing, paying for its offerings himself and asking the city to support the priests and Levites.

All Israel who were present. Not the king’s officers but the men who had just spent two weeks at the Passover dismantled the shrines in their own villages on the way home, and some kept going into Ephraim and Manasseh, which were not Hezekiah’s to govern.

Until they had destroyed them all. Royal decrees had kept failing at exactly this point, because a shrine on a hill outside a village is protected by the village. Asa and Jehoshaphat had both left high places standing (15:17; 20:33). What finally brought them down was not a stronger law but two weeks of joy. Men who had eaten the Passover, been prayed over and gone home glad had no further use for rival shrines. Grace received did what commands imposed had never done.

Every man to his possession. The feast ended, and thousands of ordinary people went back to the farm, carrying what had happened to them into an ordinary year. The rest of the chapter is the least glamorous material in these three chapters: the singing had happened, and somebody now had to make sure there would be a lamb on the altar the next morning, and a Levite fed in a country town a year from now.

Division by division. Hezekiah restores the divisions, so that priests and Levites each serve in their turn, for offerings and for thanks and praise. The text calls the temple the camp of the LORD, the language of Israel’s wilderness camp, used of a stone building two and a half centuries old. Israel’s God is still travelling with his people.

From his own possessions. Two verses in an order that matters. He pays first, from his own estate, for the whole calendar of offerings, morning and evening, Sabbaths, new moons and feasts. Then he asks the city to support the ministry.

That they might give themselves to the Law of the LORD. The reason for the clergy’s portion belongs in front of any church that sets a budget. Not that the priests had earned a standard of living, but that a man scratching for food cannot give himself to the Scriptures, and a people who will not feed their teachers have decided to be taught by men with no time to study (compare 1 Timothy 5:17–18).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — They Laid Them in Heaps
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God’s people are glad in him, they give more than enough. As soon as the command goes out, the people bring the firstfruits of grain, wine, oil and honey and the tithe of everything, piling them in heaps from the third month to the seventh (vv. 5–7). Hezekiah and the princes see the heaps and bless both the LORD and his people (v. 8). Asked about them, Azariah the chief priest reports that the priests have eaten their fill and much is left, because the LORD has blessed his people, so the king has storerooms prepared in the temple (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology: Azariah's sentence puts the credit in the right place twice over. The priests have more than they can eat, and the reason he gives is not that the priesthood is well managed or that the appeal was well run. The LORD has blessed his people. The surplus in the clergy's store is evidence of what God did in the farmers' fields.
verseByVerse.examples: Generosity here was not one spectacular collection but a whole agricultural year, harvest by harvest. Regular, unremarkable giving, from the first of what comes in rather than from what is left over, is still the kind that sustains a church. Nobody's single gift built those heaps; thousands of small ones did, and every one of them was seen.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as the command was spread abroad, the people of Israel gave in abundance the firstfruits of grain, wine, oil, honey, and of all the produce of the field. And they brought in abundantly the tithe of everything. And the people of Israel and Judah who lived in the cities of Judah also brought in the tithe of cattle and sheep, and the tithe of the dedicated things that had been dedicated to the LORD their God, and laid them in heaps. In the third month they began to pile up the heaps, and finished them in the seventh month. When Hezekiah and the princes came and saw the heaps, they blessed the LORD and his people Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people responded at once with firstfruits and tithes, piled in heaps through five months of harvest, and the king blessed both the LORD who gave the harvest and the people who brought it.

As soon as the command was spread abroad. No gap between command and response, and no campaign. Honey is on the list of firstfruits, a small surprise, because honey was never burned on the altar (Leviticus 2:11–12). It could still be given; whatever a man’s ground produced, he brought the first of it.

In the third month they began to pile up the heaps. The heaps took five months to build, from the third month, when the grain comes in, to the seventh, when the fruit and the oil are gathered: a farmer bringing the first of the wheat in early summer and the first of the olives in autumn, and the piles in the temple courts growing all summer while everyone walked past them. That is what sustained giving looks like. The Passover took two weeks; this took half a year, and the second is the harder test.

They blessed the LORD and his people Israel. The king blessed both: God for it, which is right, and then the people who carried it in, which leaders forget. The generosity was genuinely theirs, and he said so.

Does the tithe bind Christians today? Israel’s tithes supported the Levites and the worship of a nation under God’s law, and they belonged to that order. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and it calls churches to support those who teach them (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14). Many believers find a tenth a good place to start; it is not a ceiling, and it is not a debt.

Uncertain wording. “The tithe of the dedicated things” is an unusual phrase, since dedicated things were normally given whole, not tithed. It may mean a tenth of certain holy gifts, or simply the dedicated gifts brought in alongside the tithes.

verseByVerse.quote: And Hezekiah questioned the priests and the Levites about the heaps. Azariah the chief priest, who was of the house of Zadok, answered him, "Since they began to bring the contributions into the house of the LORD, we have eaten and had enough and have plenty left, for the LORD has blessed his people, so that we have this large amount left." Then Hezekiah commanded them to prepare chambers in the house of the LORD, and they prepared them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priest reported that the priests had plenty and much to spare, because the LORD had blessed his people, so the king had storerooms prepared for the surplus.

Hezekiah questioned the priests and the Levites about the heaps. The king asks the men responsible about a great deal of other people’s grain. That is not suspicion but care; somebody in authority should always be asking about the heaps.

We have eaten and had enough. Azariah the chief priest answers with two things. The first is contentment. The clergy are fed. He does not angle for more or explain what the priesthood could achieve with further resources. There was enough, and he said so.

For the LORD has blessed his people. The second is where he puts the credit: not the appeal, not even the people’s generosity, but the LORD. The surplus in the storeroom is evidence of what God had been doing all summer in other men’s fields.

Prepare chambers in the house of the LORD. The storerooms are built after the giving, not before it, once it was plain the giving would continue.

A problem of abundance. This is the third time in three chapters that Hezekiah’s problem has been abundance: too many offerings for the priests to flay (29:34), a feast extended by popular demand and paid for twice over (30:23–24), and now more grain than there is roof to keep it under. Revival brings practical problems of its own, and pleasant ones.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gifts given to God must be handled faithfully, so that every one of his servants is cared for. The contributions are brought in faithfully and put in the charge of Conaniah and his brother Shimei, with ten overseers appointed by the king and the chief priest (vv. 12–13). Kore, keeper of the east gate, oversees the freewill offerings, with six assistants in the priests’ towns who distribute the portions to old and young by their divisions (vv. 14–15). Careful rolls by family and office reach the wives and little children, and named men in the outlying towns make sure no priest or Levite is forgotten (vv. 16–19).
verseByVerse.theology: One word runs through this chapter about stores and lists: faithful. They faithfully brought in (v. 12); they were faithfully assisting (v. 15); they were faithful in keeping themselves holy (v. 18); and the king did what was good and right and faithful (v. 20).
verseByVerse.examples: If your work for the church is counting, storing, driving or delivering, this list is for you. Not one of these men preaches or sings in this chapter, and the Chronicler wrote down all nineteen names.

verseByVerse.quote: And they faithfully brought in the contributions, the tithes, and the dedicated things. The chief officer in charge of them was Conaniah the Levite, with Shimei his brother as second, while Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismachiah, Mahath, and Benaiah were overseers assisting Conaniah and Shimei his brother, by the appointment of Hezekiah the king and Azariah the chief officer of the house of God. And Kore the son of Imnah the Levite, keeper of the east gate, was over the freewill offerings to God, to apportion the contribution reserved for the LORD and the most holy offerings. Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah were faithfully assisting him in the cities of the priests, to distribute the portions to their brothers, old and young alike, by divisions, except those enrolled by genealogy, males from three years old and upward—all who entered the house of the LORD as the duty of each day required—for their service according to their offices, by their divisions. The enrollment of the priests was according to their fathers' houses; that of the Levites from twenty years old and upward was according to their offices, by their divisions. They were enrolled with all their little children, their wives, their sons, and their daughters, the whole assembly, for they were faithful in keeping themselves holy. And for the sons of Aaron, the priests, who were in the fields of common land belonging to their cities, there were men in the several cities who were designated by name to distribute portions to every male among the priests and to everyone among the Levites who was enrolled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Named men were put in charge of receiving and distributing the gifts, and they did it faithfully, keeping rolls so careful that every priest and Levite, down to the smallest child in a distant town, received a portion.

Conaniah the Levite. What follows is a deliberate list: nineteen men, named, with their exact responsibilities: two in charge, ten overseers, a gatekeeper over the freewill gifts and six more out in the priests’ towns. They receive sacks, record them, store them and hand them out, and the record of God’s dealings with Judah has their names in it permanently.

They faithfully brought in the contributions. One word keeps coming back, faithfully (vv. 12, 15, 18), and the subject throughout is other people’s food and money. Where goods belong to somebody else and are given to God, the virtue asked for is not brilliance or vision but faithfulness: the plain quality of a man who writes down what came in and hands out what was meant to go out, whether or not anybody checks. In the believer it is the Spirit’s fruit (Galatians 5:22), grown in people the faithful God has already made his own.

With all their little children. Somewhere in a country town was a Levite’s small son who could barely talk, and the national distribution system had him on a list (v. 18), with men designated by name in the outlying towns so that nobody far from Jerusalem was forgotten (v. 19). A revival is measured by more than its singing. This one can be measured by whether a small child in a village a long walk away had food that winter, and the answer is that nineteen men had been given his name.

The tyranny of the extraordinary. Ours is an age that wants every life to be remarkable: change the world, find your passion, leave a legacy. It sounds generous, but it lays a heavy weight on ordinary people, because most lives, including most good ones, will consist of something very like counting sacks. If significance has to be achieved, the storekeeper’s life is a failure, and so, quietly, is yours. The Chronicler simply ignores the idea, spends more ink on Conaniah and Shimei than on some kings, and the word he keeps attaching to them is faithfully, not brilliantly. The gospel goes further. In Christ a person’s worth is not earned by being remarkable; it is conferred. He is known by name and bought at a price (1 Corinthians 6:20). The Son of God himself spent some thirty years in a small town doing work nobody wrote down. A life that has received that kind of worth is free to be ordinary, and to do the next unnoticed thing well.

Uncertain wording. Verse 16 is compressed and hard to follow. The word rendered “except” may mean “besides” or “in addition to”, and it is not clear how the males “from three years old and upward” relate to those serving “as the duty of each day required”. Some suspect that “three” is a copying slip for “thirty”, the age at which Levites began certain service in Numbers 4:3. What verse 18 makes clear either way is that whole families, little children included, were enrolled and provided for.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The reformation is summed up in one verdict on the heart. What Hezekiah did throughout Judah was good and right and faithful before the LORD his God (v. 20). Every work he undertook, in the service of God’s house and in keeping the law, he did seeking his God and with all his heart, and he prospered (v. 21). It is praise given to very few kings in this book, and the next chapter shows how hard it was, even for Hezekiah, to keep a whole heart to the end.
verseByVerse.theology: Three chapters of reformation are summed up in two verses, and the summary is about the heart and not the results. He sought God; he did it with all his heart; and he prospered, as was once said of Uzziah (26:5), and is here said of a better man.
verseByVerse.examples: God records the good in a life honestly even when he knows what comes next. The failure of the next chapter does not erase this verdict, and a believer's later stumbles do not erase the real work God did in earlier years.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Hezekiah did throughout all Judah, and he did what was good and right and faithful before the LORD his God. And every work that he undertook in the service of the house of God and in accordance with the law and the commandments, seeking his God, he did with all his heart, and prospered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah’s whole reformation is summed up as good, right and faithful, done seeking God and with all his heart, a verdict that points beyond him to the one King who kept it to the end.

Good and right and faithful. Three words for one reign. Good: it did people real good. Right: it matched what God had commanded. Faithful: the word given to the storekeepers in verses 12–18. The king is commended in the language of the men counting sacks.

Every work that he undertook. Not just the highlights: the hinges, the sixteen days of carrying filth, the letters that were laughed at, the storerooms, the lists of small children. All of it, and all of it done seeking his God.

With all his heart. This book gives that phrase to very few kings. Amaziah did what was right yet not with a whole heart (25:2). Joash did right while his mentor lived, and Uzziah sought God while his teacher lived (24:2; 26:5). Asa’s heart was called wholly true, and he still jailed a prophet (15:17; 16:10). Jehoshaphat was remembered as one who sought the LORD with all his heart (22:9), and he too made his compromises. Here the phrase sums up a whole reformation.

Not the end of his story. The next chapter says that his heart was proud and he did not make return for the benefit done to him (32:25). The later verdict does not cancel this one, but even the best of these kings could not keep a whole heart to the end.

Why the phrase matters. Loving God with all the heart is not a high standard that a determined king can just about reach; it is the first and great commandment (Deuteronomy 6:5; Matthew 22:37–38), and the whole record of Judah is the record of people who could not keep it for a lifetime. Then a Son of David came who did every work he undertook seeking his God, with all his heart, from the carpenter’s shop to the cross, and no “yet” ever had to be added to the verdict on him. He kept the commandment whole, and he gives that obedience to the half-hearted, the lately converted and the badly prepared, so that people who have never managed a single wholehearted day are counted righteous in him (2 Corinthians 5:21).

keyVerse.quote: And every work that he undertook in the service of the house of God and in accordance with the law and the commandments, seeking his God, he did with all his heart, and prospered.
keyVerse.note: This verse sums up three chapters of reformation, and its measure is the heart, not the size of the achievements. It is praise given to very few kings, and even Hezekiah did not keep it to the end (32:25). It sends us to the one Son of David who did every work with all his heart, and whose obedience is counted to those who trust him.

31.reflection:
The shrines came down when the people went home glad from the Passover, not when a stronger law was passed (v. 1). Why does grace received often change what commands alone cannot? What “shrines” in ordinary life does joy in Christ loosen?

Hezekiah gave first from his own possessions, and the people gave for five months (vv. 3–7). What does this chapter teach about leadership in giving, and about generosity that lasts beyond a single moment of enthusiasm?

The Chronicler names nineteen men whose work was to receive, record and distribute food faithfully (vv. 12–19). Who does this kind of unseen work in your church? How does the gospel free us from needing to be remarkable?

Hezekiah did everything “with all his heart” (v. 21), yet the next chapter records his pride. How does that encourage us to look past even the best human leaders to Christ? What does it mean that his wholehearted obedience is counted to us?

32.title: He Will Not Come into This City
32.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things and these acts of faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came and invaded Judah and encamped against the fortified cities, thinking to win them for himself.<sup>2</sup>And when Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come and intended to fight against Jerusalem,<sup>3</sup>he planned with his officers and his mighty men to stop the water of the springs that were outside the city; and they helped him.<sup>4</sup>A great many people were gathered, and they stopped all the springs and the brook that flowed through the land, saying, "Why should the kings of Assyria come and find much water?"<sup>5</sup>He set to work resolutely and built up all the wall that was broken down and raised towers upon it, and outside it he built another wall, and he strengthened the Millo in the city of David. He also made weapons and shields in abundance.<sup>6</sup>And he set combat commanders over the people and gathered them together to him in the square at the gate of the city and spoke encouragingly to them, saying,<sup>7</sup>"Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or dismayed before the king of Assyria and all the horde that is with him, for there are more with us than with him.<sup>8</sup>With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God, to help us and to fight our battles." And the people took confidence from the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.<sup>9</sup>After this, Sennacherib king of Assyria, who was besieging Lachish with all his forces, sent his servants to Jerusalem to Hezekiah king of Judah and to all the people of Judah who were in Jerusalem, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Thus says Sennacherib king of Assyria, 'On what are you trusting, that you endure the siege in Jerusalem?<sup>11</sup>Is not Hezekiah misleading you, that he may give you over to die by famine and by thirst, when he tells you, "The LORD our God will deliver us from the hand of the king of Assyria"?<sup>12</sup>Has not this same Hezekiah taken away his high places and his altars and commanded Judah and Jerusalem, "Before one altar you shall worship, and on it you shall burn your sacrifices"?<sup>13</sup>Do you not know what I and my fathers have done to all the peoples of other lands? Were the gods of the nations of those lands at all able to deliver their lands out of my hand?<sup>14</sup>Who among all the gods of those nations that my fathers devoted to destruction was able to deliver his people from my hand, that your God should be able to deliver you from my hand?<sup>15</sup>Now, therefore, do not let Hezekiah deceive you or mislead you in this fashion, and do not believe him, for no god of any nation or kingdom has been able to deliver his people from my hand or from the hand of my fathers. How much less will your God deliver you out of my hand!'"<sup>16</sup>And his servants said still more against the LORD God and against his servant Hezekiah.<sup>17</sup>And he wrote letters to cast contempt on the LORD, the God of Israel, and to speak against him, saying, "Like the gods of the nations of the lands who have not delivered their people from my hands, so the God of Hezekiah will not deliver his people from my hand."<sup>18</sup>And they shouted it with a loud voice in the language of Judah to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall, to frighten and terrify them, in order that they might take the city.<sup>19</sup>And they spoke of the God of Jerusalem as they spoke of the gods of the peoples of the earth, which are the work of men's hands.<sup>20</sup>Then Hezekiah the king and Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, prayed because of this and cried to heaven.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD sent an angel, who cut off all the mighty warriors and commanders and officers in the camp of the king of Assyria. So he returned with shame of face to his own land. And when he came into the house of his god, some of his own sons struck him down there with the sword.<sup>22</sup>So the LORD saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem from the hand of Sennacherib king of Assyria and from the hand of all his enemies, and he provided for them on every side.<sup>23</sup>And many brought gifts to the LORD to Jerusalem and precious things to Hezekiah king of Judah, so that he was exalted in the sight of all nations from that time onward.<sup>24</sup>In those days Hezekiah became sick and was at the point of death, and he prayed to the LORD, and he answered him and gave him a sign.<sup>25</sup>But Hezekiah did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud. Therefore wrath came upon him and Judah and Jerusalem.<sup>26</sup>But Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the LORD did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah.<sup>27</sup>And Hezekiah had very great riches and honor, and he made for himself treasuries for silver, for gold, for precious stones, for spices, for shields, and for all kinds of costly vessels;<sup>28</sup>storehouses also for the yield of grain, wine, and oil; and stalls for all kinds of cattle, and sheepfolds.<sup>29</sup>He likewise provided cities for himself, and flocks and herds in abundance, for God had given him very great possessions.<sup>30</sup>This same Hezekiah closed the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon and directed them down to the west side of the city of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all his works.<sup>31</sup>And so in the matter of the envoys of the princes of Babylon, who had been sent to him to inquire about the sign that had been done in the land, God left him to himself, in order to test him and to know all that was in his heart.<sup>32</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Hezekiah and his good deeds, behold, they are written in the vision of Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.<sup>33</sup>And Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the upper part of the tombs of the sons of David, and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem did him honor at his death. And Manasseh his son reigned in his place.
32.overview:
Where we are. Hezekiah has reopened the temple, held the great Passover and set its worship on a lasting footing, “with all his heart” (31:21). Now, “after these things and these acts of faithfulness” (v. 1), Sennacherib of Assyria, the greatest power on earth, invades Judah (701 BC). This is the last chapter of Hezekiah’s reign.

The message. Faithfulness does not buy freedom from trouble, but it is never forsaken in it. When an empire mocks the living God as one more idol, the LORD answers prayer and saves his city without a battle. Yet the greater danger comes after the deliverance: the answered prayer that breeds pride, and the test that shows what is in the heart. The God who is “with us” (v. 8) is also the God who searches us.

Why it was said. The first readers lived under a foreign empire whose power seemed final, and they were the descendants of those carried off to Babylon (see the introduction). This chapter showed them that no empire is stronger than the God of Jerusalem, and warned them that their ruin had begun not only with enemies outside but with a proud heart showing its treasures to Babylon.

How the chapter makes its case. Hezekiah stops the springs, rebuilds the walls and arms the city, then tells the people, “with us is the LORD our God” (vv. 1–8). Sennacherib’s envoys, letters and shouted Hebrew argue that no god has ever stopped Assyria, treating the God of Jerusalem as a thing made by human hands (vv. 9–19). Hezekiah and Isaiah cry to heaven, one angel cuts down the Assyrian army, and Sennacherib dies by his own sons in his god’s house (vv. 20–23). Healed, Hezekiah grows proud, then humbles himself, and the wrath is deferred (vv. 24–26). His wealth, his tunnel and the envoys from Babylon, when “God left him to himself”, close his story (vv. 27–33).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. A son of David stands before mocking enemies with nothing but prayer, and God saves his city: a pattern of the greater victory at the cross, where Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities” (Colossians 2:15). But Hezekiah’s pride shows that even the best king is not the King. Jesus was mocked as Hezekiah’s God was mocked, “He trusts in God; let God deliver him now” (Matthew 27:43), and he was forsaken, so that those who trust him never will be (Hebrews 13:5).

For us. Do not take trouble as proof that faithfulness was wasted; work hard, and lean your weight on God’s word. Be most watchful after answered prayer. And when God seems to stand back, remember the one who was forsaken so that you will never be.
32.theology:
Verse 1 sets aside the book’s usual rule in its opening clause: the invasion follows faithfulness. Trouble is not always God’s verdict.

Verses 3-8 hold faith and work together without strain. He blocks every spring for miles and builds a second wall, and preaches that the battle belongs to God. Faith settles who the outcome belongs to; it does not settle whether to pick up a shovel.

Verse 19 names the enemy's actual error. Sennacherib's evidence was real and his reasoning was sound; he had simply counted the living God as one more idol, the work of men's hands. An argument that starts from a wrong idea of who God is cannot be saved by being well made.

And verse 31 says God withdrew on purpose. The test did not inform God; it showed the man his own heart. It was set for a king who did every work with all his heart, and even in him it found pride.
32.examples:
Hezekiah's year of crisis shows a man of faith at his best and at his most ordinary. Between the promise and the invasion he blocked the springs and built a second wall; at the gate he preached sentences God had already said to others in worse positions; and when the answer came, two men's prayer is recorded in a handful of words and the next sentence is the angel.

Then came the danger nobody expects. Pride did not get into Hezekiah through a failure. It came in through an answered prayer, and it is worth watching for in the weeks after God has been kind. The cure is the one Hezekiah found in verse 26: to go down again, before the God who gave the gift.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — With Us Is the LORD Our God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faithfulness does not exempt God’s people from trouble, but it shapes how they meet it. After all Hezekiah’s acts of faithfulness, Sennacherib invades Judah and besieges its fortified cities (v. 1). Hezekiah plans with his officers, stops the springs outside Jerusalem so that the Assyrians will find no water, rebuilds the broken wall, adds towers and an outer wall, strengthens the Millo and makes weapons in abundance (vv. 2–5). Then he gathers the people at the city gate and speaks to their hearts: be strong, for there are more with us than with him; he has an arm of flesh, but we have the LORD our God (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 1 is the most important clause in the chapter for anyone in trouble. The invasion came after the doors, the Passover, the heaps and the whole-hearted seeking of 31:21. This book normally shows a nation prospering when it obeys, and here its opening line signals that the pattern does not apply. What is happening to Hezekiah is not a verdict on Hezekiah.
verseByVerse.examples: If you are praying about a hard situation, you may still need to make the phone call, fill in the form, or see the doctor. Hezekiah trusted God and blocked the springs in the same week, and the Chronicler admires both. Prayer and planning are not rivals.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things and these acts of faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came and invaded Judah and encamped against the fortified cities, thinking to win them for himself. And when Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come and intended to fight against Jerusalem, he planned with his officers and his mighty men to stop the water of the springs that were outside the city; and they helped him. A great many people were gathered, and they stopped all the springs and the brook that flowed through the land, saying, "Why should the kings of Assyria come and find much water?" He set to work resolutely and built up all the wall that was broken down and raised towers upon it, and outside it he built another wall, and he strengthened the Millo in the city of David. He also made weapons and shields in abundance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straight after Hezekiah’s faithful reforms the Assyrian army invaded, and he met it with a faith that worked hard: cutting off the enemy’s water, rebuilding the walls and arming the city.

After these things and these acts of faithfulness. This clause does something the book almost never does. Chronicles ties a nation’s fortunes to its obedience more directly than most books: Abijah relied on the LORD and won (13:18), Asa leaned on Syria and got wars (16:9). Here the historian writes these acts of faithfulness, and the next thing in the sentence is the largest army on earth coming over the border.

What obedience does not buy. Obedience is the life of people God has already made his own, not a fee for protection. There are chapters in a faithful life that follow faithfulness and are still terrible, and the book that most insists sin brings trouble is the one that says so. The most faithful life ever lived ended on a cross.

He planned with his officers and his mighty men. Watch what a man of faith does with the warning he has. He holds a council, denies the enemy his water, rebuilds the broken wall, adds towers and a second wall, and turns out weapons and shields in quantity.

He set to work resolutely. Underneath is the verb for strengthening oneself, the resolve this book calls courage in Jehoiada (23:1) and in Amaziah before Edom (25:11): a man bracing himself and getting on with it.

Faith and planning together. He believes God will fight for Jerusalem, and he blocks the springs. Faith is not the decision to leave the shovel in the shed. It is the decision about who the outcome belongs to, and it leaves a man free to work hard at everything in front of him.

What Kings adds. For honesty’s sake: Kings records that Hezekiah sent to Sennacherib at Lachish, I have done wrong; withdraw from me, and paid three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold, stripping the gold from the temple doors he himself had overlaid (2 Kings 18:14–16; see Talent). It bought nothing; the envoys came anyway, and the speech of verse 8 is the more remarkable from a man who had tried to buy his way out.

Uncertain wording. What the Millo was is not known. The name probably means “filling”, and it was an old structure in the city of David (2 Samuel 5:9; 1 Kings 9:15), perhaps a filled, terraced embankment on the steep eastern slope. Either way it was part of the defences.

verseByVerse.quote: And he set combat commanders over the people and gathered them together to him in the square at the gate of the city and spoke encouragingly to them, saying, "Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or dismayed before the king of Assyria and all the horde that is with him, for there are more with us than with him. With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God, to help us and to fight our battles." And the people took confidence from the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah strengthened the people with words God had already spoken: Assyria had only human strength, but Judah had the LORD to fight for it, and the people leaned their weight on that.

Spoke encouragingly to them. Literally, he spoke to their heart, as he had to the temple musicians (30:22): to the choir in a good week and the militia in a bad one. The speech is almost entirely made of other people’s words.

Be strong and courageous. This is what Moses said to Israel and to Joshua, and David to Solomon (Deuteronomy 31:6–7; 1 Chronicles 22:13). Hezekiah is not improvising courage. He is handing on sentences God had already spoken to men in worse positions than his.

There are more with us than with him. This is what Elisha said to a terrified servant at Dothan: “those who are with us are more than those who are with them” (2 Kings 6:16). The king tells a crowd that can see the smoke of a burning countryside that they are, at this moment, the larger force.

With him is an arm of flesh. Not a weak arm: Assyria was the most efficient war machine the world had yet seen, and it had swallowed the northern kingdom. He does not call Sennacherib overrated; he tells them what Sennacherib is made of: flesh, mortal strength and nothing more (compare Jeremiah 17:5–7).

But with us is the LORD our God. Hanani had said the same to Asa, and Asa put him in the stocks for it: you leaned on the king of Syria and not on the LORD your God, and the eyes of the LORD run to and fro through the whole earth to give strong support to those whose heart is wholly his (16:7–10). Hezekiah has learned what Asa refused to learn, and he preaches it at the gate.

With us. The Hebrew for “with us” is the word in the name Isaiah had given Hezekiah’s father Ahaz as a sign: Immanuel, “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14). Ahaz refused the sign; his son preaches its meaning. It was fulfilled when the Son of God was born and given that name (Matthew 1:23), and his last promise to his people was “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

The people took confidence. The verb is the one for leaning your weight on something. A frightened city put its weight on a speech, and the speech held, because almost every line in it had come from God first. That is what preaching is for: giving frightened people God’s own words to lean on.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — On What Are You Trusting?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The enemy’s great mistake is to treat the living God as one more idol. From the siege of Lachish, Sennacherib sends his servants to ask Jerusalem what it is trusting in, to accuse Hezekiah of leading the people to die of hunger and thirst, and to twist his removal of the high places into an offence against the LORD (vv. 9–12). He boasts that no god of any nation has delivered its people from Assyria, so neither will theirs (vv. 13–15). More words follow, then letters, and a broadcast shouted in Hebrew to terrify the men on the wall (vv. 16–18), and the Chronicler names the error behind it all (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 12 is the cleverest sentence an enemy speaks in this book. Sennacherib takes the single most obedient act of Hezekiah's reign, pulling down the high places and centralising worship at the one altar God appointed, and presents it to the men on the wall as the reason their God will not help them. He makes obedience look like an offence, and says it in their own language.
verseByVerse.examples: The aim of the campaign is to make a frightened population stop trusting its own king and its own God. Fear still works that way. When an anxious voice says that your faith is the reason things are going badly, it is worth asking whose voice it is.

verseByVerse.quote: After this, Sennacherib king of Assyria, who was besieging Lachish with all his forces, sent his servants to Jerusalem to Hezekiah king of Judah and to all the people of Judah who were in Jerusalem, saying, "Thus says Sennacherib king of Assyria, 'On what are you trusting, that you endure the siege in Jerusalem? Is not Hezekiah misleading you, that he may give you over to die by famine and by thirst, when he tells you, "The LORD our God will deliver us from the hand of the king of Assyria"? Has not this same Hezekiah taken away his high places and his altars and commanded Judah and Jerusalem, "Before one altar you shall worship, and on it you shall burn your sacrifices"? Do you not know what I and my fathers have done to all the peoples of other lands? Were the gods of the nations of those lands at all able to deliver their lands out of my hand? Who among all the gods of those nations that my fathers devoted to destruction was able to deliver his people from my hand, that your God should be able to deliver you from my hand? Now, therefore, do not let Hezekiah deceive you or mislead you in this fashion, and do not believe him, for no god of any nation or kingdom has been able to deliver his people from my hand or from the hand of my fathers. How much less will your God deliver you out of my hand!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sennacherib’s envoys tried to break Jerusalem’s trust: they questioned what it was leaning on, accused Hezekiah of leading the people to their deaths, and argued that no god had ever stopped Assyria.

Sennacherib king of Assyria, who was besieging Lachish. The message comes from a king in the middle of taking another city of Judah, aimed past Hezekiah at the people.

On what are you trusting? The right question, asked by the wrong man for the wrong reason. Sennacherib does not begin with his siege engines. He begins by asking a hungry city what it is leaning on.

Is not Hezekiah misleading you? Then he goes after the king: your king is going to get you killed by famine and thirst, and he is doing it with a religious promise. Drive a wedge between a frightened people and the man telling them to trust God, and the wall will open by itself.

Has not this same Hezekiah taken away his high places? Verse 12 shows real intelligence and real malice. Their king, he says, has offended their own God by reducing his shrines.
