To a pagan mind it is common sense: more altars, more goodwill. To a farmer whose village high place had just been pulled down, it would have landed hard. That is how the enemy of souls generally works: not by recommending sin, but by standing next to a man who has just obeyed God at cost and whispering that this is why things are going badly.

What I and my fathers have done. He has the evidence. Nation after nation, god after god, none able to stop an Assyrian army, and he can name them. His argument from experience is sound, his evidence is real, and his conclusion is catastrophically wrong, because of one mistake: he has put the God of Israel on the same list.

verseByVerse.quote: And his servants said still more against the LORD God and against his servant Hezekiah. And he wrote letters to cast contempt on the LORD, the God of Israel, and to speak against him, saying, "Like the gods of the nations of the lands who have not delivered their people from my hands, so the God of Hezekiah will not deliver his people from my hand." And they shouted it with a loud voice in the language of Judah to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall, to frighten and terrify them, in order that they might take the city. And they spoke of the God of Jerusalem as they spoke of the gods of the peoples of the earth, which are the work of men's hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Assyrians poured out contempt for the LORD in speeches, letters and shouted Hebrew to terrify the city, and their whole case rested on one mistake: treating the living God as an idol made by human hands.

His servants said still more. Count the channels: envoys in person with a prepared speech, more speech beyond it, written letters, and a broadcast shouted in Hebrew, aimed over the government’s head at ordinary soldiers on the wall, because they would understand it and their officers could not stop them hearing it. The stated purpose is to frighten and terrify them. Fear was the weapon; the siege engines were the backup.

The work of men’s hands. Then the Chronicler names the mistake behind the whole operation: Sennacherib spoke of the God of Jerusalem as of the gods of the peoples, the work of men’s hands. His army was everything he said it was, but he classed the living God as one more local god, made by men, and reasoned faultlessly from that false start.

The same mistake today. Men do this still, usually with better manners. God is treated as one item in a range: a set of values, a cultural inheritance, a comfort, something people find helpful. Every argument built on that view of him is as tight as Sennacherib’s and as doomed, because the God of Jerusalem is not the work of anybody’s hands, and being wrong about what something is cannot be repaired by being clever about it afterwards.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the prayer of the humble and humbles the proud, whether an emperor or a king of Judah. Hezekiah and Isaiah cry to heaven, and the LORD sends an angel who cuts down the Assyrian army; Sennacherib goes home in shame and is later killed by his own sons in his god’s temple (vv. 20–21). The LORD saves Jerusalem and gives it rest on every side, and Hezekiah is honoured among the nations (vv. 22–23). Then he falls sick and is healed with a sign, but he makes no fitting return and his heart grows proud, until he humbles himself and the wrath is held back beyond his days (vv. 24–26).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 21 answers verses 13-15 in the terms Sennacherib chose. He had listed the gods who could not save their peoples out of his hand. He was killed in the temple of his own god, by his own sons, in the one place his god should have been able to protect him.
verseByVerse.examples: You do not need eloquent words to pray in a crisis. The prayer that saved this city is not even recorded; it is enough to know that two men cried to heaven, and heaven heard. Short, desperate prayers are still prayers, and God is not waiting for better ones.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Hezekiah the king and Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, prayed because of this and cried to heaven. And the LORD sent an angel, who cut off all the mighty warriors and commanders and officers in the camp of the king of Assyria. So he returned with shame of face to his own land. And when he came into the house of his god, some of his own sons struck him down there with the sword. So the LORD saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem from the hand of Sennacherib king of Assyria and from the hand of all his enemies, and he provided for them on every side. And many brought gifts to the LORD to Jerusalem and precious things to Hezekiah king of Judah, so that he was exalted in the sight of all nations from that time onward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah and Isaiah cried to heaven, and the LORD answered by sending one angel to cut down the Assyrian army; Sennacherib went home in shame to die at his sons’ hands, and Jerusalem was saved and its king honoured.

Hezekiah the king and Isaiah the prophet. The king and the prophet, Isaiah, together on their faces: a rare picture in these books, the two offices praying as a pair, in one clause with a single verb.

Cried to heaven. Kings and Isaiah record the prayer in full (2 Kings 19:15–19; Isaiah 37:14–20); here it is cried to heaven, and the next sentence is the angel. A prayer that saved the city is summarised the way a man summarises something he assumes his readers already know how to do.

The LORD sent an angel. One angel. No battle, no sortie, and none of the second wall required. Kings supplies the number, a hundred and eighty-five thousand in a night (2 Kings 19:35); the Chronicler notes instead which ranks died: the warriors, the commanders, the officers. The war machine that had swallowed the northern kingdom was taken apart in the dark by one messenger. It is the lesson of every deliverance in this book: “the battle is not yours but God’s” (20:15).

Some of his own sons struck him down. Set Sennacherib’s end beside his speech. He had asked which gods had ever delivered their people out of his hand. He died in his own god’s temple, at the hands of his own children, in the one building where his god ought to have been able to protect him.

When he died. That death came some twenty years after the siege, in about 681 BC. Kings and Chronicles pass straight to it because it ends his story, not because it happened the next week. Sennacherib’s own annals, on clay prisms found in Assyria, boast of forty-six walled towns of Judah taken and of Hezekiah shut up in Jerusalem “like a bird in a cage”. They never claim the city fell.

Exalted in the sight of all nations. Hold that word for one verse, because the next thing the Chronicler tells us is what happened inside the man who was exalted.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Hezekiah became sick and was at the point of death, and he prayed to the LORD, and he answered him and gave him a sign. But Hezekiah did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud. Therefore wrath came upon him and Judah and Jerusalem. But Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the LORD did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God healed Hezekiah in answer to prayer, but the healing made him proud instead of grateful, and though he humbled himself in time, the judgment was only postponed beyond his own days.

Hezekiah became sick. One verse for a story that fills a chapter elsewhere: the weeping, the fifteen years added, the shadow going backwards (2 Kings 20:1–11). The Chronicler writes about what the healing did to the man.

Did not make return according to the benefit done to him. The sin is ingratitude. Not idolatry, nor a broken commandment anyone could point to in court: he received an enormous kindness and made no fitting return. It was said of Joash that he did not remember the kindness (24:22), and this is the third proud heart in eight chapters, after Amaziah’s (25:19) and Uzziah’s (26:16).

For his heart was proud. This is the man who wrote the letters north and prayed for the unclean at the Passover. Pride did not get in through his failures. It came in through the answered prayer. An unanswered prayer will make a man cry out; an answered one, badly handled, can make him think he is somebody. There is no season more spiritually dangerous than the week after God does exactly what you asked.

Hezekiah humbled himself. This is the key verb of God’s promise at 7:14, and Hezekiah reaches for it in time. That is the good news of the verse, and it is real: a proud man who catches himself and goes down is not too late, because the mercy he goes down to was promised before he needed it.

In the days of Hezekiah. Then the coldest words in the chapter. The wrath was not cancelled, only put off. Kings lets us hear the tone: when Isaiah told him what was coming, Hezekiah thought, “Why not, if there will be peace and security in my days?” (2 Kings 20:19). A man can repent genuinely of his own pride and still be content that the bill falls after his funeral. The son who inherits it, Manasseh, is named in the last verse of this chapter.

After us, the flood. A phrase has long been put in the mouth of Louis XV of France, or of Madame de Pompadour: après nous le déluge, after us, the flood. Whoever said it, it names a temptation every generation knows. We borrow against our children’s income and put off the hard decisions until somebody else holds office. Hezekiah’s private thought is the creed of a culture that has stopped believing in anything beyond its own lifetime: if this life is all there is, why pay a bill that falls due after your funeral? The Bible’s answer is not first a lecture about duty. It is a Son of David who did the opposite of Hezekiah. He saw the judgment coming, and instead of letting it fall on the next generation, he walked into it himself and became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), so that it would not fall on his children at all. People who have been loved like that begin to plant trees whose shade they will never sit in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–33 — God Left Him to Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even the best king’s story ends by sending us to look for a better one. God gives Hezekiah great riches, storehouses and flocks (vv. 27–29), and he brings the waters of Gihon down inside the city (v. 30). When envoys come from Babylon to ask about the sign, God leaves him to himself, to test him and bring to light all that is in his heart (v. 31). His deeds are written in the vision of Isaiah and the book of the kings; he is buried with honour among the tombs of David’s sons, and Manasseh his son reigns in his place (vv. 32–33).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 31 says God stood back on purpose, in the words Moses used of the wilderness years: testing you to know what was in your heart (Deut 8:2). It does not mean God needed the information; the note below explains.
verseByVerse.examples: Chronicles shows its verdict on each king by his burial. Count them once more. Jehoram departed with no one's regret and was kept out of the tombs (21:20); Joash was kept out (24:25); Uzziah went into the field beside them (26:23); Ahaz was buried in the city and not carried to the chamber at all (28:27). Hezekiah is laid in the upper part of the tombs of the sons of David, and a whole nation turns out to honour him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Hezekiah had very great riches and honor, and he made for himself treasuries for silver, for gold, for precious stones, for spices, for shields, and for all kinds of costly vessels; storehouses also for the yield of grain, wine, and oil; and stalls for all kinds of cattle, and sheepfolds. He likewise provided cities for himself, and flocks and herds in abundance, for God had given him very great possessions. This same Hezekiah closed the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon and directed them down to the west side of the city of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all his works. And so in the matter of the envoys of the princes of Babylon, who had been sent to him to inquire about the sign that had been done in the land, God left him to himself, in order to test him and to know all that was in his heart. Now the rest of the acts of Hezekiah and his good deeds, behold, they are written in the vision of Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. And Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the upper part of the tombs of the sons of David, and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem did him honor at his death. And Manasseh his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave Hezekiah great wealth and success, but when the envoys of Babylon came, God left him to himself to test him and bring to light what was in his heart; then the king was buried with high honour, and his son Manasseh reigned.

God had given him very great possessions. The wealth is catalogued with pleasure, and the reason sits in the middle of it: God had given him.

This same Hezekiah closed the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon. Then the tunnel. The spring lay outside the wall, so his engineers cut a channel through solid rock under the hill, a third of a mile of it, with two teams working toward each other, and brought the water out inside the defences. A person can walk through it today, in the dark with the water round their knees, and come out where Hezekiah’s men came out.

The envoys of the princes of Babylon. Babylon was a rising power far to the east, and it had heard about the sign of the shadow on the steps. A king lately exalted in the sight of all nations showed its ambassadors everything he had, which is the part Kings tells. Isaiah’s answer to that visit was that everything in those storehouses would one day be carried to Babylon (2 Kings 20:12–18), and the Chronicler’s first readers were the descendants of those who were carried off with it.

God left him to himself, in order to test him. The strangest sentence in the chapter and the hardest to shake off: God left him to himself, deliberately, and for a stated purpose. To know all that was in his heart never means God was short of information. A test brings into daylight what was already inside, so that the man himself and everybody else can see it. The words echo Moses on the wilderness years, when God humbled and tested Israel “to know what was in your heart” (Deuteronomy 8:2).

A severe mercy. So the withdrawal was a mercy of a severe kind. Hezekiah did not know what was in his heart. He had repented at verse 26, and there was still enough pride left to walk a foreign delegation round his treasury.

When God seems to step back. Whoever has been through a season when God seemed to step back, when the nearness that carried you for years was not there, should hold on to this verse rather than panic at it. It is not desertion. The Spirit Christ gives is given to be with his people forever (John 14:16), and a felt withdrawal can be the way a believer learns what he has been leaning on.

What if being left alone is the problem? Much of modern life is organised around one wish: to be left to ourselves. Verse 31 describes exactly that condition and treats it not as liberation but as a sobering test. God gave Hezekiah what our culture calls freedom, and what came to the surface was pride. Paul says the same of whole societies: when people would not have God, God gave them up to the desires of their own hearts (Romans 1:24). One of the most dreadful things God can do to a person is give him exactly what he insists on. The cure is not a firmer grip on our own lives but being kept by another: “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). Freedom, in the Bible, is not being left alone. It is being held by someone who will not let go.

They buried him in the upper part of the tombs of the sons of David. The burial completes the series in which each king’s grave shows how he was judged (see Burial customs and tombs). Hezekiah is laid among David’s sons, and a whole city turns out to honour him.

Hezekiah’s life in sum. He was a great king, and he was not the King. He opened the doors, and stripped their gold when he was frightened; he prayed and heaven emptied an army, and came off his sickbed proud; he humbled himself, and was content that the reckoning should fall after he was gone.

Forsaken in our place. There was another Son of David whom God did not leave to himself as a test, but forsook in our place, in the dark, on a hill outside this same city, crying out about it (Matthew 27:46). He was tested in every way, and nothing came out of that heart but obedience. And because he was forsaken, no one who belongs to him is ever forsaken; the promise to them is the one Moses gave Joshua and Hezekiah preached at the gate, and it holds all the way to the grave and out the other side: “He will not leave you or forsake you” (Deuteronomy 31:6; Hebrews 13:5).

Uncertain wording. “The upper part” translates a word that can mean an ascent or a higher place: perhaps a higher, more honoured section of the royal tombs, or the approach leading up to them, perhaps because the older tombs were full. Either way, he lay among David’s sons, with honour.
verseByVerse.note: Hezekiah’s tunnel brought the Gihon spring inside the city walls. An inscription cut in its wall near the exit describes the moment the two teams of diggers heard each other and broke through.

keyVerse.quote: With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God, to help us and to fight our battles.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter is a test of this sentence. Assyria’s arm was real, and its boasts were backed by evidence, but it was flesh; the LORD answered prayer and saved the city without a battle. The same chapter warns that the people God is with must still guard their hearts, and the promise “with us” finds its fulfilment in Immanuel, who is with his people always.

32.reflection:
The invasion came “after these things and these acts of faithfulness” (v. 1). How does this verse correct the idea that obedience guarantees an easy life? How did Hezekiah combine hard work and trust in God (vv. 2–8)?

Sennacherib’s case was built on real evidence and one false assumption: that the LORD was like the gods made by human hands (vv. 13–19). In what ways do people today treat God as one option among many? How would you answer them?

Hezekiah’s pride came after answered prayer, not after failure (vv. 24–25). Why can success and answered prayer be spiritually dangerous? What helps us make a fitting return for God’s kindness?

“God left him to himself, in order to test him and to know all that was in his heart” (v. 31). Have you known a season when God seemed to step back? How does Christ’s being forsaken in our place change the way we understand such times?

33.title: When He Was in Distress He Entreated
33.text: <sup>1</sup>Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to the abominations of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.<sup>3</sup>For he rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had broken down, and he erected altars to the Baals, and made Asheroth, and worshiped all the host of heaven and served them.<sup>4</sup>And he built altars in the house of the LORD, of which the LORD had said, "In Jerusalem shall my name be forever."<sup>5</sup>And he built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And he burned his sons as an offering in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, and used fortune-telling and omens and sorcery, and dealt with mediums and with necromancers. He did much evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger.<sup>7</sup>And the carved image of the idol that he had made he set in the house of God, of which God said to David and to Solomon his son, "In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will put my name forever,<sup>8</sup>and I will no more remove the foot of Israel from the land that I appointed for your fathers, if only they will be careful to do all that I have commanded them, all the law, the statutes, and the rules given through Moses."<sup>9</sup>Manasseh led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray, to do more evil than the nations whom the LORD destroyed before the people of Israel.<sup>10</sup>The LORD spoke to Manasseh and to his people, but they paid no attention.<sup>11</sup>Therefore the LORD brought upon them the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria, who captured Manasseh with hooks and bound him with chains of bronze and brought him to Babylon.<sup>12</sup>And when he was in distress, he entreated the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers.<sup>13</sup>He prayed to him, and God was moved by his entreaty and heard his plea and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God.<sup>14</sup>Afterward he built an outer wall for the city of David west of Gihon, in the valley, and for the entrance into the Fish Gate, and carried it around Ophel, and raised it to a very great height. He also put commanders of the army in all the fortified cities in Judah.<sup>15</sup>And he took away the foreign gods and the idol from the house of the LORD, and all the altars that he had built on the mountain of the house of the LORD and in Jerusalem, and he threw them outside of the city.<sup>16</sup>He also restored the altar of the LORD and offered on it sacrifices of peace offerings and of thanksgiving, and he commanded Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>17</sup>Nevertheless, the people still sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD their God.<sup>18</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and his prayer to his God, and the words of the seers who spoke to him in the name of the LORD, the God of Israel, behold, they are in the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.<sup>19</sup>And his prayer, and how God was moved by his entreaty, and all his sin and his faithlessness, and the sites on which he built high places and set up the Asherim and the images, before he humbled himself, behold, they are written in the Chronicles of the Seers.<sup>20</sup>So Manasseh slept with his fathers, and they buried him in his house, and Amon his son reigned in his place.<sup>21</sup>Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem.<sup>22</sup>And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as Manasseh his father had done. Amon sacrificed to all the images that Manasseh his father had made, and served them.<sup>23</sup>And he did not humble himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself, but this Amon incurred guilt more and more.<sup>24</sup>And his servants conspired against him and put him to death in his house.<sup>25</sup>But the people of the land struck down all those who had conspired against King Amon. And the people of the land made Josiah his son king in his place.
33.overview:
Where we are. Hezekiah, the king who reopened the temple and kept the great Passover, has died honoured by all Judah (32:33). His twelve-year-old son inherits a cleansed house of God and a kingdom that God has just delivered from Assyria.

The message. No one is beyond the reach of God’s mercy who humbles himself before him, and no one who has seen that mercy may safely refuse it. Manasseh did more evil than the nations God destroyed, yet when he humbled himself in chains, God heard him and brought him home. His son watched that mercy at close quarters and would not humble himself.

Why it was said. The first readers had come home from Babylon after an exile their fathers’ sins had earned (see the introduction). In Manasseh they could read their own history in one man’s life: sin, exile to Babylon, humbling, and a road home. They needed to know that the promise of 7:14 still held for people like them, and that a late repentance is real even when it does not undo everything.

How the chapter makes its case. Manasseh’s evil is listed item by item, as if read off Deuteronomy’s catalogue of the nations’ abominations, and climaxes in an idol set in God’s house, beside God’s promise and its condition (vv. 1–9). God speaks and is ignored; the Assyrians take the king to Babylon, where he humbles himself greatly and God hears him (vv. 10–13). Home again, he strengthens the city, throws out his own idols and restores the altar, though the people keep their high places (vv. 14–17). The records keep his prayer and his sin side by side (vv. 18–20). Amon copies his father’s sin and not his repentance, and is murdered; the people crown Josiah (vv. 21–25).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly through the character of God revealed in him. The patience that kept speaking to Manasseh for decades is the patience Paul says Christ displayed in saving the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15–16). And God’s pardon was never a pretence that the sins did not matter: it looked ahead to the cross, where such sins were paid for (Romans 3:25–26). Manasseh himself stands, named, in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:10).

For us. No one you are praying for, and nothing you have done, lies beyond the reach of the God who heard Manasseh. But forgiveness does not undo every consequence, and grace seen up close can still be refused. Come while he is still speaking.
33.theology:
This is the promise of 7:14, that God hears and forgives those who humble themselves and pray, tested past the point where anyone would expect it to hold. A man who put an idol in God's house and burned his own children humbles himself in an Assyrian prison, and God was moved by his entreaty. The Chronicler spends nine verses making sure we cannot minimise the sins first. The mercy is not measured out according to their size.

Verses 7-8 quote God's promise with its condition attached at the moment the condition is being broken. That is this book's explanation of the exile.

And the chapter is scrupulous about what repentance does and does not do. It brought him home and restored his throne; it did not undo the country's habits (v. 17), it did not clear his record (vv. 18-19), and it did not get him into the royal tombs (v. 20).

Then verse 23 turns the mercy into a standard: Amon is condemned by comparison with his father's repentance.
33.examples:
Manasseh's life is a map of how far a person can go and how far God's mercy reaches. He undid his father's reforms, practised one by one the occult arts Moses had forbidden, and ignored God's messengers for decades. Then he was walked out of his own country on the end of a hook, and in Babylon he prayed.

He came home and threw out the idols he had spent his life installing, and offered thank offerings on the altar he had displaced. His son, who watched it all, chose to copy the first half of the reign, the idolatry. Grace seen at close quarters can still be refused.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — More Evil Than the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah’s longest reign is its worst, and the chapter makes sure we see how bad it was before we hear of mercy. Manasseh, born in the years God added to Hezekiah’s life, rebuilds the high places, serves the Baals and the stars, and puts altars to them in both temple courts (vv. 1–5). He burns his sons and works through every occult practice Moses forbade (v. 6). Then he sets a carved idol in the house where God promised to put his name, and the Chronicler quotes that promise with its condition at the moment it is broken (vv. 7–8). Judah ends up doing more evil than the nations God destroyed (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 7 and 8 print God's promise and its condition immediately before verse 9 records the breach. This is where the Chronicler explains the exile: not as bad luck or Babylonian strength, but as a stated condition that was broken in the building where the promise was made.
verseByVerse.examples: Some readers have dabbled in fortune-telling, horoscopes or attempts to contact the dead, perhaps in grief. Verse 6 shows how seriously God takes these things, and the rest of the chapter shows how readily he forgives those who turn from them.

verseByVerse.quote: Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to the abominations of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel. For he rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had broken down, and he erected altars to the Baals, and made Asheroth, and worshiped all the host of heaven and served them. And he built altars in the house of the LORD, of which the LORD had said, "In Jerusalem shall my name be forever." And he built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The longest reign in Judah’s history belonged to its worst king, and he spent it tearing down everything his father had restored. No king in this book reigned longer, not David, not Solomon, not Uzziah with his fifty-two; a long life, in Scripture, is no proof of God’s approval.

Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign. There is an arithmetic to do slowly, because the numbers are all in the text. Hezekiah reigned twenty-nine years. In the middle of that reign he was sick to the point of death, prayed, and was told: I will add fifteen years to your life (2 Kings 20:6). Fifteen from twenty-nine puts the illness in his fourteenth year. Manasseh was twelve when he came to the throne, which puts his birth in his father’s seventeenth year. Manasseh was born in the added years.

What the text does not say. The text does not comment, and neither should we. It does not say the extension was a mistake, or that the boy would have been better unborn; God had his own purposes in those fifteen years, and one of them will be visible before this chapter is out. But the sum is there for anyone who cares to do it, and it should make us slower the next time we are certain we know what to ask God for.

According to the abominations of the nations. Verse 2 opens a frame that verse 9 will close. Manasseh begins by doing what the nations did, the peoples God drove out, and ends by doing worse than the nations God destroyed. It is the same sentence that was written over his grandfather Ahaz (28:3). The one charge Israel was never supposed to face, that it had become indistinguishable from the people it replaced, has now been laid against two kings of Judah within five chapters.

He rebuilt the high places. The first thing recorded of him is aimed straight at chapter 31. The first complete clearance of the high places in the whole book, done by ordinary people walking home from a Passover, was rebuilt by the next king.

All the host of heaven. Then he escalates: Baals, Asherah poles, and the sun, moon and stars worshipped as gods. The building where God put his name forever now has star-altars in both its courtyards. Hezekiah’s cleansing lasted one generation.

verseByVerse.quote: And he burned his sons as an offering in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, and used fortune-telling and omens and sorcery, and dealt with mediums and with necromancers. He did much evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger. And the carved image of the idol that he had made he set in the house of God, of which God said to David and to Solomon his son, "In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will put my name forever, and I will no more remove the foot of Israel from the land that I appointed for your fathers, if only they will be careful to do all that I have commanded them, all the law, the statutes, and the rules given through Moses." Manasseh led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray, to do more evil than the nations whom the LORD destroyed before the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Manasseh worked through the very practices for which God had driven the Canaanites out, and then set an idol inside the house of God at the moment the Chronicler reminds us of the promise and its condition. So Judah did more evil than the nations God had destroyed before it.

He burned his sons as an offering. In the same ravine where Ahaz burned his (28:3). Three generations: Ahaz burning children, Hezekiah opening the temple doors, Manasseh back in the valley with a fire.

Fortune-telling and omens and sorcery. The rest of the verse reads like a list, and it is one. Open Deuteronomy 18 and the items come in the same order: anyone who burns his son or his daughter as an offering, anyone who practices divination or tells fortunes or interprets omens, or a sorcerer or a charmer or a medium or a necromancer (18:10–11). That passage tells Israel what the previous occupants of Canaan had done and why they were thrown out of the land. Manasseh went down it item by item, like a man working through a menu.

The carved image of the idol. Then the worst: not a shrine on a hill, not an altar in the courtyard, but a carved idol inside the temple itself. And this time the Chronicler gives God’s promise in full, condition and all.

If only. On those two words the whole history turns, and they are quoted at the exact moment the condition is broken, in the very house the promise was about. Everything in the last three chapters of this book follows from them.

To do more evil than the nations. That verdict settles whether the exile was fair. The nations were driven out of that land for exactly these practices, in front of Israel, as a demonstration. Judah watched it, was given the land, the law, the temple, the prophets and centuries of warnings, and went further than the people it replaced.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–13 — Then Manasseh Knew That the LORD Was God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When a sinner humbles himself, God hears, even this sinner. God first speaks to Manasseh and his people and is ignored (v. 10), so he sends the Assyrians, who take the king captive to Babylon (v. 11). In distress Manasseh entreats the LORD and humbles himself greatly; God is moved, hears, and brings him home to his kingdom (vv. 12–13a). The section ends with what forgiveness taught him: “Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God” (v. 13b). If the promise of 7:14 reaches this man, it reaches anyone.
verseByVerse.theology: This is 7:14 tested at its outer limit and holding. The promise was if my people ... humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn. If the offer reaches Manasseh, there is no sinner it cannot reach.
verseByVerse.examples: If you are praying for someone who seems beyond reach, these four verses are for you. God spoke to Manasseh for decades and was ignored, and still the story was not over.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Manasseh and to his people, but they paid no attention. Therefore the LORD brought upon them the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria, who captured Manasseh with hooks and bound him with chains of bronze and brought him to Babylon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God spoke to Manasseh before he struck him, and when words were ignored he sent the Assyrians, who dragged the king away to Babylon. Judgment came only after long patience, and even the judgment was aimed at bringing him back.

The LORD spoke to Manasseh and to his people. God spoke first, before the Assyrians and the hooks, and verse 18 will say there were seers with messages, plural, over years. Fifty-five years of a man setting up star-altars in God’s courtyards and killing his own children, and God kept sending people to talk to him. That is what the patience of God looks like stretched across half a century. It does not look like approval, and at the time it does not look like much of anything.

Captured Manasseh with hooks. The Assyrians handled captured kings for the benefit of the watching crowd, and their monuments show captives led by ropes fastened to rings through the lips. The man who had commanded Judah for half a century was led out of his own country like an animal.

Brought him to Babylon. Not Nineveh, where a reader would expect an Assyrian army to take its prisoners, but the city that within a lifetime will burn this temple and carry off the last king of David’s line. Manasseh went there first, in chains, and came back. The Chronicler’s first readers, who had themselves come home from Babylon, could read their own history in his: exile for sin, humbling in a foreign land, and a road back to Jerusalem.

Did Manasseh’s captivity really happen? Kings does not mention it, but Assyrian records name Manasseh as a vassal, and Assyria’s king at the time also ruled Babylon. Why then do Kings and Jeremiah still blame Manasseh for the exile (2 Kings 24:3–4)? His personal repentance did not undo the decades of idolatry and bloodshed he had taught the nation, which went on after him.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “hooks” is uncommon here. Elsewhere it means thorns or brambles, and once a hook put through a captive’s jaw (Job 41:2); older English versions read that the Assyrians took Manasseh “among the thorns”, as if caught in hiding. The likely meaning is the one the ESV gives: hooks or rings by which captives were led, matching the bronze chains in the same sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he was in distress, he entreated the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers. He prayed to him, and God was moved by his entreaty and heard his plea and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his distress Manasseh humbled himself and prayed, and God heard him and brought him home: no sinner who truly turns to God is beyond the reach of his mercy. Forgiven, the man who had known about God all his life came to know him.

When he was in distress. Not in a season of reflection, not after reading something, not because a preacher finally got through. He broke when everything else had been taken from him. That is a common road and there is no shame in it; God is not too proud to receive someone who comes because he has run out of alternatives.

He entreated the favor of the LORD his God. The word “his” has been absent from the chapter until now. It comes back in a prison.

Humbled himself greatly. The word of 7:14, which Rehoboam did under Shishak and Amon will refuse to do; only here does the book add “greatly”.

God was moved by his entreaty. He entreated, and God let himself be entreated. The God whose courtyards held star-altars, whose house had an idol standing in it, in whose sight this man had burned his own children, was moved by the prayer of that man in chains. Every argument that someone is too far gone dies here: not because Manasseh’s sins were smaller than they looked, but because the mercy of God is not measured out according to the size of the sin.

Is that fair, when the children in the valley got no such hearing? Forgiveness was never God pretending they did not matter. Every pardon in the Old Testament was given looking ahead to the day when God would put forward his Son as a propitiation, a sacrifice that turns away his wrath, to show that he is just as well as the one who justifies (Romans 3:25–26). Manasseh’s sins were not waved through; they were paid for at the cross. Paul, who called himself the foremost of sinners, says he received mercy so that Christ might display his perfect patience as an example (1 Timothy 1:15–16). Manasseh is the Old Testament’s great example of that patience.

Keep praying. Anyone who has prayed for years for someone whose life has gone past the point where decent people expect anything should keep verse 13 where they can find it. The prophets who came to Manasseh over five decades and were ignored died before it happened. The word they left in his memory was still there when the chains went on.

Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God. He had been told it since he was a boy in Hezekiah’s palace, and he learned it on the other side of being forgiven. People do not usually come to know God by being convinced of an argument. They come to know him by being forgiven.
verseByVerse.note: Manasseh’s captivity and repentance are recorded only in Chronicles.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Real repentance shows itself in deeds, and it is real even when it cannot undo everything. Back in Jerusalem, Manasseh strengthens the city and its garrisons (v. 14), throws out the foreign gods and the idol he had set up, and restores the altar of the LORD with thank offerings (vv. 15–16). Yet the people still sacrifice at the high places, though only to the LORD (v. 17). The archives keep his prayer and his sin together, divided by the words “before he humbled himself” (vv. 18–19), and he is buried in his own house, not the royal tombs (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 18 and 19 file the prayer and the sin in the same archive. The Chronicler will not let Manasseh's repentance erase his record, and he will not let the record cancel the repentance. The dividing phrase is before he humbled himself.
verseByVerse.examples: A late reformation can be real and still limited. If you came to faith after years of doing harm, you may spend some of the rest of your life watching damage you cannot repair. That is not a sign that God's forgiveness failed; it is the ordinary shape of a long wrong road, and he walks the rest of it with you.

verseByVerse.quote: Afterward he built an outer wall for the city of David west of Gihon, in the valley, and for the entrance into the Fish Gate, and carried it around Ophel, and raised it to a very great height. He also put commanders of the army in all the fortified cities in Judah. And he took away the foreign gods and the idol from the house of the LORD, and all the altars that he had built on the mountain of the house of the LORD and in Jerusalem, and he threw them outside of the city. He also restored the altar of the LORD and offered on it sacrifices of peace offerings and of thanksgiving, and he commanded Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel. Nevertheless, the people still sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Manasseh proved his repentance by tearing down his own life’s work and restoring true worship, yet the habits he had taught the nation outlived his change of heart. Forgiveness is instant; consequences keep their own timetable.

Afterward he built an outer wall. What follows shows whether the prison prayer was real. He builds an outer wall for the city of David, west of Gihon, round to the Fish Gate and about the Ophel, and raised it to a very great height, and he puts commanders in every fortified city. A restored man went back to his job and did it properly, which is usually where genuine repentance shows first.

He took away the foreign gods. Then the reversal of his own life’s work. Some of those altars he had commissioned as a young man; the image in the house was his own. There is no record that he made speeches about it. He had them taken out and thrown over the wall.

Sacrifices of peace offerings and of thanksgiving. Thank offerings, from Manasseh: the sacrifice for people with something to be grateful about.

Nevertheless, the people still sacrificed at the high places. The sentence keeps the chapter honest. He got the idols out of the temple and could not get the country back. His people went on sacrificing at the shrines, to the right God now, in the wrong places. That is the shape of a late repentance, and it should be said plainly rather than softened. Manasseh’s turning was real, and God received it, and it did not undo fifty-five years.

Come now. That is a reason to come now, while the Holy Spirit still says “Today” (Hebrews 3:7), and never a reason not to come.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and his prayer to his God, and the words of the seers who spoke to him in the name of the LORD, the God of Israel, behold, they are in the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. And his prayer, and how God was moved by his entreaty, and all his sin and his faithlessness, and the sites on which he built high places and set up the Asherim and the images, before he humbled himself, behold, they are written in the Chronicles of the Seers. So Manasseh slept with his fathers, and they buried him in his house, and Amon his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The record keeps Manasseh’s prayer and his sin together, because God’s forgiveness does not rewrite history: it pays the debt. And even a forgiven king was buried apart from the honoured kings of Judah.

His prayer to his God. The usual closing summary is longer here, and what it records is the point. His prayer is in the national archive. So are the words of the seers he ignored for decades, written down at the time, by somebody, while nobody was listening.

All his sin and his faithlessness. Verse 19 files the other half. The prayer and the sin together, not the prayer instead of the sin. The record even keeps the addresses, the sites on which he built high places, a list of the places a forgiven man ruined.

Before he humbled himself. The phrase cuts his life in two. There is a before and an after, and the hinge is a man in irons deciding to bend. Keep that within reach when the past will not stay buried. Scripture never pretends a pardoned man has a clean history, and it does not need to, because the honest record of a forgiven sin is what lets us see how great the mercy was.

They buried him in his house. Not in the tombs of the kings; Kings says it was the garden (2 Kings 21:18). Set that beside Hezekiah, buried in the upper part of the royal tombs with a nation mourning (32:33). Manasseh was forgiven, restored to his throne, and buried in his own garden. Both are true at once, and neither cancels the other.

Is the apocryphal “Prayer of Manasseh” this prayer? It was written much later, in his name, and is not Scripture.

Are these lost books Scripture? They were the prophets’ records and royal annals the inspired writer drew on, as Luke drew on earlier accounts (Luke 1:1–3). Not every writing of a prophet was given to be Scripture; God has preserved all of his word that he meant the church to have (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

Uncertain wording. “The Chronicles of the Seers” translates a Hebrew word, ḥozai, that may be a plural (“seers”) or a name, Hozai, an otherwise unknown prophet, and some versions take it as the name. An early translation already read “the seers”, as the ESV does. Either way, it was a prophetic record of Manasseh’s reign.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–25 — He Did Not Humble Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A father’s repentance becomes the measure of his son. Amon reigns two years and copies the first half of Manasseh’s life, sacrificing to the images his father had made (vv. 21–22). But he does not humble himself as his father did, and so his guilt only grows (v. 23). His own servants kill him in his house; the people of the land execute the conspirators and make his eight-year-old son Josiah king (vv. 24–25), keeping David’s line on the throne once more.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 23 is the sentence the whole chapter exists to make possible. Amon is measured not by Hezekiah or David but by Manasseh, the worst man in the book, at the one point where the worst man in the book got it right. A father's repentance becomes the standard his son is measured against.
verseByVerse.examples: Parents who came to faith late sometimes watch their children choose the old life rather than the new one. That grief is real, and it is not the end of the story either: Amon's own son would become the most thorough reformer of them all.

verseByVerse.quote: Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as Manasseh his father had done. Amon sacrificed to all the images that Manasseh his father had made, and served them. And he did not humble himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself, but this Amon incurred guilt more and more. And his servants conspired against him and put him to death in his house. But the people of the land struck down all those who had conspired against King Amon. And the people of the land made Josiah his son king in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amon copied his father’s idolatry but not his repentance, and so stands condemned by the very mercy he had watched; yet God kept David’s line alive through the boy who would follow him. Family history is a strong current, not a fate.

As Manasseh his father had done. Look at which part of his father he copied. Amon grew up in the palace Manasseh came home to from Babylon; he watched the old man pull the idols out of the temple and heard him command Judah to serve the LORD. What he chose to inherit was the first half of the reign.

Amon sacrificed to all the images. The images his father made, and had thrown out of the city: it seems he went and got them back, or made them again. A son can reach past a parent’s repentance to the sins the parent abandoned, and it happens more often than anyone likes to admit.

He did not humble himself before the LORD. That Amon is measured by Manasseh is a terrible and merciful arrangement. It means that even the darkest family history may hold an example of grace to follow. And it means that mercy shown to one man becomes evidence against everyone who watched it and refused it for themselves. Amon knew that God receives the humbled, because he had eaten at the table with the proof of it for years.

Are we only our upbringing? Two stories about families compete today. One says we are the product of what was done to us, and a person raised in a certain kind of home will repeat it. The other says the past has no hold on us at all, and we can invent ourselves from scratch. Each has truth in it, and each is too simple. This chapter sets three generations in a row and refuses both. Manasseh’s influence on Amon was real, and Amon still chose which half of his father to copy. Then the people crown Amon’s own son, Josiah, who will become the most thorough reformer in the book. The prophets said as much: the son does not bear the father’s iniquity, and each answers for his own (Ezekiel 18:20). The gospel goes further than either modern story. It neither denies what our families did to us nor pretends we built ourselves. It offers a new birth (John 3:3) and a new Father, so that no one’s family history has the last word.

His servants conspired against him. Killed by his own household staff, in his own house, after two years. He is the third king in ten chapters to die at his own people’s hands: Joash finished in his bed by servants avenging a murdered prophet (24:25), Amaziah run down at Lachish by a conspiracy from Jerusalem (25:27), and now Amon. A king who has made himself hated has nowhere private left to sleep.

The people of the land made Josiah his son king. They execute the conspirators and crown an eight-year-old named Josiah. For the third time in this book ordinary people keep the line of David on the throne, as they did with Ahaziah (22:1) and Uzziah (26:1), and their names are not written down.

Where the line was leading. And the line needed keeping, because of where it led. The first page of the New Testament reads: and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah (Matthew 1:10). The ESV prints Amos, following the oldest Greek manuscripts; Kings and Chronicles spell it Amon. It is the same man.

Manasseh in the genealogy of Christ. The man with the star-altars in God’s courtyards and his sons’ ashes in the Hinnom valley stands in the line that runs to Bethlehem, named without apology in the opening paragraph of the Gospel. God did not merely forgive him and leave him at the edge of the story. He kept him in the family, and the descendant who came of that line went down into a distress deeper than any Babylonian prison, so that people like Manasseh, which is to say people like us, could be heard when they finally entreat.

keyVerse.quote: He prayed to him, and God was moved by his entreaty and heard his plea and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God.
keyVerse.note: This is the promise of 7:14 tested at its outer limit, and holding. If God hears the prayer of the man who burned his sons and set an idol in the temple, there is no one who humbles himself whom he will not hear. And the last sentence shows what forgiveness does: it turns knowing about God into knowing him.

33.reflection:
Manasseh’s sins are listed in full before his repentance is told. Why does it matter that we see how bad things were before we hear of mercy, in his story and in our own?

Manasseh turned to God “when he was in distress”. Is a repentance that begins in desperation any less real? How has God used hard times in your life or in someone you know?

His repentance was real, yet the people kept their high places and his record kept his sins. How do forgiveness and lasting consequences fit together, and how can we help someone living with the second?

Amon watched his father’s repentance and copied his sin instead. Whose example of grace have you seen at close quarters, and what would it mean to follow it rather than merely admire it?

34.title: His Heart Was Tender
34.text: <sup>1</sup>Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, and walked in the ways of David his father; and he did not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.<sup>3</sup>For in the eighth year of his reign, while he was yet a boy, he began to seek the God of David his father, and in the twelfth year he began to purge Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the Asherim, and the carved and the metal images.<sup>4</sup>And they chopped down the altars of the Baals in his presence, and he cut down the incense altars that stood above them. And he broke in pieces the Asherim and the carved and the metal images, and he made dust of them and scattered it over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them.<sup>5</sup>He also burned the bones of the priests on their altars and cleansed Judah and Jerusalem.<sup>6</sup>And in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, and as far as Naphtali, in their ruins all around,<sup>7</sup>he broke down the altars and beat the Asherim and the images into powder and cut down all the incense altars throughout all the land of Israel. Then he returned to Jerusalem.<sup>8</sup>Now in the eighteenth year of his reign, when he had cleansed the land and the house, he sent Shaphan the son of Azaliah, and Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah the son of Joahaz, the recorder, to repair the house of the LORD his God.<sup>9</sup>They came to Hilkiah the high priest and gave him the money that had been brought into the house of God, which the Levites, the keepers of the threshold, had collected from Manasseh and Ephraim and from all the remnant of Israel and from all Judah and Benjamin and from the inhabitants of Jerusalem.<sup>10</sup>And they gave it to the workmen who were working in the house of the LORD. And the workmen who were working in the house of the LORD gave it for repairing and restoring the house.<sup>11</sup>They gave it to the carpenters and the builders to buy quarried stone, and timber for binders and beams for the buildings that the kings of Judah had let go to ruin.<sup>12</sup>And the men did the work faithfully. Over them were set Jahath and Obadiah the Levites, of the sons of Merari, and Zechariah and Meshullam, of the sons of the Kohathites, to have oversight. The Levites, all who were skillful with instruments of music,<sup>13</sup>were over the burden-bearers and directed all who did work in every kind of service, and some of the Levites were scribes and officials and gatekeepers.<sup>14</sup>While they were bringing out the money that had been brought into the house of the LORD, Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the Law of the LORD given through Moses.<sup>15</sup>Then Hilkiah answered and said to Shaphan the secretary, "I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD." And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan.<sup>16</sup>Shaphan brought the book to the king, and further reported to the king, "All that was committed to your servants they are doing.<sup>17</sup>They have emptied out the money that was found in the house of the LORD and have given it into the hand of the overseers and the workmen."<sup>18</sup>Then Shaphan the secretary told the king, "Hilkiah the priest has given me a book." And Shaphan read from it before the king.<sup>19</sup>And when the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes.<sup>20</sup>And the king commanded Hilkiah, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Abdon the son of Micah, Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah the king's servant, saying,<sup>21</sup>"Go, inquire of the LORD for me and for those who are left in Israel and in Judah, concerning the words of the book that has been found. For great is the wrath of the LORD that is poured out on us, because our fathers have not kept the word of the LORD, to do according to all that is written in this book."<sup>22</sup>So Hilkiah and those whom the king had sent went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tokhath, son of Hasrah, keeper of the wardrobe (now she lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter) and spoke to her to that effect.<sup>23</sup>And she said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: 'Tell the man who sent you to me,<sup>24</sup>Thus says the LORD, Behold, I will bring disaster upon this place and upon its inhabitants, all the curses that are written in the book that was read before the king of Judah.<sup>25</sup>Because they have forsaken me and have made offerings to other gods, that they might provoke me to anger with all the works of their hands, therefore my wrath will be poured out on this place and will not be quenched.<sup>26</sup>But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the LORD, thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Regarding the words that you have heard,<sup>27</sup>because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God when you heard his words against this place and its inhabitants, and you have humbled yourself before me and have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you, declares the LORD.<sup>28</sup>Behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your grave in peace, and your eyes shall not see all the disaster that I will bring upon this place and its inhabitants.'" And they brought back word to the king.<sup>29</sup>Then the king sent and gathered together all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem.<sup>30</sup>And the king went up to the house of the LORD, with all the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the priests and the Levites, all the people both great and small. And he read in their hearing all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD.<sup>31</sup>And the king stood in his place and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes, with all his heart and all his soul, to perform the words of the covenant that were written in this book.<sup>32</sup>Then he made all who were present in Jerusalem and in Benjamin join in it. And the inhabitants of Jerusalem did according to the covenant of God, the God of their fathers.<sup>33</sup>And Josiah took away all the abominations from all the territory that belonged to the people of Israel and made all who were present in Israel serve the LORD their God. All his days they did not turn away from following the LORD, the God of their fathers.
34.overview:
Where we are. Amon has been murdered after two years, and the people of the land have crowned his eight-year-old son (33:25). The temple is in disrepair, and somewhere inside it the Book of the Law lies forgotten.

The message. God’s word, heard with a tender heart, humbles a person and brings him to mercy, but a nation’s faithfulness cannot rest on one good king. Josiah seeks God as a boy and clears the land, and when the lost law is read to him he tears his clothes. God hears him and spares him the coming disaster, yet the sentence on the nation stands. His people follow the LORD only “all his days” (v. 33).

Why it was said. The first readers were a community rebuilding its life around the law of Moses read aloud (Nehemiah 8; see the introduction). Josiah showed them what it means to hear Scripture rightly, and warned them that renewal which depends on a leader dies with him.

How the chapter makes its case. Josiah begins to seek God at sixteen and to purge Judah at twenty, carrying the work into the ruins of the north (vv. 1–7). In his eighteenth year he repairs the temple, and the work is done faithfully (vv. 8–13). While the money is being brought out, the Book of the Law is found and read to the king, who tears his clothes and sends to inquire of the LORD (vv. 14–21). Huldah the prophetess answers: the curses will fall on the nation, but because the king’s heart was tender he will not see them (vv. 22–28). Josiah reads the covenant to all the people, binds himself to it, brings them into it, and removes the abominations; all his days they follow the LORD (vv. 29–33).

Where it leads. To Christ above all through the need it exposes. Josiah is the king who most nearly fits Deuteronomy’s picture of a king, and the obedience he produced lasted exactly as long as he lived. Jeremiah, who began to prophesy in his reign, foretold a new covenant with the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–33). That covenant was made by the Son of David whose days do not end, who kept the law with all his heart in our place, and who gives his people the tender heart God commended in Josiah.

For us. Do not merely handle Scripture; let it read you, and when it exposes you, run to the mercy it holds out. Do not rest your faithfulness on a gifted leader or a good season. Rest it on Christ, who never dies, and ask him for a tender heart.
34.theology:
Verse 14 is the quiet horror of the chapter. The covenant document was lost inside the building that existed to house it, and nobody had missed it. Two generations had not abandoned the word of God so much as mislaid it, which is how it is usually lost.

Verse 19 shows what hearing it does. Josiah had already sought God for ten years, and the reading of Scripture still tore him open.

Huldah's oracle then holds two settled things together. Judah's judgment will not be quenched; this one man is heard. The reformation that followed could not save the nation and was worth every year of it.

And what God commends in verse 27 is nothing Josiah built, but a tender heart, a humbled self, torn clothes and tears. The first of those is the one item on the list that a man cannot manufacture; it is God's gift.
34.examples:
Josiah's reign is full of small, telling scenes. He walked north through the burned-out villages of a kingdom that no longer existed to pull down its altars. The Bible turned up in the temple because somebody was carrying a chest of money out of a room. The high priest and four royal officials walked across Jerusalem to ask a woman what God was saying.

And told that his own eyes would be spared, he did not settle into a quiet old age. He called the entire nation together and read them the whole book himself, curses and all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — While He Was Yet a Boy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Reform that lasts begins with seeking God. Josiah comes to the throne at eight and does what is right, turning neither to the right nor to the left, the standard Deuteronomy set for Israel’s kings (vv. 1–2). At sixteen he begins to seek the God of David; at twenty he begins to purge Judah and Jerusalem (v. 3). Altars are chopped down in his presence, idols ground to dust over their worshippers’ graves, and the bones of the priests burned on their own altars, as a prophet had foretold three centuries before (vv. 4–5). Then he carries the work into the ruined towns of the north, where no king of Judah ruled (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 5 is the fulfilment of a word three hundred years old. At the dedication of Jeroboam's altar a man of God cried out that a son would be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, who would burn human bones on it (1 Kgs 13:2). The note on verses 4-7 takes up the question this raises.
verseByVerse.examples: If you are young and just beginning to seek God, you do not have to have everything sorted out first. Josiah began at sixteen in a household that had taught him nothing about God, and God met him there.

verseByVerse.quote: Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, and walked in the ways of David his father; and he did not turn aside to the right hand or to the left. For in the eighth year of his reign, while he was yet a boy, he began to seek the God of David his father, and in the twelfth year he began to purge Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the Asherim, and the carved and the metal images.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah was the king Deuteronomy described, and his reform began not with demolition but with four years of seeking God. At sixteen he began to look for the God of David; only at twenty did he begin to pull things down.

Josiah was eight years old. This is a boy raised in the household of Amon, grandson of Manasseh, whose father was murdered by the palace staff when he was eight. Nobody taught Josiah to seek God; the last two men on that throne had spent their lives teaching Judah the opposite.

To the right hand or to the left. This is a quotation, and knowing where it comes from changes the chapter. Deuteronomy 17, which lays down what a king of Israel may be, ends: that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers, and that he may not turn aside from the commandment, either to the right hand or to the left (17:20). So the Chronicler measures Josiah by the standard God set for kings, and he meets it. Remember that passage, because the verses just before it require every king to keep his own copy of the law and read in it all the days of his life (17:18–19), and Josiah has never seen one.

In the eighth year of his reign, while he was yet a boy. Verse 3 gives dates, and their order explains this man. The eighth year makes him sixteen and the twelfth makes him twenty. At sixteen, with the country still full of his grandfather’s shrines, he started looking for the God of David. Then he waited four years before he touched anything.

Seeking before reform. Everything that follows, the axes, the dust on the graves, the sweep through the northern ruins, the covenant read aloud to a nation, stands on those four private years. Reform that does not begin with seeking God is only ever demolition. What made Josiah different from a young man with strong opinions about other people’s religion is that he had spent four years wanting God before he lifted a hammer.

Chronicles and Kings compared. Chronicles has the reform begin before the book was found (vv. 3–7), Kings after (2 Kings 22–23). Josiah began purging idolatry in his twelfth year; the finding of the book in his eighteenth year drove the reform much further. Kings tells it all at once.

verseByVerse.quote: And they chopped down the altars of the Baals in his presence, and he cut down the incense altars that stood above them. And he broke in pieces the Asherim and the carved and the metal images, and he made dust of them and scattered it over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them. He also burned the bones of the priests on their altars and cleansed Judah and Jerusalem. And in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, and as far as Naphtali, in their ruins all around, he broke down the altars and beat the Asherim and the images into powder and cut down all the incense altars throughout all the land of Israel. Then he returned to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah ground the idols to dust, fulfilled a three-hundred-year-old prophecy without knowing it, and carried his cleansing into the ruins of the north, because the whole land belonged to God.

In his presence. He stood in the wreckage while it happened, and the verbs move from they to he in the middle of the sentence.

He made dust of them and scattered it over the graves. He ground the idols to powder and emptied the powder over the graves of the men who had worshipped them. Everyone who watched understood: this is what your gods came to, and this is where they have left you. The idol and the idolater in the same handful of dust.

He also burned the bones of the priests on their altars. And a very old prophecy comes true. A man of God had foretold that a king, Josiah by name, would burn human bones on Jeroboam’s altar (1 Kings 13:2). That was spoken some three centuries before, and nothing in this chapter suggests the king knew the prophecy existed. He was simply doing the next right thing in front of him, and an ancient word came true by his hands.

Named in advance. Many critical scholars think the name was written into 1 Kings 13 after the event. The text presents it as true prediction, of a piece with Isaiah naming Cyrus (Isaiah 44:28): the God who rules history can name his servants before they are born. The question turns, in the end, on whether such a God exists; this commentary believes he does and reads the verse as it stands.

As far as Naphtali. Then the geography opens out. Manasseh, Ephraim and Naphtali are northern tribes, and Josiah has no authority in their towns, because nobody has: the northern kingdom fell to Assyria a lifetime ago. A king of Judah walked through burned-out villages and dismantled the altars of a country that no longer existed. He could go there at all probably because Assyria’s hold on its western provinces was failing after the death of its last great king, Ashurbanipal, around 630 BC.

Why he did it. There was no political gain in it. He did it because the ground belonged to God and the altars were an offence on it, and somebody was finally in the neighbourhood who cared.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind “in their ruins all around” (v. 6) is obscure, and the consonants can be read in more than one way. Translations offer “in their ruins”, “with their swords”, or, in older English, “with their mattocks”. The ESV’s reading fits the setting of a land long since devastated by Assyria, but the point of the verse does not depend on the phrase: Josiah cleansed the north as well as the south.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Kings of Judah Had Let It Go to Ruin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cleansing comes before rebuilding, and the work of God’s house is done faithfully. In his eighteenth year, with land and temple cleansed, Josiah sends three officials to repair the house of the LORD (v. 8). The money, collected by Levites at the doors from what was left of the northern tribes as well as from Judah and Benjamin, is paid to workmen for stone and timber to restore what the kings of Judah had let fall into ruin (vv. 9–11). The men work faithfully under Levite overseers, with musicians directing the labourers and Levite scribes, officials and gatekeepers at their posts (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The repair is honest about who caused the damage: the kings of Judah, not the Assyrians or the weather. The Chronicler writes that about his own dynasty, and the confession comes before the restoration, as it does in any true repentance.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 12 puts the choir in charge of the scaffolding. If you have a gift that is usually used up front, there may be seasons when the house of God needs it on the building site instead, and that is no demotion.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the eighteenth year of his reign, when he had cleansed the land and the house, he sent Shaphan the son of Azaliah, and Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah the son of Joahaz, the recorder, to repair the house of the LORD his God. They came to Hilkiah the high priest and gave him the money that had been brought into the house of God, which the Levites, the keepers of the threshold, had collected from Manasseh and Ephraim and from all the remnant of Israel and from all Judah and Benjamin and from the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And they gave it to the workmen who were working in the house of the LORD. And the workmen who were working in the house of the LORD gave it for repairing and restoring the house. They gave it to the carpenters and the builders to buy quarried stone, and timber for binders and beams for the buildings that the kings of Judah had let go to ruin. And the men did the work faithfully. Over them were set Jahath and Obadiah the Levites, of the sons of Merari, and Zechariah and Meshullam, of the sons of the Kohathites, to have oversight. The Levites, all who were skillful with instruments of music, were over the burden-bearers and directed all who did work in every kind of service, and some of the Levites were scribes and officials and gatekeepers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having cleansed the land, Josiah repaired God’s house, and the work was paid for by north and south together and carried out faithfully by Levites who turned out to have every skill it needed.

When he had cleansed the land and the house. Cleansed first, then repaired. Six years of clearing out came before a single stone was cut.

Hilkiah the high priest. The money goes through the high priest, and one detail in its description is easy to miss. It was collected by the Levites who kept the doors, from Manasseh and Ephraim and from all the remnant of Israel and from all Judah and Benjamin. Northerners were putting money in the box. Whatever was left of the ten tribes after the Assyrian deportations was helping to pay for the temple in Jerusalem.

The men did the work faithfully. The word that ran through Hezekiah’s storerooms (31:12–20). Where the job is stone, timber and other people’s money, it is the adjective Scripture keeps reaching for.

All who were skillful with instruments of music. A detail that ought to make anyone smile: the musicians run the building site. Twice now, when the house of God has needed hard, unglamorous work, the first men to put their instruments down and pick something else up have been the singers (29:12–16).

Some of the Levites were scribes and officials and gatekeepers. The clerks who kept the accounts, the administrators and the men on the doors all came from the same tribe. A body of people set apart for the service of God turned out to contain, between them, every skill a national restoration needed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God’s word is truly heard, it humbles even the best of people. While the money is being brought out, Hilkiah the priest finds the Book of the Law of the LORD given through Moses (v. 14). Shaphan the secretary reports on the building work and then, almost in passing, mentions the book and reads it to the king (vv. 15–18). Josiah tears his clothes (v. 19) and sends five men to inquire of the LORD for himself and for the remnant of Israel and Judah, confessing that God’s wrath is great because their fathers had not kept his word (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Deuteronomy 17 required every king to keep a copy of the law and read in it all the days of his life. Josiah is measured by that same passage in verse 2, and verse 19 is the first time he hears it. The statute had been neglected so completely that the book had to be discovered before it could be obeyed.
verseByVerse.examples: It is possible to keep a Bible in the house, or a church, and lose it all the same. The remedy is not dramatic. It is to open the book and let it be read aloud, as Shaphan did, and to listen.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were bringing out the money that had been brought into the house of the LORD, Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the Law of the LORD given through Moses. Then Hilkiah answered and said to Shaphan the secretary, "I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD." And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan. Shaphan brought the book to the king, and further reported to the king, "All that was committed to your servants they are doing. They have emptied out the money that was found in the house of the LORD and have given it into the hand of the overseers and the workmen." Then Shaphan the secretary told the king, "Hilkiah the priest has given me a book." And Shaphan read from it before the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law of God had been lost inside God’s own house, and it was found not by a search but in the course of a building job. Its rediscovery, announced in the flattest sentence of the chapter, split Josiah’s reign in two.

Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the Law of the LORD. Found it. That word takes something for granted. The covenant document, the charter of the nation, was lost, inside the building whose reason for existing was to house it.

While they were bringing out the money. Nobody went looking. It surfaced because somebody was carrying money out of a room, and there it was.

What two generations can do. Manasseh reigned fifty-five years and Amon two, and by the end of it a high priest could walk through the house of God every day of his working life and not know where the Bible was. The idols in chapter 33 are more spectacular; this verse is more frightening. A nation does not usually decide to abandon the word of God. It mislays it.

Hilkiah the priest has given me a book. Shaphan’s report is a masterpiece of understatement: accounts in order, contractors paid, works proceeding, and then, as a second item, the book. Not the law of God; a book. Whether Shaphan was being careful or had no idea what he was holding, the flattest sentence in the chapter is the one everything turns on. Then he read it aloud, as a secretary does with a document, and the reign of Judah’s last good king split in two while a civil servant read.

Was this book forged then, as critics say? The people recognised it at once as the law of Moses, long neglected; Josiah grieved because their fathers had not kept it (v. 21). It was a lost copy of an old book, most likely Deuteronomy or the whole Pentateuch. Since the nineteenth century many scholars have held that Deuteronomy, or its core, was written in Josiah’s day; others answer that the reform had begun before the book was found (vv. 3–7), and that much in Deuteronomy, such as its laws for a conquest not yet made and a king not yet chosen, fits an earlier age. The date of its final form is still debated; this commentary holds that its substance comes from Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes. And the king commanded Hilkiah, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Abdon the son of Micah, Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah the king's servant, saying, "Go, inquire of the LORD for me and for those who are left in Israel and in Judah, concerning the words of the book that has been found.
