For great is the wrath of the LORD that is poured out on us, because our fathers have not kept the word of the LORD, to do according to all that is written in this book."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the law was read, the best king Judah had seen in a century tore his clothes, because God’s word measures us not against others but against God himself. Then he sent to ask for mercy, owning his fathers’ guilt as his own.

When the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes. He did not take it away to consider or ask for a summary. It was read to him and he tore his clothes in the room.

How far he had already come. He had been seeking God for ten years. He had purged Judah of its high places, walked the ruins of the north pulling down altars, and put a major restoration in hand. By any measure available to him he was the best king Judah had seen since Hezekiah.

The word genuinely heard. Such is the effect of the word of God genuinely heard rather than merely handled. It did not confirm him in his reforms; it showed him how far he and his people still fell short. The book does not measure us against the previous generation, or our own past, or what our friends think. It measures us against God, and no reading of it leaves an honest man comfortable. Anyone who can sit through the reading of Scripture week after week entirely at ease should ask whether they have been hearing it at all. But the same book that tore Josiah open sent him to the mercy of God, and the next verses show that mercy waiting.

The book that reads its reader. Modern people have been trained to read as critics: what does the author want, what can I take, what can I leave. With most books that is the right skill. But a person who stands over every text can never be stood over by one. Josiah had every reason to read as a critic: he was the king, the reformer, the man in charge. Instead he let the book do the reading, and it found him out. That is what Scripture claims for itself: it is discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart (Hebrews 4:12). We resist that kind of reading for the same reason we put off a doctor we suspect has bad news. What makes it bearable is what Josiah found next. The book that exposes us also tells us the sentence has been carried by another, and a person who knows that can come to the Bible as a patient rather than a critic, and go away healed.

Ahikam the son of Shaphan. Two of the five men he sends are from one family: Shaphan, who had just read the book aloud, and his son Ahikam. Follow that family and it runs to the end of the story. Ahikam later put himself between Jeremiah and a mob that wanted him dead (Jeremiah 26:24). And when the city has fallen, the temple is ash and the king is blinded and gone, the man Nebuchadnezzar leaves in charge of whoever is still alive in Judah is Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan (2 Kings 25:22). A secretary read a scroll aloud in a throne room, and his son and grandson spent their lives protecting what was left of the people that scroll belonged to.

For those who are left in Israel and in Judah. He knows what he is king of: a remnant in a small hill country, with the north in ruins and empires on both horizons.

Because our fathers have not kept the word of the LORD. He takes the family guilt onto himself, as Hezekiah did a century earlier (29:6). His grandfather filled the temple with idols, and he does not say they.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–28 — Because Your Heart Was Tender
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word brings both judgment and mercy, and mercy goes to the humble. The delegation goes to Huldah the prophetess (v. 22). Her answer has two halves. To the nation: every curse written in the book will fall on this place, because they have forsaken the LORD, and his wrath will not be quenched (vv. 23–25). To the king: because his heart was tender, and he humbled himself, tore his clothes and wept, God has heard him; he will be gathered to his grave in peace and will not see the disaster (vv. 26–28).
verseByVerse.theology: Both halves are spoken by the same prophet in the same breath, and neither softens the other. The judgment on Judah is settled and will not be recalled; the mercy to this one man is equally settled.
verseByVerse.examples: Some readers are carrying a judgment they cannot reverse: a marriage ended, a child estranged, a diagnosis. Huldah's word shows that God can be utterly firm about consequences and utterly tender toward the person who comes to him humbly in the middle of them, in the same breath.

verseByVerse.quote: So Hilkiah and those whom the king had sent went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tokhath, son of Hasrah, keeper of the wardrobe (now she lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter) and spoke to her to that effect. And she said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: 'Tell the man who sent you to me, Thus says the LORD, Behold, I will bring disaster upon this place and upon its inhabitants, all the curses that are written in the book that was read before the king of Judah. Because they have forsaken me and have made offerings to other gods, that they might provoke me to anger with all the works of their hands, therefore my wrath will be poured out on this place and will not be quenched.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s answer through Huldah was that the curses written in the book would fall on Judah, and that not even the best reform the nation ever saw would turn them back.

Went to Huldah the prophetess. Israel’s high priest and four officials of the crown walk across Jerusalem to ask a woman what God is saying. The Chronicler gives Huldah’s address and her husband’s job (he looked after the royal wardrobe), but no explanation of why she was the one they went to, though Jeremiah had been prophesying in Judah for five years (Jeremiah 1:2).

Tell the man who sent you to me. A delegation arrives from the throne of David with the high priest at its head, and she calls its sender a man. She is not being rude; she speaks for someone in whose presence there are no kings, only men. Two verses later she does use the title, but by then it is clear that before God he is first of all a man.

I will bring disaster upon this place. The word is not softened by a syllable, and the men who wrote it down were the men it condemned.

All the curses that are written in the book. Deuteronomy ends with a long chapter of them, siege, famine, exile, a nation scattered, read out to Israel before it entered the land, so that nobody could say afterwards they had not been told. Huldah brings no new information. She announces that a warning which had sat in the archive for some seven centuries is now to be carried out.

Because they have forsaken me. The charge this book has brought against king after king since Rehoboam is here brought against the whole nation, and the sentence is final. Will not be quenched: the reform now in progress, the best Judah would ever see, was not going to stop it.

Facing it honestly. Josiah’s reformation was real, thorough and God-honouring, and it did not save the country. Sin persisted in long enough reaches a point where its consequences can no longer be turned back. It does not follow that the reform was pointless: God sent the word, the king obeyed it, a generation heard the Scriptures read aloud, and the mercy in the second half of Huldah’s oracle exists precisely because he did.

Why go to Huldah? She was a prophetess near the palace, trusted, and God gave his word through her. This was prophecy given directly, not the office of priest or elder, which Scripture gives to men (1 Timothy 2:12).

verseByVerse.quote: But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the LORD, thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Regarding the words that you have heard, because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God when you heard his words against this place and its inhabitants, and you have humbled yourself before me and have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you, declares the LORD. Behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your grave in peace, and your eyes shall not see all the disaster that I will bring upon this place and its inhabitants.'" And they brought back word to the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgment on Judah stood, but the king who had heard God’s word with a tender heart was heard in turn, and spared the sight of the disaster. God commended him not for what he built but for how he wept.

But to the king of Judah. The same prophet, the same breath, and now a word to one man.

Because your heart was tender. Four things are named, in the order they happened. His heart was tender. He humbled himself. He tore his clothes. He wept. None of those is an achievement; not one is a reform, a demolition, a building programme or a policy. God’s commendation of the most energetic king in the book says nothing at all about what he built.

Where a tender heart comes from. A tender heart is the opposite of the stiff neck Hezekiah warned the northerners about (30:8). Where did Josiah get his, in that palace? Ezekiel would answer within a lifetime: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26), and with it God’s own Spirit within (36:27). The tenderness God commends is the tenderness God gives.

I also have heard you. Judah would not be spared and Josiah was heard, from the same mouth in the same oracle.

Gathered to your grave in peace. The reader who goes on will hit a difficulty, so it is better to meet it now: Josiah is killed by archers in a battle at Megiddo (35:23–24). That is not what anyone usually means by dying in peace, and the text is not embarrassed about it. What was promised was not a quiet death but this: he would be gathered to his fathers, buried in their tombs in his own city, mourned by his own people, and his eyes would not see the disaster. All of that happened. He died before Egypt’s puppet kings, before Nebuchadnezzar, before the walls came down and the house he had repaired was burned. God’s mercy to him was not a long life. It was that he did not have to watch.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Told that the nation’s sentence will not be revoked, Josiah still leads it back to God. He gathers the elders and all the people, great and small, and reads them the whole Book of the Covenant himself (vv. 29–30). Standing in his place, he binds himself first to keep God’s commandments with all his heart and soul (v. 31), then brings all who are present into the covenant (v. 32). He removes the abominations from all Israel’s territory, and all his days the people do not turn away from the LORD (v. 33), a faithfulness that will last exactly as long as he does.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 31 has the king binding himself to the words that had been read with all his heart and all his soul, the language of the first commandment as Israel recited it. He does not command the covenant and then watch. He makes it first, out loud, and then brings the nation in.
verseByVerse.examples: Those who lead, whether in a home, a church or a workplace, cannot ask others to go where they have not gone. Josiah's people followed a man who had bound himself first, and the note on verse 33 shows how much their faithfulness depended on him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king sent and gathered together all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem. And the king went up to the house of the LORD, with all the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the priests and the Levites, all the people both great and small. And he read in their hearing all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD. And the king stood in his place and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes, with all his heart and all his soul, to perform the words of the covenant that were written in this book.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though nothing could now save the nation, Josiah read the whole covenant to all the people and bound himself to it first, with all his heart and soul. He did the one thing that could not help him at all, because it was right.

All the people both great and small. Told that the sentence on the nation will not be revoked, he calls the whole country together. A lesser man would have taken Huldah’s second paragraph and gone quiet. He had a personal guarantee of peace in his lifetime. He could have kept the reforms ticking over and let the disaster fall in somebody else’s time, which is what Hezekiah had settled for (2 Kings 20:19).

He read in their hearing all the words. The king read it. Not the high priest, not Shaphan, not a Levite appointed for the purpose: the man on the throne stood up in front of the whole population and read the Bible aloud, the curses included. Deuteronomy had said a king should read in the law all the days of his life (17:19). Judah’s last good king found the book at twenty-six and began by reading it to everybody he had.

The king stood in his place. By the pillar where the king stood, where seven-year-old Joash had been crowned two centuries before (23:13). And what he commits himself to is the first and great commandment, with all his heart and all his soul, in the words Israel was told to talk of when they lay down and when they rose (Deuteronomy 6:5–7).

Made a covenant before the LORD. He binds himself first, in public, and only then turns to the nation. Nobody has ever been led anywhere by a man who had not gone there first.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he made all who were present in Jerusalem and in Benjamin join in it. And the inhabitants of Jerusalem did according to the covenant of God, the God of their fathers. And Josiah took away all the abominations from all the territory that belonged to the people of Israel and made all who were present in Israel serve the LORD their God. All his days they did not turn away from following the LORD, the God of their fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah brought the whole people into the covenant and cleared the land of its idols, yet their faithfulness lasted only as long as he lived. The best king in a century could not give his people a new heart; that waited for another King.

He made all who were present in Jerusalem and in Benjamin join in it. The covenant was not left as a royal gesture to be admired; he put the whole assembly into it with him.

Josiah took away all the abominations. All the abominations, from all the territory, including the northern ruins. This is the most complete reform in the book, carried out by a man who had been told it would not avert the judgment.

All his days they did not turn away. The last clause of the chapter casts a shadow. The Chronicler has used that construction before, and it never means anything good about the people it describes. Joash did right all the days of Jehoiada the priest (24:2), then buried him and turned. Uzziah sought God in the days of Zechariah (26:5), outlived his teacher and walked into the sanctuary with a censer. Now the same kind of phrase is used of a whole nation. Judah’s faithfulness had a lifespan, and it was Josiah’s. Thirteen years after this covenant he would be carried home from Megiddo in his second chariot, and within a generation the book he found would be ash and the people who swore that covenant would be walking to Babylon.

Why another King was needed. He sought God as a boy, obeyed the book the day he heard it, tore his clothes over his family’s sin, read the Scriptures to a nation with his own mouth and bound himself to them with all his heart and soul, and the obedience he produced in his people lasted exactly as long as he lived. The covenant that holds is not one made by a good man at a pillar, but one made by a Son of David whose days do not end. He kept the first commandment whole in our place, wrote the law not on a scroll to be mislaid in a storeroom but on the hearts of his people (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10), and gives to hard men and women the one thing God commended in Josiah and no one can manufacture: a tender heart.

keyVerse.quote: because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God when you heard his words against this place and its inhabitants, and you have humbled yourself before me and have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you, declares the LORD.
keyVerse.note: God’s verdict on the most energetic reformer in the book says nothing about what he built and everything about how he heard. Josiah is the clearest picture in Chronicles of the humbling that 7:14 asks for, and of the God who hears it. The tender heart commended here is the heart God promises to give (Ezekiel 36:26).

34.reflection:
Josiah spent four years seeking God before he began to pull down idols. What is the danger of zeal for reform that does not begin with seeking God, in a church or in a person?

The Book of the Law was lost inside the temple. In what ways can Christians or churches “mislay” the Bible while still keeping it on the shelf?

Josiah tore his clothes when he heard God’s word, though he was already the best king in a century. What does it look like to let Scripture read us, rather than only reading it? When has it last humbled you?

The people followed the LORD only “all his days”. How can we make sure our faith rests on Christ and not on a gifted leader or a good season in a church’s life?

35.title: No Passover Like It
35.text: <sup>1</sup>Josiah kept a Passover to the LORD in Jerusalem. And they slaughtered the Passover lamb on the fourteenth day of the first month.<sup>2</sup>He appointed the priests to their offices and encouraged them in the service of the house of the LORD.<sup>3</sup>And he said to the Levites who taught all Israel and who were holy to the LORD, "Put the holy ark in the house that Solomon the son of David, king of Israel, built. You need not carry it on your shoulders. Now serve the LORD your God and his people Israel.<sup>4</sup>Prepare yourselves according to your fathers' houses by your divisions, as prescribed in the writing of David king of Israel and the document of Solomon his son.<sup>5</sup>And stand in the Holy Place according to the groupings of the fathers' houses of your brothers the lay people, and according to the division of the Levites by fathers' household.<sup>6</sup>And slaughter the Passover lamb, and consecrate yourselves, and prepare for your brothers, to do according to the word of the LORD by Moses."<sup>7</sup>Then Josiah contributed to the lay people, as Passover offerings for all who were present, lambs and young goats from the flock to the number of 30,000, and 3,000 bulls; these were from the king's possessions.<sup>8</sup>And his officials contributed willingly to the people, to the priests, and to the Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the chief officers of the house of God, gave to the priests for the Passover offerings 2,600 Passover lambs and 300 bulls.<sup>9</sup>Conaniah also, and Shemaiah and Nethanel his brothers, and Hashabiah and Jeiel and Jozabad, the chiefs of the Levites, gave to the Levites for the Passover offerings 5,000 lambs and young goats and 500 bulls.<sup>10</sup>When the service had been prepared for, the priests stood in their place, and the Levites in their divisions according to the king's command.<sup>11</sup>And they slaughtered the Passover lamb, and the priests threw the blood that they received from them while the Levites flayed the sacrifices.<sup>12</sup>And they set aside the burnt offerings that they might distribute them according to the groupings of the fathers' houses of the lay people, to offer to the LORD, as it is written in the Book of Moses. And so they did with the bulls.<sup>13</sup>And they roasted the Passover lamb with fire according to the rule; and they boiled the holy offerings in pots, in cauldrons, and in pans, and carried them quickly to all the lay people.<sup>14</sup>And afterward they prepared for themselves and for the priests, because the priests, the sons of Aaron, were offering the burnt offerings and the fat parts until night; so the Levites prepared for themselves and for the priests, the sons of Aaron.<sup>15</sup>The singers, the sons of Asaph, were in their place according to the command of David, and Asaph, and Heman, and Jeduthun the king's seer; and the gatekeepers were at each gate. They did not need to depart from their service, for their brothers the Levites prepared for them.<sup>16</sup>So all the service of the LORD was prepared that day, to keep the Passover and to offer burnt offerings on the altar of the LORD, according to the command of King Josiah.<sup>17</sup>And the people of Israel who were present kept the Passover at that time, and the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days.<sup>18</sup>No Passover like it had been kept in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet. None of the kings of Israel had kept such a Passover as was kept by Josiah, and the priests and the Levites, and all Judah and Israel who were present, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.<sup>19</sup>In the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah this Passover was kept.<sup>20</sup>After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Neco king of Egypt went up to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates, and Josiah went out to meet him.<sup>21</sup>But he sent envoys to him, saying, "What have we to do with each other, king of Judah? I am not coming against you this day, but against the house with which I am at war. And God has commanded me to hurry. Cease opposing God, who is with me, lest he destroy you."<sup>22</sup>Nevertheless, Josiah did not turn away from him, but disguised himself in order to fight with him. He did not listen to the words of Neco from the mouth of God, but came to fight in the plain of Megiddo.<sup>23</sup>And the archers shot King Josiah. And the king said to his servants, "Take me away, for I am badly wounded."<sup>24</sup>So his servants took him out of the chariot and carried him in his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem. And he died and was buried in the tombs of his fathers. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah.<sup>25</sup>Jeremiah also uttered a lament for Josiah; and all the singing men and singing women have spoken of Josiah in their laments to this day. They made these a rule in Israel; behold, they are written in the Laments.<sup>26</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Josiah, and his good deeds according to what is written in the Law of the LORD,<sup>27</sup>and his acts, first and last, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.
35.overview:
Where we are. In the same eighteenth year in which the Book of the Law was found and the covenant renewed (34:8–33), Josiah keeps the Passover. It is Judah’s last high point before its last good king dies.

The message. God’s word obeyed produces worship that is ordered, generous and glad: the greatest Passover since Samuel, kept “according to the word of the LORD by Moses” (v. 6). But the king who heard God’s word so well in the temple failed to hear it from an unexpected mouth, and died for it. Judah’s hope could not rest on even its best king; the God who keeps his word kept even Huldah’s promise through an archer’s arrow.

Why it was said. The first readers kept the Passover again after the return (Ezra 6:19–22) and were rebuilding temple worship with its priests, Levites, singers and gatekeepers (see the introduction). Josiah’s feast showed them worship done as it is written, and his death warned them that no reformer, however faithful, can carry a people’s faith for them.

How the chapter makes its case. Josiah keeps the feast on the right date, encourages the priests and gives the Levites new work now that the ark need not be carried (vv. 1–6). King and leaders provide the animals from their own goods (vv. 7–9). The service runs in careful order, the lamb roasted according to the rule and everyone fed, down to the singers and gatekeepers at their posts (vv. 10–15). It is the greatest Passover since Samuel (vv. 16–19). Then Josiah rides out against Neco, will not listen to words the narrator says came from God, and is shot at Megiddo (vv. 20–24). The nation mourns him, and Jeremiah laments (v. 25). The record measures his life by the Law of the LORD, first and last (vv. 26–27).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern above all. Every Passover lamb pointed to the Lamb of God, and the descendant of David who kept the feast on its night took its bread and said it was his body: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). And by the need the chapter exposes: the mourning at Megiddo became, in Zechariah, the measure of Israel’s grief over “him whom they have pierced” (Zechariah 12:10–11), the King who did not fail and yet died for those who did.

For us. Worship God as he has said, generously and in good order, caring for those who serve unseen. Weigh what is said by whether it is true, not only by who says it. And grieve your losses honestly, with the hope that the true Passover Lamb has given.
35.theology:
Verse 3 shows how God's people handle a finished task: the Levites' oldest duty is retired and a new one given in the same sentence.

Verse 22 is the chapter's hardest sentence, and the narrator states it as fact rather than as Neco's claim: Josiah did not listen to Neco's words from the mouth of God. God is not confined to the channels his people find respectable, and the man in this book who heard Scripture best was deaf when the truth arrived by an unexpected road.

And Huldah's promise is kept in a shape nobody would have chosen (34:28). He was gathered to his fathers' tombs, mourned by his nation, and spared the sight of the disaster, and the means was an Egyptian arrow.
35.examples:
This time the clergy were ready, so the feast fell on the right date, and the men who paid for it were the men responsible for those who ate it. On the busiest day of the year someone made sure the Passover lamb, the one item with a rule attached, was roasted and not boiled, and someone else made sure the singers and doorkeepers were fed at their posts.

The book was found and the greatest Passover since Samuel was kept inside the same twelve months. Within a few years Israel was singing Jeremiah's lament for the king who had led it, and still singing it generations later.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — You Need Not Carry It on Your Shoulders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Obedience to the rediscovered word begins with God’s people in their places, ready to serve. Josiah keeps the Passover on its proper date, the fourteenth day of the first month, sets the priests in their offices and encourages them (vv. 1–2). He tells the Levites that the ark rests in Solomon’s house and need no longer be carried; their work now is to serve the LORD and his people, in their divisions, as David and Solomon wrote and as the LORD commanded by Moses (vv. 3–6). Then the king gives thirty-three thousand animals from his own possessions, and the leaders of temple and Levites each provide for those in their charge (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 3 formally retires the job the tribe was founded to do and supplies the replacement at once. A ministry whose original task is finished is redeployed, not disbanded.
verseByVerse.examples: Look at who gave to whom. The king gave to the lay people. The chief officers of the temple gave to the priests. The chiefs of the Levites gave to the Levites. Every man in a position of responsibility made sure the people he was responsible for could keep the feast, and paid for it himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Josiah kept a Passover to the LORD in Jerusalem. And they slaughtered the Passover lamb on the fourteenth day of the first month. He appointed the priests to their offices and encouraged them in the service of the house of the LORD. And he said to the Levites who taught all Israel and who were holy to the LORD, "Put the holy ark in the house that Solomon the son of David, king of Israel, built. You need not carry it on your shoulders. Now serve the LORD your God and his people Israel. Prepare yourselves according to your fathers' houses by your divisions, as prescribed in the writing of David king of Israel and the document of Solomon his son. And stand in the Holy Place according to the groupings of the fathers' houses of your brothers the lay people, and according to the division of the Levites by fathers' household. And slaughter the Passover lamb, and consecrate yourselves, and prepare for your brothers, to do according to the word of the LORD by Moses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah kept the Passover on its proper date, with priests encouraged and Levites given new work, everything done according to God’s word and nothing invented on the day.

On the fourteenth day of the first month. The correct date. A century earlier Hezekiah had to keep his Passover a month late because too few priests had consecrated themselves and the people had not gathered (30:3). This time the clergy were ready. That is what six years of clearing and repairing had bought.

Encouraged them in the service of the house of the LORD. As Hezekiah had encouraged the Levites (30:22) and his commanders (32:6). Good leadership in this book comes from men who took the trouble to say something personal to the people doing the work.

You need not carry it on your shoulders. Carrying the ark was the founding work of the Levites from the wilderness onwards, and Uzzah had died when it was done wrongly (1 Chronicles 13:9–10). David had already said the carrying days were over once there was a permanent house (1 Chronicles 23:26), and Josiah says it again.

Now serve the LORD your God. The old task ends and a new one is handed over in the same breath. And the same verse calls them the Levites who taught all Israel. That began as Jehoshaphat’s initiative, sending Levites round the towns with the Book of the Law (17:7–9); two and a half centuries later it is simply what Levites do. Any church that has had to retire a ministry knows how hard this is. Josiah tells the men who gave their lives to it plainly, and does not leave them without work.

The writing of David king of Israel. The instructions name three authorities: the writing of David, the document of Solomon, and the word of the LORD by Moses. Nothing here is being invented on the day.

Uncertain wording. “Put the holy ark in the house” seems to assume the ark had been moved, perhaps during Manasseh’s reign or the recent repairs, but we are not told why or where. Some read the words as “Leave the holy ark in the house”: it is already there, so you need not carry it. The Chronicler does not explain, and it is better to leave the gap open than to fill it. Either way the point is the same: the ark’s travelling days are over, and the Levites have other work.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Josiah contributed to the lay people, as Passover offerings for all who were present, lambs and young goats from the flock to the number of 30,000, and 3,000 bulls; these were from the king's possessions. And his officials contributed willingly to the people, to the priests, and to the Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the chief officers of the house of God, gave to the priests for the Passover offerings 2,600 Passover lambs and 300 bulls. Conaniah also, and Shemaiah and Nethanel his brothers, and Hashabiah and Jeiel and Jozabad, the chiefs of the Levites, gave to the Levites for the Passover offerings 5,000 lambs and young goats and 500 bulls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king and the leaders paid for the feast out of their own goods, each providing for those in his care, so that no one was turned away from God’s table for being poor.

These were from the king’s possessions. Thirty-three thousand animals out of the royal estate, so that ordinary families who had come up to Jerusalem would have something to sacrifice. And the officials gave willingly, not under a levy. Hezekiah’s great feast, itself the largest since Solomon, had seen king and princes give two thousand bulls and seventeen thousand sheep between them (30:24). Josiah’s contribution alone far outstrips it.

The chief officers of the house of God. The list explains itself: the three chief officers of the temple provided for the priests, and the six chiefs of the Levites provided for their own tribe. Each man provisioned his own people. Nobody passed the cost down to the men who would be working, and nobody waited for somebody further up to notice.

Why they gave. They gave at a feast that remembered the rescue from Egypt, which nobody in Israel had paid for. Generosity to the people under your care grows from that: the God who rescued us gave first. And bearing the cost for those in your charge is the difference between leading them and merely being over them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Worship ordered by God’s word becomes a feast in which everyone is fed. The priests and Levites stand in their places; the blood is thrown, the animals flayed, the burnt offerings shared out as written in the Book of Moses (vv. 10–12). The lamb is roasted according to the rule, the other offerings boiled and carried quickly to the people (v. 13). The Levites cook last, for themselves and the priests who serve till night, and feed the singers and gatekeepers at their posts (vv. 14–15). The verdict: no Passover like it since Samuel, and none by any king, kept in the very year the book was found (vv. 16–19).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 shows what obedience looks like when nobody is watching the detail: two ways of cooking kept going side by side at enormous scale, because the Passover lamb had to be roasted (Exod 12:8-9).
verseByVerse.examples: Nobody had to abandon his post to look after himself: those who could not leave their work were fed at it.

verseByVerse.quote: When the service had been prepared for, the priests stood in their place, and the Levites in their divisions according to the king's command. And they slaughtered the Passover lamb, and the priests threw the blood that they received from them while the Levites flayed the sacrifices. And they set aside the burnt offerings that they might distribute them according to the groupings of the fathers' houses of the lay people, to offer to the LORD, as it is written in the Book of Moses. And so they did with the bulls. And they roasted the Passover lamb with fire according to the rule; and they boiled the holy offerings in pots, in cauldrons, and in pans, and carried them quickly to all the lay people. And afterward they prepared for themselves and for the priests, because the priests, the sons of Aaron, were offering the burnt offerings and the fat parts until night; so the Levites prepared for themselves and for the priests, the sons of Aaron. The singers, the sons of Asaph, were in their place according to the command of David, and Asaph, and Heman, and Jeduthun the king's seer; and the gatekeepers were at each gate. They did not need to depart from their service, for their brothers the Levites prepared for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The feast ran as God’s word directed, down to the way the lamb was cooked, and it was organised so that everyone was fed, including the priests who worked till night and the singers and gatekeepers who could not leave their posts.

The priests stood in their place. This is a very large organisation working properly, and the Chronicler evidently enjoys it. Every man knows where he stands and what is in his hands, and the burnt offerings are distributed as it is written in the Book of Moses.

They roasted the Passover lamb with fire according to the rule. A detail only a careful man would record. Exodus is explicit that the Passover lamb is not to be eaten raw or boiled in water, but roasted (12:9); the other holy offerings were normally boiled. So on a day when tens of thousands of animals were being prepared at speed, somebody made sure the one item with a rule attached was done by the rule. That is obedience in the small technical matter nobody in the crowd would have checked, on the busiest day of the year, from people who had just been given back the book.

Carried them quickly to all the lay people. Hot, and served fast, to families who had walked a long way.

Until night. The priests were at the altar until dark and had no chance to eat. So the Levites, who had spent the day flaying carcasses, cooked the priests’ dinner after everyone else had been fed. The singers sang all day without breaking off, and the men on the doors never left the doors, because others brought them food where they stood.

A well-ordered body. That is what a well-ordered body of people looks like, and it is a better picture of a healthy church than most in circulation. Nobody had to choose between doing his job and eating. Nobody’s post was left unmanned because he had needs of his own. Somebody had thought about the singers’ stomachs, and the Chronicler gave it two verses in the account of the greatest Passover since Samuel.

Roasted or boiled? The Hebrew verb behind both “roasted” and “boiled” in verse 13 means “cook” in general; “with fire” and “in pots” show which is meant. The same verb in Deuteronomy 16:7, sometimes translated “boil”, need mean no more than “cook”, so that law does not conflict with the rule in Exodus.

verseByVerse.quote: So all the service of the LORD was prepared that day, to keep the Passover and to offer burnt offerings on the altar of the LORD, according to the command of King Josiah. And the people of Israel who were present kept the Passover at that time, and the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days. No Passover like it had been kept in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet. None of the kings of Israel had kept such a Passover as was kept by Josiah, and the priests and the Levites, and all Judah and Israel who were present, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. In the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah this Passover was kept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No king had ever kept a Passover like this one, and it came in the very year the lost book was found. A rediscovered Scripture, obeyed, can renew a people within a single year.

All the service of the LORD was prepared. Prepared is the word that has run through these chapters. It means putting things in order and in place, and that is what a reformation actually consists of once the shouting is over.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days. The Passover night opened a week of eating bread without yeast, as at the first Passover, when Israel left Egypt in haste (see Feast of Unleavened Bread).

Since the days of Samuel the prophet. The comparison reaches further back than the one used for Hezekiah, whose Passover was unmatched since the time of Solomon (30:26). This one reaches back past Solomon, past David, past the whole monarchy, to Samuel, the last man to lead Israel before there were any kings at all. And then he says it a second way, so that nobody misses it: none of the kings of Israel had kept such a Passover. Not one, in four hundred years of them.

In the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah. Turn back one chapter: that is the year he sent Shaphan to repair the temple, the book was found and read aloud, he tore his clothes, Huldah answered, and he made the covenant at his pillar. All of that is one year. The Bible turned up in the temple, and within that same year the nation kept the greatest Passover since Samuel. That is what a rediscovered Scripture can do when the man who hears it does not put it down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–25 — From the Mouth of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even the best of kings can fail to listen, and God’s word stands whoever brings it. When Neco of Egypt marches north to Carchemish, Josiah goes out to stop him (v. 20). Neco warns him that God has sent him and that Josiah is opposing God (v. 21). Josiah disguises himself and fights at Megiddo, not listening to words the narrator says came from the mouth of God (v. 22). Archers wound him; he is carried to Jerusalem in his second chariot, dies and is buried with his fathers, and all Judah mourns (vv. 23–24). Jeremiah laments him, and the singers still sing his lament (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 22 settles whether Neco spoke the truth: the warning really was from God, though it came through a pagan king with an agenda of his own.
verseByVerse.examples: A disguise made no difference to an arrow, for Josiah any more than for Ahab.

verseByVerse.quote: After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Neco king of Egypt went up to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates, and Josiah went out to meet him. But he sent envoys to him, saying, "What have we to do with each other, king of Judah? I am not coming against you this day, but against the house with which I am at war. And God has commanded me to hurry. Cease opposing God, who is with me, lest he destroy you." Nevertheless, Josiah did not turn away from him, but disguised himself in order to fight with him. He did not listen to the words of Neco from the mouth of God, but came to fight in the plain of Megiddo.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah, who had listened so well to God’s word in the temple, would not listen when God warned him through a pagan king, and he went to his death at Megiddo. God’s word is to be weighed by its truth, not by the mouth that carries it.

After all this. The building work finished, the book found and obeyed, the covenant made, the Passover kept. Everything a king could do had been done, and the chapter has seven verses left.

Neco king of Egypt went up to fight at Carchemish. Egypt was marching north to prop up the last of Assyria against Babylon, and the road ran past Josiah’s border. He went out to stop it, probably for good reasons, since an Egyptian victory would have left a great power on both sides of him. The year was 609 BC. Nineveh had fallen to the Babylonians and Medes three years before, and the last king of Assyria was holding out at Harran, far to the north.

Cease opposing God, who is with me. A pharaoh telling a son of David to stop opposing God. Everything in a reader wants to dismiss it: he is a pagan with an army on the move and every reason to say whatever gets Judah out of his way.

From the mouth of God. This is not Neco’s claim repeated; it is the historian’s own verdict on it. The warning was genuine.

He did not listen to the words of Neco. The hardest thing in this chapter is aimed at good people. Josiah is the man who tore his clothes the moment a book was read to him; nobody in this book listens better. And when God’s word came to him through the wrong sort of mouth, from a man whose religion was false and whose motives were mixed, he did not hear it at all. A believer can become so practised at hearing God through the expected channels (the pulpit, the page, the people who talk as we do) that a true word arriving by another route is dismissed before it is weighed. The test is never the messenger’s credentials. It is whether the thing said is true, and that has to be asked even when asking it is humiliating.

Disguised himself. The last king in this book to do that was Ahab, who went up against a prophet’s word in somebody else’s clothes and was hit by an arrow shot at random (18:29–33). The king who turned to God as none before him died copying the tactic of the worst king Israel ever had, with the same result.

A note for KJV readers. In the KJV, 2 Kings 23:29 says that Neco went up against the king of Assyria. The Hebrew can mean either, and Babylonian records show Egypt was marching to Assyria’s aid, as modern translations have it.
verseByVerse.note: Carchemish lay on the Euphrates; Neco was hurrying to support Assyria against Babylon in 609 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: And the archers shot King Josiah. And the king said to his servants, "Take me away, for I am badly wounded." So his servants took him out of the chariot and carried him in his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem. And he died and was buried in the tombs of his fathers. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah. Jeremiah also uttered a lament for Josiah; and all the singing men and singing women have spoken of Josiah in their laments to this day. They made these a rule in Israel; behold, they are written in the Laments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah died of his wound and was mourned by the whole nation, and in his death God kept every word of his promise that the king would not see the coming disaster. Jeremiah’s lament made the grief permanent, and it would become the measure of a greater mourning.

Take me away, for I am badly wounded. He was thirty-nine years old. Eight when he came to the throne, thirty-one years on it, and the last thing he says in this book is a request to be lifted out of a chariot.

Kings and Chronicles together. Kings says Neco killed him at Megiddo and his servants carried him dead to Jerusalem (2 Kings 23:29–30). Chronicles gives the fuller picture: struck down at Megiddo, he died once they had brought him home. Kings speaks of the fatal wound as the killing; the two accounts tell of the same death.

Huldah’s promise kept. Every word of her promise is kept, in a form nobody would have chosen: you shall be gathered to your grave in peace, and your eyes shall not see all the disaster (34:28). He was buried in his fathers’ tombs and mourned by his whole nation, and he did not live to watch Nebuchadnezzar’s men break the walls, burn the house he had repaired, and lead the last son of David out of the city in chains. God’s mercies do not always arrive looking like mercies. This one arrived through an Egyptian archer.

Jeremiah also uttered a lament for Josiah. Jeremiah wrote a funeral song for him. It is not the book of Lamentations, which mourns the fall of the city a generation later; it was most likely collected in the book called the Laments that we no longer have. And Israel did something nations rarely do: they made the grief permanent. Singers were still performing it when the Chronicler wrote, generations later, because somebody had decided this loss should be remembered on purpose rather than allowed to fade.

Why are we in such a hurry to stop grieving? Our culture is uneasy with grief. We give the bereaved a few days off work, speak of closure and moving on, and grow quietly worried when someone is still sad a year later, as if grief were a malfunction to be repaired. A society that has lost confidence in anything beyond death has no idea what to do with death except hurry past it. Israel wrote the lament down and sang it on purpose. That is not morbid; it is honest. Death is an enemy, not a natural transition, and Scripture never asks believers to pretend otherwise. Jesus stood at the grave of a friend he was about to raise, and wept (John 11:35). Christians do not grieve less than others, but differently: Paul writes so that we may not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Hope does not cut the lament short. It gives it somewhere to go, because the One who wept at the tomb has broken the power of the thing we are weeping over.

Another mourning at Megiddo. Zechariah, writing after the exile, says that on a coming day Jerusalem will mourn for one they have pierced, and that the mourning will be as great as the mourning for Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo (Zechariah 12:10–11). Many take that to be the mourning for Josiah. The deepest grief Israel could remember became the measure for the grief of a people looking at the one their sins had killed (John 19:37).

The last Passover that mattered. The last Passover in this book, kept better than any since Samuel, was not the last that mattered. Six centuries later a descendant of this same house sat down with twelve men at the Passover, took the bread of the feast Josiah had spent a kingdom’s wealth on, and said that it was his body. The lamb Josiah killed by the thousand was pointing at him the whole time: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The record of a life is measured by God’s word, and it keeps first and last together. The rest of Josiah’s acts, and his good deeds, are judged according to what is written in the Law of the LORD, the book found in his own reign (v. 26). His acts, first and last, are written in the book of the kings (v. 27): the great Passover and the fatal ride to Megiddo stand in the same file.
verseByVerse.theology: His deeds are recorded against a standard: according to what is written in the Law of the LORD. The book once lost in the temple has become the measure by which his whole life is recorded.
verseByVerse.examples: Some things in a good man's story are simply recorded, not explained.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Josiah, and his good deeds according to what is written in the Law of the LORD, and his acts, first and last, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah’s life is measured by the Law of the LORD he rediscovered, and the record keeps his first and last deeds together, his great Passover and his fatal ride.

His good deeds according to what is written in the Law of the LORD. That is the book that lay forgotten in the temple until men came to carry out the money. It was found in his eighteenth year, read to him by a secretary who called it a book, and by the end of that year read aloud to the whole nation and sworn to in the temple. Now, at the end of his life, it is the standard his deeds are measured by. He did not merely obey it; it became the measure of his own reign.

His acts, first and last. Both are in the file: the Passover that reached back past every king to Samuel, and the ride to Megiddo against a warning he would not weigh. The Chronicler does not reconcile them, and there is no reconciling them; the same man did both, and the second cost him his life and the country its last good reign.

First and last together. That is worth remembering when we are inclined to sort people into the useful and the failed. God’s record of a servant keeps first and last together, and the mercy is that God does not judge his servants by an average of the two. The account ends with a Passover lamb, and with a King who came after Josiah and did not put a foot wrong from Nazareth to the cross, whose obedience is counted to us in place of our own.

keyVerse.quote: No Passover like it had been kept in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet.
keyVerse.note: This is what God’s rediscovered word produced within a single year: worship ordered by Scripture, paid for generously, with everyone fed. It is the last high point of Judah’s history before the end. And every Passover lamb pointed beyond itself to Christ, the Passover lamb sacrificed for us (1 Corinthians 5:7).

35.reflection:
Josiah gave the Levites new work when their old task ended, and fed the singers and gatekeepers at their posts. What does this chapter teach about caring for those who serve in a church, especially those whose work is unseen?

The king and leaders paid for the people’s sacrifices from their own goods. How does God’s free rescue shape the way we give and the way we lead?

Josiah listened to God’s word in the temple but not when it came from Neco. Have you ever dismissed something true because of who said it? How can we weigh what we hear by whether it is true?

Israel sang Josiah’s lament for generations. How does Christian hope change the way we grieve, without hurrying us past grief?

36.title: Let Him Go Up
36.text: <sup>1</sup>The people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah and made him king in his father's place in Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem.<sup>3</sup>Then the king of Egypt deposed him in Jerusalem and laid on the land a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold.<sup>4</sup>And the king of Egypt made Eliakim his brother king over Judah and Jerusalem, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. But Neco took Jehoahaz his brother and carried him to Egypt.<sup>5</sup>Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD his God.<sup>6</sup>Against him came up Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon.<sup>7</sup>Nebuchadnezzar also carried part of the vessels of the house of the LORD to Babylon and put them in his palace in Babylon.<sup>8</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, and the abominations that he did, and what was found against him, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. And Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place.<sup>9</sup>Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned three months and ten days in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD.<sup>10</sup>In the spring of the year King Nebuchadnezzar sent and brought him to Babylon, with the precious vessels of the house of the LORD, and made his brother Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem.<sup>11</sup>Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.<sup>12</sup>He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD his God. He did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke from the mouth of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God. He stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>14</sup>All the officers of the priests and the people likewise were exceedingly unfaithful, following all the abominations of the nations. And they polluted the house of the LORD that he had made holy in Jerusalem.<sup>15</sup>The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place.<sup>16</sup>But they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD rose against his people, until there was no remedy.<sup>17</sup>Therefore he brought up against them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary and had no compassion on young man or virgin, old man or aged. He gave them all into his hand.<sup>18</sup>And all the vessels of the house of God, great and small, and the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king and of his princes, all these he brought to Babylon.<sup>19</sup>And they burned the house of God and broke down the wall of Jerusalem and burned all its palaces with fire and destroyed all its precious vessels.<sup>20</sup>He took into exile in Babylon those who had escaped from the sword, and they became servants to him and to his sons until the establishment of the kingdom of Persia,<sup>21</sup>to fulfill the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths. All the days that it lay desolate it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years.<sup>22</sup>Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and also put it in writing:<sup>23</sup>"Thus says Cyrus king of Persia, 'The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whoever is among you of all his people, may the LORD his God be with him. Let him go up.'"
36.overview:
Where we are. Josiah has died at Megiddo, mourned by the whole nation (35:24–25), and with him the last good reign. In twenty-two years four of his sons and grandsons will sit on David’s throne, and every one of them will be put there or taken away by a foreign king.

The message. God’s patience is long because his compassion is great, but it can be mocked until there is no remedy. Even then his judgment is measured and his word kept to the letter, and his last word is not ruin but return. The book ends with the house burned, and then with a door thrown open: “Let him go up” (v. 23).

Why it was said. The first readers were the people who had gone up, or their children (see the introduction). This chapter told them why the exile came: not because Babylon was strong or God was weak, but because Judah laughed at the messengers God sent in compassion. And it assured them that the same word which had foretold the seventy years had opened the way home.

How the chapter makes its case. Egypt deposes Jehoahaz, renames his brother and taxes the land (vv. 1–4). Babylon takes Jehoiakim and Jehoiachin, and the temple vessels go east in loads (vv. 5–10). Zedekiah will not humble himself before Jeremiah and breaks an oath sworn by God, and priests and people are as unfaithful as he is (vv. 11–14). Then the explanation of four centuries: God sent his messengers persistently because he had compassion, and they mocked them until there was no remedy (vv. 15–16). The Chaldeans burn the house, and the survivors go into exile while the land keeps its Sabbaths for seventy years (vv. 17–21). Then the LORD stirs up Cyrus, whose decree sends God’s people home (vv. 22–23).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by the need the chapter leaves open. David’s line comes home but never reigns again, the rebuilt house is smaller, and the promises still wait. Last of all God sent his Son (Mark 12:6). He was mocked as the prophets were; he humbled himself where Zedekiah would not (Philippians 2:8); he spoke of his own body as the temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19–21). Through him the call to go up now reaches anyone at all.

For us. Do not laugh off God’s warnings: his patience is compassion, not indifference, and it is not endless. But no ruin is so complete that God cannot open a way back, and in Christ the gate stands open. Whoever is among his people, let him go up.
36.theology:
Verse 15 gives God's motive for every prophet in this book, and it is compassion. No remedy ends the book's longest theme, the offer of healing made at the dedication of the temple (7:14). Judah did not fall short of that offer; Judah laughed at it.

Even the empty land shows the covenant being carried out as written: the land keeps the Sabbath years it was denied. Then the LORD stirred up Cyrus, as he had once stirred up the nations against his people (21:16; 1 Chr 5:26). The hand that scattered gathers, and the book ends not with a ruin but with an open gate: let him go up.
36.examples:
Judah's independence ended when a pharaoh renamed a son of David, and its temple was emptied in three loads over some twenty years. By the final generation the chief priests were as unfaithful as the king, and the people did not argue with the prophets; they laughed at them.

The house that took six chapters to build is destroyed in one sentence with no adjectives, and the fields get the rest they had been denied because nobody is left to work them. And the last words of the Hebrew Bible are a permission to go home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — A Foreign King Changed His Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Once Judah’s kings stopped listening to God, foreign powers decided who reigned. The people make Jehoahaz king, but within three months Pharaoh Neco deposes him, fines the land, makes his brother Eliakim king with a new name, Jehoiakim, and takes Jehoahaz to Egypt (vv. 1–4). Jehoiakim does evil for eleven years; Nebuchadnezzar binds him and carries off part of the temple vessels (vv. 5–8). His son Jehoiachin lasts three months and ten days before he too is taken to Babylon, with the precious vessels, and Zedekiah is put in his place (vv. 9–10). The pace of the telling quickens as the end approaches.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 4 is the whole political situation in one clause: a pharaoh takes a son of David and changes his name.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch the temple vessels through this chapter: it took some twenty years and three deportations to empty the room Solomon had filled.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah and made him king in his father's place in Jerusalem. Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. Then the king of Egypt deposed him in Jerusalem and laid on the land a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. And the king of Egypt made Eliakim his brother king over Judah and Jerusalem, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. But Neco took Jehoahaz his brother and carried him to Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Within three months of Josiah’s death, Egypt removed his son, taxed the land and renamed the next king: from now on foreign powers decide who sits on David’s throne.

The people of the land took Jehoahaz. Ordinary Judeans have kept the line of David in place through every emergency of two centuries: after the raid that emptied the palace (22:1), after two assassinations (26:1; 33:25), and now at Josiah’s grave. This is the last time they will manage it. Every king after this one is appointed or removed by a foreigner.

He reigned three months in Jerusalem. Neco has come back from the north along the road where Josiah rode out to stop him, and this time nobody stops him. He removes a king of Judah and makes the country pay tribute.

A hundred talents of silver. That sum has moved through this book like a coin passed from hand to hand. Amaziah paid it for mercenaries he had to send home (25:6–10); Jotham received it from Ammon three years running (27:5). Now Judah pays it to Egypt as the price of keeping a king at all.

Changed his name to Jehoiakim. Naming is what an owner does. Adam named the animals; God renamed Abram and Jacob; a Babylonian official will shortly rename four Hebrew boys (Daniel 1:7). Judah’s independence does not end here with a siege. It ends with a foreign king writing a different word on a list, and everyone accepting it.

Neco took Jehoahaz his brother and carried him to Egypt. The nation God brought Israel out of has one of David’s sons back, some four hundred years after David, as a prisoner.
verseByVerse.note: A talent was about 75 pounds (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD his God. Against him came up Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar also carried part of the vessels of the house of the LORD to Babylon and put them in his palace in Babylon. Now the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, and the abominations that he did, and what was found against him, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. And Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place. Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned three months and ten days in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. In the spring of the year King Nebuchadnezzar sent and brought him to Babylon, with the precious vessels of the house of the LORD, and made his brother Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon replaced Egypt as master, and the temple’s treasures began to go east in loads, while kings were moved about like pieces on a board. Nothing in God’s house was safe because it was old, beautiful or costly.

The pace of the end. The story speeds up now, and the speed is the point: eleven years, then three months and ten days, told in six verses.

Part of the vessels of the house of the LORD. Egypt is finished as the ruling power; Babylon has arrived, under Nebuchadnezzar, and it will not leave until there is nothing left to take. And the Chronicler starts counting: part of the vessels here, the precious vessels in verse 10, all the vessels of the house of God, great and small in verse 18. Three visits, three loads, some twenty years.

The day the house was finished. Turn back to the day the house was completed: Thus all the work that Solomon did for the house of the LORD was finished. And Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, and stored the silver, the gold, and all the vessels in the treasuries of the house of God (5:1). David saved for them; Solomon carried them in; Joash’s chest at the gate paid to replace what Athaliah’s sons had plundered (24:7, 14); Hezekiah’s Levites cleaned the ones Ahaz threw out and set them before the altar (29:18–19). Now they go onto carts and end up as ornaments in a Babylonian palace. Vessels were never the point of a temple.

Jehoiachin was eighteen years old. He reigned three months and ten days, and the Chronicler gives him one line of verdict and one of removal. These are not kings any more; they are men being moved about a board by somebody else’s hand.

Was Jehoiakim taken to Babylon? He was bound to be taken (v. 6), and Daniel says vessels and nobles were carried off (Daniel 1:1–2), but Kings says he died in Jerusalem (2 Kings 24:6): he was probably released and kept as a vassal.

His brother Zedekiah. Zedekiah was Jehoiachin’s uncle (2 Kings 24:17); “brother” is used broadly of a kinsman.
verseByVerse.note: Most Hebrew manuscripts give Jehoiachin’s age as eight; the Greek and 2 Kings read eighteen (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — He Did Not Humble Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last king of Judah refuses the very thing this book has called every king to do. Zedekiah reigns eleven years and does evil (v. 11). He will not humble himself before Jeremiah, who speaks from the mouth of the LORD (v. 12). He breaks the oath he swore by God to Nebuchadnezzar, and stiffens his neck and hardens his heart against turning to the LORD (v. 13). Nor is the guilt the king’s alone: the leading priests and the people are exceedingly unfaithful, following the nations’ abominations and polluting the house God had made holy (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The verb the whole book turns on, humble himself, appears one last time, with “not” in front of it, and the door of mercy that had stood open since 7:14 closes on the man who refused to walk through it.
verseByVerse.examples: A promise made in God's name to a man who does not know God is still made in God's name.

verseByVerse.quote: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD his God. He did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke from the mouth of the LORD. He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God. He stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the LORD, the God of Israel. All the officers of the priests and the people likewise were exceedingly unfaithful, following all the abominations of the nations. And they polluted the house of the LORD that he had made holy in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zedekiah refused to humble himself before God’s prophet, broke an oath sworn in God’s name, and hardened his heart, and the priests and people were as unfaithful as their king. The verb this whole book was built on is used one last time, with “not” in front of it.

He did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet. It was God’s own word at the dedication: if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven (7:14). And it was answered by the least likely people: Rehoboam with Shishak at the gate, Hezekiah over his pride, men of Asher and Zebulun walking to a Passover, and Manasseh, who had burned his sons, in an Assyrian prison.

Who spoke from the mouth of the LORD. Almost the phrase used of Neco’s warning to Josiah (35:22). Josiah could not hear God in a pagan’s mouth; his son could not hear him in a prophet’s. The problem was never the quality of the messenger.

Who had made him swear by God. He had sworn an oath in the name of the LORD to a Babylonian emperor, and he broke it; Ezekiel condemned him for it in the LORD’s name (Ezekiel 17:15–19). A promise made in God’s name is made before God, whoever is on the other side of the table, and a man who breaks one has not outwitted an enemy; he has lied about God.

He stiffened his neck and hardened his heart. This echoes Hezekiah’s letter a century earlier: Do not now be stiff-necked as your fathers were, but yield yourselves to the LORD (30:8). Neither the stiff neck nor the hard heart happens in a day; they are what a man ends up with after a long career of small refusals. The way back is the one Manasseh found: humbling oneself while the word is still being sent.

The officers of the priests and the people likewise. This book has tied the nation’s fortunes to its kings, but at the end it will not let anybody else escape the verdict. Judah had the leaders it was content with, and by the last generation the men in the temple were as unfaithful as the man on the throne.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — Until There Was No Remedy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The exile came because God’s compassion was refused, not because his power failed. Out of compassion for his people and his house, God sent his messengers again and again, but they mocked the messengers, despised his words and scoffed at his prophets until there was no remedy (vv. 15–16). So he brought the king of the Chaldeans, who had no compassion: the young are killed in the sanctuary, the treasures carried off, the house burned and the walls broken down (vv. 17–19). The survivors serve in Babylon until Persia rises, while the land keeps the Sabbaths it was denied, seventy years, as Jeremiah said (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 15 gives God's motive for four centuries of prophets, and it is compassion, for the people and for the building. Two verses later the same word comes back with a “no”: the Chaldean king God finally used had no compassion.
verseByVerse.examples: The book that has been about healing since chapter 7 says at last that there was no remedy left, and then, in its final verses, opens the gate again.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place. But they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD rose against his people, until there was no remedy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sent prophet after prophet because he had compassion on his people, and the exile came only when they had mocked his messengers until there was no remedy left. The sentence that explains four hundred years is not about wrath but about love refused.

Sent persistently to them by his messengers. Shemaiah to Rehoboam, Azariah and Hanani to Asa, Jehu to Jehoshaphat, Micaiah at the gate of Samaria, Zechariah stoned in the courtyard, Oded, Elijah’s letter, the seers who came to Manasseh, Huldah, Jeremiah: four centuries of men walking into throne rooms with unwelcome news. And the historian tells us at last why they were sent.

Because he had compassion on his people. Not because a case had to be built. He kept sending them because he loved his people and his house, and every messenger was an attempt to avoid what he finally had to do. Hold on to that if you think of the Old Testament as the volume where God is angry. The prophets are not the sound of God losing his temper. They are the sound of God holding his anger back.

They kept mocking the messengers of God. Three verbs, all about contempt rather than disagreement: they mocked the men, despised the words and scoffed at the prophets. Nobody argues with the message. They laugh at it, which is a far more effective defence and requires no thought at all.

The sneer as an argument. Our age has made an art of that defence. We rarely refute faith now; we roll our eyes at it. A joke on a late-night programme or a clever caption does more work than a shelf of philosophy, because ridicule needs no evidence and keeps the one who laughs safely above the conversation. C. S. Lewis saw the danger in The Screwtape Letters, where the senior devil prizes flippancy, the habit of treating everything as a joke, as fine armour against God. Mockery is the stance of someone who will not risk being addressed. The gospel has a strange answer to it. The Son God sent last, after all the prophets, was mocked himself: soldiers knelt before him in a scarlet robe, and the chief priests jeered at the foot of the cross (Matthew 27:28–29, 41). He did not answer the sneer with one of his own. He bore it, and prayed for the men who were killing him (Luke 23:34). The God who is laughed at goes on sending.

Until there was no remedy. This ends the book’s longest theme. A remedy is a healing, and healing is what God promised in the courtyard of this house: I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land (7:14). It is what happened when Hezekiah prayed for a crowd of unclean northerners: And the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people (30:20). The offer had been open since chapter 7, and it was taken up by a fool, a coward, a proud man and a murderer; every one of them was healed, not because their humbling was perfect but because God is merciful. Judah at the end did not fail to qualify for it. Judah laughed at the men who brought it, until there was nothing left to say.

The remedy open again. What Judah’s kings would not do, the last son of David did in their place: he humbled himself to the point of death (Philippians 2:8), and in him the remedy is open again.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore he brought up against them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary and had no compassion on young man or virgin, old man or aged. He gave them all into his hand. And all the vessels of the house of God, great and small, and the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king and of his princes, all these he brought to Babylon. And they burned the house of God and broke down the wall of Jerusalem and burned all its palaces with fire and destroyed all its precious vessels. He took into exile in Babylon those who had escaped from the sword, and they became servants to him and to his sons until the establishment of the kingdom of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths. All the days that it lay desolate it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God handed his people to a king without compassion, the house of God was burned, and the land rested its unpaid Sabbaths for seventy years, exactly as his word had said. The exile was not God losing control of his history but the covenant carried out as written.

Had no compassion on young man or virgin. The word used of God two verses earlier is now used, with a “no”, of the man God sent. God’s pity had held the sword back for centuries. The man who finally carried it had none.

In the house of their sanctuary. They were killed in the building cleansed by Hezekiah, repaired by Josiah, filled with glory in Solomon’s day and defended by an angel in Hezekiah’s (32:21). And verse 18 empties it: all the vessels. The counting that began in verse 7 finishes here.

They burned the house of God. Burned. Broke down. Burned. Destroyed. The Chronicler has spent six chapters on the building of that house: the cedar from Lebanon, the gold on the walls, the cherubim, the veil, the fire that came down and the glory that filled it so that the priests could not stand to minister. He gives its destruction one sentence and no adjectives at all. Sometimes that is the only decent way to report a thing.

Until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths. Then he looks at a burned city and an empty country and reaches for Leviticus. Moses had written it some seven or eight centuries earlier: Then the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths as long as it lies desolate ... the rest that it did not have on your Sabbaths when you were dwelling in it (Leviticus 26:34–35). Israel was commanded to let the fields lie fallow every seventh year (see Sabbath year), and for centuries had not done it. So the land takes what it was owed while there is nobody there to work it.

To fulfill seventy years. Even in the emptiness the commandment is being kept, just not by the people. It is the covenant being carried out exactly as written, for the exact number of years Jeremiah had said.

The rest the land took back. There is something uncomfortably modern about verse 21. Judah worked its fields without the pause God commanded, and the land took back, all at once, the rest it had been denied. A culture that measures worth by output treats soil, bodies and hours alike as things to be maximised, with rest a concession to weakness. The phone comes to bed, the weekend becomes catch-up time, and we are tired in ways sleep does not fix. Abraham Heschel, the Jewish writer, called the Sabbath a palace in time, a day that declares we are more than what we make. Refusing it is not only a scheduling problem; underneath lies a belief that everything depends on us. The gospel strikes at that belief. Jesus invites the weary to come to him and promises them rest (Matthew 11:28), and Hebrews says that whoever enters God’s rest has rested from his own works (Hebrews 4:10). The deepest Sabbath is not a day off but a finished work, his, and a life that has received it can finally stop.

Counting the seventy years. The seventy years most likely run from the first deportation in 605 BC to the return in 538 BC. Others count from the temple’s fall in 586 BC to its rebuilding in 516 BC, which is also seventy years. Either way, Jeremiah’s number came true.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath years were commanded in Leviticus 25:4.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s last word in this book is not judgment but return. In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfil the word spoken through Jeremiah, the LORD stirs up the emperor’s spirit (v. 22). Cyrus proclaims through his whole kingdom, by speech and in writing, that the God of heaven has given him the kingdoms of the earth and charged him to build a house at Jerusalem, and he ends with an invitation to all God’s people: “Let him go up” (v. 23). The story closes with a gate standing open.
verseByVerse.theology: The verb in verse 22 has been used twice before in these two books: God stirred up the Philistines and Arabians against Jehoram (21:16), and the kings of Assyria who carried the northern tribes into exile (1 Chr 5:26). The same hand that moved empires to take Israel away moves an empire to send it home.
verseByVerse.examples: Cyrus issued the decree as state policy; the historian records it as God keeping his promise, and the rest of Scripture reads it that way.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and also put it in writing: "Thus says Cyrus king of Persia, 'The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whoever is among you of all his people, may the LORD his God be with him. Let him go up.'"
