verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who sent his people into exile stirred up a pagan emperor to send them home, and the book ends not with ruin but with an open invitation: let him go up. The story is left unfinished, waiting for the Son of David who would bring it to its end.

Cyrus king of Persia. Isaiah had named the man long before: who says of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose (Isaiah 44:28). Many modern scholars hold that these chapters of Isaiah were written during the exile, so that the name was no prediction; the book presents them as Isaiah’s, and its own argument is that the LORD alone declares things before they happen (Isaiah 48:3–5). This commentary reads them so, while recognising that the question is debated. And Jeremiah had put a number on the years. The return is not an accident of Persian policy, and Cyrus is not merely being generous. He is being used, and the historian says so in the same sentence that names him.

Put it in writing. The decree was spoken and written throughout the empire, so that a Jewish family in a provincial town could hold it in their hands. Ezra preserves it twice: the proclamation as it was published (Ezra 1:2–4), and a memorandum in Aramaic later found in the royal archive (Ezra 6:3–5).

To build him a house at Jerusalem. The last thing said about that building was that it had been burned; the next is that a foreign emperor has been charged to build it again. Between those two sentences lie seventy years, and the Chronicler does not fill them.

Let him go up. In most printed Hebrew Bibles, Chronicles stands last of all, which makes let him go up the final sentence of the Old Testament. Jesus seems to have known that order. He spoke of the blood of the righteous from Abel to Zechariah (Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51): Abel, the first murder in Genesis, and Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, stoned in the temple court near the end of Chronicles (24:20–22). From the first book to the last, he meant, every martyr in Scripture. (Matthew calls Zechariah the son of Barachiah, a known puzzle; most take the same martyr to be meant.) Zechariah died crying for the LORD to see and avenge; the blood of Jesus, Hebrews says, speaks a better word than Abel’s (Hebrews 12:24).

Where the two volumes started. The first word of 1 Chronicles is Adam. Nine chapters of names follow, then Saul’s death, David’s reign, the ark, the temple, the division, twenty kings, a locked door, an open door, a boy with a crown and a law book, a man in chains who prayed, a scroll found in the temple, and a fire. It ends without a summary, without a moral, and without telling us whether anyone went: a gate standing open and four words of permission.

Why the story was unfinished. That is exactly right, because the story was never finished. The house Cyrus authorised was built, and it was smaller, and the glory did not fall on it as it fell on Solomon’s. The line of David came home and never sat on a throne again. The promises were still waiting to be kept.

The gate is open. Five centuries later a descendant of that line stood in the courts of the second temple and said that if they destroyed this temple he would raise it up in three days, and he was speaking of his own body (John 2:19–21). He went up to Jerusalem to be killed, went down into an exile deeper than Babylon, came up out of it on the third day, and then went up where no one could follow him yet. He left behind him the same four words, addressed now to anyone at all. The captivity is over. The gate is open. Whoever is among you of all his people: let him go up.

Was Cyrus a believer? He spoke of the LORD as Persian kings spoke of every nation’s gods, and his own inscription credits Marduk. God used him as his servant without Cyrus knowing him (Isaiah 45:4–5).
verseByVerse.note: In most printed Hebrew Bibles the canon ends here, with Cyrus’s decree (539/538 BC) and a call to go up, the same words that open Ezra.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place.
keyVerse.note: This verse gives God’s motive for every prophet in the book: not to build a case but to spare his people. The exile came only when that compassion had been mocked “until there was no remedy” (v. 16). And the God whose compassion was refused still has the last word in the book, sending his people home (v. 23), and at last sending his Son.

36.reflection:
Verse 15 says God kept sending his messengers “because he had compassion”. How does that change the way you read the warnings of the prophets, and the warnings of Scripture to you?

Judah did not argue with God’s word; it mocked it. Where do you see ridicule used today to avoid taking God seriously, and how should Christians respond when they meet it?

Zedekiah’s hard heart was the end of a long road of small refusals. What small refusals might be stiffening your own neck, and what would humbling yourself look like this week?

The book ends with a ruined temple and an open gate: “Let him go up.” How does Jesus fulfil the hope of this ending, and to whom might you pass on his invitation?
